chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Loomings
paragraphs: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — never mind how long exactly — having little or no money and nothing of interest to keep me on shore, I decided to sail around a bit and see the watery part of the world. It's my way of shaking off the blues and getting my blood flowing. Whenever I catch myself scowling; whenever it's a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself pausing in front of coffin shops and trailing every funeral I encounter; and especially whenever my dark moods get such a grip on me that only strong moral principle keeps me from deliberately walking into the street and methodically knocking people's hats off — then I know it's high time to get to sea. This is my substitute for a pistol and a bullet. Cato, with a philosophical flourish, throws himself on his sword; I quietly take to a ship. There's nothing surprising in this. Almost every person, at some point, feels the same pull toward the ocean that I do.

There stands your island city of Manhattan, surrounded by wharves the way Pacific isles are surrounded by coral reefs — commerce laps at it like surf. Left and right, every street leads you toward the water. The downtown tip is the Battery, where that noble seawall is washed by waves and cooled by breezes that were out of sight of land just hours before. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and then north by way of Whitehall. What do you see? Standing like silent sentinels all around the town are thousands upon thousands of people lost in ocean reveries. Some lean against the pilings; some sit on the pier heads; some gaze over the sides of ships from China; some perch high in the rigging, trying to get an even better view of the sea. But these are all landlocked people — weekdays they're penned up in plaster and wood, chained to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. What's going on? Have all the green fields vanished? What are they doing here?

But look! Here come more crowds, heading straight for the water, seemingly ready to dive in. Strange! Nothing satisfies them but the very edge of the land; lounging in the shade of those warehouses won't do. No. They have to get as close to the water as humanly possible without falling in. And there they stand — miles of them — leagues. They come from every neighborhood, every direction — north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all converge. Do the compass needles of all those ships somehow attract them?

Consider one more thing. Say you're in the country, on some high plateau of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and nine times out of ten it will lead you down into a valley and leave you at a stream. There's something magical in it. Take the most absent-minded person alive, deep in thought, put them on their feet and set them walking — and they will inevitably lead you to water, if there's water anywhere around. If you're ever dying of thirst in the American desert, try this experiment, provided your caravan includes a philosophy professor. Yes, as everyone knows, contemplation and water are wedded forever.

And here's an artist who wants to paint the dreamiest, shadiest, most enchanting landscape in the Saco Valley. What's the essential element? Here stand his trees, each hollow-trunked as if sheltering a hermit and a crucifix; here sleeps his meadow, there rest his cattle; a sleepy trail of smoke rises from a cottage. A winding path disappears into distant woodlands, reaching toward mountain spurs bathed in blue. But though the picture seems entranced, and though the pine tree sighs leaves down upon the shepherd's head, it would all be meaningless if the shepherd's eyes weren't fixed on the magic stream before him. Visit the Prairies in June and wade knee-deep through tiger lilies for miles — what's the one thing missing? Water — not a drop to be found! If Niagara were a waterfall of sand, would you travel a thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor Tennessee poet, suddenly handed two fistfuls of silver, agonize over whether to buy the coat he desperately needed or spend the money on a trip to Rockaway Beach? Why does almost every strong, healthy young person, at some point, go crazy with the urge to go to sea? Why, on your first voyage as a passenger, did you feel that mystical vibration when told your ship was now out of sight of land? Why did the ancient Persians consider the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it its own god, Poseidon, brother of Zeus? Surely none of this is meaningless. And deeper still is the meaning of the story of Narcissus, who plunged into the fountain and drowned because he could not grasp the tormenting, gentle image he saw there. But that same image, we see it in every river and ocean. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

Now, when I say I go to sea whenever my eyes grow hazy and I become too aware of my own breathing, don't imagine I ever go as a passenger. Passengers need money, and a wallet is just a rag without anything in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don't sleep at night, and generally don't enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I know my way around a ship, do I ever go as a Commodore, Captain, or Cook. I leave the glory of such positions to those who want them. I personally despise all honorable, respectable labor, trials, and tribulations. I have quite enough to do just looking after myself without looking after ships, barques, brigs, and schooners. And as for going as cook — though there's considerable prestige in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board — I never much liked the idea of broiling chickens. Though once broiled, properly buttered, judiciously salted and peppered, there's no one who speaks of a broiled chicken with more respect — even reverence — than I do. It's from the ancient Egyptians' worship of broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you find mummies of those creatures in their enormous bake-houses, the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, down into the forecastle, up to the royal masthead. True, they order me around and make me jump from spar to spar like a grasshopper in a May meadow. At first, this kind of thing is unpleasant enough. It stings your pride, especially if you come from an old established family — the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And even more so if, just before dipping your hand into the tar bucket, you'd been lording it as a country schoolteacher, making the tallest boys tremble before you. The transition from schoolmaster to sailor is a sharp one, I assure you, and requires a strong dose of Seneca and the Stoics to help you grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

So what if some crusty old sea captain orders me to grab a broom and sweep the deck? What does that humiliation amount to, weighed on the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks any less of me because I obey that old grouch? Who isn't a slave, in one way or another? Tell me that. Well, however the old captains may boss me around, thump me, and shove me, I have the satisfaction of knowing it's all fair; that everyone else gets served the same way, physically or metaphysically speaking. The universal thump gets passed around, and we should all just rub each other's shoulders and be content.

Another reason I always go as a sailor: they actually pay me for my trouble, while no one has ever paid a passenger a single penny. On the contrary, passengers have to pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most painful curse that Adam and Eve inflicted on us. But being paid — what compares with it? The cheerful eagerness with which a person accepts money is truly remarkable, considering how earnestly we believe money to be the root of all evil, and that no rich man can enter heaven. How gladly we consign ourselves to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the fresh air and healthy exercise on the forecastle deck. In this world, headwinds are far more common than tailwinds (at least, if you follow the Pythagorean rule), so the Commodore on the quarterdeck mostly breathes secondhand air from the sailors up front. He thinks he breathes it first; but he doesn't. In much the same way, ordinary people lead their leaders in many things, though the leaders rarely suspect it. But why, after repeatedly going to sea as a merchant sailor, did I suddenly decide to go on a whaling voyage? That invisible police officer of Fate, who constantly watches me, secretly follows me, and steers me in mysterious ways — he can answer that better than I can. No doubt my whaling voyage was part of the grand plan of Providence, drawn up long ago. It came in as a brief interlude and solo between the larger acts. I imagine this part of the program read something like this:
“GRAND CONTESTED ELECTION FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE UNITED STATES.” “WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL.” “BLOODY BATTLE IN AFGHANISTAN.”

Though I cannot tell exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were assigned magnificent parts in high tragedies, short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces — though I cannot tell exactly why this was; yet, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives which, being cunningly presented to me under various disguises, induced me to set about performing the part I did. They also coaxed me into the delusion that it was a choice resulting from my own unbiased free will and discriminating judgment.

Chief among those motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a gigantic, mysterious creature roused all my curiosity. Then the wild, distant seas where he rolled his enormous bulk; the nameless, unimaginable dangers of the whale hunt; these, along with all the wonders of a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, swayed me toward my decision. Other men might not have been tempted by such things, but I am tormented by an unending itch for things far away. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on savage coasts. Not that I ignore what's good — I'm simply quick to sense a horror, and willing to keep company with it, if they'd let me. After all, it's wise to be on good terms with all the inhabitants of the place where you're staying.

For all these reasons, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fantasies that drove me toward my purpose, two by two there floated into my deepest soul endless processions of whales — and in the middle of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The Carpet-Bag
paragraphs: I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and headed for Cape Horn and the Pacific. Leaving the good city of old Manhattan, I arrived in New Bedford. It was a Saturday night in December. I was very disappointed to learn that the little packet boat to Nantucket had already sailed, and there was no way to get there until Monday.

Since most young candidates for the punishments of whaling stop in this same New Bedford before embarking, I should mention that I had no intention of doing the same. I was determined to sail on a Nantucket ship, because there was something fine and wild about everything connected with that famous old island that pleased me enormously. Besides, though New Bedford has gradually been taking over the whaling business, and poor old Nantucket now trails far behind, Nantucket was the original — the Tyre to New Bedford's Carthage, the place where the first dead American whale washed ashore. Where else but Nantucket did those original whalemen, the Native Americans, first paddle out in canoes to chase the great beast? And where else did that first small, daring sloop set sail, partly loaded — so the story goes — with cobblestones to throw at whales, to judge when they were close enough to risk a harpoon?

Now, facing a night, a day, and another night in New Bedford before I could set out for my destination, the question of where to eat and sleep became pressing. It was a grim-looking night — dark, dismal, bitingly cold, and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. I'd anxiously searched my pocket and found only a few silver coins. So, wherever you go, Ishmael, I said to myself, standing in the middle of a dreary street with my bag on my shoulder, comparing the gloom to the north with the darkness to the south — wherever you decide to sleep tonight, my dear Ishmael, be sure to ask the price, and don't be too picky.

With halting steps I walked the streets and passed the sign of 'The Crossed Harpoons' — but it looked too expensive and festive in there. Further on, from the bright red windows of the 'Sword-Fish Inn,' such warm light poured out that it seemed to have melted the packed snow in front of the building, while everywhere else the frozen ground lay ten inches thick like hard pavement. Rough going for me, striking my foot against the flinty ridges, since my boot soles were in miserable shape from hard service. Too expensive and festive again, I thought, pausing to watch the bright glow in the street and hear the clinking glasses inside. But move along, Ishmael, I told myself at last — don't you hear? Get away from the door; your patched boots are blocking the way. So on I went, instinctively following streets that led me toward the water, where the cheapest — if not the cheeriest — inns were sure to be.

What dreary streets! Solid blocks of blackness, not houses, on either side, and here and there a candle, like a flame moving in a tomb. At this hour of night, on the last day of the week, that part of town was all but deserted. But soon I came to a dim, smoky light from a low, wide building with its door standing invitingly open. It had a careless look, as if it were meant for public use. I walked in and immediately stumbled over an ash-box in the entrance. Ha! I thought, choking on the flying particles — are these ashes from that destroyed city, Gomorrah? But 'The Crossed Harpoons' and 'The Sword-Fish'? Then this must be the sign of 'The Trap.'

It looked like some great dark parliament sitting in Hell. A hundred dark faces turned in their rows to stare, and beyond them, a dark figure was pounding a book in a pulpit. It was a Black church, and the preacher's text was about the blackness of darkness, the weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth. Ha, Ishmael, I muttered, backing out — what wretched entertainment at the sign of 'The Trap'!

Moving on, I eventually came to a faint light not far from the docks and heard a forlorn creaking in the air. Looking up, I saw a swinging sign over a door with a white painting on it, faintly depicting a tall, straight jet of misty spray, and these words underneath: 'The Spouter Inn: — Peter Coffin.'

Coffin? Spouter? Rather ominous in that particular combination, I thought. But it's a common name in Nantucket, they say, and I suppose this Peter is originally from there. Since the light was dim, the place seemed quiet enough, and the dilapidated little wooden house looked as if it might have been carted here from the ruins of some burned district — and since the swinging sign had a poverty-stricken creak to it — I figured this was exactly the spot for cheap lodgings and decent coffee.

It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side almost paralyzed, leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner where the tempestuous northeast wind howled worse than it ever did around poor Saint Paul's storm-tossed ship. But that same wind is a perfectly pleasant breeze if you're indoors with your feet on the hearth, getting ready for bed. 'In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon,' says an old writer whose works only I possess, 'it makes a marvelous difference whether you look at it from a glass window with the frost all on the outside, or from a sashless window where the frost is on both sides, and Death is the only glazier.' True enough, I thought — old black-letter, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a shame they didn't seal up the cracks and stuff in some insulation. But it's too late for improvements now. The universe is finished; the capstone is on, and the scraps were hauled away a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone as his pillow, shaking off his rags with his shivering — he might plug both ears with scraps and stick a corncob in his mouth, and still the freezing wind would find him. 'Euroclydon!' says old Dives in his red silk robe — he'd have a redder one later — 'Bah! What a fine frosty night! How Orion glitters! What northern lights! Let them talk about their tropical conservatories — give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.'

But what does Lazarus think? Can he warm his blue hands by holding them up to the northern lights? Wouldn't Lazarus rather be in Sumatra than here? Wouldn't he far rather stretch himself out along the equator — or even descend to the fiery pit itself — just to escape this frost?

Now, that Lazarus should lie stranded on the curb outside the door of Dives — this is more astonishing than an iceberg moored to a tropical island. Yet Dives himself lives like a czar in an ice palace made of frozen sighs, and being president of a temperance society, he drinks only the lukewarm tears of orphans.
But enough of this blubbering — we're going whaling, and there's plenty of that to come. Let's scrape the ice from our frozen feet and see what kind of place this 'Spouter' is.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Spouter-Inn
paragraphs: Entering the gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, rambling entryway with old-fashioned wood paneling that reminded you of the bulkheads of some condemned old ship. On one side hung a very large oil painting, so thoroughly covered in soot and grime that you could only figure out what it depicted through careful study, repeated visits, and asking the neighbors. Such unfathomable masses of shadow that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the days of the New England witch trials, had tried to paint chaos itself under a spell. But through much earnest contemplation and a great deal of pondering — and especially by throwing open the little back window to let in more light — you finally concluded that such an interpretation, however wild, might not be completely off the mark.

But what puzzled you most was a long, dark, ominous mass of something hovering in the center of the painting, above three blue, dim, vertical lines floating in a nameless froth. A boggy, soggy, squelchy picture — enough to drive a nervous person crazy. Yet there was something almost sublime about it that froze you in place until you swore to yourself you'd figure out what it meant. Bright ideas would flash through you: It's the Black Sea in a midnight gale. It's the four primal elements at war. It's a blasted heath. It's an Arctic winter scene. It's the breaking up of the frozen river of Time. But eventually all these theories gave way to that one ominous something in the center. Once you figured that out, everything else fell into place. But wait — doesn't it look faintly like a gigantic fish? The great Leviathan himself?

In fact, the artist's intention seemed to be this (my own theory, partly based on the combined opinions of many old-timers I'd consulted): the painting shows a ship rounding Cape Horn in a massive hurricane. The half-sunk vessel is wallowing in the waves with its three broken masts barely visible, and a furious whale, trying to leap clean over the ship, is in the act of impaling itself on all three mastheads.

The opposite wall was covered with a barbaric display of monstrous clubs and spears. Some were studded with glittering teeth like ivory saws; others were tufted with knots of human hair; one was sickle-shaped, with a huge sweeping handle like the arc a long-armed mower cuts through fresh grass. You shuddered as you looked, wondering what monstrous cannibal could have gone harvesting death with such a terrifying weapon. Mixed in were rusty old whaling lances and harpoons, all broken and bent. Some had stories behind them. With this lance, now wildly twisted, Nathan Swain had killed fifteen whales between sunrise and sunset fifty years ago. And that harpoon — now bent like a corkscrew — was thrown in the Java seas and run off with by a whale, which was killed years later off the Cape of Blanco. The original iron had entered near the tail and, like a restless needle traveling through a human body, migrated forty feet before lodging in the hump.

Crossing the dusky entry and passing through a low archway — cut through what must once have been a great central chimney — you entered the public room. An even darker place, with such heavy low beams above and such worn, wrinkled planks below that you'd almost think you were treading the decks of some ancient ship, especially on a howling night when the old building rocked like an anchored ark. On one side stood a long, low, shelf-like table covered with cracked glass cases full of dusty curiosities gathered from the world's most remote corners. Projecting from the far corner was a dark den — the bar — a crude imitation of a right whale's head. Whatever the intention, there stood the vast arched jawbone of a whale, so wide a coach could nearly drive beneath it. Inside were shabby shelves with old bottles, decanters, and flasks; and within those jaws of destruction, like another cursed Jonah (which was indeed his nickname), a little withered old man hustled about, selling the sailors delirium and death for their money.

Terrible were the glasses he served his poison in. Though perfectly cylindrical on the outside, the villainous green tumblers tapered deceptively on the inside to a cheating bottom. Lines were crudely etched into the glass like latitude markings. Fill to this line and it costs a penny; to this line, a penny more; all the way up to the full glass — the Cape Horn measure — which you could gulp down for a shilling.

When I entered, I found several young seamen gathered around a table, examining by dim light various specimens of scrimshaw. I found the landlord and told him I wanted a room. He said his house was full — not a bed available. 'But hold on,' he added, tapping his forehead, 'you wouldn't mind sharing a harpooneer's blanket, would you? I expect you're going whaling, so you'd better get used to that sort of thing.'

I told him I never liked sleeping two to a bed; that whether I'd agree would depend on who the harpooneer was; and that if there really was no other option, and the harpooneer wasn't too objectionable, then rather than wander any further through a strange town on such a bitter night, I'd put up with sharing any decent man's blanket.
'Thought so. All right, have a seat. Supper? You want supper? It'll be ready shortly.'

I sat down on an old wooden bench carved all over like a seat on the Battery. At one end, a ruminative sailor was further decorating it with his jackknife, stooping over and working diligently at the space between his knees. He was attempting a ship under full sail, but he wasn't making much progress.

At last four or five of us were called to eat in an adjoining room. It was cold as Iceland — no fire at all; the landlord said he couldn't afford it. Nothing but two gloomy tallow candles, each in a paper sleeve. We had to button up our jackets and hold our cups of scalding tea with half-frozen fingers. But the food was substantial — not just meat and potatoes but dumplings. Good heavens, dumplings for supper! One young fellow in a green coat attacked those dumplings in a most alarming manner.
'My boy,' said the landlord, 'you're going to have nightmares for sure.'
'Landlord,' I whispered, 'that's not the harpooneer, is it?'
'Oh no,' he said, with a sort of diabolically amused look, 'the harpooneer is a dark-complexioned fellow. He never eats dumplings — nothing but steaks, and he likes them rare.'
'The devil he does,' I said. 'Where is this harpooneer? Is he here?'
'He'll be here before long,' was the answer.
I couldn't help it — I was starting to feel suspicious of this 'dark-complexioned' harpooneer. At the very least, I resolved that if we were to share a bed, he'd have to undress and get in before me.
After supper, the company returned to the bar room. Having nothing else to do, I decided to spend the rest of the evening as a spectator.

Soon a riotous noise was heard from outside. Jumping up, the landlord cried, 'That's the Grampus's crew! I saw her reported offshore this morning — three-year voyage, full ship. Hurrah, boys! Now we'll have the latest news from the Fiji Islands!'

The tramping of sea boots echoed in the entry; the door burst open, and in rolled a wild set of sailors. Wrapped in shaggy watch coats, heads muffled in wool scarves, all patched and ragged, beards stiff with icicles, they looked like an eruption of bears from Labrador. They'd just come from their boat, and this was the first building they'd entered. No wonder they made straight for the whale's mouth — the bar — where the wrinkled little old Jonah poured them full glasses all around. One complained of a bad cold, so Jonah mixed him a tar-like brew of gin and molasses, swearing it was a guaranteed cure for all colds whatsoever, no matter how long-standing or where they'd been caught.
The liquor quickly went to their heads, as it usually does with even the heaviest drinkers who've just come ashore, and they began leaping about wildly.

I noticed, however, that one of them held somewhat apart. Though he clearly didn't want to dampen his shipmates' fun with his own sober expression, he mostly refrained from joining the noise. This man interested me at once. Since fate had decreed he'd soon become my shipmate — though only a sleeping partner, as far as this story goes — I'll describe him briefly. He stood a full six feet tall, with noble shoulders and a chest like a vault. I've rarely seen such powerful build in a man. His face was deeply tanned, making his white teeth dazzle by contrast, and in the depths of his eyes floated memories that didn't seem to bring him much joy. His voice marked him as a Southerner, and from his fine build I guessed he must be one of those tall mountaineers from Virginia's Allegheny Ridge. When his companions' revelry reached its peak, this man slipped away unnoticed. I didn't see him again until he became my comrade at sea. Within minutes, though, his shipmates missed him, and being apparently a great favorite, they raised a cry of 'Bulkington! Bulkington! Where's Bulkington?' and rushed out in pursuit.

It was now about nine o'clock. The room felt almost supernaturally quiet after the commotion, and I began congratulating myself on a little plan that had occurred to me just before the sailors arrived.

Nobody prefers to sleep two in a bed. In fact, you'd rather not share one even with your own brother. People like privacy when they sleep. And when it comes to sharing a bed with a complete stranger, in a strange inn, in a strange town — and that stranger a harpooneer — your objections multiply enormously. And there was no reason I, as a sailor, should be any more willing than anyone else. Sailors don't share beds at sea any more than bachelor kings do on land. True, they all sleep in one room, but each man has his own hammock, his own blanket, and sleeps in his own skin.

The more I thought about this harpooneer, the less I wanted to share a bed with him. Being a harpooneer, his clothes were probably not the tidiest. I began fidgeting all over. Besides, it was getting late, and my supposedly decent harpooneer should have been home and heading to bed by now. What if he stumbled in at midnight — what nasty dive might he be coming from?
'Landlord! I've changed my mind about the harpooneer. I won't sleep with him. I'll try this bench.'

'Suit yourself. Sorry I can't spare you a tablecloth for a mattress — this is a rough board,' he said, feeling the knots and notches. 'But wait, Scrimshander — I've got a carpenter's plane behind the bar. Hold on, I'll make you nice and comfortable.' With that he produced the plane, dusted the bench with his old silk handkerchief, and set to planing away at my bed, grinning like an ape. Shavings flew everywhere until the blade hit an indestructible knot. He nearly sprained his wrist. I told him for heaven's sake to stop — the bed was soft enough, and all the planing in the world couldn't turn a pine plank into a featherbed. So, gathering the shavings with another grin and tossing them into the big stove, he went about his business and left me to my thoughts.

I now took the measure of the bench, and found that it was a foot too short — but that could be remedied with a chair. It was also a foot too narrow, and the other bench in the room was about four inches higher than the planed one, so there was no yoking them together. I then placed the first bench lengthwise along the only clear space against the wall, leaving a little interval between it and the wall for my back to settle down in. But I soon found that such a draft of cold air came over me from under the sill of the window that this plan would never do at all, especially as another current from the rickety door met the one from the window, and the two together formed a series of small whirlwinds in the immediate vicinity of the very spot where I had thought to spend the night.

To hell with that harpooneer, I thought. But wait — couldn't I sneak into his room, bolt the door from inside, and jump into his bed, too soundly asleep to be roused by even the loudest knocking? It wasn't a bad idea, but on second thought I dropped it. Who knew but the next morning, the moment I stepped out, the harpooneer might be standing in the hallway, ready to knock me down!

Still, looking around and seeing no possible way to spend a bearable night except in someone else's bed, I began to think I might be harboring unwarranted prejudice against this unknown harpooneer. I'll wait a while, I thought. He must be showing up soon. I'll get a good look at him, and maybe we'll become perfectly good bedfellows after all — you never know.
But though the other boarders kept arriving one by one and going to bed, there was no sign of my harpooneer.
'Landlord!' I said. 'What sort of fellow is he — does he always keep such late hours?' It was now nearly midnight.

The landlord chuckled with his dry chuckle, looking mightily amused about something beyond my understanding. 'No,' he answered, 'usually he's an early bird — early to bed and early to rise. But tonight he went out peddling, you see, and I can't imagine what's keeping him so late, unless maybe he can't sell his head.'

'Can't sell his head? What kind of crazy story is this?' I said, getting furious. 'Do you mean to tell me, landlord, that this harpooneer is actually out this Saturday night — or rather Sunday morning — peddling his head around town?'
'That's exactly it,' said the landlord, 'and I told him he couldn't sell it here. The market's overstocked.'
'Overstocked with what?' I shouted.
'With heads, of course. Aren't there too many heads in the world?'
'Look here, landlord,' I said, quite calmly, 'you'd better stop spinning that yarn. I wasn't born yesterday.'
'Maybe not,' he said, pulling out a stick and whittling a toothpick, 'but I think you'll be done brown if that harpooneer hears you slandering his head.'
'I'll break it for him,' I said, flying into a rage again at the landlord's incomprehensible nonsense.
'It's already broken,' he said.
'Broken?' I said. 'Broken, you mean?'
'Yep, and that's the very reason he can't sell it, I guess.'

'Landlord,' I said, walking up to him cool as a glacier in a blizzard, 'landlord, stop whittling. You and I need to come to an understanding, and right now. I come to your house wanting a bed; you tell me you can only give me half of one, the other half belonging to some harpooneer. And about this harpooneer, whom I haven't seen, you keep telling me the most mystifying, infuriating stories, designed to make me deeply uncomfortable about the man you're assigning as my bedfellow — an arrangement, landlord, which is among the most intimate known to man. I now demand that you speak plainly and tell me who and what this harpooneer is, and whether I'll be safe spending the night with him. And first, please retract that story about selling his head — because if it's true, that's strong evidence the man is stark mad, and I have no intention of sleeping with a madman. And you, sir — you, landlord — by knowingly trying to make me do so, you'd be making yourself liable for criminal prosecution.'

'Well,' said the landlord, drawing a long breath, 'that's a mighty long speech for a fellow who swears a little now and then. But take it easy — this harpooneer I've been telling you about just arrived from the South Seas, where he bought up a batch of embalmed New Zealand heads — great curiosities, you know — and he's sold all of them except one, which he's trying to sell tonight because tomorrow is Sunday, and it wouldn't do to be selling human heads on the streets when people are going to church. He wanted to last Sunday, but I stopped him just as he was heading out the door with four heads strung together like a string of onions.'

This explanation cleared up the mystery and showed the landlord hadn't been trying to fool me. But still — what was I to think of a harpooneer who stayed out on a Saturday night deep into the Sabbath, engaged in the cannibal business of selling dead men's heads?
'Mark my words, landlord — that harpooneer is a dangerous man.'

'He pays regular,' was the reply. 'But come, it's getting terribly late. You'd better turn in — it's a nice bed. My wife Sal and I slept in it the night we were married. There's plenty of room for two; it's an enormous bed. Before we gave it up, Sal used to put little Sam and Johnny at the foot of it. But one night I went thrashing around in my sleep and poor Sam got thrown on the floor and nearly broke his arm. After that, Sal said it wouldn't do. Come along, I'll give you a light.' He lit a candle and held it toward me, offering to lead the way. But I stood undecided. Then, glancing at a clock in the corner, he exclaimed, 'By George, it's Sunday! You won't see that harpooneer tonight — he must have anchored somewhere. Come along, then — come on, won't you?'
I thought it over for a moment, then upstairs we went. I was shown into a small room, cold as a clam, furnished with an enormous bed — big enough for four harpooneers to sleep side by side.

'There,' said the landlord, setting the candle on a battered old sea chest that doubled as a washstand and table. 'Make yourself comfortable. Good night.' I turned from examining the bed, but he'd already vanished.

Folding back the bedspread, I leaned over and inspected the bed. Not the most elegant, but it passed muster. I glanced around the room: besides the bed and the chest, the only furniture was a crude shelf, the four bare walls, and a wallpapered fireboard showing a man harpooning a whale. The room also contained a hammock rolled up in one corner, a large sailor's bag — the harpooneer's wardrobe, no doubt, serving as a suitcase — some strange bone fishhooks on the shelf above the fireplace, and a tall harpoon standing at the head of the bed.

But what was this on the chest? I picked it up, held it to the light, felt it, smelled it, and tried every possible way to figure out what it was. The closest comparison I could make was a large doormat, trimmed at the edges with little jingling tags like the stained porcupine quills around a Native American moccasin. There was a hole in the middle, like a South American poncho. But could any sober harpooneer actually wear a doormat through the streets of a Christian town? I tried it on. It weighed me down like a heavy basket — shaggy, thick, and I thought a little damp, as if the mysterious harpooneer had been wearing it in the rain. I went to a bit of mirror stuck on the wall. I never saw such a sight in my life. I tore myself out of it so fast I nearly wrenched my neck.

I sat on the edge of the bed, thinking about this head-peddling harpooneer and his doormat. After a while I stood up and took off my jacket, then stood in the middle of the room thinking some more. Then I took off my coat and thought further in my shirtsleeves. But starting to feel very cold, half-undressed as I was, and remembering the landlord's comment that the harpooneer might not come back at all tonight, I wasted no more time. I jumped out of my trousers and boots, blew out the light, tumbled into bed, and commended myself to heaven.

Whether that mattress was stuffed with corn cobs or broken crockery, I can't say, but I tossed and turned for a long time. At last I drifted into a light doze and had nearly reached the land of Nod when I heard a heavy footstep in the hallway and saw a glimmer of light under the door.

Lord save me, I thought — that must be the harpooneer, the infernal head-peddler. But I lay perfectly still, determined not to say a word until spoken to. Holding a light in one hand and that very New Zealand head in the other, the stranger entered the room and, without looking at the bed, placed his candle on the floor in a far corner. Then he started working at the knotted cords of the large bag I'd noticed earlier. I was desperate to see his face, but he kept it turned away while he unlaced the bag. When he finally turned around — good heavens! What a sight! Such a face! It was a dark, purplish-yellow color, covered here and there with large, blackish squares. Just as I thought — he's a terrible bedfellow; he's been in a fight, gotten horribly cut up, and just come from the surgeon. But then he turned his face toward the light, and I could plainly see those black squares weren't bandages at all. They were stains of some kind. At first I didn't know what to make of it. Then it hit me. I remembered a story about a white whaleman who'd been tattooed by cannibals. I concluded that this harpooneer, during his distant voyages, must have had a similar experience. And what of it? It's only his outside; a man can be honest in any kind of skin. But what about his unearthly complexion — the part independent of the tattoos? It might just be a heavy tropical tan, but I'd never heard of the sun turning a white man purplish-yellow. Then again, I'd never been to the South Seas. While all these thoughts were racing through my mind, the harpooneer hadn't noticed me at all. Having opened his bag, he rummaged around and pulled out a sort of tomahawk and a sealskin wallet with the fur still on. Setting these on the chest, he then took the New Zealand head — a ghastly thing — and crammed it into the bag. Then he took off his hat — a new beaver hat — and I nearly cried out in fresh surprise. There was no hair on his head to speak of — nothing but a small topknot twisted up on his forehead. His bald, purplish head looked exactly like a mildewed skull. If the stranger hadn't been standing between me and the door, I'd have bolted faster than I've ever bolted a dinner.

Even as it was, I thought something of slipping out the window, but it was the second floor at the back. I am no coward, but what to make of this head-peddling, purple-skinned rascal altogether passed my comprehension. Ignorance is the parent of fear, and being completely nonplussed and confounded about the stranger, I confess I was now as much afraid of him as if it were the devil himself who had broken into my room at the dead of night. In fact, I was so afraid of him that I wasn't game enough, just then, to address him and demand a satisfactory answer concerning what seemed inexplicable in him.

Meanwhile, he continued undressing, eventually baring his chest and arms. As I live, those parts were covered with the same dark squares as his face; his back too. He looked like he'd survived a Thirty Years' War wearing nothing but bandages. Even his legs were marked, as if dark green frogs were climbing up young palm trunks. It was now obvious: he must be some savage or other who'd shipped aboard a whaler in the South Seas and landed in this Christian country. I trembled at the thought. A peddler of heads, too — maybe even the heads of his own brothers. What if he took a fancy to mine? God — look at that tomahawk!

But there was no time for shuddering, for now the savage went about something that completely fascinated my attention and convinced me that he must indeed be a heathen. Going to his heavy grego, or wraparound, or dreadnaught coat, which he had previously hung on a chair, he fumbled in the pockets and at length produced a curious little deformed image with a hunch on its back, exactly the color of a three-day-old Congo baby. Remembering the embalmed head, at first I almost thought this black manikin was a real baby preserved in some similar manner. But seeing that it was not at all limber, and that it glistened a good deal like polished ebony, I concluded it must be nothing but a wooden idol — which indeed it proved to be. For now the savage went up to the empty fireplace, removed the papered fire-board, and set up this little hunchbacked image, like a tenpin, between the andirons. The chimney jambs and all the bricks inside were very sooty, so that I thought this fireplace made a very appropriate little shrine or chapel for his Congo idol.

I strained my eyes toward the half-hidden image, feeling very uneasy, wanting to see what came next. First he took a double handful of shavings from his coat pocket and placed them carefully before the idol. Then he laid a piece of ship biscuit on top, lit the shavings from the lamp, and kindled a little sacrificial blaze. After many hasty snatches into the fire and even hastier withdrawals of his scorched fingers, he managed to fish out the biscuit. Blowing off the heat and ashes, he politely offered it to the little figure. But the little devil didn't seem to fancy such dry fare; he never moved his lips. All these strange rituals were accompanied by still stranger guttural noises — the worshipper seemed to be praying in a singsong or chanting some pagan hymn, his face twitching in the most unnatural way. Finally, putting out the fire, he picked up the idol unceremoniously and stuffed it back in his coat pocket as casually as a hunter bagging a dead bird.

All these strange doings made me increasingly uncomfortable. Seeing that he was now showing every sign of finishing up and jumping into bed with me, I decided it was high time — now or never, before the light went out — to break the spell I'd been under.

But the moment I hesitated, deciding what to say, was fatal. Picking up his tomahawk from the table, he examined the head for a moment, then held it to his mouth by the handle and puffed out great clouds of tobacco smoke. The next instant the light went out, and this wild cannibal, tomahawk between his teeth, sprang into bed with me. I screamed — I couldn't help it. With a sudden grunt of surprise, he started feeling me all over.

Stammering out something, I knew not what, I rolled away from him against the wall, and then conjured him, whoever or whatever he might be, to keep quiet and let me get up and light the lamp again. But his guttural responses satisfied me at once that he barely understood my meaning.
'Who the devil are you?' he finally said. 'You no speak, damn me, I kill you.' And the lit tomahawk began waving around me in the dark.
'Landlord! For God's sake, Peter Coffin!' I shouted. 'Landlord! Help! Coffin! Angels! Save me!'

'Speak! Tell me who you are, or damn me, I kill you!' growled the cannibal again, his tomahawk scattering hot tobacco ashes over me until I thought my sheets would catch fire. But thank heaven, at that moment the landlord burst in with a light. I leaped from the bed and ran to him.
'Don't be afraid,' he said, grinning again. 'Queequeg here wouldn't harm a hair on your head.'
'Stop grinning!' I shouted. 'Why didn't you tell me that infernal harpooneer was a cannibal?'
'I thought you knew! Didn't I tell you he was peddling heads around town? But turn in again and go to sleep. Queequeg, look here — you understand me? This man sleep with you — you understand?'
'Me understand plenty,' grunted Queequeg, puffing away at his pipe and sitting up in bed.

'You get in,' he added, motioning to me with his tomahawk and throwing back the covers. He really did this in not only a polite but a genuinely kind and generous way. I stood looking at him for a moment. Despite all his tattoos, he was, on the whole, a clean and decent-looking cannibal. What have I been making such a fuss about? I thought. The man is a human being, just like me. He has just as much reason to fear me as I have to fear him. Better to sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

'Landlord,' I said, 'tell him to put away that tomahawk, or pipe, or whatever it is. Tell him to stop smoking — I'll share his bed. But I don't like sleeping next to a man who's smoking. It's dangerous. Besides, I'm not insured.'
When this was communicated to Queequeg, he immediately complied and politely motioned me into bed again, rolling over to one side as if to say, 'I won't touch a leg of you.'
'Good night, landlord,' I said. 'You can go.'
I turned in, and never slept better in my life.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Counterpane
paragraphs: Waking next morning around daylight, I found Queequeg's arm thrown over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You'd have thought I was his wife. The bedspread was patchwork, full of odd little multicolored squares and triangles; and his arm, tattooed all over with an endless Cretan labyrinth of patterns — no two parts exactly the same shade, probably from keeping his arm at sea in random patches of sun and shade, his sleeves rolled up unevenly at different times — this arm, I say, looked exactly like a strip of that same patchwork quilt. Lying partly on the quilt as it was when I first woke, I could barely tell arm from bedspread, they blended their colors so perfectly. Only the sense of weight and pressure told me Queequeg was hugging me.

My feelings were strange. Let me try to explain. When I was a child, something very similar happened to me — whether it was real or a dream, I could never decide. Here's what happened. I'd been getting into some kind of mischief — trying to crawl up the chimney, I think, having seen a little chimney sweep do it a few days before. My stepmother, who was always either whipping me or sending me to bed without supper, dragged me out by my legs and packed me off to bed, though it was only two in the afternoon on June 21st — the longest day of the year. I felt miserable. But there was nothing to be done, so up I went to my little room on the third floor, undressed as slowly as possible to kill time, and with a bitter sigh crawled between the sheets.

I lay there miserably calculating that sixteen full hours had to pass before I could hope for freedom. Sixteen hours in bed! My back ached just thinking about it. And it was so bright out — sunshine pouring through the window, coaches rattling in the streets, cheerful voices throughout the house. I felt worse and worse. Finally I got up, dressed, and tiptoed downstairs in my stockings to find my stepmother. I threw myself at her feet and begged her, as a special favor, to give me a good spanking for my misbehavior — anything rather than condemning me to that unbearable time in bed. But she was the most conscientious of stepmothers, and back I went to my room. For several hours I lay wide awake, feeling worse than I've ever felt since, even in my greatest misfortunes. At last I must have fallen into a troubled doze, and slowly waking from it — half-steeped in dreams — I opened my eyes. The room, which had been sunlit before, was now wrapped in total darkness. Instantly a shock ran through me. Nothing could be seen, nothing heard — but a supernatural hand seemed to be placed in mine. My arm hung over the bedspread, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form to which the hand belonged seemed seated right beside my bed. For what felt like ages upon ages, I lay there frozen with the most terrible fear, not daring to pull my hand away, yet thinking that if I could just move it one inch, the horrible spell would break. I don't know how this sensation finally faded. But waking in the morning, I remembered it all with a shudder, and for days and weeks and months afterward I lost myself in futile attempts to explain the mystery. Even now, I still puzzle over it.

Now, take away the awful fear, and my feelings at sensing that supernatural hand were very similar to what I experienced waking up to find Queequeg's tattooed arm around me. But gradually the events of last night came back, one by one, in solid reality, and I realized the comedy of my situation. I tried to move his arm — to unlock his bridegroom's embrace — but he hugged me tight in his sleep, as if nothing but death could part us. I tried to wake him: 'Queequeg!' — but his only answer was a snore. I rolled over, my neck feeling like it was in a horse collar, and suddenly felt a scratch. Throwing back the bedspread, there lay the tomahawk, sleeping by the savage's side like a hatchet-faced baby. Fine situation, I thought — in bed in a strange house in broad daylight, with a cannibal and a tomahawk! 'Queequeg! In the name of goodness, Queequeg, wake up!' After much wriggling and loud protests about the impropriety of one man hugging another in such a matrimonial fashion, I managed to extract a grunt. He drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog fresh from the water, and sat up stiff as a board, looking at me and rubbing his eyes as if he didn't quite remember how I came to be there — though a dim awareness of knowing me seemed to be slowly dawning. Meanwhile I lay quietly studying him, no longer seriously worried, determined to observe this curious creature closely. When his mind was finally made up about me, he jumped out of bed and through signs and gestures let me know that, if I wished, he would dress first and then leave the entire room to me. Very civilized of you, Queequeg, I thought. The truth is, these so-called savages have an innate sense of courtesy, say what you will. I pay Queequeg this particular compliment because he treated me with such kindness, while I was guilty of great rudeness — staring at him from bed and watching his every move, my curiosity getting the better of my manners. But a man like Queequeg you don't see every day.

He began dressing from the top down — first putting on his very tall beaver hat, and then, still without trousers, hunting for his boots. What on earth he was doing, I can't say, but his next move was to cram himself — boots in hand, hat on head — under the bed. From various violent gaspings and strainings, I gathered he was battling to get his boots on, though no rule of propriety I've ever heard of requires a man to be private while putting on boots. Queequeg, you see, was a creature in transition — neither caterpillar nor butterfly. He was just civilized enough to display his oddness in the strangest ways. His education wasn't yet complete; he was still an undergraduate. If he'd been less civilized, he probably wouldn't have bothered with boots at all. But if he'd been less savage, he'd never have dreamed of getting under the bed to put them on. He finally emerged with his hat badly dented over his eyes, creaking and limping around the room — those damp, wrinkled cowhide boots clearly pinching him on this bitter cold morning.

Seeing that there were no curtains on the window, and that the narrow street gave the neighbors a clear view into the room, and noticing what an indecent figure Queequeg made in nothing but his hat and boots, I begged him to speed up and especially to get into his trousers as soon as possible. He complied, then proceeded to wash himself. Any Christian at that hour would have washed his face, but Queequeg, to my amazement, restricted his washing to his chest, arms, and hands. He then put on his vest, picked up a piece of hard soap from the washstand, lathered his face, and — I was watching for his razor when, lo and behold, he grabbed the harpoon from the bed corner, slid off the wooden shaft, unsheathed the head, honed it a little on his boot, and striding to the mirror on the wall, began vigorously scraping — or rather harpooning — his cheeks. Using the finest cutlery with a vengeance, I thought. Later, I was less surprised when I learned how fine the steel of a harpoon head is, and how razor-sharp the edges are always kept.
The rest of his grooming was quickly finished, and he marched proudly out of the room wrapped in his great pilot jacket, carrying his harpoon like a marshal's baton.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Breakfast
paragraphs: I quickly followed suit and went down to the bar room, greeting the grinning landlord pleasantly enough. I bore him no grudge, despite his pranks regarding my bedfellow.

A good laugh is a mighty good thing, and too rare in this world. So if any person naturally provides material for a good joke, they shouldn't hold back — let them cheerfully spend themselves that way. And anyone who has something genuinely laughable about them, you can be sure there's more to them than meets the eye.

The bar room was now full of boarders who'd been arriving the night before, and whom I hadn't yet gotten a good look at. They were nearly all whalemen — chief mates, second mates, third mates, ship carpenters, coopers, blacksmiths, harpooneers, and ship keepers. A brown, brawny company with bushy beards — an unshaven, shaggy bunch, all wearing their monkey jackets as morning robes.

You could easily tell how long each one had been ashore. This young fellow's ruddy cheek was the color of a sun-ripened pear and seemed to smell just as sweet — he couldn't have been off his ship more than three days. The man next to him was a few shades lighter — a touch of satinwood in his complexion. A third still showed a tropical tan, though slightly faded — he'd probably been ashore for weeks. But who could match Queequeg's cheek? Striped with various shades, it looked like the western slope of the Andes, displaying a whole array of contrasting climates, zone by zone.
'Grub, ho!' cried the landlord, throwing open a door, and in we went to breakfast.

They say that men who've seen the world become perfectly at ease in any company. Not always, though. Ledyard, the great New England traveler, and Mungo Park, the Scottish one — of all men, they had the least social confidence. But perhaps crossing Siberia in a dog sled, or taking a long solitary walk on an empty stomach through the heart of Africa, may not be the best training for polite society. Still, that kind of worldly awkwardness can be found anywhere.

These reflections occurred to me because after we were all seated at the table, and I was expecting to hear some good whaling stories, nearly everyone maintained a profound silence. And not only that — they looked embarrassed. Here were sea dogs, many of whom had boarded great whales on the open ocean without flinching — complete strangers to them — and fought them to the death without blinking. Yet here they sat at a social breakfast table, all in the same profession, all sharing the same interests, looking around as sheepishly as if they'd never left some mountain farm. A strange sight — these bashful bears, these timid warrior whalemen!

But Queequeg sat among them — at the head of the table, as it happened — cool as an icicle. I can't say much for his table manners. His greatest admirer couldn't have justified his bringing the harpoon to breakfast and using it without ceremony — reaching across the table with it, endangering many heads, and spearing beefsteaks toward himself. But he did it so coolly, and everyone knows that in most people's estimation, doing anything coolly is doing it with style.

We won't dwell on all of Queequeg's peculiarities here — how he avoided coffee and hot rolls and devoted his full attention to beefsteaks, done rare. Enough to say that after breakfast he withdrew like the others to the public room, lit his tomahawk-pipe, and sat there quietly digesting and smoking with his inseparable hat on, while I headed out for a walk.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — The Street
paragraphs: If I'd been astonished at first seeing someone as outlandish as Queequeg strolling through the polite society of a civilized town, my surprise quickly vanished during my first daylight walk through New Bedford's streets.

Near any major port's docks, you'll regularly encounter the strangest-looking characters from foreign lands. Even on Broadway and Chestnut Street, Mediterranean sailors sometimes startle the ladies. London's Regent Street isn't unfamiliar with Lascars and Malays; and in Bombay, live Yankees have often frightened the locals. But New Bedford outdoes them all. In those other haunts you see only sailors; in New Bedford, actual cannibals stand chatting on street corners — genuine savages, many still carrying unholy flesh on their bones. It makes a stranger stare.

But besides the Fijians, Tongans, Erromangans, and other South Sea islanders, and besides the wild specimens of the whaling trade who stagger unnoticed through the streets, you'll see even more curious sights. Every week, scores of fresh young Vermonters and New Hampshire boys arrive, all hungry for fortune and glory in the whale fishery. They're mostly young and powerfully built — men who've felled forests and now want to trade the axe for the whale-lance. Many are as green as the Green Mountains they came from. In some ways, they seem only hours old. Look at that fellow strutting around the corner: he wears a beaver hat and a tailcoat, cinched with a sailor's belt and sheath-knife. Here comes another in a sou'wester and a shabby cloak.

No city-bred dandy compares to a country-bred one — a real backwoods dandy, the kind who mows his field in buckskin gloves to avoid tanning his hands. When a country dandy like this decides to make his name and joins the great whale fishery, you should see what he does when he reaches the seaport. Ordering his sea outfit, he requests bell-buttons on his waistcoat and straps on his canvas trousers. Ah, poor Hay-Seed! How bitterly those straps will burst in the first howling gale, when you're driven, straps, buttons, and all, down the throat of the storm.

But don't think this famous town has only harpooneers, cannibals, and country boys to show its visitors. Not at all. Still, New Bedford is an unusual place. If it weren't for us whalemen, this stretch of land might still be as desolate as the coast of Labrador. As it is, parts of the surrounding countryside look almost skeletal. The town itself is perhaps the most expensive place to live in all of New England. It's a land of oil, certainly — though not like Canaan, a land of milk and honey. The streets don't flow with milk; in spring they aren't paved with fresh eggs. Yet despite this, nowhere in all America will you find more aristocratic houses, more magnificent parks and gardens. Where did they come from? How were they planted on this once barren ground?

Go and look at the iron decorative harpoons around that grand mansion, and your question will be answered. Yes, all these beautiful houses and flowery gardens came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. They were harpooned and dragged up here from the bottom of the sea.

In New Bedford, fathers give whales as dowries for their daughters and set aside a few porpoises for each niece. You have to visit New Bedford to see a brilliant wedding; they say every house has reservoirs of oil, and every night they recklessly burn the finest spermaceti candles.

In summer, the town is beautiful — full of fine maple trees, long avenues of green and gold. In August, the magnificent horse-chestnuts hold up their tapering, upright cones of blossoms like candelabras to every passerby. So powerful is human art; in many parts of New Bedford, it has planted bright terraces of flowers on the barren refuse rocks cast aside on creation's final day.

And the women of New Bedford bloom like their own red roses. But roses bloom only in summer; the fine color of their cheeks is perennial as sunlight in the seventh heaven. Nowhere else can you match that bloom — except in Salem, where they say the young women breathe such perfume that their sailor sweethearts can smell them miles offshore, as if they were approaching the fragrant Moluccas instead of the Puritan sands.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — The Chapel
paragraphs: In this same New Bedford stands a Whaleman's Chapel, and few moody fishermen, shortly bound for the Indian Ocean or Pacific, fail to pay it a Sunday visit. I certainly didn't.

Returning from my morning stroll, I set out on this particular errand. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold to driving sleet and mist. Wrapping myself in my shaggy bearskin jacket, I fought my way through the stubborn storm. Inside, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, broken only by shrieks of the storm. Each worshipper seemed deliberately sitting apart from the others, as if each grief were an island, incommunicable. The chaplain hadn't arrived yet. These silent islands of men and women sat steadfastly gazing at several marble tablets with black borders, set into the walls on either side of the pulpit. Three of them read something like this, though I don't pretend to quote exactly:

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF JOHN TALBOT, Who, at the age of eighteen, was lost overboard, Near the Isle of Desolation, off Patagonia, November 1st, 1836. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS SISTER.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF ROBERT LONG, WILLIS ELLERY, NATHAN COLEMAN, WALTER CANNY, SETH MACY, AND SAMUEL GLEIG, Forming one of the boats' crews OF THE SHIP ELIZA Who were towed out of sight by a Whale, On the Off-shore Ground in the PACIFIC, December 31st, 1839. THIS MARBLE Is here placed by their surviving SHIPMATES.

SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF The late CAPTAIN EZEKIEL HARDY, Who in the bows of his boat was killed by a Sperm Whale on the coast of Japan, August 3d, 1833. THIS TABLET Is erected to his Memory BY HIS WIDOW.

Shaking the sleet from my ice-glazed hat and jacket, I sat down near the door and was surprised to see Queequeg nearby. Moved by the solemnity of the scene, he wore a look of wondering, incredulous curiosity. He was the only person who seemed to notice my arrival — because he was the only one who couldn't read, and therefore wasn't reading those cold inscriptions on the wall. Whether any of the dead sailors' relatives were in the congregation, I didn't know. But so many are the unrecorded accidents in the whale fishery, and so plainly did several women present wear the look of unceasing grief, that I felt sure these were people in whose unhealed hearts the sight of those bleak tablets made old wounds bleed fresh.

Oh, you whose dead lie buried beneath green grass, who can stand among flowers and say, 'Here lies my beloved' — you don't know the desolation that haunts hearts like these. What bitter blanks in those black-bordered marble tablets that cover no ashes! What despair in those immovable inscriptions! What deadly emptiness in lines that seem to gnaw at all Faith, refusing resurrection to those who have perished without a place, without a grave. Those tablets might as well stand in the caves of Elephanta.

In what census of living creatures are the dead of mankind included? Why does the universal proverb say the dead tell no tales, though they contain more secrets than the Goodwin Sands? Why do we prefix such a significant and faithless word to the name of someone who departed yesterday for the other world, yet don't use that word for someone who merely embarks for the remotest shores of this living earth? Why do life insurance companies pay death-claims on supposedly immortal souls? In what eternal, unstirring paralysis lies ancient Adam, who died sixty centuries ago? Why do we refuse to be comforted for those we insist are dwelling in unspeakable bliss? Why do the living strive so hard to silence the dead? Why does the mere rumor of a knocking in a tomb terrify an entire city? All these things have their meanings.
But Faith, like a jackal, feeds among the tombs, and even from these dead doubts she gathers her most vital hope.

I hardly need to describe with what feelings, on the eve of a Nantucket voyage, I gazed at those marble tablets and read — by the murky light of that dark, doleful day — the fate of whalemen who had gone before me. Yes, Ishmael, the same fate could be yours. But somehow I grew cheerful again. Delightful inducements to go whaling! Fine chance for advancement, it seems — a smashed boat will make me immortal by reputation. Yes, there is death in this whaling business — a speechlessly quick, chaotic bundling of a man into Eternity. But what of it? I think we've made a tremendous mistake about this matter of Life and Death. I think what they call my shadow here on earth is my true substance. I think that in looking at spiritual things, we're too much like oysters observing the sun through water, thinking the thick water is the thinnest air. My body is just the dregs of my better being. Take my body, whoever wants it — take it, I say — it is not me. And so three cheers for Nantucket; and let the boat be smashed and the body staved when they will, for stave my soul, Jove himself cannot.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — The Pulpit
paragraphs: I hadn't been seated long before a man of impressive, weathered strength entered. The moment the storm-battered door swung open to admit him, every eye in the congregation turned toward him, confirming that this fine old man was the chaplain. Yes, it was the famous Father Mapple — so called by the whalemen, among whom he was a great favorite. He'd been a sailor and harpooneer in his youth but had devoted his life to the ministry for many years. At the time I write of, Father Mapple was in the hardy winter of a healthy old age — the kind that seems to merge into a second blooming youth, for among the crevices of his wrinkles shone mild gleams of a newly developing vitality, like spring green peeping out beneath February's snow. Anyone seeing Father Mapple for the first time couldn't help being fascinated, because his manner carried certain clerical quirks clearly rooted in his adventurous life at sea. When he entered, I noticed he carried no umbrella and certainly hadn't arrived by carriage — his oilskin hat was streaming with melting sleet, and his heavy pilot jacket seemed ready to drag him to the floor under the weight of water it had absorbed. But hat, coat, and overshoes were removed one by one and hung in a little corner space. Then, wearing a decent suit, he quietly approached the pulpit.

Like most old-fashioned pulpits, it was very high, and since a regular staircase would have taken up too much of the chapel's already small floor space, the architect — apparently acting on Father Mapple's suggestion — had built the pulpit without stairs, using instead a perpendicular side ladder, like those used to board a ship from a boat at sea. A whaling captain's wife had provided a handsome pair of red woolen hand-ropes for this ladder, which itself was neatly made and stained mahogany. The whole setup, considering what kind of chapel this was, seemed in perfectly good taste. Pausing at the foot of the ladder and grasping the ornamental knobs of the hand-ropes, Father Mapple cast a look upward, then with a truly sailor-like but still reverent agility, hand over hand, climbed the steps as if ascending the mainmast of his vessel.

The vertical sides of this ladder were cloth-covered rope, with only the rungs made of wood, so every step had a joint. At first glance, it struck me that these joints, however practical on a ship, seemed unnecessary here. I wasn't prepared for what came next: Father Mapple, having reached the top, slowly turned around, leaned over the pulpit, and deliberately pulled the ladder up behind him, step by step, until the whole thing was deposited inside — leaving him impregnable in his little Quebec.

I puzzled over this for some time. Father Mapple had such a wide reputation for sincerity and holiness that I couldn't suspect him of seeking attention through stage tricks. No, I thought, there must be a serious reason for this. And it must symbolize something unseen. Could it be that by physically isolating himself, he was signifying a spiritual withdrawal from all worldly ties and connections? Yes — for replenished with the bread and wine of God's word, this pulpit becomes, for the faithful man of God, a self-contained fortress — a lofty stronghold with a perpetual spring of water within its walls.

But the side ladder wasn't the only feature borrowed from the chaplain's seafaring days. Between the marble memorial tablets on either side of the pulpit, the back wall displayed a large painting of a brave ship battling a terrible storm off a rocky lee shore of black cliffs and white breakers. But high above the flying spray and dark rolling clouds floated a little island of sunlight, from which beamed an angel's face. This bright face cast a distinct spot of radiance on the ship's tossing deck, like the silver plate set into the Victory's planking where Nelson fell. 'Ah, noble ship,' the angel seemed to say, 'beat on, noble ship, and hold a steady helm; for the sun is breaking through, the clouds are rolling away — clear blue sky lies ahead.'

The pulpit itself also carried traces of the same sea-inspiration. Its paneled front was shaped like a ship's bluff bow, and the Holy Bible rested on a projecting piece of scrollwork fashioned after a ship's figurehead.

What could be more fitting? For the pulpit is the earth's foremost part; everything else follows in its wake. The pulpit leads the world. From there, the storm of God's swift wrath is first spotted, and the bow must bear the earliest blow. From there, the God of fair winds and foul is first called upon. Yes, the world is a ship on an outward voyage, not yet complete; and the pulpit is its prow.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — The Sermon
paragraphs: Father Mapple rose and in a mild voice of quiet authority ordered the scattered congregation to move together. 'Starboard gangway, there! Move over to port — port gangway to starboard! Midships! Midships!'
There was a low rumbling of heavy sea boots among the benches and an even slighter shuffling of women's shoes, and then all was quiet again, every eye on the preacher.

He paused a moment, then kneeled in the bow of the pulpit, folded his large brown hands across his chest, raised his closed eyes, and offered a prayer so deeply reverent that he seemed to be kneeling and praying at the bottom of the sea.

When he finished, in prolonged, solemn tones — like the continuous tolling of a bell on a ship foundering at sea in fog — he began reading the following hymn. But as he reached the final stanzas, his manner changed, and he burst forth with pealing joy and exultation:
'The ribs and terrors in the whale / Arched over me a dismal gloom, / While all God's sunlit waves rolled by, / And lifted me deepening down to doom.
'I saw the opening maw of hell, / With endless pains and sorrows there; / Which none but they that feel can tell — / Oh, I was plunging to despair.
'In black distress, I called my God, / When I could scarce believe him mine, / He bowed his ear to my complaints — / No more the whale did me confine.
'With speed he flew to my relief, / As on a radiant dolphin borne; / Awful, yet bright, as lightning shone / The face of my Deliverer God.
'My song forever shall record / That terrible, that joyful hour; / I give the glory to my God, / His all the mercy and the power.'

Nearly everyone joined in singing this hymn, which swelled high above the howling storm. A brief pause followed. The preacher slowly turned the pages of the Bible and at last, pressing his hand down on the right page, said: 'Beloved shipmates, hold tight to the last verse of the first chapter of Jonah: "And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah."'

'Shipmates, this book — just four chapters, four yarns — is one of the smallest strands in the mighty cable of Scripture. Yet what depths of the soul does Jonah's deep sea-line plumb! What a powerful lesson this prophet teaches us! What a magnificent canticle from the fish's belly! How surging and grandly it billows! We feel the floods washing over us; we sink with him to the kelp-covered bottom; seaweed and all the slime of the sea is around us! But what is this lesson that the book of Jonah teaches? Shipmates, it's a two-stranded lesson: a lesson to us all as sinful men, and a lesson to me as a pilot of the living God. As sinful men, it's a story of sin, hard-heartedness, sudden fear, swift punishment, repentance, prayer, and finally deliverance and joy. Like all sinners, Jonah's sin was willful disobedience of God's command — never mind what the command was or how it was delivered — a command he found hard. But everything God wants us to do is hard for us — remember that — which is why he more often commands than persuades. And if we obey God, we must disobey ourselves; and it's in this disobeying of ourselves that the hardness of obeying God consists.'

'With this sin of disobedience in him, Jonah further defies God by trying to flee from Him. He thinks a man-made ship can carry him to countries where God doesn't rule — where only the captains of this earth hold power. He skulks around the wharves of Joppa, looking for a ship bound for Tarshish. And there may be a deeper meaning here. By all accounts, Tarshish was the modern Cadiz. And where is Cadiz, shipmates? Cadiz is in Spain — as far by water from Joppa as Jonah could possibly have sailed in those ancient days, when the Atlantic was an almost unknown sea. Joppa — modern Jaffa — sits on the easternmost coast of the Mediterranean, and Tarshish is more than two thousand miles to the west, just outside the Straits of Gibraltar. Don't you see, shipmates? Jonah tried to flee as far from God as the world allowed! Miserable man! Skulking from his God with a slouched hat and guilty eyes, prowling among the shipping like a burglar rushing to cross the seas. He looks so disordered and self-condemning that if there had been police in those days, he'd have been arrested on suspicion before he touched a deck. He's obviously a fugitive — no luggage, no hat-box, no bag — no friends seeing him off at the wharf. After much dodging around, he finds the Tarshish ship loading its last cargo. As he steps aboard to find the captain's cabin, all the sailors stop hoisting goods to study the stranger's guilty eyes. Jonah sees this and tries in vain to look confident — tries his wretched smile. But strong instinct tells the sailors he's no innocent man. In their half-joking, half-serious way, one whispers to another: "Jack, he's robbed a widow." "Joe, mark him — he's a bigamist." "Harry, I bet he's that adulterer who broke jail in Gomorrah, or one of the missing murderers from Sodom." Another runs to read the wanted poster nailed to the wharf, offering five hundred gold coins for a parricide. He reads, looks from Jonah to the poster. All the sailors crowd around Jonah, ready to seize him. Frightened Jonah trembles, and trying to put on a brave face, only looks more cowardly. He won't confess — but that itself deepens suspicion. He makes the best of it, and when they decide he's not the wanted man, they let him pass. He goes below to the cabin.'

'"Who's there?" cries the captain at his busy desk, hurriedly filling out customs papers. "Who's there?" Oh, how that harmless question torments Jonah! For an instant he almost turns to flee again. But he rallies. "I want passage to Tarshish. How soon do you sail, sir?" The busy captain hadn't even looked up, but the moment he hears that hollow voice, he shoots Jonah a piercing glance. "We sail with the next tide," he says slowly, still studying him intently. "No sooner?" "Soon enough for any honest man traveling as a passenger." Ha! Jonah — another stab. But he quickly distracts the captain from that scent. "I'll sail with you — the passage money, how much? I'll pay now." Because it's specifically noted, shipmates, as if it were a detail not to be overlooked, that "he paid the fare" before the ship sailed. And in context, this is full of meaning.'

'Now Jonah's captain, shipmates, was a man whose judgment could detect crime in anyone, but whose greed would expose it only in the penniless. In this world, sin that pays its way travels freely, without a passport, while Virtue, if poor, is stopped at every border. So the captain tests the depth of Jonah's purse before judging him openly. He charges triple the normal fare — and Jonah agrees. Now the captain knows Jonah is a fugitive, but he's willing to assist a flight that paves its trail with gold. Yet when Jonah actually opens his purse, the captain's suspicions persist. He tests every coin for counterfeits. "Not a forger, anyway," he mutters, and books Jonah's passage. "Show me my room, sir," says Jonah. "I'm weary from traveling. I need sleep." "You look it," says the captain. "There's your room." Jonah enters and tries to lock the door, but there's no key. Hearing him fumble, the captain laughs quietly and mutters something about convicts' cell doors never being locked from inside. Fully dressed and dusty, Jonah throws himself into his berth, finding the ceiling almost touching his forehead. The air is stifling, and Jonah gasps. In that cramped hole, sunk below the ship's waterline, Jonah feels a foreshadowing of that suffocating hour when the whale will hold him in the tightest chamber of its belly.'

'Screwed to the wall, a swinging lamp rocks gently in Jonah's room. The ship heels toward the wharf under the weight of the last cargo, and the lamp, flame and all, though swaying, maintains a constant angle to the room — perfectly straight itself, but making obvious the crooked, lying levels around it. The lamp terrifies Jonah. Lying in his berth, his tormented eyes scan the room, and this so-far-successful fugitive finds no rest for his restless gaze. The lamp's contradiction appalls him more and more. The floor, ceiling, and walls are all askew. "Oh! So my conscience hangs in me!" he groans. "Straight upward it burns, but the chambers of my soul are all twisted!"'

'Like a man who after a night of drunken revelry staggers to bed, still reeling, but with conscience pricking him — who turns and turns in agony, praying for oblivion until the episode passes — and at last, amid the whirl of suffering, a deep stupor steals over him, like the numbness of bleeding to death, for conscience is the wound and nothing can stanch it — so, after sore wrestling in his berth, Jonah's ponderous misery drags him drowning down to sleep.'

'Now the tide has turned. The ship casts off, and from the deserted wharf the cheerless vessel for Tarshish glides to sea, all leaning to one side.
