That ship, my friends, was the first recorded smuggler! The contraband was Jonah. But the sea rebels — it will not bear the wicked burden. A terrible storm comes on; the ship is about to break apart. But when the boatswain calls all hands to lighten her, when boxes, bales, and jars are clattering overboard, when the wind is shrieking and the men are shouting and every plank thunders with trampling feet right over Jonah's head — in all this raging chaos, Jonah sleeps his horrible sleep. He sees no black sky, feels no reeling timbers, barely notices the rush of the mighty whale already cleaving the seas after him with open mouth. Yes, shipmates, Jonah had gone down into the sides of the ship and was fast asleep. But the terrified captain comes and screams in his deaf ear: "What do you mean, sleeper? Arise!" Startled from his stupor, Jonah staggers to his feet, stumbles to the deck, and grabs a rope to look out at the sea. But at that moment a panther-wave leaps over the bulwarks and pounces on him. Wave after wave floods the ship; the sailors nearly drown while still afloat. And whenever the pale moon shows her frightened face through steep canyons in the black sky overhead, Jonah sees the bowsprit rearing skyward, then plunging back down toward the tormented deep.'

'Terrors upon terrors run screaming through his soul. In all his cringing postures, the God-fugitive is now unmistakable. The sailors watch him. Their suspicions grow, and finally, to test the truth by referring the matter to Heaven itself, they cast lots to discover whose fault this tempest is. The lot falls on Jonah. Then how furiously they mob him with questions: "What is your occupation? Where are you from? What country? What people?" But mark, shipmates, the behavior of poor Jonah. The eager sailors only ask who he is and where he's from. But they receive not only an answer to those questions — they get an answer to a question they never asked, an unsolicited confession forced from Jonah by the hard hand of God upon him.'

'"I am a Hebrew," he cries — and then: "I fear the Lord God of Heaven, who made the sea and the dry land!" Fear Him, Jonah? Yes, well might you fear the Lord God then! He goes on to make a full confession, and the sailors grow more and more appalled — but still they pity him. When wretched Jonah, not yet asking God for mercy because he knows all too well the darkness of what he deserves, cries out for them to throw him into the sea, knowing the storm is his fault — they mercifully turn away and try other means to save the ship. But it's no use. The furious gale howls louder. Then, with one hand raised to God in prayer, with the other they reluctantly take hold of Jonah.'

'And now Jonah is taken up like an anchor and dropped into the sea. Instantly, an oily calm spreads from the east, and the sea goes still — as if Jonah carried the gale down with him, leaving smooth water behind. He sinks into the whirling heart of such a masterless chaos that he barely notices the moment he drops, seething, into the yawning jaws waiting for him. The whale snaps shut all its ivory teeth like white bolts upon his prison. Then Jonah prayed to the Lord from the fish's belly. But notice his prayer, and learn a weighty lesson. Sinful as he is, Jonah does not weep and beg for immediate rescue. He feels his terrible punishment is just. He leaves all deliverance to God, contenting himself with this: that despite all his agony, he will still look toward God's holy temple. And here, shipmates, is true and faithful repentance — not clamoring for pardon, but grateful for punishment. And how pleasing to God this was is shown in Jonah's eventual deliverance from the sea and the whale. Shipmates, I don't hold up Jonah as a model of sin, but I do hold him up as a model of repentance. Don't sin — but if you do, repent like Jonah.'

While he spoke these words, the howling, slanting storm outside seemed to add new power to the preacher. Describing Jonah's storm, he seemed tossed by a storm himself. His deep chest heaved like a ground swell; his arms seemed the warring elements at work; and the thunder rolling from his dark brow and the light leaping from his eyes made every simple listener watch him with a strange, quick fear.
Then a lull came over his expression as he silently turned the pages of the Book once more. At last, standing motionless with closed eyes, he seemed for a moment to be communing with God and himself.
But again he leaned toward the congregation, and bowing his head with an expression of the deepest yet manliest humility, he spoke these words:

'Shipmates, God has laid only one hand upon you; both His hands press upon me. I have read you, by whatever murky light is mine, the lesson Jonah teaches to all sinners — and therefore to you, and even more to me, for I am a greater sinner than you. And now how gladly I would come down from this masthead and sit on the hatches where you sit, and listen as you listen, while one of you reads me that other, more terrible lesson that Jonah teaches to me as a pilot of the living God. How, being an anointed pilot-prophet, a speaker of truth, and commanded by the Lord to sound unwelcome truths in the ears of wicked Nineveh, Jonah — dreading the hostility he would provoke — fled from his mission and tried to escape his duty and his God by taking ship at Joppa. But God is everywhere; Tarshish he never reached. As we have seen, God came upon him in the whale and swallowed him down to living gulfs of doom, tearing him along "into the midst of the seas," where the swirling depths sucked him ten thousand fathoms down and "the weeds were wrapped about his head" and all the watery world of misery poured over him. Yet even then, beyond the reach of any plumb line — "out of the belly of hell" — when the whale grounded on the ocean's deepest bones, even then God heard the engulfed, repenting prophet when he cried. Then God spoke to the fish, and from the shuddering cold and blackness of the sea, the whale rose breaching toward the warm, pleasant sun and all the delights of air and earth, and "vomited out Jonah upon the dry land." And when the word of the Lord came a second time, Jonah — bruised and beaten, his ears still echoing with the ocean like two sea shells — did the Almighty's bidding. And what was that, shipmates? To preach the Truth to the face of Falsehood! That was it!'

'This, shipmates, is that other lesson — and woe to the pilot of the living God who ignores it. Woe to him whom this world charms away from Gospel duty! Woe to him who tries to pour oil on the waters when God has brewed them into a gale! Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to shake! Woe to him whose reputation means more to him than righteousness! Woe to him who, in this world, doesn't court dishonor! Woe to him who would not be true, even though being false would save him! Yes, woe to him who, as the great Pilot Paul said, while preaching to others is himself a castaway!'

He sank and fell away from himself for a moment. Then lifting his face again, a deep joy shone in his eyes as he cried out with heavenly passion: 'But oh! Shipmates! On the starboard side of every woe, there is a sure delight — and the peak of that delight is higher than the depth of that woe is deep. Isn't the masthead higher than the keel is low? Delight is to him — a far, far upward and inward delight — who against the proud gods and commodores of this earth, stands forever forth as his own inexorable self. Delight is to him whose strong arms still support him when the ship of this base, treacherous world has gone down beneath him. Delight is to him who gives no quarter to the truth, and kills, burns, and destroys all sin, though he pluck it from under the robes of senators and judges. Delight — topgallant delight — is to him who acknowledges no law or lord but the Lord his God, and is only a patriot to heaven. Delight is to him whom all the waves of the billows of the seas of the raging mob can never shake from this sure Keel of the Ages. And eternal delight and blessedness will be his, who coming to lay himself down, can say with his final breath — O Father! — chiefly known to me by Thy rod — mortal or immortal, here I die. I have striven to be Thine, more than to be this world's, or my own. Yet this is nothing; I leave eternity to Thee; for what is man that he should live out the lifetime of his God?'
He said no more. Slowly waving a benediction, he covered his face with his hands and remained kneeling until every person had left and he was alone in the place.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — A Bosom Friend
paragraphs: Returning to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel, I found Queequeg there alone. He'd left the service before the benediction. He was sitting on a bench by the fire with his feet on the stove hearth, holding his little idol close to his face, peering hard into it and gently whittling its nose with a jackknife, meanwhile humming to himself in his heathen way.

When I interrupted him, he put the idol away. Soon he went to the table, picked up a large book, placed it on his lap, and began counting the pages with careful regularity. Every fifty pages or so, he'd stop, look vaguely around, and let out a long, gurgling whistle of astonishment. Then he'd start again at the next fifty, seeming to begin at one each time, as if he couldn't count past fifty — and it was only the sheer number of fifties that amazed him.

I watched him with great interest. Savage though he was, and hideously scarred about the face — at least to my taste — there was something in his expression that wasn't at all disagreeable. You can't hide the soul. Through all his unearthly tattoos, I thought I could see traces of a simple, honest heart. And in his large, deep eyes — fiery black and bold — there were signs of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils. Beyond all this, there was a certain dignity about the man that even his roughness couldn't destroy. He looked like someone who had never groveled and never owed a debt. Whether it was because his shaved head made his forehead stand out in clearer, broader relief, I won't say — but his head was phrenologically excellent. Ridiculous as it may sound, it reminded me of General Washington's head, as you see it in popular busts: the same long, evenly sloping forehead retreating from projecting brows that jutted out like two wooded promontories. Queequeg was George Washington, cannibalistically developed.

While I studied him closely — half-pretending to watch the storm through the window — he never noticed me at all. He appeared completely absorbed in counting the pages of that marvelous book. Considering how sociably we'd slept together the night before, and especially the affectionate arm I'd found thrown over me that morning, his indifference seemed very strange. But savages are strange beings. Sometimes you don't know how to take them. At first they're overawing; their calm self-possession seems like Socratic wisdom. I'd also noticed that Queequeg never mingled with the other sailors at the inn. He made no effort to widen his circle of acquaintances. All this struck me as remarkable, yet on second thought, there was something almost sublime about it. Here was a man twenty thousand miles from home — by way of Cape Horn, the only route available to him — thrown among people as alien to him as if he'd landed on Jupiter. Yet he seemed completely at ease, perfectly serene, content with his own company, always equal to himself. Surely this was a touch of fine philosophy, even though he'd probably never heard such a thing existed. But perhaps to be true philosophers, we mortals shouldn't be conscious of living or striving as such. The moment I hear someone calls himself a philosopher, I conclude that, like the dyspeptic old woman, he must have broken his digester.

As I sat in that now-lonely room — the fire burning low, in that gentle stage when, having warmed the air, it just glows to be looked at; the evening shadows and phantoms gathering at the windows, peering in at us, a silent, solitary pair; the storm booming outside in solemn swells — I began to feel strange sensations. Something was melting in me. My splintered heart and furious fist were no longer turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it. There he sat, his very indifference revealing a nature free of civilized hypocrisies and smooth deceits. Wild he was — a sight of sights to see. Yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn to him. And the very things that would have repelled most people were the magnets that attracted me. I'll try a pagan friend, I thought, since Christian kindness has proved to be hollow courtesy. I moved my bench closer and made friendly signs and hints, doing my best to talk with him. At first he barely noticed, but when I mentioned his hospitality the night before, he managed to ask whether we'd be bedfellows again. I said yes, and he seemed pleased — perhaps a little flattered.

We turned over the book together, and I tried to explain the purpose of printing and the meaning of the few pictures in it. This caught his interest, and from there we moved on to chattering as best we could about the various sights to see in this famous town. Soon I suggested we smoke together. He produced his pouch and tomahawk-pipe and quietly offered me a puff. And then we sat, exchanging puffs from that wild pipe of his, passing it regularly back and forth.

If there still lingered any ice of indifference between us, that friendly pipe thawed it away. He seemed to feel a warm regard for me from the start, and when our smoke was over, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me around the waist, and said that from now on we were married — meaning, in his country's way, that we were bosom friends. He would gladly die for me, if need be. In a country where they don't regulate these things by law, I suppose they use this simple, savage way. In any case, he seemed to consider us joined.

After supper, we went up to our room together. He brought out his giant tobacco pouch, which also served as a pillow — with the tomahawk he smoked with tucked inside. He offered me the pillow and the tomahawk-pipe, and we sat together on the edge of the bed. He then produced about thirty dollars in silver, spread them on the table, divided them into two equal piles, pushed one toward me, and insisted I keep it. I tried to refuse, but he swept it into my trousers pocket. He then went through a sort of ceremony, emptied his pipe's ashes, held up his idol, and made a ritual of fire — offering me the idol to worship along with him.

I was a good Christian, born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church. How then could I unite with this wild idolator in worshipping his piece of wood? But what is worship? thought I. Do you suppose now, Ishmael, that the magnanimous God of heaven and earth — pagans and all included — can possibly be jealous of an insignificant bit of black wood? Impossible! But what is worship? — to do the will of God — that is worship. And what is the will of God? — to do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man to do to me — that is the will of God. Now, Queequeg is my fellow man. And what do I wish that this Queequeg would do to me? Why, unite with me in my particular Presbyterian form of worship. Consequently, I must then unite with him in his; ergo, I must turn idolator. So I kindled the shavings; helped prop up the innocent little idol; offered him burnt biscuit with Queequeg; salamed before him twice or thrice; kissed his nose; and that done, we undressed and went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and all the world. But we did not go to sleep without some little chat.

How it is I know not; but there is no place like a bed for confidential disclosures between friends. Man and wife, they say, there open the very bottom of their souls to each other; and some old couples often lie and chat over old times till nearly morning. Thus, then, in our hearts' honeymoon, lay I and Queequeg — a cozy, loving pair.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Nightgown
paragraphs: We had lain in bed chatting and napping in short intervals, with Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine and drawing them back. We were entirely relaxed and comfortable. At last, our conversation chased away the last traces of sleepiness, and we felt like getting up — though dawn was still some way off.

We grew so wide awake that lying down became tiresome. Little by little we sat up, bedclothes tucked snugly around us, leaning against the headboard with our four knees drawn up close together and our two noses bent over them, as if our kneecaps were warming pans. We felt wonderfully cozy, especially since it was so cold outside — and outside the blankets too, since there was no fire in the room. To truly enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, because no quality in this world exists except by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you believe you've been perfectly comfortable for a long time, then you can no longer be said to be comfortable at all. But if, like Queequeg and me in that bed, only the tip of your nose or the crown of your head is slightly chilled, then in your general consciousness you feel most deliciously warm. For this reason, a bedroom should never have a fire — that's one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. The height of this kind of bliss is having nothing but the blanket between your warmth and the cold outside air. Then you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the feeling of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object when Queequeg suggested we light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that although I'd been so against his smoking in bed the night before, see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, lit by the flame of the newly lit lamp.

Whether that undulating canopy of smoke carried the savage away to distant scenes, I don't know, but he began speaking of his native island. Eager to hear his story, I asked him to go on. He gladly agreed. Though at the time I barely understood half his words, later conversations — when I'd grown more familiar with his broken English — now allow me to present the whole story, such as it is, in the bare skeleton I give here.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Biographical
paragraphs: Queequeg was a native of Rokovoko, an island far away to the west and south. It isn't on any map; true places never are.

Even as a child running wild through the woods in nothing but a grass cloth, followed by nibbling goats as if he were a green sapling — even then, Queequeg's ambitious soul harbored a strong desire to see more of the Christian world than a whaling ship or two. His father was a High Chief, a King; his uncle a High Priest; and on his mother's side he boasted aunts married to unconquerable warriors. He had excellent blood in his veins — royal stuff, though sadly contaminated, I'm afraid, by the cannibal tendencies he'd picked up in his unschooled youth.

A ship from Sag Harbor visited his father's bay, and Queequeg tried to get passage to Christian lands. But the ship had a full crew and turned him down — even all the influence of his father the King couldn't help. So Queequeg made a vow. Alone in his canoe, he paddled to a distant strait that the ship had to pass through when leaving the island. On one side was a coral reef; on the other, a low tongue of land covered with mangrove thickets growing out into the water. Hiding his canoe among the thickets with its prow seaward, he sat in the stern, paddle in hand. When the ship glided past, he shot out like lightning, reached the ship's side, kicked his canoe over and sank it with one backward thrust of his foot, scrambled up the chains, and threw himself full-length on the deck, grabbing a ring-bolt. He swore not to let go even if they hacked him to pieces.

The captain threatened to throw him overboard and dangled a cutlass over his bare wrists. But Queequeg was a king's son, and Queequeg wouldn't budge. Struck by his desperate fearlessness and his wild desire to see Christendom, the captain finally relented and told him he could stay. But this fine young savage — this sea Prince of Wales — never saw the captain's cabin. They put him below with the sailors and made a whaleman of him. But like Czar Peter, content to toil in foreign shipyards, Queequeg didn't mind the indignity if it meant learning enough to help his people. At heart, he told me, he was driven by a deep desire to learn the arts of the Christians — to make his people happier and better than they already were. But alas, the practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be miserable and wicked — infinitely more so than all his father's heathens. Arriving in Sag Harbor and seeing how the sailors lived there, then going on to Nantucket and seeing how they spent their wages — poor Queequeg gave up hope. It's a wicked world in every direction, he thought. I'll die a pagan.
And so, an idolator at heart, he lived among these Christians, wore their clothes, and tried to speak their language. That explained his odd ways, though he'd been away from home for some time.

Through hints, I asked whether he planned to go home and claim his throne — since his father, very old and feeble by last report, was probably dead by now. He said no, not yet. He was afraid that Christianity — or rather Christians — had made him unfit to ascend the pure, undefiled throne of thirty pagan kings before him. But eventually, he said, he would return — once he felt properly cleansed again. For now, he planned to sail around and sow his wild oats in all four oceans. They'd made him a harpooneer, and that barbed iron was his scepter now.

I asked about his immediate plans. He said he wanted to go to sea again in his old line of work. I told him whaling was my plan too, and that I intended to sail from Nantucket, the most promising port for an adventurous whaleman. He immediately decided to come with me — to ship on the same vessel, join the same watch, the same boat, the same mess — in short, to share every stroke of luck. With both my hands in his, we'd boldly dip into the potluck of both worlds. I agreed joyfully. Beyond the affection I now felt for Queequeg, he was an experienced harpooneer, which would be invaluable to someone like me — a complete novice at whaling, though well acquainted with the sea from merchant sailing.
His story finished with his pipe's last dying puff. Queequeg embraced me, pressed his forehead against mine, and blowing out the light, we rolled apart and were soon asleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Wheelbarrow
paragraphs: Next morning, Monday, after selling the embalmed head to a barber for a wig block, I settled our bill — using Queequeg's money, however. The grinning landlord and boarders seemed enormously amused by the sudden friendship between me and Queequeg — especially since Peter Coffin's wild stories had previously made me so terrified of the very person I now kept company with.

We borrowed a wheelbarrow, loaded our things — my poor carpet-bag, Queequeg's canvas sack and hammock — and headed down to the Moss, the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. People stared as we walked — not so much at Queequeg, since they were used to seeing cannibals in their streets, but at seeing us on such friendly terms. We ignored them, taking turns wheeling the barrow, Queequeg occasionally stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked why he carried such a cumbersome thing ashore when surely all whaling ships provided their own harpoons. He answered that while what I said was true, he had a special fondness for his own harpoon — it was made of proven steel, tested in many mortal combats and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland farmers who bring their own scythes to other men's fields, Queequeg preferred his own harpoon for his own private reasons.

Switching the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he'd ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. His ship's owners had lent him one to carry his heavy sea chest to his boarding house. Not wanting to appear ignorant — though he was entirely ignorant of how to use the thing — Queequeg placed his chest on the barrow, lashed it tight, then hoisted the whole contraption onto his shoulders and marched up the wharf. 'Queequeg,' I said, 'you should have known better! Didn't people laugh?'

At that, he told me another story. On his island of Rokovoko, at wedding feasts, they press the fragrant water of young coconuts into a large stained calabash like a punchbowl. This punchbowl is always the great centerpiece of the braided mat where the feast is held. Once, a grand merchant ship visited, and its captain — by all accounts a very stately, punctilious gentleman — was invited to the wedding feast of Queequeg's sister, a pretty young princess who had just turned ten. When the wedding guests gathered at the bride's bamboo cottage, the captain marched in and was given the seat of honor, directly across from the punchbowl, between the High Priest and King Queequeg's father. Grace was said — for those people say grace as well as we do, though Queequeg told me that unlike us, who look down at our plates, they look upward to the great Giver of all feasts, copying the ducks. Then the High Priest opened the banquet with the island's ancient ceremony: dipping his consecrated fingers into the bowl before the blessed drink could circulate. The captain, seated next to the Priest and watching this ritual, concluded that as captain of a ship he clearly outranked a mere island king — especially in the king's own house — and calmly proceeded to wash his hands in the punchbowl, apparently mistaking it for a large finger bowl. 'Now,' said Queequeg, 'what you think? Didn't our people laugh?'

At last, passage paid and luggage safe, we stood aboard the schooner. Hoisting sail, she glided down the Acushnet River. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, its ice-covered trees glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of barrels were piled on the wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent, safely moored at last — while from others came sounds of carpenters and coopers, fires and forges melting pitch, all signaling that new voyages were being prepared. One long, perilous voyage ends, and a second begins; the second ends, and a third starts — forever and ever. Such is the endlessness of all earthly effort.

Reaching the open water, the bracing breeze freshened. The little Moss tossed quick foam from her bows, like a young colt snorting. How I breathed in that brisk, wild air! How I scorned the common highway, all dented with the marks of slavish heels, and turned to admire the magnificence of the sea, which permits no records.

Queequeg seemed to drink and reel at the same spray fountain with me. His dark nostrils flared wide; he bared his filed and pointed teeth. On we flew, and once we'd gained the open sea, the Moss paid homage to the blast — ducking and diving her bow like a slave before a sultan. Leaning sideways, we darted sideways; every rope hummed like a wire; the two tall masts bent like Indian canes in a tornado. So absorbed were we in this thrilling scene, standing by the plunging bowsprit, that for a while we didn't notice the jeering looks from the other passengers — a landlubber bunch who marveled that two people should be so friendly, as though a white man were somehow more dignified than a whitewashed Black man. Among them were some real bumpkins who, by their extreme greenness, must have come from the very heart of the countryside. Queequeg caught one of these yokels mimicking him behind his back. I thought the fool's hour had come. Dropping his harpoon, Queequeg grabbed the man in his arms and, with almost miraculous dexterity and strength, launched him bodily into the air. With a light tap to his backside at the peak of the somersault, the fellow landed on his feet, lungs bursting, while Queequeg calmly turned away, lit his tomahawk pipe, and passed it to me for a puff.
'Captain! Captain!' yelled the bumpkin, running toward the officer. 'Captain! Here's the devil!'
'Hey, you!' cried the captain, a gaunt scarecrow of the sea, stalking up to Queequeg. 'What the hell do you mean by that? Don't you know you could have killed that man?'
'What him say?' said Queequeg, mildly turning to me.
'He says,' I said, 'that you nearly killed that man there' — pointing to the still-shivering greenhorn.
'Kill him?' cried Queequeg, twisting his tattooed face into an unearthly look of disdain. 'Him very small fish. Queequeg no kill such small fish. Queequeg kill big whale!'
'Listen here,' roared the captain. 'I'll kill you, you cannibal, if you try any more tricks on this ship. Watch yourself!'

But just then the captain had to watch himself. The enormous strain on the mainsail had snapped the weather sheet, and the huge boom was now swinging wildly from side to side, sweeping the entire stern deck. The poor fellow Queequeg had tossed was knocked overboard. Everyone panicked. Trying to grab the boom seemed suicidal — it flew left and right, almost in one tick of a watch, threatening to splinter at any moment. Nothing could be done. Everyone rushed to the bow, staring at the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an enraged whale. In the midst of this chaos, Queequeg dropped to his knees, crawled under the boom's path, grabbed a rope, secured one end to the railing, and then, flinging the other like a lasso, caught it around the boom as it swept over his head. At the next jerk, the spar was trapped. The schooner was turned into the wind. While the crew prepared the rescue boat, Queequeg stripped to the waist and dove from the side in a long, living arc. For three minutes or more we watched him swimming like a dog, his powerful arms cutting straight through the freezing foam, his brawny shoulders breaking through the water. I looked at that grand, glorious man but saw no one to be saved — the greenhorn had gone under. Queequeg shot himself vertically out of the water, took a quick look around, and dived down and vanished. A few minutes later he surfaced, one arm still stroking, the other dragging a lifeless form. The boat picked them up. The bumpkin was revived. Everyone voted Queequeg a hero. The captain begged his pardon. From that hour I clung to Queequeg like a barnacle — until poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

Was there ever such lack of self-importance? He didn't seem to think he deserved a medal. He only asked for water — fresh water — and something to wipe off the brine. That done, he put on dry clothes, lit his pipe, leaned against the railing, and gazing mildly at those around him, seemed to be thinking: 'It's a mutual, joint-stock world in every latitude. We cannibals must help these Christians.'

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Nothing else noteworthy happened during the crossing, so after a fine run, we arrived safely in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Pull out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies — way offshore, lonelier than the Eddystone lighthouse. A mere hillock, an elbow of sand, all beach without a background. There's more sand there than you'd use in twenty years as blotting paper. Jokers will tell you they have to plant weeds because nothing grows naturally, that they import Canadian thistles, that they send overseas for a wooden plug to stop a leak, that wood is carried around like relics of the True Cross in Rome, that people plant toadstools for shade in summer, that one blade of grass makes an oasis and three blades a prairie, that they wear quicksand shoes like Lapland snowshoes, and that they're so enclosed by the ocean that small clams sometimes attach to their chairs and tables, as barnacles cling to sea turtles. But these exaggerations only prove that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Consider the wonderful legend of how the island was first settled by the Native Americans. An eagle swooped down on the New England coast and carried off an infant in its talons. With loud cries the parents watched their child disappear over the wide water. They resolved to follow. Setting out in canoes, after a dangerous crossing they discovered the island — and there they found an empty ivory casket: the poor little skeleton.

No wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, took to the sea for a living! First they caught crabs and clams in the sand. Growing bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel. More experienced, they pushed off in boats for cod. And at last, launching a navy of great ships, they explored the watery world, put an unbroken belt of voyages around it, peeked through the Bering Strait, and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war on the mightiest living creature that has survived the Flood — the most monstrous, most mountainous beast! That Himalayan, salt-sea mastodon, clothed with such tremendous unconscious power that its very panics are more dangerous than its most malicious attacks!

And so these naked Nantucketers, these sea hermits, swarming from their anthill in the ocean, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders — dividing the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans among themselves the way three pirate powers divided Poland. Let America annex Mexico and pile Cuba on top of Canada; let England swarm across all India and hang its banner from the sun — two-thirds of this watery globe belong to the Nantucketer. The sea is his; he owns it as emperors own empires. Other sailors have only a right of passage. Merchant ships are merely floating bridges; warships are floating forts; even pirates, though they live on the sea the way highwaymen live on the road, only plunder other ships — other fragments of land like themselves — without drawing their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer alone lives and revels on the sea. He alone, in the Bible's words, goes down to it in ships, plowing it back and forth as his private plantation. There is his home; there lies his business — a business that Noah's flood couldn't interrupt even if it drowned all of China. He lives on the sea as prairie chickens live on the prairie. He hides among the waves, he climbs them like chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years he doesn't see land, and when he finally reaches it, it smells like another world — stranger than the moon would seem to an Earthling. Like the landless gull that folds its wings at sunset and is rocked to sleep between the swells — so at nightfall the Nantucketer, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lies down to rest, while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Chowder
paragraphs: It was late in the evening when the little Moss came snugly to anchor, and Queequeg and I went ashore. We couldn't attend to any business that day — nothing but supper and a bed. The landlord of the Spouter-Inn had recommended us to his cousin Hosea Hussey of the Try Pots, who he claimed ran one of the best hotels in all Nantucket and was famous for his chowders. In short, he strongly hinted we couldn't do better than try our luck at the Try Pots. But his directions — keep a yellow warehouse on your starboard until you see a white church to port, then keep that to port until you reach a corner three points to starboard, then ask the first person you meet — confused us badly. Especially since Queequeg insisted the yellow warehouse should be to port, while I was sure Peter Coffin had said starboard. After stumbling around in the dark for a while, occasionally waking a peaceful resident to ask directions, we finally came to something unmistakable.

Two enormous wooden pots, painted black and suspended by handles, swung from the crossbeams of an old topmast planted in front of an old doorway. The opposite ends of the crossbeams had been sawn off, making the topmast look disturbingly like a gallows. Maybe I was oversensitive at the time, but I couldn't help staring at it with a vague dread. My neck felt stiff as I gazed up at the two remaining arms — yes, two of them: one for Queequeg, one for me. Ominous, I thought. A Coffin for an innkeeper at my first whaling port; tombstones staring at me in the whalemen's chapel; and now a gallows! Plus a pair of enormous black pots! Were these throwing out hints about Hell?

I was pulled from these reflections by the sight of a freckled woman with yellow hair and a yellow dress, standing in the porch under a dull red lamp that looked like a bruised eye, having a brisk argument with a man in a purple wool shirt.
'Get along with you,' she said to the man, 'or I'll give you a thrashing!'
'Come on, Queequeg,' I said. 'That's Mrs. Hussey.'

And so it was. Mr. Hosea Hussey was away, but Mrs. Hussey was entirely capable of managing everything. When we told her we wanted supper and a bed, she paused her scolding, led us into a little room, sat us at a table covered with the remains of a recent meal, turned to us and said: 'Clam or cod?'
'What's that about cod, ma'am?' I said politely.
'Clam or cod?' she repeated.
'A clam for supper? A cold clam? Is that what you mean, Mrs. Hussey?' I said. 'That's rather cold and clammy for a winter reception, isn't it?'

But being in a great hurry to resume scolding the man in the purple shirt, who was waiting in the hall, and apparently hearing only the word 'clam,' Mrs. Hussey rushed to an open kitchen door, yelled 'Clam for two!' and disappeared.
'Queequeg,' I said, 'do you think we can make a supper out of one clam?'

But a warm, savory steam from the kitchen belied the cheerless prospect. When the smoking chowder arrived, the mystery was deliciously explained. Oh, friends, listen to me! It was made of small, juicy clams barely bigger than hazelnuts, mixed with crushed ship biscuit and salt pork cut into little flakes, the whole enriched with butter and generously seasoned with pepper and salt. Our appetites sharpened by the frosty voyage, and Queequeg especially delighted to see his favorite seafood, we demolished it at great speed. The chowder was supremely excellent. Then, leaning back and remembering Mrs. Hussey's 'clam or cod' announcement, I decided to try an experiment. I stepped to the kitchen door, pronounced the word 'cod' with great emphasis, and sat back down. In a few moments the savory steam returned, but with a different flavor, and presently a fine cod chowder was placed before us.

We got back to business. Plying our spoons, I thought: I wonder if chowder has any effect on the brain? What's that expression about 'chowder-headed' people? 'But look, Queequeg — isn't that a live eel in your bowl? Where's your harpoon?'

The fishiest of all fishy places was the Try Pots, which fully deserved its name — the pots were always boiling with chowder. Chowder for breakfast, chowder for dinner, chowder for supper, until you started expecting fish bones to come through your clothes. The yard was paved with clam shells. Mrs. Hussey wore a polished necklace of codfish vertebrae, and Hosea Hussey's account books were bound in superior old sharkskin. Even the milk tasted fishy, which I couldn't explain until one morning, strolling along the beach among the fishing boats, I saw Hosea's cow feeding on fish scraps and marching along the sand with each foot stuck in a decapitated cod's head — looking very slovenly, I assure you.

After supper, we received a lamp and directions from Mrs. Hussey to the nearest bed. But as Queequeg was about to go up the stairs ahead of me, she reached out her arm and demanded his harpoon. No harpoons in her rooms. 'Why not?' I said. 'Every true whaleman sleeps with his harpoon.' 'Because it's dangerous,' she said. 'Ever since young Stiggs came back from that unfortunate voyage — gone four and a half years with only three barrels of oil — and was found dead in my first-floor back room with his harpoon in his side, I allow no boarders to take such dangerous weapons to their rooms at night. So, Mr. Queequeg' — she had learned his name — 'I'll just take this iron and keep it for you till morning. But the chowder — clam or cod for breakfast, men?'
'Both,' I said. 'And let's have a couple of smoked herrings for variety.'

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — The Ship
paragraphs: That night in bed, we made our plans for the next day. But to my surprise and real concern, Queequeg informed me that he had been consulting Yojo — the name of his small black idol — and Yojo had told him two or three times over, insisting on the point, that instead of going together to the harbor to pick out a whaling ship, the choice should rest entirely with me. Yojo intended to help us, and had already selected a vessel. If left to myself, I, Ishmael, would find it as if by chance. I was to sign on immediately, without waiting for Queequeg.

I should mention that Queequeg placed great trust in Yojo's judgment and remarkable ability to predict things. He regarded Yojo with considerable respect, as a fairly decent sort of god who probably meant well overall, but who didn't always succeed in his well-meaning plans.

Now, this plan of Queequeg's — or rather Yojo's — about choosing our ship, I didn't like it one bit. I had been counting on Queequeg's good judgment to point out the whaler best suited to carry us safely. But since all my objections had no effect on him, I had to give in. So I prepared to tackle the business with a determined burst of energy that should quickly settle the matter. Early the next morning, I left Queequeg shut up with Yojo in our little bedroom — it seemed to be some sort of Lent or Ramadan, a day of fasting, self-denial, and prayer for Queequeg and Yojo. How it all worked, I could never figure out, since I never managed to master his rituals and articles of faith. So, leaving Queequeg fasting with his tomahawk pipe, and Yojo warming himself by his little sacrificial fire of wood shavings, I headed out among the ships. After much wandering and many random questions, I learned there were three ships preparing for three-year voyages: The Devil-Dam, the Tit-Bit, and the Pequod. Devil-Dam — I have no idea where the name came from. Tit-Bit is obvious. Pequod, you'll probably remember, was the name of a famous Massachusetts Indian tribe, now extinct as the ancient Medes. I looked over the Devil-Dam, hopped across to the Tit-Bit, and finally, going aboard the Pequod and looking around for a moment, I decided this was the ship for us.

You may have seen plenty of strange vessels in your time, for all I know — square-toed luggers, towering Japanese junks, boxy galliots, and who knows what else. But take my word for it, you never saw such a rare old ship as this Pequod. She was old school, on the small side if anything, with an old-fashioned, claw-footed look about her. Seasoned and weather-stained through the typhoons and calms of all four oceans, her old hull had darkened like a French soldier who has fought in both Egypt and Siberia. Her sturdy bow looked bearded with age. Her masts — cut somewhere on the coast of Japan, after she lost the originals overboard in a gale — stood stiffly upright like the spines of three old Cologne kings. Her ancient decks were worn and wrinkled, like the pilgrim-worshipped flagstone in Canterbury Cathedral where Becket bled. But on top of all these antiquities, she had new and marvelous features related to the wild business she had followed for more than half a century. Old Captain Peleg, who served many years as her chief mate before commanding his own vessel and was now retired and one of the Pequod's principal owners — this old Peleg, during his time as chief mate, had built upon the ship's original strangeness and decorated it all over with a uniqueness of material and design matched by nothing except perhaps a Viking's carved shield or bedstead. She was decked out like some barbarian African emperor, his neck heavy with polished ivory pendants. She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, adorning herself with the carved bones of her enemies. All around, her open bulwarks were lined like one continuous jaw, set with the long sharp teeth of sperm whales, used as pins to fasten her old ropes and rigging. Those ropes didn't run through ordinary wooden blocks but traveled smoothly over sheaves of sea-ivory. Scorning a standard wheel at her noble helm, she carried instead a tiller — and that tiller was carved in one mass from the long narrow lower jaw of her hereditary enemy. The helmsman steering by that tiller in a storm felt like a Tartar holding back his wild horse by gripping its jaw. A noble craft, but somehow deeply melancholy. All noble things carry that touch.

When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, wanting to offer myself for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't miss a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, set up a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be a temporary structure used only in port. It was cone-shaped, about ten feet high, made from the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of a right whale's jaw. Planted with their broad ends on the deck, a circle of these slabs leaned inward toward each other, joined at the top in a tufted point where loose hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on some old Native chief's head. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, giving whoever sat inside a clear view forward.

Half hidden in this strange shelter, I finally found someone who looked like he had authority. It was noon, the ship's work was paused, and he was enjoying a break from the burden of command. He sat in an old-fashioned oak chair, elaborately carved all over, its seat woven from the same springy material as the wigwam.

There was nothing especially remarkable about the elderly man I saw. He was brown and muscular, like most old seamen, and heavily bundled in blue pilot-cloth cut in the Quaker style. The only notable thing was a fine, almost microscopic network of the tiniest wrinkles around his eyes, which must have come from years of sailing through hard gales and always squinting into the wind — that habit tightens the muscles around the eyes. Wrinkles like that are very effective in a scowl.
"Is this the Captain of the Pequod?" I said, stepping up to the entrance of the tent.
"Supposing it is the captain of the Pequod, what do you want with him?" he demanded.
"I was thinking of signing on."
"Were you now? I can see you're no Nantucketer. Ever been in a stove boat?"
"No, Sir, I never have."
"Don't know anything at all about whaling, I suppose — eh?"
"Nothing, Sir, but I have no doubt I'll learn quickly. I've made several voyages in the merchant service, and I think that —"

"Merchant service be damned. Don't talk that language to me. See this leg? I'll take that leg off your stern if you ever mention the merchant service to me again. Merchant service indeed! I suppose you feel quite proud of having served on those merchant ships. But flukes! Man, what makes you want to go whaling, eh? Looks a little suspicious, doesn't it? Haven't been a pirate, have you? Didn't rob your last captain, did you? Aren't planning to murder the officers once you're at sea?"

I protested my innocence. I could see that behind these half-humorous accusations, this old seaman, as a sheltered Quaker Nantucketer, was full of his island prejudices. He was suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.
"But what draws you to whaling? I want to know that before I think about signing you on."
"Well, sir, I want to see what whaling is. I want to see the world."
"Want to see what whaling is, eh? Have you set eyes on Captain Ahab?"
"Who is Captain Ahab, sir?"
"That's what I thought. Captain Ahab is the captain of this ship."
"I'm mistaken then. I thought I was speaking to the captain himself."

"You're speaking to Captain Peleg — that's who you're speaking to, young man. It's my job, mine and Captain Bildad's, to see the Pequod fitted out for the voyage and supplied with everything she needs, including crew. We're part owners and agents. But as I was saying, if you want to know what whaling is, as you say you do, I can show you a way to find out before you commit yourself past backing out. Take a look at Captain Ahab, young man, and you'll find he has only one leg."
"What do you mean, sir? Was the other one lost to a whale?"
"Lost to a whale! Young man, come closer: it was devoured, chewed up, crunched by the most monstrous sperm whale that ever smashed a boat! — ah, ah!"

I was a little alarmed by his intensity, and perhaps also a little moved by the genuine grief in that final exclamation. But I said as calmly as I could, "What you say is no doubt true enough, sir. But how could I have known there was anything especially ferocious about that particular whale, though I might have guessed as much from the simple fact of the accident."
"Look here, young man, you're a bit soft, do you see? You don't talk tough at all. You have been to sea before, surely?"
"Sir," said I, "I thought I told you that I'd been on four voyages in the merchant —"

"Stop right there! Remember what I said about the merchant service — don't push me — I won't have it. But let's understand each other. I've given you a hint about what whaling involves. Do you still feel inclined to try it?"
"I do, sir."
"Very good. Now, are you the kind of man who'd throw a harpoon down a live whale's throat and then jump in after it? Answer quick!"
"I am, sir, if it were absolutely necessary and there were no alternative — which I don't believe is actually the case."

"Good again. So you not only want to go whaling to find out what it's like, but you also want to see the world? Wasn't that what you said? I thought so. Well then, just step forward there and take a look over the weather bow. Then come back and tell me what you see."

For a moment I stood puzzled by this odd request, not sure whether to take it as a joke or seriously. But when Captain Peleg concentrated all his crow's feet into one fierce scowl, he sent me on my way.

Walking forward and looking over the weather bow, I saw that the ship, swinging on her anchor with the rising tide, was now pointing toward the open ocean. The view was unlimited but utterly monotonous and forbidding. Not the slightest variety that I could see.
"Well, what's the report?" said Peleg when I came back. "What did you see?"
"Not much," I replied. "Nothing but water. Plenty of horizon, though, and there's a squall coming up, I think."
"Well, what do you think now about seeing the world? Still want to go around Cape Horn to see more of it, eh? Can't you see the world right where you stand?"

I was a little taken aback, but go whaling I must and would. The Pequod was as good a ship as any — I thought the best — and I repeated all this to Peleg. Seeing how determined I was, he agreed to sign me on.
"You might as well sign the papers right now," he added. "Come along." And with that, he led the way below deck into the cabin.

Sitting on the stern bench was what struck me as a most unusual and surprising figure. This turned out to be Captain Bildad, who along with Captain Peleg was one of the largest owners of the vessel. The remaining shares, as is sometimes the case in these ports, were held by a crowd of old pensioners — widows, orphaned children, and wards of the court — each owning about the value of a timber head, a foot of plank, or a nail or two in the ship. People in Nantucket invest their money in whaling vessels the same way you invest yours in government bonds.

Now, Bildad, like Peleg and indeed many Nantucketers, was a Quaker. The island had originally been settled by that sect, and to this day its inhabitants generally retain Quaker peculiarities to an unusual degree, though strangely modified by completely foreign influences. Some of these Quakers are the most bloodthirsty of all sailors and whale hunters. They are fighting Quakers — Quakers with a vengeance.

Among them you find men who were given Scripture names — a remarkably common custom on the island — and who grew up naturally absorbing the stately "thee" and "thou" of Quaker speech. Yet from the bold, daring, boundless adventure of their later lives, they strangely blend these inherited mannerisms with a thousand dashing traits worthy of a Scandinavian sea-king or a heroic pagan Roman. And when these qualities come together in a man of greatly superior natural force, with a powerful mind and a deep heart — a man who, through the stillness and solitude of many long night watches in remote waters, under constellations never seen in the north, has been led to think independently and unconventionally, taking in all of nature's sweet or savage impressions straight from her own wild breast, and thereby learning a bold, forceful, elevated way of speaking — that man is one in a million, a mighty figure shaped for noble tragedies. It won't detract from him, dramatically speaking, if by birth or circumstance he carries what seems a half-willful, overriding darkness at the bottom of his nature. For all tragically great men are made so through a certain darkness. Be sure of this, young ambition: all mortal greatness is but disease. But we're not dealing with such a man yet — rather with quite another, and still a man whose peculiarities stem from yet another strain of the Quaker character, shaped by individual circumstances.

Like Captain Peleg, Captain Bildad was a well-off, retired whaleman. But unlike Peleg — who didn't give a damn about what people call serious things and considered those very serious things the biggest trifles of all — Captain Bildad had been raised in the strictest Nantucket Quaker tradition. And all his years at sea, all the sights of lovely unclothed island women round the Horn — none of it had moved this born Quaker one inch or changed a single angle of his vest. Yet for all this unchangeableness, there was something inconsistent about worthy Captain Bildad. Though his conscience wouldn't allow him to bear arms against invaders on land, he had boundlessly invaded the Atlantic and Pacific. Though a sworn enemy of human bloodshed, he had, in his strait-laced coat, spilled barrels upon barrels of whale blood. How, in the reflective evening of his days, the pious Bildad reconciled these things in his memory, I don't know. But it didn't seem to bother him much. Very likely he had long since reached the wise and practical conclusion that a man's religion is one thing and the real world quite another. This world pays dividends. Rising from a little cabin boy in drab short pants to a harpooner in a wide-bellied waistcoat, then boat-header, chief mate, captain, and finally ship owner, Bildad, as I mentioned, had capped off his adventurous career by retiring completely from active life at the respectable age of sixty. He dedicated his remaining days to the quiet collection of his well-earned income.

Now, Bildad, I'm sorry to say, had the reputation of being a hopeless old miser, and in his sea-going days, a bitter, hard taskmaster. They told me in Nantucket, though it certainly seems a curious story, that when he sailed the old Categut whaler, his crew, upon arriving home, were mostly all carried ashore to the hospital, utterly exhausted and worn out. For a pious man, especially a Quaker, he was certainly rather hard-hearted, to say the least. He never swore at his men, they said. But somehow he got an enormous amount of cruel, unrelenting hard work out of them. When Bildad was chief mate, having his drab-colored eye fixed intently on you made you feel completely nervous until you could grab something — a hammer or a marlinspike — and go to work like a madman at something or other, never mind what. Laziness and idleness withered before him. His own body was the perfect expression of his utilitarian character. On his long, gaunt frame, he carried no spare flesh and no unnecessary beard — just a soft, economical fuzz on his chin, like the worn nap of his broad-brimmed hat.

Such was the person I saw sitting on the stern bench when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small. There, bolt upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat that way and never leaned — this to preserve his coat tails. His broad-brimmed hat was placed beside him. His legs were stiffly crossed. His drab vest was buttoned up to his chin. And with spectacles on his nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a heavy volume.
"Bildad," cried Captain Peleg, "at it again, Bildad, eh? You've been studying those Scriptures now for the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge. How far have you got, Bildad?"
As if long accustomed to such irreverent talk from his old shipmate, Bildad paid no attention to the disrespect. He quietly looked up, saw me, and glanced inquiringly at Peleg.
"He says he's our man, Bildad," said Peleg. "He wants to sign on."
"Does thee?" said Bildad, in a hollow tone, turning to face me.
"I does," I said, unconsciously mimicking him — he was that intense a Quaker.
"What do you think of him, Bildad?" said Peleg.
"He'll do," said Bildad, looking me over. Then he went back to reading from his book in a mumbling tone, quite audible.

I thought him the strangest old Quaker I'd ever seen, especially since Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed like such a blowhard. But I said nothing, only looking around me sharply. Peleg threw open a chest, pulled out the ship's articles, set pen and ink before him, and sat down at a small table. I began to think it was time to figure out what terms I'd accept for the voyage. I already knew that in the whaling business they paid no wages. Instead, everyone, including the captain, received shares of the profits called lays. These lays were proportional to the importance of each man's duties. I also knew that as a greenhand at whaling, my own lay wouldn't be large. But considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship and splice a rope, I felt confident I'd be offered at least the 275th lay — that is, the 275th part of the voyage's net profits, whatever that might amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they called a rather long lay, it was better than nothing. If we had a lucky voyage, it might nearly cover the cost of the clothes I'd wear out, to say nothing of three years' food and board, for which I wouldn't have to pay a penny.

You might think this was a poor way to build a fortune — and so it was, a very poor way indeed. But I'm one of those people who never fuss about fortunes. I'm quite content if the world is ready to feed and house me while I'm staying at this grim sign of the Thunder Cloud. All things considered, the 275th lay seemed about fair, though I wouldn't have been surprised to be offered the 200th, given my broad shoulders.

But one thing made me uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other smaller shareholders left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. I suspected that stingy old Bildad might have a lot of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was struggling to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"
"Well, Captain Bildad," Peleg interrupted, "what do you say? What lay shall we give this young man?"
"Thou knowest best," came the sepulchral reply. "The seven hundred and seventy-seventh wouldn't be too much, would it? — 'where moth and rust do corrupt, but lay —'"

Lay indeed, I thought, and what a lay! The seven hundred and seventy-seventh! Well, old Bildad, you're determined that I, for one, won't be laying up many lays down here where moth and rust corrupt. It was an absurdly long lay. Though the number sounds impressive to a landlubber, the slightest thought will show you that the seven hundred and seventy-seventh part of a farthing is a great deal less than seven hundred and seventy-seven gold doubloons. And so I thought at the time.
"Why, blast your eyes, Bildad," cried Peleg, "you don't want to swindle this young man! He must have more than that."
"Seven hundred and seventy-seventh," Bildad said again, without lifting his eyes. Then he went on mumbling: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
"I'm putting him down for the three hundredth," said Peleg. "Do you hear that, Bildad? The three hundredth lay, I say."

Bildad laid down his book and, turning solemnly toward Peleg, said, "Captain Peleg, thou hast a generous heart. But thou must consider thy duty to the other owners of this ship — widows and orphans, many of them — and that if we reward this young man too generously, we may be taking bread from those widows and orphans. The seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, Captain Peleg."

"Bildad!" roared Peleg, jumping up and stomping around the cabin. "Blast you, Captain Bildad, if I had followed your advice in these matters, I would by now have a conscience heavy enough to sink the largest ship that ever sailed around Cape Horn."

"Captain Peleg," said Bildad steadily, "thy conscience may draw ten inches of water, or ten fathoms — I can't tell. But since thou art still an unrepentant man, Captain Peleg, I greatly fear thy conscience is a leaky one. In the end it will sink thee down to the fiery pit, Captain Peleg."

"Fiery pit! Fiery pit! You insult me, man — beyond all natural bearing, you insult me. It's an outrage to tell any human being he's bound for hell. Flukes and flames! Bildad, say that to me again, and I'll — I'll — yes, I'll swallow a live goat with all his hair and horns on. Out of the cabin, you droning, drab-colored son of a wooden gun — straight out with you!"
As he thundered this out, he rushed at Bildad. But with a marvelous sideways, sliding quickness, Bildad dodged him.

Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he still twitched a little with nervous agitation. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."
"Captain Peleg," said I, "I have a friend who wants to sign on too — shall I bring him down tomorrow?"
"Of course," said Peleg. "Bring him along and we'll have a look at him."
"What lay does he want?" groaned Bildad, glancing up from the book in which he had again buried himself.
"Oh, never mind about that, Bildad," said Peleg. "Has he ever whaled?" turning to me.
"Killed more whales than I can count, Captain Peleg."
"Well, bring him along then."
And after signing the papers, off I went, fully confident that I had done a good morning's work and that the Pequod was the very ship Yojo had chosen to carry Queequeg and me around the Cape.

But I hadn't gone far before it struck me that the captain I was to sail with still remained unseen. In many cases, a whale ship will be completely fitted out and take on her entire crew before the captain shows up to take command. Sometimes these voyages last so long, and the time ashore between them is so short, that if the captain has a family or any pressing personal matters, he doesn't bother much with his ship in port but leaves everything to the owners until she's ready for sea. Still, it's always wise to have a look at him before irrevocably putting yourself in his hands. Turning back, I found Captain Peleg and asked where Captain Ahab might be.
"And what do you want with Captain Ahab? Everything's fine — you're signed on."
"Yes, but I'd like to see him."

"I don't think you'll be able to right now. I don't know exactly what's the matter with him, but he stays shut up inside his house. He's a sort of sick, and yet he doesn't look it. Actually, he isn't sick — but he isn't well either. Anyway, young man, he won't always see even me, so I don't suppose he'll see you. He's a strange man, Captain Ahab — so some think — but a good one. Oh, you'll like him well enough, no fear. He's a grand, ungodly, god-like man, Captain Ahab. He doesn't talk much, but when he does, you'd better listen. Be warned: Ahab is above the common run. He's been in colleges as well as among cannibals. He's faced deeper wonders than the waves and driven his fiery lance into mightier, stranger enemies than whales. His lance! The keenest and truest that ever came from all our island! Oh, he's not Captain Bildad, no, and he's not Captain Peleg. He's Ahab, boy. And Ahab of old, as you know, was a crowned king!"
"And a very wicked one. When that evil king was killed, the dogs licked his blood, did they not?"

"Come here — closer, closer," said Peleg, with a look in his eye that nearly startled me. "Listen, lad. Never say that aboard the Pequod. Never say it anywhere. Captain Ahab did not name himself. It was a foolish, ignorant whim of his crazy, widowed mother, who died when he was only a year old. And yet the old woman Tistig, at Gay Head, said the name would somehow prove prophetic. Other fools may tell you the same. I want to warn you — it's a lie. I know Captain Ahab well. I've sailed with him as mate, years ago. I know what he is — a good man. Not a pious, good man like Bildad, but a swearing good man — something like me — only there's a good deal more of him. I'll admit he was never very cheerful. And I know that on the way home last voyage, he was a little out of his mind for a while. But that was the sharp, shooting pains in his bleeding stump — anyone could see that. I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg on the last voyage to that accursed whale, he's been moody — desperately moody, and savage sometimes. But that will pass. And once and for all, let me tell you and assure you, young man: it's better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one. So goodbye — and don't wrong Captain Ahab just because he happens to have a wicked name. Besides, my boy, he has a wife — married not three voyages ago — a sweet, patient girl. Think about that. By that sweet girl, the old man has a child. Can you really believe there's any utter, hopeless evil in Ahab? No, no, my lad. Stricken and blasted as he may be, Ahab still has his humanity!"

As I walked away, I was full of thoughts. What had been revealed to me about Captain Ahab filled me with a strange, vague unease. Somehow, I felt both sympathy and sorrow for him, though I couldn't say why — unless it was the cruel loss of his leg. And yet I also felt a strange awe of him, though not exactly awe. I don't know what it was. But I felt it, and it didn't turn me against him, even though I was frustrated by what seemed like mystery surrounding him, as little as I knew of him then. Eventually, though, my thoughts turned in other directions, and for the time being, dark Ahab slipped from my mind.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — The Ramadan
paragraphs: Since Queequeg's Ramadan, or day of Fasting and Humiliation, was to continue all day, I decided not to disturb him until nightfall. I have the greatest respect for everyone's religious practices, no matter how odd they might seem. I couldn't bring myself to look down on even a congregation of ants worshipping a toadstool, or those people in certain parts of the world who, with a degree of servility unmatched anywhere else, bow down before the preserved body of a dead landowner simply because of the enormous property still held and rented in his name.

I say, we good Presbyterian Christians should be charitable about these things. We shouldn't consider ourselves so vastly superior to other people — pagans and whoever else — because of their half-crazy ideas on these subjects. There was Queequeg, certainly holding the most absurd beliefs about Yojo and his Ramadan — but so what? Queequeg thought he knew what he was doing, I suppose. He seemed content, and there I should let him be. All our arguing with him wouldn't help. Let him be, I say, and Heaven have mercy on us all — Presbyterians and Pagans alike — for we are all somehow dreadfully cracked in the head and badly need mending.

Toward evening, when I felt sure all his rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked on the door. No answer. I tried to open it, but it was locked from inside. "Queequeg," I said softly through the keyhole. All silent. "I say, Queequeg! Why don't you answer? It's me — Ishmael." But everything stayed still as before. I started to worry. I had given him plenty of time. I thought he might have had a stroke. I looked through the keyhole, but since the door opened into an odd corner of the room, the view was narrow and useless. I could only see part of the footboard of the bed and a strip of wall, nothing more. I was surprised to see Queequeg's harpoon shaft leaning against the wall — the landlady had taken it from him the previous evening, before we went up to the room. That's strange, I thought. But since the harpoon was there, and he hardly ever went anywhere without it, he must be inside. No question about it.

"Queequeg! — Queequeg!" — still nothing. Something must have happened. A stroke! I tried to force the door open, but it held firm. Running downstairs, I quickly explained my fears to the first person I met — the chambermaid. "Oh my!" she cried. "I thought something must be wrong. I went to make the bed after breakfast and the door was locked. Not a sound from inside, and it's been just as silent ever since. But I thought maybe you'd both gone out and locked your things in for safekeeping. Oh my! — Ma'am! Murder! Mrs. Hussey! A stroke!" And with those cries she ran toward the kitchen, with me right behind her.
Mrs. Hussey soon appeared, with a mustard pot in one hand and a vinegar bottle in the other, having just been pulled away from setting the table and scolding her little kitchen boy.

"The woodshed!" I cried. "Which way to it? Run, for God's sake, and get something to pry open the door — the axe! The axe! He's had a stroke, I'm sure of it!" And saying this, I was rushing back upstairs empty-handed when Mrs. Hussey blocked my way with the mustard pot, the vinegar bottle, and the full authority of her expression.
"What's the matter with you, young man?"
"Get the axe! For God's sake, someone run for the doctor while I pry it open!"

"Look here," said the landlady, quickly putting down the vinegar bottle to free up a hand. "Look here — are you talking about prying open one of my doors?" And with that she grabbed my arm. "What's the matter with you? What's the matter with you, shipmate?"

As calmly and quickly as I could, I explained the situation. Unconsciously pressing the vinegar bottle against one side of her nose, she thought for a moment, then exclaimed, "No! I haven't seen it since I put it there." Running to a small closet under the stairs, she looked inside, came back, and told me Queequeg's harpoon was missing. "He's killed himself," she cried. "It's that poor Stiggs all over again — there goes another bedspread — God pity his poor mother! It'll be the ruin of my house. Does the poor lad have a sister? Where's that girl? — there, Betty, go to Snarles the Painter, and tell him to paint me a sign: 'No suicides permitted here, and no smoking in the parlor.' Might as well kill both birds at once. Kill? The Lord be merciful to his ghost! What's that noise up there? You, young man, stop right there!"
And running up after me, she caught me as I was again trying to force the door open.

"I won't allow it. I won't have my property damaged. Go for the locksmith — there's one about a mile from here. But wait —" putting her hand in her pocket — "here's a key that might fit; let's see." She turned it in the lock. But Queequeg's bolt on the inside was still thrown.

"Have to break it down," I said, and was running back down the hall to get a running start when the landlady grabbed me again, insisting I not break down her property. But I tore free and, with a sudden full-body charge, threw myself against the door.

With a tremendous crash the door flew open, the knob slamming into the wall and sending plaster to the ceiling. And there — good heavens! — there sat Queequeg, perfectly cool and composed, right in the middle of the room, squatting on his heels, holding Yojo on top of his head. He looked neither one way nor the other but sat like a carved statue with barely a sign of life.
"Queequeg," I said, going up to him, "Queequeg, what's the matter with you?"
"He hasn't been sitting like that all day, has he?" said the landlady.

But no matter what we said, we couldn't drag a single word out of him. I almost felt like pushing him over just to change his position, which was almost unbearable to look at — so painfully and unnaturally stiff. Especially since, in all likelihood, he had been sitting that way for eight or ten hours, going without his regular meals the whole time.
"Mrs. Hussey," said I, "he's alive, at any rate. So leave us, please, and I'll deal with this strange business myself."

Closing the door on the landlady, I tried to get Queequeg to sit in a chair, but it was useless. There he sat. Despite all my polite efforts and coaxing, he wouldn't budge an inch, say a single word, look at me, or show the slightest awareness that I was there.

I wonder, I thought, if this could be part of his Ramadan. Do they fast while squatting like this on his native island? It must be so. Yes, it's part of his religion, I suppose. Well, let him be. He'll get up sooner or later. It can't last forever, thank God. And his Ramadan only comes once a year — and I don't think it's very punctual even then.

I went down to supper. After sitting a long time listening to the rambling stories of some sailors who had just come from a "plum-pudding voyage," as they called it — meaning a short whaling trip in a schooner or brig, limited to waters north of the equator in the Atlantic Ocean — after listening to these plum-puddingers until nearly eleven o'clock, I went upstairs to bed, feeling quite sure by then that Queequeg must have finished his Ramadan. But no — there he was, exactly where I had left him. He hadn't moved an inch. I started getting annoyed with him. It seemed so utterly senseless and insane to sit there all day and half the night on his heels in a cold room, holding a piece of wood on his head.
"For heaven's sake, Queequeg, get up and move around. Get up and have some supper. You'll starve. You'll kill yourself, Queequeg." But not a word did he reply.

Giving up on him, I decided to go to bed and sleep. No doubt he would follow before long. But before turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket and threw it over him, since it promised to be a very cold night and he had nothing but his ordinary light jacket on. For some time, no matter what I did, I couldn't fall asleep. I had blown out the candle, and the mere thought of Queequeg — not four feet away — sitting in that miserable position, completely alone in the cold and dark — it made me truly wretched. Think of it: sleeping all night in the same room with a wide-awake pagan squatting in this dreary, inexplicable Ramadan!

But somehow I drifted off at last and knew nothing more until daybreak. Looking over the side of the bed, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been bolted to the floor. But as soon as the first rays of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and creaking joints but a cheerful face. He limped over to where I lay, pressed his forehead against mine, and said his Ramadan was over.

Now, as I mentioned before, I have no objection to anyone's religion, whatever it may be, as long as that person doesn't kill or insult anyone else for not sharing it. But when a person's religion becomes truly fanatical — when it's a source of real torment, and when, in short, it makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable place to live — then I think it's high time to take that individual aside and have a serious talk.

And that's exactly what I did with Queequeg. "Queequeg," I said, "get into bed and lie down and listen to me." I then launched into a review, beginning with the rise and development of primitive religions and working my way down to the various religions of today. Throughout, I tried to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and long hours of squatting in cold, cheerless rooms were complete nonsense — bad for the health, useless for the soul, and contrary to the basic laws of hygiene and common sense. I told him that since he was in other respects such an extremely sensible and wise person, it pained me — deeply pained me — to see him being so foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, I argued, fasting weakens the body, which weakens the spirit, and all thoughts born of fasting are necessarily half-starved. This is why most sickly religious people hold such gloomy ideas about the afterlife. In a word, Queequeg, I said, getting somewhat off track: hell is an idea first born from an undigested apple dumpling, and has been perpetuated ever since through the hereditary indigestion caused by Ramadans.

I then asked Queequeg whether he himself was ever troubled with indigestion, putting the question very plainly so he could understand. He said no — except on one memorable occasion. It was after a great feast given by his father, the king, celebrating a great battle in which fifty of the enemy had been killed by about two in the afternoon and all cooked and eaten that very evening.

"No more, Queequeg," I said, shuddering. "That will do." I knew what he was implying without him spelling it out.
