I had met a sailor who had visited that very island, and he told me that when a great battle was won there, the custom was to barbecue all the slain in the victor's yard or garden. Then, one by one, they were placed on great wooden platters, garnished around like a pilaf with breadfruit and coconuts, and with parsley in their mouths, were sent round with the victor's compliments to all his friends — just as though these gifts were so many Christmas turkeys.

In the end, I don't think my remarks about religion made much of an impression on Queequeg. In the first place, he seemed somewhat deaf to that particular subject, unless it was approached from his own point of view. In the second place, he didn't understand more than a third of what I said, no matter how simply I put it. And finally, he no doubt believed he knew a good deal more about true religion than I did. He looked at me with a sort of condescending pity and compassion, as though he thought it a great shame that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to proper pagan devotion.

At last we got up and dressed. Queequeg ate a tremendously hearty breakfast of chowders of every kind, making sure the landlady wouldn't profit too much from his Ramadan. Then we headed out to board the Pequod, strolling along and picking our teeth with halibut bones.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — His Mark
paragraphs: As we walked down the wharf toward the ship, Queequeg carrying his harpoon, Captain Peleg loudly called out to us from his wigwam in his gruff voice. He said he hadn't realized my friend was a cannibal, and he didn't allow any cannibals on board unless they could produce their papers first.
"What do you mean by that, Captain Peleg?" said I, jumping up onto the ship's rail and leaving my companion standing on the wharf.
"I mean," he replied, "he has to show his papers."

"Yes," said Captain Bildad in his hollow voice, poking his head out from behind Peleg's in the wigwam. "He must prove he's been converted. Son of darkness," he added, turning to Queequeg, "are you currently in communion with any Christian church?"
"Why," said I, "he's a member of the First Congregational Church." I should mention that many tattooed islanders who sail on Nantucket ships eventually end up joining the local churches.

"First Congregational Church!" cried Bildad. "What! The one that meets in Deacon Deuteronomy Coleman's meeting house?" And saying this, he took out his spectacles, wiped them with his big yellow handkerchief, put them on very carefully, came out of the wigwam, and, leaning stiffly over the rail, took a good long look at Queequeg.
"How long has he been a member?" he then said, turning to me. "Not very long, I'd guess, young man."
"No," said Peleg, "and he hasn't been properly baptized either, or it would have washed some of that devil's blue off his face."
"Is that so?" cried Bildad. "Is this Philistine really a member of Deacon Deuteronomy's congregation? I never saw him there, and I pass it every Sunday."
"I don't know anything about Deacon Deuteronomy or his meeting," said I. "All I know is that Queequeg here is a born member of the First Congregational Church. He's a deacon himself, Queequeg is."
"Young man," said Bildad sternly, "thou art playing games with me — explain thyself, thou young heathen. What church dost thou mean? Answer me."

Pressed hard like this, I replied: "I mean, sir, the same ancient universal Church to which you and I, and Captain Peleg there, and Queequeg here, and all of us — every mother's son and soul of us — belong. The great and everlasting First Congregation of this whole worshipping world. We all belong to that. Some of us just hold some odd notions that don't touch the grand belief. In that, we all join hands."

"Splice — you mean splice hands," cried Peleg, coming closer. "Young man, you'd better sign on as a missionary instead of a common sailor. I never heard a better sermon. Deacon Deuteronomy — why, Father Mapple himself couldn't beat it, and he's considered something. Come aboard, come aboard — never mind about the papers. I say, tell Quohog there — what do you call him? Tell Quohog to step along. By the great anchor, what a harpoon he's got there! Looks like good steel, and he handles it just right. I say, Quohog, or whatever your name is, have you ever stood in the bow of a whale-boat? Have you ever struck a whale?"

Without saying a word, Queequeg, in his wild way, jumped up onto the ship's rail, from there into the bow of one of the whale-boats hanging alongside, and then, bracing his left knee and balancing his harpoon, cried out something like this:

"Cap'ain, you see that little drop of tar on the water there? You see it? Well, suppose that's a whale's eye. Well, then!" And taking careful aim, he hurled the iron right over old Bildad's broad brim, clean across the ship's decks, and struck the glistening tar spot out of sight.
"Now," said Queequeg, calmly hauling in the line, "suppose that whale eye. Well, then — that whale dead."

"Quick, Bildad," said Peleg, his partner, who had retreated toward the cabin entrance, shaken by how close the flying harpoon had come. "Quick, I say, Bildad — get the ship's papers. We need Hedgehog there — I mean Quohog — in one of our boats. Listen, Quohog, we'll give you the ninetieth lay, and that's more than any harpooner out of Nantucket has ever been given."
So down we went into the cabin, and to my great joy, Queequeg was soon enrolled in the same ship's company as me.

When all the formalities were done and Peleg had everything ready for signing, he turned to me and said, "I guess Quohog there doesn't know how to write, does he? I say, Quohog — blast you! Do you sign your name or make your mark?"

But Queequeg, who had taken part in similar ceremonies two or three times before, looked not at all embarrassed. Taking the offered pen, he copied onto the paper, in the proper place, an exact replica of a strange round figure tattooed on his arm. So, thanks to Captain Peleg's stubborn error with his name, it looked something like this:
Quohog. his X mark.

Meanwhile, Captain Bildad sat earnestly studying Queequeg. At last he rose solemnly, fumbled in the huge pockets of his broad-skirted drab coat, and pulled out a bundle of religious pamphlets. Selecting one titled "The Latter Day Coming; or No Time to Lose," he placed it in Queequeg's hands. Then, grasping both Queequeg's hands and the booklet in his own, he looked earnestly into his eyes and said, "Son of darkness, I must do my duty by thee. I am part owner of this ship and feel responsible for the souls of all its crew. If thou still clingest to thy pagan ways, which I sadly fear, I beg thee — do not remain forever a servant of wickedness. Reject the idol Baal and the hideous dragon. Turn from the wrath to come. Watch thyself, I say. Oh, goodness gracious — steer clear of the fiery pit!"
Something of the salt sea still lingered in old Bildad's speech, oddly mixed with scriptural and domestic phrases.

"Hold on there, hold on, Bildad — stop ruining our harpooner," cried Peleg. "Pious harpooners never make good sailors — it takes the fight out of them. No harpooner is worth a straw who isn't pretty fierce. There was young Nat Swaine, once the bravest boat-header out of all Nantucket and the Vineyard. He joined the church, and nothing good came of it. He got so worried about his wretched soul that he flinched and shied away from whales, afraid of consequences in case he got smashed up and sent to Davy Jones."

"Peleg! Peleg!" said Bildad, raising his eyes and hands. "Thou thyself, just as I have, hast seen many a dangerous time. Thou knowest, Peleg, what it is to fear death. How then canst thou talk in such an ungodly way? Thou art lying to thine own heart, Peleg. Tell me — when this same Pequod lost all three masts in that typhoon off Japan, that same voyage when thou sailed as mate with Captain Ahab — didst thou not think of Death and Judgment then?"

"Hear him! Hear him now!" cried Peleg, marching across the cabin and thrusting his hands deep into his pockets. "Hear him, all of you. Think of that! When every moment we thought the ship would go down! Death and Judgment then? What? With all three masts making such an endless thundering against the hull, and every wave breaking over us fore and aft? Think of Death and Judgment then? No! No time to think about death. Life was what Captain Ahab and I were thinking about — and how to save every hand on board. How to rig emergency masts. How to reach the nearest port. That was what I was thinking about."

Bildad said no more. He buttoned up his coat and walked out on deck, where we followed him. There he stood, very quietly watching some sailmakers who were mending a topsail amidships. Now and then he stooped to pick up a patch or save a length of tarred twine that might otherwise have been wasted.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — The Prophet
paragraphs: "Shipmates, have you signed on to that ship?"

Queequeg and I had just left the Pequod and were strolling away from the water, each lost in his own thoughts, when a stranger spoke these words to us. Pausing in front of us, he aimed his heavy forefinger at the ship in question. He was shabbily dressed in a faded jacket and patched trousers, with a rag of a black handkerchief around his neck. A severe case of smallpox had flowed across his face in every direction and left it like the scarred, ribbed bed of a dried-up stream.
"Have you signed on to her?" he repeated.
"You mean the ship Pequod, I suppose," said I, trying to buy a little more time for a good look at him.
"Yes, the Pequod — that ship there," he said, pulling his whole arm back and then thrusting it straight out, his pointed finger aimed like a bayonet at the vessel.
"Yes," said I, "we've just signed the articles."
"Anything in there about your souls?"
"About what?"

"Oh, maybe you haven't got any," he said quickly. "No matter though. I know plenty of fellows who haven't got any — good luck to them. They're all the better off for it. A soul is a sort of fifth wheel on a wagon."
"What are you going on about, shipmate?" said I.
"He's got enough soul, though, to make up for what's missing in other men," the stranger said abruptly, placing a nervous emphasis on the word he.
"Queequeg," said I, "let's go. This fellow has escaped from somewhere. He's talking about something and somebody we don't know."
"Stop!" cried the stranger. "You spoke true — you haven't seen Old Thunder yet, have you?"
"Who's Old Thunder?" said I, caught again by the unsettling intensity of his manner.
"Captain Ahab."
"What! The captain of our ship, the Pequod?"
"Yes, some of us old sailor types call him that. You haven't seen him yet, have you?"
"No, we haven't. They say he's sick, but getting better, and he'll be fine again before long."
"Fine again before long!" the stranger laughed — a solemn, mocking kind of laugh. "Listen: when Captain Ahab is fine, then this left arm of mine will be fine. Not before."
"What do you know about him?"
"What did they tell you about him? Tell me that!"
"They didn't say much of anything about him. I've only heard he's a good whale-hunter and a good captain to his crew."

"That's true — both true enough. But you'd better jump when he gives an order. Obey and complain — complain and obey — that's how it works with Captain Ahab. But nothing about what happened to him off Cape Horn, long ago, when he lay like a dead man for three days and nights? Nothing about that deadly fight with the Spaniard in front of the altar in Santa? Heard nothing about that, eh? Nothing about the silver cup he spat into? And nothing about losing his leg last voyage, just as was prophesied? Didn't you hear a word about any of that and more? No, I don't think you did — how could you? Who knows about it? Not all of Nantucket, I expect. But anyhow, maybe you've heard about the leg and how he lost it. Yes, you have heard about that, I'm sure. Oh yes, that everyone knows — almost. I mean they know he's got only one leg, and that a sperm whale took the other."

"My friend," said I, "I have no idea what all this rambling of yours is about, and I don't much care. It seems to me you must be a little damaged in the head. But if you're talking about Captain Ahab of that ship there, the Pequod, then let me tell you — I know all about the loss of his leg."
"All about it, eh? Sure you do? All?"
"Pretty sure."

With finger pointed and eye fixed on the Pequod, the beggar-like stranger stood a moment, as if in a troubled daydream. Then, starting slightly, he turned and said: "So you've signed on, have you? Names down on the papers? Well, well, what's signed is signed. And what's to be will be — and then again, maybe it won't be after all. Anyway, it's all fixed and arranged already. Some sailors or other have to go with him, I suppose — might as well be you as anyone. God pity them! Good morning to you, shipmates, morning. The heavens bless you. I'm sorry I stopped you."
"Look here, friend," said I, "if you have something important to tell us, out with it. But if you're just trying to trick us, you've picked the wrong men. That's all I have to say."

"And well said — I like hearing a man speak up like that. You're just the right sort for him — exactly the type. Good morning, shipmates, morning! Oh! And when you get there, tell them I've decided not to be one of the crew."
"Ah, my friend, you can't fool us that way — you can't fool us. It's the easiest thing in the world for a man to act as though he carries a great secret."
"Good morning, shipmates, morning."
"Morning it is," said I. "Come along, Queequeg, let's leave this crazy man. But stop — tell me your name, will you?"
"Elijah."

Elijah! I thought. And we walked away, both commenting in our own way on this ragged old sailor, and agreed he was nothing but a fraud trying to scare us. But we hadn't gone a hundred yards when, turning a corner and glancing back, who should I see but Elijah following us at a distance. The sight struck me so forcefully that I said nothing to Queequeg about it. I just walked on with my companion, wanting to see if the stranger would turn the same corner we did. He did. And then it seemed he was following us, though for what purpose I couldn't imagine. This, combined with his vague, half-hinting, half-revealing way of talking, stirred up all kinds of shadowy suspicions in me — all connected with the Pequod, and Captain Ahab, and his lost leg, and the Cape Horn incident, and the silver cup, and what Captain Peleg had said about him the day before, and the prediction of the old woman Tistig, and the voyage we had committed ourselves to, and a hundred other dark things.

I decided to find out for certain whether this ragged Elijah was truly following us. Queequeg and I crossed to the other side of the street and retraced our steps. But Elijah walked straight past without seeming to notice us. This was a relief, and once more — and finally, as it seemed to me — I decided in my heart that he was nothing but a fraud.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — All Astir
paragraphs: A day or two passed, and there was great activity aboard the Pequod. Old sails were being mended, new sails were coming on board, along with bolts of canvas and coils of rigging. Everything indicated that the ship's preparations were hurrying to a close. Captain Peleg seldom or never went ashore, but sat in his wigwam keeping a sharp eye on the crew. Bildad handled all the purchasing and provisioning at the shops. And the men working in the hold and up in the rigging kept at it long after dark.

The day after Queequeg signed the articles, word was sent to all the inns where the crew was staying that their sea chests had to be on board before nightfall — there was no telling how soon the ship might sail. So Queequeg and I brought our belongings down, though we planned to sleep ashore until the last possible night. But as usual, they gave very long notice in these cases, and the ship didn't actually sail for several more days. No surprise there — there was a great deal to be done, and no telling how many details needed attending to before the Pequod was fully equipped.

Everyone knows what a multitude of things — beds, saucepans, knives and forks, shovels and tongs, napkins, nutcrackers, and whatnot — are indispensable for running a household. It's just the same with whaling, which requires three years of housekeeping on the open ocean, far from any grocers, doctors, bakers, or supply shops. This is true of merchant ships too, but nowhere near to the same extent as with whalers. Besides the great length of the voyage and the many specialized items needed for the whale hunt, and the impossibility of replacing them at the remote harbors these ships usually visit, you have to remember that of all ships, whalers are the most exposed to accidents of every kind — especially the destruction and loss of the very equipment on which the voyage's success depends. Hence the spare boats, spare masts, spare lines, spare harpoons, and spare everything else — everything, that is, except a spare captain and a duplicate ship.

By the time we arrived at the island, most of the Pequod's heavy stores had already been loaded — her beef, bread, water, fuel, iron hoops, and barrel staves. But as I mentioned, there was a constant stream of odds and ends, both large and small, being carried on board.

Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once she was properly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for someone's aching back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a true sister of mercy, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a tidy sum of carefully saved dollars.

But it was startling to see this kind-hearted Quaker woman come aboard on the last day carrying a long oil ladle in one hand and an even longer whaling lance in the other. Neither Bildad nor Captain Peleg held back either. Bildad carried a long checklist of needed supplies, and at every delivery, he made a mark next to that item on his list. Every now and then, Peleg hobbled out of his whalebone den, roaring at the men down the hatchways, roaring up at the riggers on the masthead, and then concluded by roaring back into his wigwam.

During these days of preparation, Queequeg and I often visited the ship, and each time I asked about Captain Ahab — how he was and when he planned to come aboard. They always answered that he was getting better and better and was expected any day. In the meantime, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, could handle everything needed to ready the vessel. If I had been truly honest with myself, I would have seen plainly that I only half liked the idea of being committed to such a long voyage without once laying eyes on the man who would be its absolute ruler the moment the ship reached open sea. But when a man suspects something is wrong and is already caught up in the matter, he tends to bury his own suspicions, even from himself. And that's exactly what I did. I said nothing and tried to think nothing.
At last the word came that the ship would definitely sail the next day. So the following morning, Queequeg and I got a very early start.

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Going Aboard
paragraphs: It was nearly six o'clock, but only a gray, imperfect, misty dawn when we approached the wharf.
"There are some sailors running ahead there, if I'm seeing right," said I to Queequeg. "Those can't be shadows. She must be leaving by sunrise, I think. Come on!"

"Stop!" cried a voice. Its owner came up close behind us, laid a hand on both our shoulders, and then pushed himself between us. Stooping forward slightly in the uncertain twilight, he peered strangely from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.
"Going aboard?"
"Hands off, will you," said I.
"Look here," said Queequeg, shaking himself free, "go away!"
"Not going aboard, then?"
"Yes, we are," said I, "but what business is that of yours? Do you know, Mr. Elijah, that I consider you rather rude?"
"No, no, no — I wasn't aware of that," said Elijah, slowly looking from me to Queequeg and back with the strangest glances.
"Elijah," said I, "you would do my friend and me a favor by going away. We're heading to the Indian and Pacific Oceans and would prefer not to be delayed."
"Are you, are you? Coming back before breakfast?"
"He's crazy, Queequeg," said I. "Come on."
"Hello there!" cried Elijah, calling after us when we had gone a few steps.
"Ignore him," said I. "Queequeg, come on."
But he crept up to us again and, suddenly clapping his hand on my shoulder, said, "Did you see anything that looked like men heading toward that ship a little while ago?"
Struck by this straightforward, matter-of-fact question, I answered, "Yes, I thought I saw four or five men, but it was too dim to be sure."
"Very dim, very dim," said Elijah. "Morning to you."
Once more we left him behind. But once more he came softly after us, and touching my shoulder again, said, "See if you can find them now, will you?"
"Find who?"

"Morning to you! Morning to you!" he called back, moving off again. "Oh! I was going to warn you against — but never mind, never mind — it's all one, all in the family too. Sharp frost this morning, isn't it? Goodbye to you. Won't be seeing you again very soon, I guess — unless it's before the Grand Jury." And with those wild words he finally departed, leaving me for the moment in no small amazement at his frantic boldness.

At last, stepping aboard the Pequod, we found everything in deep quiet. Not a soul was moving. The cabin entrance was locked from inside. The hatches were all closed and piled with coils of rigging. Going forward to the forecastle, we found the scuttle slide open. Seeing a light, we went down and found only an old rigger there, wrapped in a tattered jacket. He was stretched out full length across two sea chests, face down, his head buried in his folded arms. The deepest sleep had taken hold of him.

"Those sailors we saw, Queequeg — where could they have gone?" said I, looking doubtfully at the sleeper. But it seemed that Queequeg hadn't noticed what I was referring to when we were on the wharf. I would have thought I was seeing things, if not for Elijah's otherwise inexplicable question. But I pushed the thought aside. Looking again at the sleeper, I jokingly suggested to Queequeg that perhaps we should sit up with the body, and told him to make himself comfortable. He put his hand on the sleeper's rear end, as if testing whether it was soft enough, and then, without further hesitation, sat right down on it.
"Good Lord! Queequeg, don't sit there," said I.
"Oh! Very good seat," said Queequeg. "My country way. Won't hurt him face."

"Face!" said I. "You call that his face? A very friendly-looking face, then. But listen to how hard he's breathing — he's heaving up and down. Get off, Queequeg, you're heavy. You're crushing the poor man's face. Get off, Queequeg! Look, he'll throw you off any second. I'm amazed he doesn't wake up."

Queequeg moved himself just past the sleeper's head and lit his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We passed the pipe back and forth over the sleeper between us. Meanwhile, when I questioned him in his broken way, Queequeg explained that in his land, due to the complete lack of benches and sofas, the king, chiefs, and important people had the custom of fattening some of the lower classes to use as furniture. To furnish a house comfortably, you only had to buy eight or ten lazy fellows and scatter them around the rooms. Besides, they were very convenient on outings — much better than those garden chairs that fold into walking sticks. On occasion, a chief would simply call his attendant and order him to make himself into a bench under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy spot.
While telling these stories, every time Queequeg took the tomahawk from me, he flourished the hatchet end of it over the sleeper's head.
"What's that for, Queequeg?"
"Very easy, kill him. Oh! Very easy!"

He was going on with some wild memories about his tomahawk-pipe, which had apparently both brained his enemies and soothed his soul, when we were suddenly drawn to the sleeping rigger. The thick smoke had completely filled the cramped space and was starting to affect him. He breathed with a sort of muffled sound, then seemed bothered in his nose, then rolled over once or twice, then sat up and rubbed his eyes.
"Hey there!" he finally wheezed. "Who are you smokers?"
"Signed-on crew," I answered. "When does she sail?"
"Oh, you're going on her, are you? She sails today. The captain came aboard last night."
"What captain — Ahab?"
"Who else?"
I was about to ask him more questions about Ahab when we heard noise on deck.

"Hey! Starbuck's up and about," said the rigger. "He's a sharp chief mate, that one — good man and religious. But he's fully awake now, so I've got to get to work." And with that he went up on deck, and we followed.

It was now clear sunrise. Soon the crew came aboard in twos and threes. The riggers got to work. The mates were busy giving orders. And several people from shore were bringing various last things on board. Meanwhile, Captain Ahab remained invisibly shut away inside his cabin.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — Merry Christmas
paragraphs: At length, toward noon, after the ship's riggers were finally dismissed, and after the Pequod had been hauled out from the wharf, and after the ever-thoughtful Charity had come out in a whale-boat with her last gifts — a nightcap for Stubb, the second mate and her brother-in-law, and a spare Bible for the steward — after all this, the two captains, Peleg and Bildad, emerged from the cabin. Turning to the chief mate, Peleg said:
"Now, Mr. Starbuck, are you sure everything is ready? Captain Ahab is all set — just spoke to him — nothing more to get from shore, eh? Well, call all hands, then. Gather them aft here — blast them!"
"No need for profane words, however great the hurry, Peleg," said Bildad. "But off with you, friend Starbuck, and carry out our orders."

How about that! Here at the very moment of departure, Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad were running the show on the quarter-deck, just as if they were going to be the joint commanders at sea as well as in port. As for Captain Ahab, there was still no sign of him. They said he was in the cabin. But the idea was that his presence wasn't at all necessary for getting the ship underway and steering her out to sea. That was really the pilot's job, and since he hadn't fully recovered — so they said — Captain Ahab stayed below. All of this seemed natural enough. In the merchant service, many captains never show themselves on deck for some time after the anchor is raised, but stay at the cabin table having a farewell party with their shore friends before those friends leave the ship with the pilot.
But there wasn't much time to think it over, because Captain Peleg was now fully energized. He seemed to do most of the talking and commanding, not Bildad.
"Get back here, you sons of bachelors!" he cried, as the sailors lingered at the mainmast. "Mr. Starbuck, drive them aft."

"Strike the tent!" was the next order. As I mentioned before, this whalebone shelter was only set up in port. Aboard the Pequod, for thirty years, the order to strike the tent was well known to be the step right before raising the anchor.
"Man the capstan! Blood and thunder — jump!" was the next command, and the crew sprang for the handspikes.

Now, when getting underway, the pilot usually stations himself at the front of the ship. And there was Bildad, who — along with Peleg, you should know — was one of the port's licensed pilots in addition to his other roles. He was suspected of having got himself licensed just to save the Nantucket pilot fee for every ship he had a stake in, since he never piloted any other vessel. Bildad, I say, could now be seen looking over the bow for the approaching anchor, and at intervals singing what sounded like a dismal hymn to encourage the men at the windlass. They roared back a chorus about girls in some alley, with hearty enthusiasm. This despite the fact that not three days before, Bildad had declared that no profane songs would be permitted aboard the Pequod, especially while getting underway. And Charity, his sister, had placed a small hymnal in each seaman's berth.

Meanwhile, overseeing the other end of the ship, Captain Peleg cursed and swore at the stern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he'd sink the ship before the anchor could be raised. I involuntarily paused at my handspike and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the dangers we faced in starting a voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself with the thought that pious Bildad might offer some salvation, despite his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, when I felt a sudden sharp jab in my rear. Turning around, I was horrified to see Captain Peleg pulling his boot back from my immediate area. That was my first kick.

"Is that how they heave in the merchant service?" he roared. "Get moving, you blockhead — move and break your backbone! Why don't you all move — move! Quohog! Move, you fellow with the red whiskers! Move, Scotch-cap! Move, green pants! Move, I say, all of you, and spring your eyes out!" And with that, he worked his way along the windlass, freely using his boot here and there, while the unflappable Bildad kept leading off with his hymn. That captain must have had something to drink today, I thought.

At last the anchor was up, the sails were set, and off we glided. It was a short, cold Christmas Day. As the brief northern daylight merged into night, we found ourselves nearly out on the wintry ocean, whose freezing spray coated us in ice like polished armor. The long rows of whale teeth along the bulwarks gleamed in the moonlight. And like the white ivory tusks of some enormous elephant, vast curving icicles hung from the bow.

Gaunt Bildad, as pilot, headed the first watch. And again and again, as the old ship plunged deep into the green seas and sent shivering frost everywhere, and the winds howled, and the rigging sang, his steady voice could be heard:
"Sweet fields beyond the swelling flood, stand dressed in living green. So to the Jews old Canaan stood, while Jordan rolled between."

Never did those sweet words sound more beautiful to me than at that moment. They were full of hope and fulfillment. Despite this frigid winter night on the wild Atlantic, despite my wet feet and even wetter jacket, it seemed to me there were still many pleasant harbors ahead — meadows and glades so eternally green that the grass, springing up untrodden and unwilted, remains fresh at midsummer.
At last we reached such a distance from shore that the two pilots were no longer needed. The sturdy sailboat that had accompanied us came alongside.

It was touching, and not unpleasant, to see how Peleg and Bildad were affected at this moment, especially Captain Bildad. He was reluctant to leave — deeply reluctant to part, for good, from a ship bound on so long and dangerous a voyage, beyond both stormy Capes. A ship in which thousands of his hard-earned dollars were invested. A ship in which an old shipmate sailed as captain — a man almost as old as himself, heading out once more to face all the terrors of the pitiless sea. Reluctant to say goodbye to something so full of personal significance. Poor old Bildad lingered long. He paced the deck anxiously. He ran below to speak one more farewell word in the cabin. He came back on deck and looked windward. He looked toward the wide, endless waters, bounded only by far-off, unseen continents. He looked toward the land. He looked up. He looked right and left. He looked everywhere and nowhere. And at last, mechanically coiling a rope on its pin, he gripped Peleg's hand hard, and holding up a lantern, stood gazing heroically into his face for a moment, as if to say, "Nevertheless, friend Peleg, I can bear it. Yes, I can."

As for Peleg, he took it more philosophically. But for all his composure, there was a tear glistening in his eye when the lantern came too close. And he, too, kept running from cabin to deck — a word below, then a word with Starbuck, the chief mate.

But at last he turned to his companion with a final sort of look about him. "Captain Bildad — come, old shipmate, we must go. Back the main yard there! Boat ahoy! Stand by to come alongside now! Careful, careful — come, Bildad, old friend — say your last. Good luck to you, Starbuck. Good luck, Mr. Stubb. Good luck, Mr. Flask. Goodbye and good luck to you all — and three years from today, I'll have a hot supper waiting for you in old Nantucket. Hurrah and away!"

"God bless you, and have you in His holy keeping, men," murmured old Bildad, almost incoherently. "I hope you'll have fine weather now, so Captain Ahab may soon be moving among you. A pleasant sun is all he needs, and you'll have plenty of those on the tropical voyage ahead. Be careful in the hunt, you mates. Don't smash the boats needlessly, you harpooners — good white cedar plank has gone up three percent this year. Don't forget your prayers, either. Mr. Starbuck, make sure that cooper doesn't waste the spare staves. Oh! The sail needles are in the green locker! Don't whale it too much on Sundays, men, but don't miss a fair chance either — that's rejecting Heaven's good gifts. Keep an eye on the molasses barrel, Mr. Stubb — I thought it was a little leaky. Be careful with the butter — twenty cents a pound it was, and mind you, if —"
"Come, come, Captain Bildad — stop chattering — away!" And with that, Peleg hurried him over the side, and both dropped into the boat.

Ship and boat parted ways. The cold, damp night breeze blew between them. A screaming gull flew overhead. The two hulls rolled wildly. We gave three heavy-hearted cheers and plunged blindly, like fate, into the lonely Atlantic.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — The Lee Shore
paragraphs: Some chapters back, a man named Bulkington was mentioned — a tall, recently landed sailor encountered at the inn in New Bedford.

When, on that shivering winter's night, the Pequod thrust her vengeful bow into the cold, hostile waves, who should I see standing at the helm but Bulkington! I looked at the man with sympathetic awe and dread. Here was someone who, in the dead of winter, having just returned from a four-year dangerous voyage, could so restlessly push off again for yet another stormy stint at sea. The land seemed to scorch his feet. The most wondrous things are always the ones that cannot be spoken. Deep memories yield no epitaphs. This six-inch chapter is the gravestone — without a stone — of Bulkington. Let me say only that it went with him as with a storm-tossed ship driven helplessly along a lee shore. The port would gladly give shelter. The port is compassionate. In the port there is safety, comfort, a warm hearth, supper, blankets, friends — everything kind to our mortal selves. But in that gale, the port, the land, is the ship's greatest danger. She must refuse all hospitality. One touch of land, even grazing the keel, would make her shudder from stem to stern. With all her might she crowds on sail to get offshore. In doing so, she fights the very winds that would blow her home. She seeks the open, landless sea again — rushing into danger for the sake of refuge. Her only friend is her bitterest enemy!

Do you understand now, Bulkington? Do you catch a glimpse of that unbearable truth — that all deep, earnest thinking is nothing but the brave effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea, while the wildest winds of heaven and earth conspire to cast her on the treacherous, enslaving shore?

But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and infinite as God — it is better to die in that howling infinity than to be shamefully smashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who, worm-like, would crawl cringing to land! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Stand firm, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up leaps your immortality!

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — The Advocate
paragraphs: Since Queequeg and I are now properly launched in this business of whaling, and since whaling has somehow come to be seen by people on land as a rather unpoetic and disreputable trade, I am anxious to convince you landlubbers of the injustice done to us whale hunters.

First, it may seem unnecessary to establish the fact that, among the general public, whaling is not considered on the same level as the so-called liberal professions. If a stranger were introduced into any mixed gathering of city society, it would hardly raise the general opinion of his merits to present him as a harpooner. And if, in imitation of naval officers, he were to add the letters S.W.F. (Sperm Whale Fishery) after his name on his business card, that would be considered extremely presumptuous and ridiculous.

No doubt one main reason the world refuses to honor us whalemen is this: people think that our occupation amounts to a butchering sort of business, and that when we're actively at work, we're surrounded by filth and gore. Butchers we are — that's true. But butchers, too, and butchers of the bloodiest sort, have been all the military commanders whom the world loves to honor. And as for the alleged uncleanliness of our business, you'll soon learn certain facts generally unknown which will place the sperm whale ship among the cleanest operations on this tidy earth. But even granting the charge to be true — what messy, slippery decks of a whale ship can compare with the unspeakable carnage of those battlefields from which so many soldiers return to drink in the applause of ladies? And if the idea of danger so greatly enhances the popular admiration of the soldier's profession, let me assure you that many a veteran who has bravely marched toward a cannon battery would quickly turn and run at the sight of a sperm whale's vast tail churning the air above his head. For what are the dangers men can understand compared with the intertwined terrors and wonders of God!

But though the world looks down on us whale hunters, it unknowingly pays us the deepest tribute — indeed, an overwhelming devotion! For almost all the candles, lamps, and tapers that burn around the globe burn, like offerings before so many shrines, to our glory!
But look at this from other angles. Weigh it on every scale. See what we whalemen are and have been.

Why did the Dutch in De Witt's time have admirals of their whaling fleets? Why did Louis XVI of France personally fund whaling ships from Dunkirk, and politely invite a couple dozen families from our own island of Nantucket to that town? Why did Britain, between 1750 and 1788, pay its whalemen over one million pounds in bounties? And finally, how is it that American whalemen now outnumber all the other whalemen in the world combined, sailing a fleet of over seven hundred vessels, manned by eighteen thousand men, spending four million dollars a year, with ships worth twenty million dollars at the time of sailing, and importing a well-harvested seven million dollars into our harbors annually? How do you explain all this, if there isn't something mighty in whaling?
But that's only half of it. Look again.

I assert freely that the most worldly philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has had more powerful impact on the entire world, taken as a whole, than the grand business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so endlessly significant in their consequences, that whaling may well be compared to that mythical Egyptian mother who bore children already pregnant in the womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to list them all. A handful will do. For many years the whale ship has been the pioneer in discovering the most remote and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and island chains that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once-savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor of the whale ship, which showed them the way and first served as interpreter with the natives. They may celebrate the heroes of exploring expeditions — your Cooks, your Krusensterns — but I say that scores of unnamed captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great, and greater, than Cook and Krusenstern. In their helpless, empty-handed state, in shark-infested waters and on the beaches of uncharted islands, they battled with unknown dangers and wonders that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not have willingly faced. All the feats that fill three chapters in the old South Sea voyage accounts were just everyday life for our heroic Nantucketers. Adventures that Vancouver devoted whole chapters to, these men didn't consider worth noting in the ship's log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

Until the whale fishery rounded Cape Horn, no trade but colonial, and hardly any contact but colonial, existed between Europe and the long line of wealthy Spanish provinces on the Pacific coast. It was the whaleman who first broke through the jealous trade policies of the Spanish crown regarding those colonies. And if space allowed, it could be clearly shown how the efforts of those whalemen eventually led to the liberation of Peru, Chile, and Bolivia from the yoke of Spain, and the establishment of democracy in those lands.

That great America on the other side of the globe, Australia, was opened to the civilized world by the whaleman. After its first accidental discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long avoided those shores as dangerously savage. But the whale ship went there. The whale ship is the true mother of that now mighty nation. In the early days of the first Australian settlement, the colonists were several times saved from starvation by the generous provisions of whale ships that happened to anchor in their waters. The countless islands of Polynesia tell the same story, owing a commercial debt to the whale ship that cleared the way for missionaries and merchants, and in many cases actually carried the first missionaries to their destinations. If that sealed-off nation, Japan, is ever to become welcoming, it is the whale ship alone that will deserve the credit — for she is already at the doorstep.
But if, despite all this, you still insist that whaling has no noble or artistic associations, then I am ready to break fifty lances with you right here, and knock you off your horse every time.
The whale has no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler, you say.

The whale no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler? Who wrote the first account of our great Leviathan? None other than mighty Job! And who composed the first whaling narrative? No less a prince than Alfred the Great, who with his own royal pen took down the words of Ohthere, the Norwegian whale hunter of those times! And who delivered our glowing praise in Parliament? Edmund Burke!
True enough, you say, but whalemen themselves are lowly types with no noble blood.

No noble blood? They have something better than royal blood. The grandmother of Benjamin Franklin was Mary Morrel, later Mary Folger by marriage, one of the original settlers of Nantucket and ancestor to a long line of Folgers and harpooners — all kin to noble Benjamin — to this day hurling the barbed iron from one side of the world to the other.
Fine, you say, but everyone agrees that whaling somehow just isn't respectable.
Whaling not respectable? Whaling is imperial! By old English law, the whale is officially declared "a royal fish."
Oh, that's only a technicality! The whale itself has never figured in anything grand or imposing.

The whale never figured in anything grand or imposing? In one of the mighty triumphs staged for a Roman general upon his entry into the world's capital, the bones of a whale, brought all the way from the Syrian coast, were the most prominent objects in the cymbal-clashing procession.
See later chapters for more on this subject.
All right, since you bring it up. But say what you will, there's no real dignity in whaling.

No dignity in whaling? The very heavens proclaim the dignity of our calling. Cetus is a constellation in the southern sky! Enough said! Bow your head before the Czar, but take off your hat to Queequeg! Enough! I know a man who has taken three hundred and fifty whales in his lifetime. I consider that man more honorable than the great ancient general who boasted of capturing as many walled cities.

And as for me, if there's any undiscovered quality worth noting in me, if I ever deserve any real reputation in that small but lofty world I might reasonably aspire to, if I ever accomplish anything that a man might rather have done than left undone, if when I die my executors — or more accurately, my creditors — find any valuable manuscripts in my desk, then I give all the honor and glory to whaling. For a whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — Postscript
paragraphs: In defense of the dignity of whaling, I would prefer to offer nothing but proven facts. But when an advocate has marshaled his facts, wouldn't it be wrong to suppress an entirely reasonable speculation that might speak powerfully in support of his case?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious seasoning process is performed on them. There is a ceremonial salt cellar, and possibly a ceremonial spice shaker. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of lettuce being dressed for salad. Could it be that they anoint it to make the interior run smoothly, the way one oils machinery? Much could be said here about the essential dignity of this royal process, because in ordinary life we look down on anyone who oils his hair and obviously smells of it. In truth, a grown man who uses hair oil, unless for medical reasons, probably has a soft spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can't amount to much overall.

But the only question to consider here is this: what kind of oil is used at coronations? It certainly can't be olive oil, or macassar oil, or castor oil, or bear's grease, or train oil, or cod liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its pure, unprocessed state — the finest of all oils?
Think about that, you loyal Britons! We whalemen supply your kings and queens with coronation oil!

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: The chief mate of the Pequod was Starbuck, a native of Nantucket and a Quaker by ancestry. He was a tall, serious man. Though born on an icy coast, he seemed perfectly suited to endure hot climates, his flesh being hard as twice-baked biscuit. Shipped to the tropics, his living blood would not spoil like bottled ale. He must have been born during some time of drought and famine, or on one of those fast days for which his state is famous. Only about thirty dry summers had he seen, and those summers had burned away all excess from his body. But this thinness was no sign of wasting anxiety or physical decline. It was simply the condensation of the man. He was by no means bad-looking — quite the opposite. His clean, tight skin was an excellent fit. Closely wrapped in it, and preserved by inner health and strength, like a restored Egyptian mummy, this Starbuck seemed prepared to endure for ages to come, and to endure always as he was now. Whether in polar snow or tropical sun, like a fine chronometer, his internal vitality was guaranteed to perform well in all climates. Looking into his eyes, you seemed to see the lingering images of a thousand dangers he had calmly faced throughout his life. A steady, reliable man, whose life was mostly a powerful pantomime of action, not a tame chapter of words. Yet for all his tough sobriety and courage, certain qualities in him sometimes threatened to outweigh everything else. Uncommonly conscientious for a seaman, and gifted with a deep natural reverence, the wild, watery loneliness of his life strongly inclined him toward superstition — but the kind that, in some minds, seems to spring from intelligence rather than ignorance. He was attuned to outward omens and inner premonitions. And if these things sometimes bent the welded iron of his soul, his far-off memories of his young wife and child on Cape Cod bent him even further from his natural toughness, opening him to those hidden influences which, in some honest-hearted men, hold back the rush of reckless daring so often displayed by others in the most dangerous moments of the whale hunt. "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." By this he seemed to mean not only that the most reliable courage comes from a fair assessment of the danger, but that a man who feels no fear at all is a far more dangerous companion than a coward.

"That's right," said Stubb, the second mate. "Starbuck there is as careful a man as you'll find anywhere in this business." But we shall soon see what the word "careful" means when used by a man like Stubb, or almost any other whale hunter.

Starbuck was no crusader chasing after danger. For him, courage was not a feeling but a practical tool, always at hand when needed. Besides, he thought that in the whaling business, courage was one of the ship's essential supplies, like her beef and bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. He had no taste for chasing whales after sunset, nor for fighting a whale that fought back too fiercely. For, Starbuck thought, I am here on this dangerous ocean to kill whales for my living, not to be killed by them for theirs. And he knew well that hundreds of men had died that way. What doom had befallen his own father? Where, in the bottomless deep, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

With memories like these, and given to a certain superstition as I've mentioned, the courage that could nevertheless still flourish in Starbuck must indeed have been extraordinary. But it was only natural that a man built this way, with such terrible experiences and memories, would harbor deep within him an element that, under the right circumstances, would break free and burn all his courage away. Brave as he was, it was the kind of bravery, visible in some fearless men, that while holding firm against seas, winds, whales, or any of the ordinary irrational horrors of the world, cannot withstand those more terrible, because more spiritual, terrors that sometimes confront you from the concentrated brow of an enraged and powerful man.

But if the coming story were to reveal any complete collapse of poor Starbuck's courage, I would hardly have the heart to write it. For it is a most sorrowful thing — shocking, even — to expose the failure of valor in a soul. Humanity in the mass may seem hateful — like joint-stock companies and nations — full of knaves, fools, and murderers, with mean and meager faces. But the individual man, in the ideal, is so noble and so radiant, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any shameful blemish in him, all his fellows should rush to throw their finest cloaks. That immaculate dignity we feel deep within ourselves, so far within that it remains intact even when the outer character seems gone — it bleeds with the sharpest anguish at the sight of a man stripped of valor. Not even piety itself, at such a shameful spectacle, can completely silence its accusations against the stars that permitted it. But this grand dignity I speak of is not the dignity of kings and robes. It is that overflowing dignity which needs no ceremonial dress. You shall see it shining in the arm that swings a pickaxe or drives a spike — that democratic dignity which radiates endlessly in all directions from God Himself! The great God absolute! The center and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence — our divine equality!

If, then, I should hereafter ascribe high qualities, though dark ones, to the lowliest sailors, renegades, and castaways — if I should weave tragic graces around them — if even the most sorrowful, perhaps the most degraded among them all, should at times rise to noble heights — if I should touch that workman's arm with some heavenly light — if I should spread a rainbow over his disastrous sunset — then against all critics defend me, thou Spirit of Equality, who has spread one royal mantle of humanity over all my kind! Defend me, thou great democratic God! Thou who didst not deny to the imprisoned convict Bunyan the pale, poetic pearl. Thou who didst clothe the mutilated, impoverished arm of old Cervantes in leaves of the finest gold. Thou who didst pluck Andrew Jackson from the dirt and hurl him onto a warhorse, thundering him higher than a throne! Thou who, in all Thy mighty earthly marches, ever choosest Thy finest champions from the common people — defend me, O God!

chapters.title: Chapter 27 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: Stubb was the second mate, a native of Cape Cod, and therefore known as a Cape Cod man. He was a happy-go-lucky type — neither cowardly nor heroic — taking dangers as they came with an air of indifference. In the most critical moment of the chase, he worked away as calmly as a carpenter hired by the year. Good-humored, easy, and carefree, he ran his whale-boat as if the most deadly encounter were just a dinner party and his crew the invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat as an old stagecoach driver is about the coziness of his seat. When close to the whale, in the very death grip of the fight, he handled his merciless lance coolly and casually, like a whistling handyman tapping his hammer. He would hum his old tunes while fighting flank to flank with the most enraged beast. Long experience had, for Stubb, converted the jaws of death into a comfortable chair. What he thought about death itself, there's no telling. Whether he ever thought about it at all was debatable. But if he did happen to turn his mind that way after a good dinner, no doubt, like a sensible sailor, he took it as a sort of call of the watch — an order to tumble up on deck and get busy with something he'd learn about when he obeyed the order, and not before.

What helped make Stubb such an easygoing, fearless man, so cheerfully carrying the burden of life in a world full of solemn worriers bent double under their loads — what contributed to his almost irreverent good humor — that must have been his pipe. For like his nose, his short black little pipe was one of the permanent features of his face. You'd have sooner expected him to climb out of his bunk without his nose than without his pipe. He kept a whole row of them, pre-loaded, in a rack within easy reach. Whenever he turned in, he smoked them all in succession, lighting each from the last until they were done, then reloading them all for next time. When Stubb got dressed, instead of putting his legs into his trousers first, he put his pipe into his mouth.

I say this constant smoking must have been one cause, at least, of his peculiar temperament. For everyone knows that the earthly air, whether on land or sea, is terribly infected with the nameless miseries of the countless people who have died breathing it. And just as during a cholera outbreak some people walk around pressing camphor-soaked handkerchiefs to their mouths, so too, against all mortal troubles, Stubb's tobacco smoke may have served as a kind of disinfectant.

The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury on Martha's Vineyard. A short, stocky, ruddy young fellow, tremendously combative when it came to whales. He somehow seemed to believe that the great creatures had personally and hereditably insulted him, and therefore it was a point of honor to destroy them whenever he found them. He had so completely lost all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic size and mysterious ways, and was so utterly deaf to any possibility of danger from them, that in his humble opinion a whale was nothing but a species of oversized mouse — or at least a water rat — requiring only a little cleverness and some time and effort to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness made him playful about whales. He hunted them for the fun of it. A three-year voyage around Cape Horn was just a long-running joke. As a carpenter's nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails, so mankind can be similarly divided. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones — made to grip tight and last long. They called him King-Post aboard the Pequod, because in shape he resembled the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers, which, by means of many radiating side timbers, braces the ship against the battering ice.

Now these three mates — Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask — were important men. By universal tradition, they commanded three of the Pequod's boats as headsmen. In the grand battle formation in which Captain Ahab would likely arrange his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were like company captains. Or, armed with their long, keen whaling lances, they were a chosen trio of lancers, just as the harpooners were throwers of javelins.

And since in this famous fishery, each mate or headsman, like a Gothic knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooner — who in certain tight spots provides him with a fresh lance when the first one has been bent or broken in the attack — and since a close friendship generally exists between the two, it is fitting that we record here who the Pequod's harpooners were and which headsman each of them served.
First was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had chosen as his squire. But Queequeg is already known to us.

Next was Tashtego, a pure-blooded Indian from Gay Head, the westernmost point of Martha's Vineyard, where the last remnant of a Native village still exists — a community that has long supplied neighboring Nantucket with many of its boldest harpooners. In the fishery, they usually go by the general name of Gay-Headers. Tashtego's long, lean, jet-black hair, his high cheekbones, and his dark, rounded eyes — large like an Oriental's but with an Antarctic glitter — all proclaimed him the inheritor of the pure blood of those proud warrior-hunters who, bow in hand, had once ranged the ancient forests of the mainland in pursuit of the great New England moose. But no longer tracking wild beasts through the woods, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea. The unerring harpoon of the son had fittingly replaced the infallible arrow of his ancestors. Looking at the tawny muscle of his lithe, snake-like limbs, you could almost credit the superstitions of the early Puritans and half-believe this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was Stubb's squire.

Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black African, with a lion-like stride — a magnificent sight to behold. From his ears hung two golden hoops so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts and joked about tying the topsail ropes to them. In his youth, Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler anchored in a lonely bay on his native coast. Having never been anywhere in the world except Africa, Nantucket, and the remote ports most visited by whalemen — and having lived for years the bold life of the fishery on ships whose owners were unusually particular about their crews — Daggoo retained all his untamed virtues. Standing straight as a giraffe, he moved about the decks in all the majesty of six feet five in his socks. There was a physical humility in looking up at him. A white man standing before him seemed like a white flag come to beg a truce from a fortress. Curiously, this magnificent Daggoo was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's crew, it should be said that today, not one in two of the many thousands of common sailors in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. It's the same with the American whale fishery as with the American army, navy, and merchant marine, and the workers who built the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases native Americans generously supply the brains, while the rest of the world generously supplies the muscle. Many of these whaling sailors come from the Azores, where outbound Nantucket whalers frequently stop to add to their crews from the hardy islanders. Similarly, Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London stop at the Shetland Islands to pick up their full complement and drop them off again on the way home. Why it is, there's no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders on the Pequod — Isolatoes, as I call them, not acknowledging the common continent of mankind, but each living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, joined along one keel, what a crew these Isolatoes made! A delegation from all the islands of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab on the Pequod to present the world's grievances before that bar from which not many of them would ever return. Black little Pip — he never did. Oh no, he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle, you shall soon see him beating his tambourine — a prelude to the eternal time when, summoned to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to join the angels and beat his tambourine in glory. Called a coward here, hailed a hero there!

chapters.title: Chapter 28 — Ahab
paragraphs: For several days after leaving Nantucket, Captain Ahab was nowhere to be seen above decks. The mates relieved each other at their watches as usual, and to all appearances they seemed to be the only commanders of the ship. But sometimes they emerged from the cabin with orders so sudden and absolute that it was clear they were only commanding on someone else's authority. Yes, their supreme lord and ruler was down there, though still unseen by any eyes not permitted to enter the now sacred retreat of the cabin.

Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft for any strange face. My first vague unease about the unknown captain, now intensified by the isolation of the open sea, had become a real anxiety. This was strangely heightened at times by ragged Elijah's wild, incoherent warnings, which kept coming back to me uninvited, with a disturbing power I hadn't imagined possible. I couldn't resist them, even though in calmer moments I was almost ready to laugh at the solemn absurdities of that odd prophet of the wharves. But whatever my apprehension — if I can call it that — whenever I looked around the ship, it seemed completely unjustified. The harpooners and the bulk of the crew were a far more wild, heathen, and mixed lot than any merchant ship company I had known. But I attributed this, rightly, to the fierce uniqueness of the wild Scandinavian trade I had so recklessly joined. What truly calmed my nameless fears and inspired confidence about the voyage was the character of the three chief officers — the mates. Three better, more capable sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American — a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, and a Cape man. Now, since the ship had left harbor on Christmas Day, we had biting polar weather for a while, though always running south away from it. With every degree of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter behind. It was one of those less threatening but still gray and gloomy transitional mornings, when the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping, melancholy speed, that I came up on deck at the call of the forenoon watch. The moment I leveled my gaze toward the stern, a shiver of foreboding ran through me. Reality outran my worst fears: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

There was no sign of ordinary illness about him, nor of recovery from any. He looked like a man cut down from the burning stake, when the fire has consumed all his limbs' outer surface without destroying them or diminishing their compact, aged strength. His entire tall, broad frame seemed made of solid bronze, cast in an unchangeable mold, like Cellini's statue of Perseus. Threading its way out from among his gray hairs and continuing down one side of his tawny, scorched face and neck until it disappeared into his clothing, you could see a slender, rod-like mark, lividly white. It resembled the vertical seam sometimes left in the straight, tall trunk of a great tree when lightning tears down it, peeling and grooving the bark from top to bottom without breaking a single branch, then running off into the ground, leaving the tree still greenly alive but branded. Whether that mark was something he was born with, or the scar of some desperate wound, no one could say for sure. By unspoken agreement, throughout the voyage little or no mention was made of it, especially by the mates. But once an old Gay Head Indian among the crew, Tashtego's elder, superstitiously claimed that Ahab didn't get that mark until he was a full forty years old, and that it came upon him not in any human fight but in an elemental struggle at sea. Yet this wild theory seemed to be contradicted by what a gray old Manxman suggested — an ancient, grave man who, having never before sailed out of Nantucket, had never seen wild Ahab before. Nevertheless, old sea traditions and ancient superstitions credited this Manxman with supernatural powers of perception. So no white sailor seriously argued when he said that if Captain Ahab should ever be peacefully laid out — which might hardly come to pass, he muttered — then whoever performed that last service for the dead would find a birthmark on him running from crown to sole.

So powerfully did Ahab's entire grim appearance affect me, and the livid brand that streaked his face, that for the first few moments I hardly noticed that much of this overpowering grimness was due to the barbaric white leg on which he partly stood. I had heard that this ivory leg had been fashioned at sea from the polished bone of a sperm whale's jaw. "Yes, he lost his mast off Japan," the old Gay Head Indian once said, "but like his dismasted ship, he fitted another mast without going home for it. He has a whole supply of them."

I was struck by the singular posture he maintained. On each side of the Pequod's quarter-deck, close to the mizzen shrouds, an auger hole had been bored about half an inch into the plank. His bone leg was steadied in that hole. One arm raised, holding onto a shroud, Captain Ahab stood erect, staring straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching bow. There was an infinity of iron determination in that gaze — a fixed, fearless, forward dedication that would not surrender. He spoke not a word, nor did his officers say anything to him. Yet by their every small gesture and expression, they clearly showed their uneasy, even painful awareness of being under a troubled master's eye. And more than that — moody, stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face, with all the nameless, regal, overpowering dignity of some mighty grief.

Before long, after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the now sunny deck, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. Nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing the mates were fully capable of handling. So there was little outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab, and nothing to chase away the clouds that piled, layer upon layer, upon his brow — just as storm clouds always choose the tallest peaks to gather on.

Nevertheless, before long, the warm, coaxing charm of the pleasant, holiday weather we sailed into seemed to gradually draw him from his dark mood. For just as when the rosy, dancing girls of April and May come tripping home to the wintry, bitter woods, even the barest, roughest, most thunder-split old oak will at least send out a few green sprouts to welcome such cheerful visitors — so Ahab did, in the end, respond a little to the playful temptations of that gentle air. More than once, he put forth the faint blossom of a look which, in any other man, would soon have flowered into a smile.

chapters.title: Chapter 29 — Enter Ahab; to Him, Stubb
paragraphs: Some days passed. With ice and icebergs all behind us, the Pequod now rolled through the bright spring of the equatorial regions, which at sea reigns almost perpetually on the threshold of the eternal summer of the Tropics. The warm yet cool, clear, ringing, fragrant, overflowing days were like crystal goblets of Persian sherbet, heaped up and flaked with rose-water snow. The starry, stately nights seemed like proud ladies in jeweled velvet, nursing at home in lonely pride the memory of their absent conquering lords, the golden-helmeted suns! For a sleeping man, it was hard to choose between such enchanting days and such seductive nights. But all the magic of that endless fair weather didn't just add new spells to the outer world. It worked inward upon the soul too, especially during the mild evening hours, when memory formed its crystals like clear ice in the noiseless twilight. And all these subtle forces worked more and more on Ahab's nature.

Old age is always wakeful, as if the longer a man is linked with life, the less he wants anything to do with what resembles death. Among sea captains, the old graybeards are the ones who most often leave their beds to visit the night-wrapped deck. So it was with Ahab, except that lately he seemed to live so much in the open air that, truly speaking, his visits were more to the cabin than from it. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter to himself, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow hatch to my grave-dug bed."

So almost every twenty-four hours, when the night watches were set and the men on deck guarded the sleep of those below — when if a rope needed hauling on the forecastle, the sailors dropped it gently to its place rather than flinging it down, for fear of waking their shipmates — when this sort of steady quiet would settle in, the silent helmsman would watch the cabin hatch, and before long the old man would emerge, gripping the iron railing to help his crippled way. There was some touch of human consideration in him. At times like these, he usually avoided pacing the quarter-deck, because to his exhausted mates, trying to sleep within six inches of his ivory heel, the reverberating crack of that bony step would have filled their dreams with the crunching teeth of sharks. But once, his mood ran too deep for such consideration. As he paced the ship with a heavy, lumbering stride from stern to mainmast, Stubb, the old second mate, came up from below. With a certain uneasy, apologetic humor, he suggested that if Captain Ahab was pleased to walk the planks, then no one could argue. But there might be some way of muffling the noise — hinting vaguely and hesitantly about a ball of rope fiber and inserting it around the ivory heel. Ah, Stubb! You didn't know Ahab then.

"Am I a cannonball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that you'd want to pad me like that? But go your way — I forgot. Down to your nightly grave, where the likes of you sleep wrapped in shrouds, getting used to the one you'll fill at last. Down, dog, and to your kennel!"

Startled by this unexpected, suddenly scornful outburst from the old man, Stubb was speechless for a moment. Then he said with agitation, "I'm not used to being spoken to that way, sir. I don't half like it, sir."
"Enough!" Ahab growled through clenched teeth, moving violently away as if to avoid some passionate temptation.
"No, sir, not yet," said Stubb, growing bolder. "I won't meekly accept being called a dog, sir."
"Then be called ten times a donkey, and a mule, and an ass, and get out of my sight, or I'll rid the world of you!"
As he said this, Ahab advanced on him with such overpowering menace in his bearing that Stubb involuntarily backed away.

"I was never treated like that without throwing a punch for it," Stubb muttered as he found himself going down the cabin hatch. "This is very strange. Stop, Stubb. Somehow, I don't quite know whether to go back and hit him, or — what's that? — get down here on my knees and pray for him? Yes, that was the thought rising up in me. But it would be the first time I ever prayed. It's strange. Very strange. And he's strange too. Take him front to back, he's about the strangest old man Stubb ever sailed with. How he flashed at me! His eyes like gunpowder! Is he mad? Either way, there's something on his mind, as sure as there must be something on a deck when it cracks. He doesn't sleep in his bed more than three hours out of twenty-four, and he doesn't really sleep even then. Didn't Dough-Boy, the steward, tell me that every morning the old man's hammock is all rumpled and twisted, sheets kicked to the foot, covers nearly tied in knots, and the pillow frightfully hot, as though a baked brick had been on it? A restless old man! I guess he's got what some folks ashore call a conscience — a kind of torture, they say — worse than a toothache. Well, well, I don't know what it is, but the Lord keep me from catching it. He's full of riddles. I wonder what he goes into the aft hold for every night, as Dough-Boy suspects. What's that about? Who's he meeting in the hold? Isn't that strange? But there's no telling — it's the same old game. Time for a nap. Damn me, it's worth being born just to fall right asleep. And now that I think about it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's sort of strange too. Damn me, but everything's strange when you think about it. But that's against my principles. Don't think — that's my eleventh commandment. And sleep when you can — that's my twelfth. So here goes again. But wait — didn't he call me a dog? Blazes! He called me ten times a donkey, and piled a load of jackasses on top of that! He might as well have kicked me and been done with it. Maybe he did kick me, and I didn't notice — I was so stunned by that brow of his. It flashed like bleached bone. What the devil's wrong with me? I don't feel steady on my legs. Running into that old man has sort of turned me inside out. By the Lord, I must have been dreaming — how? how? how? But the only thing to do is forget it. So back to the hammock, and in the morning I'll see how this damned puzzle looks by daylight."

chapters.title: Chapter 30 — The Pipe
paragraphs: When Stubb had gone, Ahab stood for a while leaning over the bulwarks. Then, as had become his habit lately, he called a sailor on watch and sent him below for his ivory stool and his pipe. Lighting the pipe at the compass lamp and planting the stool on the windward side of the deck, he sat and smoked.

In old Norse times, the thrones of the sea-loving Danish kings were built, according to tradition, from the tusks of the narwhal. How could anyone look at Ahab then, seated on that tripod of bones, without thinking of the royalty it symbolized? For Ahab was a king of the planks, a lord of the sea, and a great ruler of Leviathans.

Some moments passed while thick smoke came from his mouth in quick, constant puffs that blew back into his face. "What's this?" he said at last, pulling the pipe from his mouth. "This smoking no longer soothes me. Oh, my pipe! Things must be going badly for me if your charm is gone! I've been toiling here without realizing it, not taking pleasure — yes, and foolishly smoking to windward all the while, with such nervous, anxious puffs, as if, like the dying whale, my final gasps were the strongest and most troubled. What business do I have with this pipe? This thing is meant for serenity, for sending up mild white vapors among mild white hairs — not among torn iron-gray locks like mine. I'll smoke no more —"

He tossed the still-lit pipe into the sea. The fire hissed in the waves. At the same instant, the ship shot past the bubble the sinking pipe made. With his hat pulled low, Ahab lurched across the planks.

chapters.title: Chapter 31 — Queen Mab
paragraphs: The next morning, Stubb approached Flask.

"What a strange dream, King-Post, I never had anything like it. You know the old man's ivory leg? Well, I dreamed he kicked me with it. And when I tried to kick back, upon my soul, little man, I kicked my own leg right off! And then, suddenly, Ahab turned into a pyramid, and I, like a complete fool, kept kicking at it. But here's what was even stranger, Flask — you know how strange dreams are — through all that rage, I somehow kept thinking to myself that, after all, Ahab's kick wasn't really much of an insult. 'Why,' I thought, 'what's the fuss? It's not a real leg, only a false one.' And there's a huge difference between a kick from a living leg and one from a dead leg. That's what makes a blow from a hand, Flask, fifty times worse than a blow from a cane. It's the living limb that makes the living insult, little man. And the whole time, mind you — while I was stubbing my stupid toes against that cursed pyramid — so ridiculously contradictory was it all — the whole time, I was thinking, 'What's his leg now but a cane — a whalebone cane? Yes,' I thought, 'it was just a playful beating — really just a whaleboning he gave me — not a vulgar kick. Besides,' I thought, 'look at it: the end of it — the foot part — what a tiny point it is. Whereas if a broad-footed farmer kicked me, now there's a great broad insult. But this insult is whittled down to a mere point.' But now comes the best part of the dream, Flask. While I was battering away at the pyramid, a sort of badger-haired old merman with a hump on his back grabs me by the shoulders and spins me around. 'What are you doing?' says he. Lord! I was scared. What a face! But somehow the next moment I was over the fright. 'What am I doing?' says I at last. 'And what business is that of yours, Mr. Humpback? Do you want a kick?' By the lord, Flask, I had no sooner said that than he turned his backside to me, bent over, and pulled up a bunch of seaweed he was wearing — and what do you think I saw? Thunder alive, man, his rear was stuck full of marlinspikes, with the points sticking out! Says I, on second thought, 'I guess I won't kick you, old fellow.' 'Wise Stubb,' said he, 'wise Stubb.'
