And he kept muttering it, sort of chewing his own gums like an old hag. Seeing he wasn't going to stop with his 'wise Stubb, wise Stubb,' I figured I might as well go back to kicking the pyramid. But I'd barely lifted my foot when he roared, 'Stop that kicking!' 'What now, old fellow?' says I. 'Look here,' says he, 'let's think about this insult. Captain Ahab kicked you, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I — 'right here.' 'Very good,' says he. 'He used his ivory leg, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I. 'Well then,' says he, 'wise Stubb, what do you have to complain about? Didn't he kick with real force? It wasn't a common pine leg he kicked with, was it? No, you were kicked by a great man, and with a beautiful ivory leg, Stubb. It's an honor. I consider it an honor. Listen, wise Stubb. In old England the greatest lords consider it a great glory to be slapped by a queen and made knights of the garter. But let it be your boast, Stubb, that you were kicked by old Ahab and made a wise man of. Remember what I say: accept his kicks as honors, and on no account kick back — for you can't help yourself, wise Stubb. Don't you see that pyramid?' With that, he suddenly seemed to swim off into the air. I snored, rolled over — and there I was in my hammock! Now, what do you think of that dream, Flask?"
"I don't know. Seems kind of silly to me, though."

"Maybe. Maybe. But it's made a wise man of me, Flask. Do you see Ahab standing there, looking sideways over the stern? Well, the best thing you can do, Flask, is leave the old man alone. Never speak to him, no matter what he says. Wait! What's that he's shouting? Listen!"
"Masthead, there! Look sharp, all of you! There are whales around here!"
"If you see a white one, scream your lungs out for him!"

"What do you think of that, Flask? Isn't there something a little strange about it? A white whale — did you catch that? Look here — there's something special going on. Be ready for it, Flask. Ahab has something bloody on his mind. But shh — he's coming this way."

chapters.title: Chapter 32 — Cetology
paragraphs: Already we are boldly launched upon the deep. But soon we shall be lost in its shoreless, harborless vastness. Before that happens — before the Pequod's weedy hull rolls alongside the barnacled hulls of whales — it would be wise at the outset to attend to a matter almost essential for a thorough understanding of the many whale-related revelations and references that are to follow.

What I want to put before you is a systematic overview of the whale in his broad categories. Yet this is no easy task. What I am attempting here is nothing less than the classification of chaos. Listen to what the best and most recent authorities have said.
"No branch of Zoology is so confused as that which is called Cetology," says Captain Scoresby, 1820.

"It is not my intention, were it in my power, to inquire into the true method of dividing the cetacea into groups and families. Utter confusion exists among the historians of this animal" (the sperm whale), says Surgeon Beale, 1839.

"Unfitness to pursue our research in the unfathomable waters." "Impenetrable veil covering our knowledge of the cetacea." "A field strewn with thorns." "All these incomplete indications but serve to torture us naturalists."

So speak the great Cuvier, John Hunter, and Lesson — those lights of zoology and anatomy. Nevertheless, though real knowledge is scarce, books are plentiful. And so it is, to some small degree, with cetology, the science of whales. Many men, small and great, old and new, landsmen and seamen, have written about the whale at length or in brief. Let me run over a few: the authors of the Bible; Aristotle; Pliny; Aldrovandi; Sir Thomas Browne; Gesner; Ray; Linnaeus; Rondeletius; Willoughby; Green; Artedi; Sibbald; Brisson; Marten; Lacepede; Bonneterre; Desmarest; Baron Cuvier; Frederick Cuvier; John Hunter; Owen; Scoresby; Beale; Bennett; J. Ross Browne; the author of Miriam Coffin; Olmstead; and the Reverend T. Cheever. But to what useful generalizing purpose all these have written, the extracts cited above will show.

Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw a living whale. And only one of them was an actual professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the specific subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority available. But Scoresby knew nothing and said nothing about the great sperm whale, compared to which the Greenland whale is almost not worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a pretender to the throne of the seas. He is not even close to being the largest of the whales. Yet, because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then mythical or completely unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still prevails everywhere except in a few scientific circles and whaling ports — this usurpation has been total. Check nearly all the whale references in the great poets of the past, and you'll find that the Greenland whale, without a rival, was their monarch of the seas. But the time has finally come for a new proclamation. Hear ye, hear ye, good people all — the Greenland whale is dethroned — the great sperm whale now reigns!

There are only two books in existence that claim to present the living sperm whale and actually succeed to any degree. Those are Beale's and Bennett's. Both authors were surgeons on English South Sea whale ships, and both are accurate, reliable men. The original material about the sperm whale in their volumes is necessarily small, but what there is of it is excellent in quality, though mostly limited to scientific description. As yet, however, the sperm whale — whether scientific or poetic — lives complete in no literature. Far above all other hunted whales, his is an unwritten life.

Now the various species of whales need some sort of popular, comprehensive classification, if only a rough outline for now, to be filled in later by others. Since no better person steps forward, I offer my own humble efforts. I promise nothing complete, because anything human that claims to be complete must, for that very reason, be flawed. I won't attempt detailed anatomical descriptions of the various species — not here, at least — or much description of any kind. My goal is simply to sketch out a system of cetology. I am the architect, not the builder.

But it is a weighty task. No ordinary mail sorter at the Post Office is equal to it. To grope down to the bottom of the sea after these creatures, to have one's hands among the unspeakable foundations, ribs, and very pelvis of the world — this is a fearful thing. Who am I to try to hook this leviathan by the nose! The terrifying challenges in the Book of Job might well unnerve me: "Will he make a covenant with thee? Behold, the hope of him is in vain!" But I have swum through libraries and sailed through oceans. I have handled whales with these very hands. I am serious, and I will try. First, some preliminaries to settle.

First: The uncertain, unsettled state of this science of Cetology is demonstrated right at the door by the fact that in some quarters it is still debated whether a whale is a fish. In his System of Nature, 1776, Linnaeus declares: "I hereby separate the whales from the fish." But from my own knowledge, I know that as recently as 1850, sharks and shad and herring were still found sharing the same seas with whales, in defiance of Linnaeus's decree.

The grounds on which Linnaeus would have banished the whales from the waters are these: "On account of their warm, two-chambered heart, their lungs, their movable eyelids, their hollow ears," and their reproductive and nursing anatomy, and finally, "by the law of nature, justly and deservedly." I submitted all this to my friends Simeon Macey and Charley Coffin, both Nantucketers and my former shipmates, and they agreed that the reasons given were altogether insufficient. Charley bluntly called them nonsense.

Let it be known that, setting aside all argument, I take the good old-fashioned position that the whale is a fish, and I call on holy Jonah to back me up. With this fundamental point settled, the next question is: in what internal way does the whale differ from other fish? Linnaeus has given you the details above. But in brief, they are these: lungs and warm blood, whereas all other fish are lungless and cold-blooded.

Next: how shall we define the whale by his obvious external features, so as to label him unmistakably for all time? To be brief, then: a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. There you have him. However condensed, that definition is the result of careful thought. A walrus spouts much like a whale, but the walrus is not a fish because he is amphibious. The last part of the definition is even more decisive when paired with the first. Almost anyone has noticed that all fish familiar to landlubbers have not a flat but a vertical — that is, an up-and-down — tail. Whereas among spouting fish, the tail, though it may be similarly shaped, always assumes a horizontal position.

By this definition of what a whale is, I do not exclude from the whale brotherhood any sea creature previously identified as a whale by the best-informed Nantucketers. Nor, on the other hand, do I include any fish previously considered to be something else. Hence, all the smaller spouting, horizontal-tailed fish must be included in this plan of Cetology. Now, then, come the grand divisions of the entire whale family.

I am aware that to this day, the fish called Manatees and Dugongs (Pig-fish and Sow-fish to the Coffins of Nantucket) are classified by many naturalists among the whales. But since these pig-fish are a noisy, contemptible lot, mostly lurking in river mouths and feeding on wet hay, and especially since they do not spout, I deny their credentials as whales and have given them their passports to leave the Kingdom of Cetology.
First: according to size, I divide the whales into three primary BOOKS (subdivided into CHAPTERS), which shall include them all, both small and large.
I. THE FOLIO WHALE; II. THE OCTAVO WHALE; III. THE DUODECIMO WHALE.
As the type of the FOLIO I present the Sperm Whale; of the OCTAVO, the Grampus; of the DUODECIMO, the Porpoise.

FOLIOS. Under this heading I include the following chapters: I. The Sperm Whale; II. The Right Whale; III. The Fin-Back Whale; IV. The Humpbacked Whale; V. The Razor Back Whale; VI. The Sulphur Bottom Whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER I (Sperm Whale). — This whale, known vaguely by the old English as the Trumpa whale, the Physeter whale, and the Anvil-Headed whale, is the present Cachalot of the French and the Pottfisch of the Germans. He is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe, the most formidable of all whales to encounter, the most majestic in appearance, and by far the most valuable commercially — being the only creature from which that precious substance, spermaceti, is obtained. All his peculiarities will be discussed at length elsewhere. For now, it is chiefly his name that concerns me. Considered linguistically, it is absurd. Centuries ago, when the sperm whale was almost completely unknown as an individual species, and his oil was only accidentally obtained from stranded specimens, spermaceti was popularly supposed to come from the creature then known in England as the Greenland or Right Whale. The idea was also that this spermaceti was a certain fluid of the Greenland Whale, which the first syllable of the word literally expresses. In those days, spermaceti was extremely rare, used not for light but only as an ointment and medicine. It could only be bought from druggists, the way you might buy an ounce of rhubarb today. When, as I believe, the true nature of spermaceti eventually became known, its original name was kept by the dealers — no doubt to inflate its value with an air of exotic rarity. And so the name must at last have been transferred to the whale from which this spermaceti actually came.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER II (Right Whale). — In one respect this is the most venerable of all whales, being the first to be regularly hunted by man. It produces the substance commonly known as whalebone or baleen, and the oil known as "whale oil," an inferior product commercially. Among fishermen, he goes by all the following names: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. There is considerable confusion about the identity of the species so multiply baptized. What, then, is the whale I include as the second species of my Folios? It is the Great Mysticetus of the English naturalists, the Greenland Whale of the English whalemen, the Baleine Ordinaire of the French whalemen, and the Gronlands Walfish of the Swedes. It is the whale that for more than two centuries has been hunted by the Dutch and English in the Arctic seas, and the whale that American fishermen have long pursued in the Indian Ocean, on the Brazil Banks, on the Northwest Coast, and various other parts of the world designated by them as Right Whale Cruising Grounds.

Some claim to see a difference between the Greenland whale of the English and the right whale of the Americans. But they agree precisely in all their major features, and no one has yet presented a single definitive fact on which to base a real distinction. It is by endless subdivisions based on the most inconclusive differences that some branches of natural history become so repulsively complicated. The right whale will be discussed elsewhere at length, in connection with the sperm whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster known by various names — Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John — seen in almost every sea. This is commonly the whale whose distant spout is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on New York packet ships. In length and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but is less stout in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by interlocking, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often easy to spot — some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear of his back, angular in shape and sharp-pointed. Even when no other part of the creature is visible, this lone fin will sometimes be seen projecting clearly from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and slightly rippled, and this fin stands up casting shadows on the wrinkled surface, the surrounding circle of water somewhat resembles a sundial, with its pointer and wavy hour-lines etched upon it. The Fin-Back is not social. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are misanthropes. Very shy — always solitary — rising unexpectedly to the surface in the most remote and desolate waters. His straight, single, tall spout rises like a misanthropic spear on a barren plain. Gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all human pursuit, this whale seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that fin upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale among a theoretical class called Whalebone Whales — that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone Whales, there appear to be several varieties, most of them poorly known: broad-nosed whales, beaked whales, pike-headed whales, bunched whales, under-jawed whales, and rostrated whales, to give the fishermen's names for a few.

Regarding the name "Whalebone Whales," it is important to note that while such a term is convenient for referring to a certain kind of whale, it is useless to try to classify whales based on their baleen, hump, fin, or teeth, even though those features might seem the most obvious basis for a system. The problem is this: baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth are features distributed randomly among all sorts of whales, with no regard for the nature of their other, more essential characteristics. The sperm whale and the humpback whale both have a hump, but there the resemblance ends. The humpback whale and the Greenland whale both have baleen, but again the resemblance ends. And it's the same with the other features listed above. Among the various species of whales, they form such irregular combinations — or, taken individually, such random occurrences — that they completely defy any orderly system based on them. On this rock every whale-naturalist has wrecked.

But perhaps, you might think, in the whale's internal parts — his anatomy — there we could find the right classification. Not so. What feature of the Greenland whale's anatomy is more striking than his baleen? Yet we've seen that baleen is useless for classification. And if you look inside the various whales, you'll find distinctions a fiftieth as useful to the classifier as the external ones already listed. What remains? Nothing but to take hold of the whales physically, in their full liberal volume, and sort them boldly by size. And this is the bibliographical system I adopt here. It is the only one that can possibly work, for it alone is practical. Let us proceed.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER IV (Humpback). — This whale is often seen off the northern American coast. He has been frequently captured there and towed into harbor. He carries a great hump on his back like a peddler's pack — you might call him the pack-horse whale. In any case, his popular name doesn't sufficiently distinguish him, since the sperm whale also has a hump, though a smaller one. His oil is not very valuable. He has baleen. He is the most playful and lighthearted of all the whales, making more joyful foam and white water than any other.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER V (Razor Back). — Of this whale, little is known but his name. I have seen him at a distance off Cape Horn. Of a retiring nature, he eludes both hunters and scholars. Though no coward, he has never shown any part of himself but his back, which rises in a long, sharp ridge. Let him go. I know little more of him, and neither does anyone else.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER VI (Sulphur Bottom). — Another shy gentleman, with a yellow belly, doubtless acquired by scraping along the ocean floor in some of his deepest dives. He is seldom seen — at least I have never seen him except in the remote southern seas, and always at too great a distance to study his appearance. He is never chased — he would run off with whole warehouses of rope. Amazing things are told about him. Farewell, Sulphur Bottom! I can say nothing more that is true of you, and neither can the oldest Nantucketer.
Thus ends BOOK I (Folio), and now begins BOOK II (Octavo).
OCTAVOES. — These include the whales of middling size, among which we may count: I. The Grampus; II. The Blackfish; III. The Narwhal; IV. The Thrasher; V. The Killer.

Why this book of whales is not called the Quarto is quite obvious. While the whales of this order, though smaller than the Folios, retain a proportionate resemblance to them in shape, the bookbinder's quarto volume does not preserve the shape of the folio, but the octavo does.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER I (Grampus). — Though this fish, whose loud, sonorous breathing has supplied a proverb for landlubbers, is a well-known resident of the deep, he is not popularly classified among whales. But possessing all the grand distinctive features of the whale, most naturalists have recognized him as one. He is moderate octavo size, ranging from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length, with corresponding girth. He swims in herds. He is never regularly hunted, though his oil is considerable in quantity and fairly good for light. Some fishermen regard his appearance as a sign that the great sperm whale is approaching.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER II (Blackfish). — I use the popular fishermen's names for all these fish, as they are generally the best. When any name happens to be vague or misleading, I will say so and suggest another. I do so now with the Blackfish, so called, because blackness is the rule among almost all whales. So call him the Hyena Whale, if you prefer. His voracity is well known, and because the inner angles of his lips curve upward, he wears an everlasting devilish grin on his face. This whale averages sixteen to eighteen feet in length and is found in almost all latitudes. He has a peculiar way of showing his hooked dorsal fin while swimming, which looks something like a Roman nose. When not more profitably employed, sperm whale hunters sometimes capture the Hyena Whale to maintain a supply of cheap oil for domestic use — as some thrifty housekeepers, in the absence of company, burn smelly tallow instead of fragrant wax. Though their blubber is very thin, some of these whales will yield upwards of thirty gallons of oil.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhal), that is, Nostril Whale. — Another curiously named whale, so called I suppose because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a pointed nose. The creature is about sixteen feet long, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is an elongated tusk growing out from the jaw at a slightly downward angle. But it only grows from the left side, which gives its owner a look somewhat like a clumsy left-handed man. What purpose this ivory horn or lance serves is hard to say. It doesn't seem to be used like the blades of the swordfish or billfish, though some sailors tell me the narwhal uses it as a rake for turning over the sea bottom for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer: the narwhal, rising to the surface of the polar sea and finding it covered with ice, thrusts his horn up and breaks through. But you can't prove either theory correct. My own opinion is that, however the narwhal actually uses his one-sided horn, it would certainly be very convenient as a bookmark for reading pamphlets. The narwhal has also been called the Tusked Whale, the Horned Whale, and the Unicorn Whale. He is certainly a curious example of the unicorn idea found in almost every kingdom of nature. From certain old authors I have learned that this sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient times believed to be a great antidote against poison, and preparations of it fetched enormous prices. It was also distilled into smelling salts for fainting ladies, much as deer antlers are made into hartshorn. Originally it was considered a great curiosity in itself. Old accounts tell me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from a voyage, when Queen Elizabeth waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," the old records say, "on bended knee he presented to Her Highness a prodigious long horn of the narwhal, which for a long period hung in Windsor Castle." An Irish author claims that the Earl of Leicester, also on bended knee, presented to Her Highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn variety.

The narwhal has a very picturesque, leopard-like appearance, being milk-white with round and oblong spots of black. His oil is very fine and clear, but there is little of it, and he is seldom hunted. He is mostly found in the Arctic seas.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER IV (Killer). — Of this whale, the Nantucketer knows little with certainty, and the professional naturalist knows nothing at all. From what I have seen of him at a distance, I would say he is about the size of a grampus. He is very savage — a sort of cannibal fish. He sometimes seizes great Folio whales by the lip and hangs there like a leech until the mighty brute is worried to death. The Killer is never hunted. I have never heard what sort of oil he has. His name might be objected to on the grounds of vagueness. For we are all killers, on land and on sea — Napoleons and sharks included.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER V (Thrasher). — This gentleman is famous for his tail, which he uses like a rod for whipping his enemies. He mounts the Folio whale's back and, as he swims, works his passage by flogging him — as some schoolmasters get through the world by a similar method. Even less is known about the Thrasher than the Killer. Both are outlaws, even in the lawless seas.
Thus ends BOOK II (Octavo), and begins BOOK III (Duodecimo).
DUODECIMOS. — These include the smaller whales: I. The Huzza Porpoise. II. The Algerine Porpoise. III. The Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise.

To those who haven't studied the subject, it may seem strange that fish commonly no more than four or five feet long should be ranked among WHALES — a word that always carries an idea of hugeness. But the creatures listed above as Duodecimos are undeniably whales, by my definition of what a whale is: a spouting fish with a horizontal tail.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER I (Huzza Porpoise). — This is the common porpoise found almost everywhere on the globe. The name is my own invention, since there are more than one sort of porpoise and something must be done to tell them apart. I call him this because he always swims in cheerful schools that keep tossing themselves skyward like caps in a Fourth of July crowd. Their appearance is generally greeted with delight by sailors. Full of high spirits, they always come from the breezy waves to windward. They are the lads who always live before the wind. They are considered a lucky omen. If you can't manage three cheers at the sight of these lively fish, then heaven help you — the spirit of joyful fun is not in you. A well-fed, plump Huzza Porpoise will yield about one good gallon of oil. But the fine, delicate fluid extracted from his jaws is extremely valuable and sought after by jewelers and watchmakers. Sailors use it on their whetstones. Porpoise meat is good eating, you know. It may never have occurred to you that a porpoise spouts. Indeed, his spout is so small that it's not easily noticed. But next time you have a chance, watch him — and you'll see the great sperm whale himself in miniature.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER II (Algerine Porpoise). — A pirate. Very savage. He is only found, I think, in the Pacific. He is somewhat larger than the Huzza Porpoise but much the same in general build. Provoke him and he'll take on a shark. I've gone after him many times but have never seen one captured.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER III (Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise). — The largest kind of porpoise, found only in the Pacific as far as is known. His only English name is the one given by fishermen — Right-Whale Porpoise — from the fact that he is mainly found near that great whale. In shape he differs somewhat from the Huzza Porpoise, being less round and stout — indeed, quite trim and gentlemanly in figure. He has no fins on his back (most other porpoises do). He has a lovely tail and sentimental hazel eyes with an Indian look. But his mealy mouth ruins everything. Though his entire back down to his side fins is deep black, a boundary line, sharp as the mark on a ship's hull called the "bright waist," streaks him from stem to stern in two separate colors — black above and white below. The white extends over part of his head and his whole mouth, making him look as if he just got caught raiding a flour bag. A most pitiful and mealy appearance! His oil is much like the common porpoise's.

Beyond the DUODECIMO, this system does not go, since the porpoise is the smallest of the whales. Above, you have all the notable Leviathans. But there is a rabble of uncertain, fleeting, half-mythical whales that I, as an American whaleman, know by reputation but not personally. I will list them by their deck-hand names, since such a list may prove valuable to future researchers who may complete what I have only begun. If any of the following whales should be caught and identified, they can easily be added to this system according to their Folio, Octavo, or Duodecimo size: the Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale; and so on. From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English sources, other lists of uncertain whales could be quoted, blessed with all manner of outlandish names. But I omit them as completely obsolete, and I can't help suspecting them of being mere words — full of whale-like grandeur but signifying nothing.

Finally: it was stated at the outset that this system would not be perfected here and now. You can plainly see that I have kept my word. But I now leave my cetological system standing unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing atop the uncompleted tower. Small structures may be finished by their first builders. Grand ones, true ones, always leave the capstone to posterity. God keep me from ever completing anything. This whole book is but a draft — no, but the draft of a draft. Oh, Time, Strength, Cash, and Patience!

chapters.title: Chapter 33 — The Specksnyder
paragraphs: Concerning the officers of the whale ship, this seems as good a place as any to describe a small domestic peculiarity on board, arising from the existence of the harpooner class of officers — a class unknown, of course, in any other service but the whale fleet.

The great importance attached to the harpooner's profession is shown by the fact that originally, in the old Dutch Fishery two centuries and more ago, command of a whale ship was not entirely in the hands of the person now called the captain. It was divided between him and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally, this word means Fat-Cutter, though in time it came to mean Chief Harpooner. In those days, the captain's authority was limited to navigation and the general management of the vessel, while over the whale-hunting department and everything related to it, the Specksnyder reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch post still exists, but with much reduced authority. At present he ranks simply as senior harpooner and is merely one of the captain's lesser subordinates. Nevertheless, since the success of a whaling voyage largely depends on the harpooners' performance, and since in the American Fishery the harpooner is not only an important officer in the boat but also, under certain circumstances like night watches on a whaling ground, has command of the ship's deck — the grand political principle of the sea demands that he should officially live apart from the common sailors and be distinguished as their professional superior, though they always regard him as their social equal.

Now, the key distinction between officer and ordinary seaman at sea is this: the officer lives aft, the seaman lives forward. Hence, on whale ships and merchant vessels alike, the mates have their quarters with the captain. And on most American whalers, the harpooners are also housed in the aft part of the ship — meaning they eat their meals in the captain's cabin and sleep in a space connected to it.

Though the long duration of a southern whaling voyage (by far the longest of all voyages ever made by man), the peculiar dangers of it, and the shared interest among a crew who all depend not on fixed wages but on common luck, vigilance, bravery, and hard work — though all these things sometimes produce a less rigid discipline than on merchant ships, and though these whalemen may in some cases live together like one big primitive family — for all that, the formal manners of the quarter-deck are seldom seriously relaxed and never entirely abandoned. Indeed, on many Nantucket ships you'll see the captain parading his quarter-deck with a lofty grandeur unmatched in any military navy — demanding nearly as much outward respect as if he wore imperial purple instead of the shabbiest pilot cloth.

And though of all captains, the moody master of the Pequod was the least given to this sort of shallow pretension — though the only obedience he ever demanded was instant and absolute — though he required no man to remove his shoes before stepping on the quarter-deck — and though there were times when, owing to special circumstances that will be described later, he spoke to his crew in unusual terms, whether condescending, threatening, or otherwise — even Captain Ahab was by no means careless about the established forms and customs of the sea.

Nor, perhaps, will it escape notice that behind those forms and customs, he sometimes masked himself, using them for other, more private purposes than they were designed for. That certain tyrannical quality in his mind, which might otherwise have stayed largely hidden, became through those forms an irresistible dictatorship made flesh. For no matter how great a man's intellectual superiority, it can never achieve practical, real-world dominance over other men without the help of some kind of external ceremony and trappings — which are always, in themselves, rather petty and base. This is what forever keeps God's true princes from the world's public stage, and awards the highest honors that this world can give to men who become famous more through their infinite inferiority to the chosen hidden few, than through any genuine superiority over the average mass. Such great power lurks in these small things, when extreme political superstition invests them, that in some royal cases they have given authority even to utter imbeciles. But when, as with Nicholas the Czar, the ringed crown of a geographic empire encircles a truly imperial brain — then the common masses cower before the tremendous power at the center. Nor will the tragic playwright who wants to depict indomitable human will in its fullest sweep ever overlook a hint so important to his art as the one I have just described.

But my Captain Ahab still stands before me in all his Nantucket grimness and roughness. And in this digression about emperors and kings, I must not forget that I am dealing only with a poor old whale hunter like him. Therefore, all outward majestic trappings are denied me. Oh, Ahab! Whatever is grand in you must be plucked from the skies, and dived for in the deep, and found in the invisible air!

chapters.title: Chapter 34 — The Cabin-Table
paragraphs: It is noon, and Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusts his pale bread-dough face from the cabin hatch to announce dinner to his lord and master. Ahab, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking a reading of the sun and is now silently calculating the latitude on the smooth, medallion-shaped tablet set into the upper part of his ivory leg for this daily purpose. From his complete inattention to the news, you'd think moody Ahab hadn't heard his servant. But presently, catching hold of the mizzen shrouds, he swings himself to the deck and, in an even, unenthusiastic voice, says, "Dinner, Mr. Starbuck," and disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan's step has faded and Starbuck, the first Emir, has every reason to believe he is seated, then Starbuck rouses from his stillness, takes a few turns along the deck, and after a serious glance into the compass, says with some touch of pleasantness, "Dinner, Mr. Stubb," and goes below. The second Emir lounges about the rigging a while, then slightly shakes the main brace to make sure it's secure. He likewise takes up the old refrain and, with a quick "Dinner, Mr. Flask," follows his predecessors.

But the third Emir, now finding himself alone on the quarter-deck, seems relieved of some curious restraint. Tipping all sorts of knowing winks in every direction and kicking off his shoes, he breaks into a sharp but silent hornpipe right over the Grand Turk's head below. Then, by a clever trick, he tosses his cap up to the mizzentop for a shelf, and goes down rollicking — at least as far as he's visible from the deck — reversing all other processions by bringing up the rear with music. But before stepping into the cabin doorway, he pauses, puts on a completely new face, and then the lively, independent little Flask enters King Ahab's presence in the role of the humble slave.

It is not the least of the strange things bred by the artificial customs of the sea that, while on the open deck some officers will speak boldly and defiantly to their commander, those same officers, the very next moment going down to dinner in that commander's cabin, will show an inoffensive, almost apologetic and humble manner toward him as he sits at the head of the table. This is remarkable, and sometimes quite comical. Why the difference? A puzzle? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon, and to have been Belshazzar not arrogantly but graciously — in that there must have been some touch of worldly grandeur. But the man who presides in a truly royal and intelligent spirit over his own dinner table of invited guests exercises an unchallenged power and personal influence that transcends even Belshazzar's, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Anyone who has once dined with friends has tasted what it is to be Caesar. There is a social spell in it that no one can resist. Now, if you add to this the official authority of a ship's captain, you can work out the cause of that peculiarity of sea life just described.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on a white coral beach, surrounded by his fierce but still respectful cubs. Each officer waited to be served in his proper turn. They were like small children before Ahab. And yet in Ahab there seemed to lurk not the slightest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened on the old man's knife as he carved the main dish. I don't think that for anything in the world they would have broken that moment with the slightest remark, even on a topic as neutral as the weather. No! And when Ahab, reaching out his knife and fork — the slice of beef locked between them — motioned Starbuck's plate toward him, the mate received his meat as though receiving charity, and cut it tenderly, and flinched a little if the knife happened to scrape the plate, and chewed it silently, and swallowed it carefully. For like the Coronation banquet at Frankfurt, where the German Emperor formally dines with the seven Imperial Electors, these cabin meals were somehow solemn events, eaten in terrible silence. And yet old Ahab never actually forbade conversation — he himself simply said nothing. What a relief it was to stifled Stubb when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below. And poor little Flask — he was the youngest son, the little boy of this grim family party. His were the shinbones of the salt beef — his would have been the drumsticks. For Flask to have presumed to serve himself would have felt like committing theft. If he had helped himself at that table, he probably could never have held his head up again in honest company. Nevertheless, strange to say, Ahab never actually forbade him. And had Flask helped himself, chances are Ahab would never have so much as noticed. Least of all did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the ship's owners denied it to him on account of its clouding his clear, sunny complexion, or whether he believed that on so long a voyage in such remote waters butter was a luxury not meant for a subordinate — however it was, Flask, alas, was a butterless man!

Another thing: Flask was the last person down to dinner and the first one back up. Consider! This meant Flask's dinner was badly squeezed for time. Starbuck and Stubb both got a head start on him, yet they also had the privilege of lingering. If even Stubb, who ranks only one peg above Flask, happened to have a small appetite and showed signs of finishing his meal, then Flask had to hurry — he wouldn't get more than three mouthfuls that day, for it was against sacred custom for Stubb to leave the table before Flask. Therefore Flask once confided in private that ever since he had risen to the dignity of an officer, he had never known what it was to be anything other than hungry, more or less. What he ate didn't so much relieve his hunger as keep it alive forever. Peace and satisfaction, Flask thought, have departed from my stomach for good. I am an officer — but how I wish I could grab a bit of good old-fashioned beef in the forecastle, the way I used to as a common sailor. There's the fruit of promotion. There's the vanity of glory. There's the insanity of life! Besides, if any ordinary sailor on the Pequod had a grudge against Flask in his official capacity, all that sailor had to do for ample revenge was go aft at dinnertime and peek at Flask through the cabin skylight, sitting there tongue-tied and dumbfounded before the awesome Ahab.

Now, Ahab and his three mates formed what might be called the first table in the Pequod's cabin. After their departure, in reverse order of their arrival, the tablecloth was cleared — or rather restored to some hasty order by the pale steward. Then the three harpooners were invited to eat, being the leftover heirs of the feast. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the grand cabin.

In sharp contrast to the barely tolerable restraint and nameless invisible domination of the captain's table was the complete carefree liberty of the harpooners. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of their own jaws, the harpooners chewed their food with such gusto that you could hear it. They dined like lords. They filled their bellies like cargo ships being loaded with spices. Such tremendous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego that to fill the gaps left by the previous meal, poor pale Dough-Boy often had to bring out a huge slab of salt beef that looked as if it had been quarried from a solid ox. And if he wasn't quick about it, Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of hurrying him along by throwing a fork at his back, harpoon-style. And once Daggoo, seized by a sudden whim, helped Dough-Boy's memory by snatching him up bodily and shoving his head into a big empty wooden platter, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began tracing the circle on his scalp preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, trembling sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward — the offspring of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the constant terrifying spectacle of the dark Ahab and the periodic tumultuous visits of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continuous quivering lip. Usually, after providing the harpooners with everything they demanded, he would escape into his little pantry next door and fearfully peek out at them through the slats of the door until it was all over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated facing Tashtego, filing his teeth against the Indian's. Across from them, Daggoo sat on the floor, since a bench would have brought his plumed head up against the low ceiling beams. With every motion of his enormous limbs, the low cabin framework shook, as when an African elephant rides as a passenger in a ship. But for all that, the great man was wonderfully restrained, even dainty, in his eating. It seemed hardly possible that such comparatively small bites could fuel the vitality spread through so broad, lordly, and magnificent a person. But doubtless this noble savage fed deeply on the abundant element of air, breathing in the sublime life of the worlds through his wide nostrils. Not by beef or bread are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg had a savage, barbaric smacking of the lips while eating — an ugly sound — so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost checked his own lean arms for teeth marks. And when he heard Tashtego call for him to come out so his bones could be picked, the simple-witted steward nearly shattered all the crockery around him in the pantry with sudden fits of terror. Nor did the whetstones the harpooners carried in their pockets for their lances — and with which, at dinner, they would pointedly sharpen their knives — do anything to calm poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his island days, Queequeg must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, cannibalistic indiscretions? Alas, Dough-Boy! Hard life for the white waiter who serves cannibals. He should carry not a napkin on his arm but a shield. In good time, though, to his great relief, the three sea-warriors would rise and depart — to his credulous, story-hungry ears, their martial bones jingling at every step, like Moorish swords in scabbards.

But though these harpooners dined in the cabin and officially lived there, being anything but sedentary in their habits, they were hardly ever in it except at mealtimes and just before bedtime, when they passed through it to their own quarters.

In this one matter, Ahab was no different from most American whale captains, who generally believe that by rights the ship's cabin belongs to them and that anyone else is allowed in only as a courtesy. So in truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more properly be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. When they did enter, it was like a street door entering a house — swinging in for a moment only to swing back out — with their permanent residence being the open air. Nor did they lose much by this arrangement. In the cabin there was no companionship. Socially, Ahab was unreachable. Though officially counted among Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world as the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as when spring and summer have departed, that wild creature buries himself in a hollow tree to live out the winter, sucking his own paws — so in his bitter, howling old age, Ahab's soul, shut up in the cave of his body, fed upon the sullen paws of its gloom!

chapters.title: Chapter 35 — The Mast-Head
paragraphs: It was during the more pleasant weather that my first turn at the masthead came around, in due rotation with the other seamen.

On most American whalers, the mastheads are manned almost as soon as the ship leaves port, even though she may have fifteen thousand miles or more to sail before reaching her proper cruising ground. And if, after a three, four, or five-year voyage, she's heading home with anything unfilled — even an empty vial — then her mastheads stay manned to the last. Not until her very topmost poles sail in among the port's church spires does she give up the hope of catching one more whale.

Now, since the business of standing mastheads, whether on land or at sea, is very ancient and interesting, let us dwell on it a while. I believe the earliest masthead-standers were the old Egyptians, because in all my research I find no one who came before them. Though their predecessors, the builders of Babel, must certainly have intended their tower to be the tallest masthead in all Asia or Africa, that great stone mast went by the board in the terrible gale of God's wrath before the final piece was put on top. So we can't give those Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of masthead-standers is supported by the common belief among archaeologists that the first pyramids were built for astronomical purposes — a theory nicely supported by the stair-like formation of all four sides, by which those old astronomers would climb to the summit with prodigious leg-stretches and call out for new stars, just as the lookouts on a modern ship call out for a sail or a whale. In Saint Stylites, the famous early Christian hermit who built himself a tall stone pillar in the desert and spent the rest of his life on top of it, hauling up his food from the ground — in him we have a remarkable example of a dauntless masthead-stander, who wouldn't be driven from his post by fog, frost, rain, hail, or sleet, but bravely faced everything to the end, literally dying at his post. Of modern masthead-standers we have only a lifeless set: statues of stone, iron, and bronze who, though capable of withstanding a stiff gale, are completely useless at the business of calling out when they spot something. There is Napoleon, standing atop the column of Vendome, arms folded, some hundred and fifty feet in the air, unconcerned about who rules the decks below. Great Washington, too, stands high on his towering mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules' pillars, his column marks the point of human greatness beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson also stands his masthead on a gun-metal capstan in Trafalgar Square. Even when obscured by London smoke, the sign is still there that a hidden hero stands above — for where there's smoke, there must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single call from below, however desperately invoked for their counsel by the troubled decks they look down upon — however much we might suppose their spirits can see through the thick haze of the future and spot what dangers must be avoided.

It may seem wrong to compare the masthead-standers on land with those at sea, but they're not so different, as demonstrated by a detail for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, is our source. Worthy Obed tells us that in the early days of the whale fishery, before ships were regularly sent out in pursuit, the islanders erected tall poles along the coast, to which lookouts climbed by means of nailed rungs, like chickens going up stairs in a henhouse. A few years ago, the same system was adopted by the bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon spotting whales, signaled the waiting boats near the beach. But this custom is now obsolete. So let us turn to the proper masthead: that of a whale ship at sea. The three mastheads are manned from sunrise to sunset, the sailors taking regular turns (as at the helm) and relieving each other every two hours. In the calm weather of the tropics, the masthead is delightful — especially for a dreamy, meditative man. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding across the deep as if the masts were giant stilts. Beneath you and between your legs, so to speak, swim the largest monsters of the sea, just as ships once sailed between the legs of the famous Colossus of Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite expanse of the ocean, with nothing stirred but the waves. The hypnotized ship lazily rolls. The drowsy trade winds blow. Everything dissolves you into lethargy. For the most part, in this tropical whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness wraps around you. You hear no news. You read no newspapers. No extras with alarming reports of ordinary events trick you into unnecessary excitement. You hear of no family troubles or bankrupt investments or falling stocks. You never worry about what to have for dinner — all your meals for three years or more are neatly stowed in barrels, and your menu is fixed.

On one of those southern whalers, on a long three or four-year voyage, as often happens, the total hours you spend at the masthead would add up to several entire months. And it is a great pity that the place where you devote such a large portion of your natural life should be so completely lacking in anything cozy or comfortable — so poorly suited to creating any sense of domestic warmth, like a bed, a hammock, a coffin, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any other of those snug little enclosures in which men temporarily shut themselves away. Your usual perch is the head of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (found almost only on whalers) called the topgallant cross-trees. Here, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels about as comfortable as he would standing on a bull's horns. In cold weather you can carry your house aloft in the form of a watch-coat, but strictly speaking the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than the naked body. For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly dwelling and can't freely move about in it, or even leave it, without risking death (like an ignorant traveler crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as just another layer of skin. You can't put shelves or drawers in your body, and no more can you make a closet out of your coat.

On this subject, it is greatly to be regretted that the mastheads of southern whale ships are not provided with those wonderful little tents or platforms called crow's-nests, which protect the lookouts of Greenland whalers from the brutal weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled A Voyage Among the Icebergs, in Quest of the Greenland Whale, and Incidentally for the Re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland, all masthead-standers are treated to a charmingly detailed account of the then recently invented crow's-nest aboard the Glacier, which was Captain Sleet's ship. He called it Sleet's Crow's-Nest in honor of himself, being the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false modesty. He held that if we name our children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors), we should likewise name any other apparatus we create. In shape, the crow's-nest is something like a large barrel — open at the top but fitted with a movable side-screen to shield your head from the wind in a gale. Being fixed atop the mast, you climb into it through a small trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side there's a comfortable seat with a locker underneath for umbrellas, scarves, and coats. In front is a leather rack for your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical necessities. When Captain Sleet stood his own masthead in this crow's-nest, he tells us he always had a rifle with him (also in the rack), along with powder flask and shot, for popping off stray narwhals or vagrant sea-unicorns in those waters — you can't shoot them successfully from the deck because of the water's resistance, but shooting down at them is quite another thing. Now, it was clearly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe all the detailed comforts of his crow's-nest. And though he gives us a very scientific account of his experiments there with a small compass he kept for correcting the errors caused by what's called the "local attraction" of the ship's iron — I say, though the Captain is very careful and scientific about his "compass deviations" and "approximate errors," he knows perfectly well that he was not so absorbed in those deep magnetic studies as to fail reaching for that well-stocked little case-bottle tucked neatly within arm's reach in one corner of his crow's-nest. Though on the whole I greatly admire and even love the brave, honest, learned Captain, I hold it very much against him that he so completely ignores that bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comfort it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we southern whale-fishers aren't as snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlanders were, that disadvantage is greatly offset by the wonderfully serene weather of those seductive seas where we mostly sail. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging quite leisurely, resting in the top for a chat with Queequeg or anyone else off duty I might find there. Then I'd climb a little higher, throw a lazy leg over the topsail yard, take a preliminary survey of the watery pastures, and at last reach my final destination.

Let me make a clean confession here and frankly admit that I kept a poor watch. With the problem of the universe revolving in my head, how could I — left completely alone at such a thought-provoking altitude — how could I take seriously my duty to observe all whale-ship standing orders: "Keep your weather eye open and sing out every time."

And let me right here give a solemn warning to you ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your watchful fisheries any young man with a lean brow and hollow eye, given to untimely philosophizing, who offers to ship with Plato instead of Bowditch in his head. Beware of such a one, I say. Your whales must be seen before they can be killed, and this sunken-eyed young philosopher will tow you ten times around the world and never make you one pint of sperm oil richer. Nor are these warnings unnecessary. For nowadays, the whale fishery serves as a refuge for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the grinding cares of life on land and seeking feeling in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not infrequently perches himself on the masthead of some unlucky, disappointed whale ship and, in moody tones, declaims:
"Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain."

Very often the captains of such ships scold these absent-minded young philosophers, criticizing them for not taking enough "interest" in the voyage — hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition that they would secretly rather not see whales at all. But it's useless. These young Platonists have a theory that their vision is imperfect. They are nearsighted. What use, then, to strain their eyes? They've left their opera glasses at home.

"Why, you monkey," said a harpooner to one of these lads, "we've been cruising now hard on three years, and you haven't spotted a whale yet. Whales are as scarce as hen's teeth whenever you're up here." Perhaps they were. Or perhaps there might have been whole schools of them on the far horizon. But lulled into such an opium-like daze of vacant, unconscious daydreaming is this absent-minded youth — by the blending rhythm of waves and thoughts — that at last he loses his identity. He takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul pervading all mankind and nature. Every strange, half-glimpsed, gliding, beautiful thing that escapes him, every dimly perceived rising fin of some unidentifiable form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that populate the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted state, your spirit ebbs away to where it came from, becoming diffused through time and space, like scattered ashes forming at last a part of every shore around the globe.

There is no life in you now, except the rocking life given by a gently rolling ship — borrowed from the sea, and by the sea from the unfathomable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is upon you, move your foot or hand an inch — slip your grip even slightly — and your identity comes rushing back in horror. Over spiraling vortexes you hover. And perhaps, at midday, in the fairest weather, with one half-strangled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, never to rise again. Take heed, you Pantheists!

chapters.title: Chapter 36 — The Quarter-Deck
paragraphs: (Enter Ahab: Then, all.)

It was not long after the affair of the pipe that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as usual, climbed the cabin gangway to the deck. There most sea captains usually walk at that hour, the way country gentlemen take a turn in the garden after the same meal.

Soon his steady, ivory stride could be heard as he paced back and forth on his old rounds, over planks so familiar to his step that they were dented all over, like geological stones, with the distinctive marks of his walk. If you stared fixedly at his ribbed and dented brow, you would see still stranger footprints there — the footprints of his one sleepless, ever-pacing thought.

But on this particular occasion, those dents looked deeper, just as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. Ahab was so full of his thought that at every regular turn — now at the mainmast, now at the compass — you could almost see that thought turn inside him as he turned, and pace inside him as he paced. It so completely possessed him that it seemed the inner mold of every outward movement.
"Do you notice him, Flask?" whispered Stubb. "The chick inside him is pecking at the shell. It'll be out soon."
The hours wore on — Ahab now shut up in his cabin, then pacing the deck again, with the same intense, fanatical purpose in his face.
The day was drawing to a close. Suddenly he stopped by the bulwarks, inserted his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand gripping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everyone aft.
"Sir!" said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on a ship except in some extraordinary situation.
"Send everybody aft," repeated Ahab. "Mastheads, there! Come down!"

When the entire ship's company was assembled and, with curious and somewhat uneasy faces, was watching him — for he looked much like the horizon when a storm is coming — Ahab, after glancing quickly over the bulwarks and then scanning the crew, left his post. As though no one were near him, he resumed his heavy pacing across the deck. With bent head and half-slouched hat, he continued to pace, ignoring the wondering whispers among the men, until Stubb cautiously whispered to Flask that Ahab must have assembled them to witness some kind of walking performance. But this didn't last long. Pausing forcefully, he cried:
"What do you do when you see a whale, men?"
"Sing out for him!" was the instant answer from a score of voices in unison.
"Good!" cried Ahab, with a wild approval in his voice, observing the hearty excitement into which his unexpected question had so magnetically thrown them.
"And what do you do next, men?"
"Lower away, and after him!"
"And what tune do you pull to, men?"
"A dead whale or a stove boat!"

Stranger and fiercer grew the glad, approving look on the old man's face with every shout. Meanwhile, the sailors began glancing curiously at each other, as if marveling at how they themselves had become so excited by such seemingly pointless questions.
But they were all eagerness again as Ahab, now half-revolving in his pivot-hole, one hand reaching high up a shroud and gripping it tightly, almost convulsively, addressed them:

"All you masthead-standers have already heard me give orders about a white whale. Look here! Do you see this Spanish gold ounce?" — holding up a broad, bright coin to the sun — "It's a sixteen-dollar piece, men. Do you see it? Mr. Starbuck, hand me that top-maul."

While the mate went for the hammer, Ahab, without speaking, slowly rubbed the gold piece against the front of his jacket, as if to heighten its shine. Without using any words, he hummed softly to himself, making a sound so strangely muffled and unclear that it seemed like the mechanical humming of the wheels of his inner vitality.

Taking the top-maul from Starbuck, he advanced toward the mainmast with the hammer raised in one hand and the gold coin displayed in the other, and in a loud, raised voice he cried: "Whichever of you spots me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw — whichever of you spots me that white-headed whale with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke — look here, whichever of you spots me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!"
"Hurrah! Hurrah!" cried the seamen, swinging their tarpaulin hats as they cheered the act of nailing the gold to the mast.
"It's a white whale, I say," Ahab continued, throwing down the hammer. "A white whale. Keep your eyes peeled for him, men. Watch for white water. If you see so much as a bubble, sing out."

All this time, Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg had been watching with even more intense interest and surprise than the rest. At the mention of the wrinkled brow and crooked jaw, they had each started as if individually touched by some specific memory.
"Captain Ahab," said Tashtego, "that white whale must be the same one some call Moby Dick."
"Moby Dick?" shouted Ahab. "Do you know the white whale, then, Tash?"
"Does he spread his tail a little strangely, sir, before he dives?" said the Gay-Header deliberately.
"And does he have an unusual spout, too," said Daggoo, "very bushy, even for a sperm whale, and very quick, Captain Ahab?"

"And he have one, two, three — oh! many many iron in him hide, too, Captain," cried Queequeg in his broken way, "all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him — him —" struggling for the word and screwing his hand round and round as if uncorking a bottle — "like him — him —"

"Corkscrew!" cried Ahab. "Yes, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and wrenched in him. Yes, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole sheaf of wheat, and white as a pile of Nantucket wool after the annual shearing. Yes, Tashtego, and he spreads his tail like a split sail in a squall. Death and devils! Men, it is Moby Dick you have seen — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!"

"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, who with Stubb and Flask had been watching his superior with growing surprise but now seemed struck by a thought that somewhat explained the wonder, "Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick — but it was not Moby Dick that took off your leg?"

"Who told you that?" cried Ahab. Then, pausing: "Yes, Starbuck. Yes, my hearties, all of you. It was Moby Dick that dismasted me. Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now. Yes, yes!" he shouted with a terrible, loud, animal sob, like that of a heart-stricken moose. "Yes, yes! It was that accursed white whale that cut me down, made a poor stumping cripple of me forever and a day!" Then, throwing both arms wide with measureless curses, he shouted: "Yes, yes! And I'll chase him around the Cape of Good Hope, and around the Horn, and around the Norway Maelstrom, and around the flames of hell before I give him up. And this is what you have signed on for, men! To chase that white whale on both sides of every land, and across every ocean, until he spouts black blood and rolls over dead. What say you, men? Will you join hands on it? I think you look brave."
"Yes! Yes!" shouted the harpooners and seamen, running closer to the excited old man. "A sharp eye for the white whale! A sharp lance for Moby Dick!"

"God bless you," he seemed to half sob and half shout. "God bless you, men. Steward! Go draw the great measure of grog. But what's this long face about, Mr. Starbuck? Won't you chase the white whale? Aren't you game for Moby Dick?"

"I'll face his crooked jaw, and the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it fairly comes in the way of the business we're here for. But I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's vengeance. How many barrels will your vengeance yield you, even if you get it, Captain Ahab? It won't fetch you much in our Nantucket market."

"Nantucket market! Ha! But come closer, Starbuck — you need a little deeper layer. If money is to be the measure, man, and the accountants have calculated their great counting-house the globe by circling it with gold coins, one to every three parts of an inch — then let me tell you that my vengeance will fetch a great premium here!"
"He strikes his chest," whispered Stubb. "What's that for? It seems to ring vast, but hollow."
"Vengeance on a dumb animal!" cried Starbuck. "That simply struck you from blindest instinct! Madness! To be enraged with a mindless creature, Captain Ahab, seems blasphemous."

"Listen again — the deeper layer. All visible things, man, are nothing but cardboard masks. But in each event — in the living act, the undeniable deed — there, some unknown but still thinking thing pushes its features through from behind the unthinking mask. If a man would strike, strike through the mask! How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved close against me. Sometimes I think there's nothing behind it. But that's enough. He drives me. He burdens me. I see in him monstrous strength, with an unfathomable malice powering it. That unfathomable thing is chiefly what I hate. And whether the white whale is the agent or the principal, I will unleash that hate upon him. Don't talk to me of blasphemy, man — I'd strike the sun if it insulted me. For if the sun could do that, then I could strike back, since there is always a kind of fair play in things, with jealousy presiding over all creation. But not even that fair play is my master, man. Who is above me? Truth knows no boundaries. Take your eyes off me! More unbearable than a fiend's glare is a dull, stupid stare! So, so — you flush red and go pale. My heat has melted your anger into a glow. But listen, Starbuck — what is said in heat unsays itself. There are men for whom hot words are no real offense. I didn't mean to provoke you. Let it go. Look! See those Turkish cheeks of spotted gold — living, breathing pictures painted by the sun. The pagan leopards — the unthinking, unworshipping things that live and seek and give no reasons for the fierce life they feel! The crew, man, the crew! Aren't they one and all with Ahab in this matter of the whale? See Stubb — he laughs! See that Chilean — he snorts just thinking of it. Stand against the general hurricane? Your one bent sapling cannot, Starbuck! And what is it? Think about it. It's only helping to strike a fin — no great feat for Starbuck. What more? You mean to tell me the best lance out of all Nantucket will hang back from this one poor hunt, when every common sailor has already grabbed a whetstone? Ah! I can see it seizing you — the wave lifts you! Speak — speak! Yes, yes! Your silence speaks for you. (Aside) Something shot from my flaring nostrils, and he has breathed it in. Starbuck is mine now. He cannot oppose me without rebellion."
"God keep me! — keep us all!" murmured Starbuck, quietly.

But in his joy at the mate's enchanted, silent consent, Ahab did not hear his ominous prayer. Nor the low laugh from the hold. Nor the foreboding vibrations of the wind in the rigging. Nor the hollow flap of the sails against the masts, as if for a moment their hearts sank. For again Starbuck's downcast eyes lit up with the stubbornness of life. The subterranean laugh died away. The winds blew on. The sails filled out. The ship heaved and rolled as before. Ah, you warnings and omens! Why don't you stay when you come? But rather than warnings, you are predictions — you shadows! Yet not so much predictions from outside as confirmations of what was already inside. For with little to restrain us from without, the deepest necessities within our being still drive us on.
"The measure! The measure!" cried Ahab.

Receiving the brimming pewter mug and turning to the harpooners, he ordered them to produce their weapons. Then, lining them up before him near the capstan with their harpoons in hand, while his three mates stood at his side with their lances and the rest of the crew formed a circle around the group, he stood for a moment searching every man's face. Those wild eyes met his the way the bloodshot eyes of prairie wolves meet the eye of their leader before he rushes ahead of the pack on the trail of the buffalo — but alas, only to fall into the hidden trap of the Indian.

"Drink and pass!" he cried, handing the heavy, full flagon to the nearest seaman. "The crew alone drinks now. Pass it round! Short sips — long swallows, men. It's hot as Satan's hoof. Good, good — it goes round well. It spirals into you. It forks out at the serpent-snapping eye. Well done — nearly drained. That way it went, this way it comes. Hand it back — here's a hollow! Men, you seem the years: life, brimming, is gulped and gone. Steward, refill!"

"Listen now, my brave ones. I have gathered you all around this capstan. You mates, flank me with your lances. You harpooners, stand there with your irons. And you, stout sailors, ring me in, so I may in some fashion revive a noble custom of my fisherman ancestors. O men, you will yet see that — Ha! Boy, back again? Bad pennies always return. Hand it here. Why, now, this pewter had run full again — wouldn't it, you twitching imp — away with you!"

"Advance, you mates! Cross your lances before me. Good! Let me touch the center." So saying, with extended arm he grasped the three level, radiating lances at their crossed center point. As he did so, he suddenly and nervously twitched them, meanwhile looking intently from Starbuck to Stubb, from Stubb to Flask. It seemed as though by some nameless, inner force of will, he wanted to shock into them the same fiery emotion stored in the Leyden jar of his own magnetic life. The three mates quailed before his strong, sustained, mystic presence. Stubb and Flask looked sideways away from him. The honest eye of Starbuck fell straight to the deck.

"In vain!" cried Ahab. "But maybe that's for the best. For if you three had taken the full-forced shock, then my own electric force might have drained out of me. Perhaps it would have killed you too. Perhaps you don't need it. Lower lances! And now, you mates, I appoint you three cupbearers to my three pagan kinsmen there — those three most honorable gentlemen and noblemen, my valiant harpooners. You disdain the task? What — when the great Pope washes the feet of beggars, using his crown for a water basin? Oh, my dear cardinals! Your own gracious condescension will bend you to it. I don't command you — you will it. Cut loose and draw the poles, you harpooners!"
Silently obeying the order, the three harpooners now stood holding the detached iron tips of their harpoons, about three feet long, barbs pointing up, before him.

"Don't stab me with that sharp steel! Turn them — turn them over! Don't you know the socket end? Turn up the sockets! Good, good. Now, you cupbearers, step forward. The irons! Take them. Hold them while I fill!" Then, slowly going from one officer to the next, he filled the harpoon sockets to the brim with the fiery liquor from the pewter.

"Now, three and three, you stand. Raise the murderous chalices! Pass them, you who are now partners in this unbreakable bond. Ha! Starbuck! — but the deed is done! That ratifying sun waits to set its seal on it. Drink, you harpooners! Drink and swear, you men who man the deadly whaleboat's bow — Death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!" The long, barbed steel goblets were raised. To cries and curses against the white whale, the spirits were gulped down with a hiss. Starbuck paled, turned, and shuddered. Once more, and finally, the refilled pewter went the rounds among the frenzied crew. Then, waving his free hand to them, they all dispersed, and Ahab retired to his cabin.

chapters.title: Chapter 37 — Sunset
paragraphs: The cabin, by the stern windows. Ahab sitting alone, gazing out.
I leave a white and troubled wake. Pale waters, paler cheeks, wherever I sail. The jealous waves swell sideways to swallow my track. Let them — but first I pass.

Yonder, at the ever-brimming goblet's rim, the warm waves blush like wine. The golden brow sinks into the blue. The diving sun — slowly descended from noon — goes down. My soul rises up! She tires of her endless climb. Is, then, the crown too heavy that I wear? This Iron Crown of Lombardy. Yet it is bright with many a gem. I, the wearer, cannot see its distant flashing — but I darkly feel that I wear something that dazzles and confounds. It is iron — that I know — not gold. It is cracked, too — I feel it. The jagged edge chafes me so, my brain seems to beat against the solid metal. Yes, a steel skull, mine — the kind that needs no helmet in the most brutal fight!

Dry heat upon my brow? Oh! There was a time when the sunrise nobly stirred me and the sunset soothed. No more. This lovely light — it doesn't light me. All beauty is agony to me, since I can never enjoy it. Gifted with the high perception, I lack the low, enjoying power. Damned — most subtly and most cruelly! Damned in the midst of Paradise! Good night — good night! (Waving his hand, he moves from the window.)

It was not so hard a task. I expected to find at least one man stubborn, but my one geared circle fits into all their various wheels, and they revolve. Or, if you prefer, like so many anthills of gunpowder, they all stand before me — and I am their match. Oh, how hard! That to set others ablaze, the match itself must burn away! What I have dared, I have willed. And what I have willed, I will do! They think me mad — Starbuck does. But I am demonic. I am madness gone mad! That wild madness which is only calm enough to comprehend itself! The prophecy said I would be dismembered — and yes! I lost this leg. I now prophesy that I will dismember my dismemberer. So let me be both prophet and fulfiller in one. That's more than you great gods ever were. I laugh at you and mock you, you cricket-players, you boxers, you deaf Burkes and blinded Bendigoes! I will not say as schoolboys say to bullies: pick on someone your own size, don't beat me! No — you've knocked me down, and I am back on my feet. But you have run and hidden. Come out from behind your barricades! I have no gun to reach you. Come, Ahab sends his compliments — come and see if you can turn me aside. Turn me? You cannot turn me — or else you turn yourselves! There, mankind has the advantage. Turn me? The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, and my soul is grooved to run on them. Over bottomless gorges, through the rifled hearts of mountains, under the beds of torrents, I rush without swerving! Nothing is an obstacle, nothing is a detour on the iron way!

chapters.title: Chapter 38 — Dusk
paragraphs: By the mainmast. Starbuck leaning against it.

My soul is more than matched — she's overpowered, and by a madman! What an unbearable sting, that sanity should lay down its arms on such a battlefield! But he drilled deep down and blasted all my reason out of me! I think I see his impious end, but I feel that I must help him reach it. Whether I will or not, the unspeakable thing has tied me to him, towing me with a cable I have no knife to cut. Horrible old man! "Who's above me?" he cries — yes, he would be a democrat to all above, but look how he lords it over all below! Oh! I can plainly see my miserable duty: to obey while rebelling, and worse still, to hate with a touch of pity! For in his eyes I read some terrible grief that would shrivel me up if I had it. Yet there is still hope. Time and tide flow wide. The hated whale has the whole round watery world to swim in, as a small goldfish has its glass globe. His heaven-insulting purpose — God may push it aside. I would take heart, if my heart were not like lead. But my whole clock has run down. My heart is the weight that controls everything, and I have no key to wind it again.
(A burst of revelry from the forecastle.)

Oh, God! To sail with such a heathen crew that have so little of human mothers in them! Whelped somewhere by the shark-infested sea. The white whale is their demon god. Listen! Those infernal celebrations! That revelry is forward. Notice the unbroken silence aft! It seems to me a picture of life. The bow shoots forward, gay and combative, through the sparkling sea — but only to drag dark Ahab after it, where he broods inside his cabin at the stern, built over the dead water of the wake, and further on, haunted by its wolfish gurgling. The long howl thrills me through! Quiet, you revelers, and set the watch! Oh, life! It is in an hour like this, with the soul beaten down and forced to face knowledge — as wild, untamed creatures are forced to feed — oh, life! It is now that I feel the hidden horror in you! But it is not in me! That horror is outside of me! And with the soft human feeling still in me, I will try to fight you, grim phantom futures! Stand by me, hold me, bind me, O you blessed influences!

chapters.title: Chapter 39 — First Night-Watch
paragraphs: Fore-Top.
(Stubb alone, mending a brace.)
