In more than one instance he has been known not only to chase the attacking boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself and hold out for a long time against all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that score; and as for his strength, let me say that there have been cases where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship and made fast there, the whale towing her great hull through the water as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that if the sperm whale, once struck, is given time to rally, he then acts not so often with blind rage as with willful, deliberate designs of destruction against his pursuers; and it says something eloquent about his character that, when attacked, he will often open his mouth and hold it in that dreadful gape for several minutes on end. But I must be content with only one more, concluding illustration — a remarkable and most significant one, from which you will not fail to see not only that the most marvelous event in this book is corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — truly, there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth century of the Christian era lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius was general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work of uncommon value in every way. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unsensational historian, except in one or two particulars that do not affect the matter I am about to mention.

Now, in this history of his, Procopius mentions that, during the term of his prefecture at Constantinople, a great sea-monster was captured in the neighboring Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after it had destroyed vessels at intervals in those waters for more than fifty years. A fact set down like this in substantial history cannot easily be denied. Nor is there any reason it should be. What precise species this sea-monster was is not mentioned. But since he destroyed ships, as well as for other reasons, he must have been a whale; and I am strongly inclined to think a sperm whale. And I will tell you why. For a long time I imagined that the sperm whale had always been unknown in the Mediterranean and the deep waters connecting with it. Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place he habitually resorts to in herds. But further investigations have recently proved to me that in modern times there have been isolated instances of the sperm whale's presence in the Mediterranean. I am told, on good authority, that on the Barbary coast a Commodore Davis of the British navy found the skeleton of a sperm whale. Now, since a vessel of war passes readily through the Dardanelles, a sperm whale could by the same route pass out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that sort, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century stove in the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

chapters.title: Chapter 46 — Surmises
paragraphs: Though, consumed by the hot fire of his purpose, Ahab in all his thoughts and actions always had in view the ultimate capture of Moby Dick; though he seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion; it may nevertheless have been that he was by nature and long habit far too wedded to a fiery whaleman's ways to give up altogether pursuing the ordinary business of the voyage alongside it. Or at least, if this was not so, there was no lack of other motives with much more influence on him. It would perhaps be too fine a point, even allowing for his monomania, to hint that his vindictiveness toward the White Whale might possibly have extended in some degree to all sperm whales, and that the more monsters he killed, the more he multiplied the chances that each whale he met afterward would prove to be the hated one he hunted. But if such a hypothesis is indeed open to objection, there were still further considerations which, though not so strictly in keeping with the wildness of his ruling passion, were by no means incapable of swaying him.

To accomplish his object Ahab had to use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are the most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendancy over Starbuck was in some respects, that ascendancy did not cover the whole spiritual man, any more than mere bodily superiority implies intellectual mastery; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual stands only in a sort of bodily relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still, he knew that for all this the chief mate in his soul abhorred his captain's quest, and if he could, would joyfully cut himself loose from it, or even thwart it. It might be a long time before the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would always be liable to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear on him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab concerning Moby Dick was nowhere more significantly shown than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should somehow be stripped of the strange imaginative impiety that naturally clothed it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept back in the dim background (for few men's courage can hold out against long brooding unrelieved by action); and that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think about than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, all sailors of every sort are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the changing outer weather, and they breathe in its fickleness — and when they are kept at a long pursuit of some remote and blank object, however much it promises life and passion in the end, it is above all necessary that temporary interests and occupations should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

Nor did Ahab forget another thing. In times of strong emotion mankind scorns all base considerations; but such times are fleeting. The permanent, constitutional condition of the manufactured man, thought Ahab, is sordidness. Granted that the White Whale fully stirs the hearts of this savage crew of mine, and, playing around their savageness, even breeds a certain generous knight-errantry in them — still, while they chase Moby Dick for the love of it, they must also have food for their more common, everyday appetites. For even the lofty, chivalric Crusaders of old were not content to cross two thousand miles of land to fight for their holy sepulchre without committing burglaries, picking pockets, and gaining other pious perks along the way. Had they been held strictly to their one final and romantic object, too many would have turned from that final and romantic object in disgust. I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hope of cash — yes, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by with no prospect of it in view, and then this same dormant cash, suddenly mutinying in them, would soon cashier Ahab — dismiss him from his command.

There was yet another precautionary motive, more closely related to Ahab personally. Having revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod's voyage — impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely — Ahab was now fully aware that in doing so he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation; and with perfect impunity, both moral and legal, his crew, if they were so inclined and able to carry it out, could refuse all further obedience to him, and even take the command from him by force. Ahab must of course have been most anxious to protect himself from even the barest hint of a charge of usurpation, and from the possible consequences of such a suppressed feeling gaining ground. That protection could lie only in his own dominating brain and heart and hand, backed by a careful, closely calculating attention to every minute atmospheric influence to which his crew could possibly be subjected.

For all these reasons, and others perhaps too subtle to spell out here, Ahab plainly saw that he must still in good measure stay true to the natural, stated purpose of the Pequod's voyage — observe all customary practices, and not only that, but force himself to show all his well-known passionate interest in the general pursuit of his profession.

Be all this as it may, his voice was now often heard hailing the three mastheads and warning them to keep a sharp lookout, and not to skip reporting even a porpoise. This vigilance was not long without reward.

chapters.title: Chapter 47 — The Mat-Maker
paragraphs: It was a cloudy, sultry afternoon. The seamen were lazily lounging about the decks or gazing vacantly over the rail into the lead-colored waters. Queequeg and I were quietly weaving what is called a sword-mat, to use as an additional lashing for our boat. So still and subdued was the whole scene, and yet somehow so full of anticipation, and such a spell of daydreaming lurked in the air, that each silent sailor seemed dissolved into his own invisible self.

I was Queequeg's attendant, or page, while he was busy at the mat. As I kept passing the filling, or woof, of marline back and forth between the long yarns of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, every now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads and, idly looking off at the water, carelessly and unthinkingly drove every yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess reigned then over all the ship and all the sea, broken only by the intermittent dull sound of the sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself a shuttle mechanically weaving and weaving away at the Fates. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one single, ever-returning, unchanging vibration, and that vibration just enough to allow other threads to be interwoven crosswise with its own. This warp seemed necessity; and here, I thought, with my own hand I ply my own shuttle and weave my own destiny into these unalterable threads. Meanwhile Queequeg's impulsive, indifferent sword sometimes hit the woof slantwise, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be, and by this difference in the concluding blow produced a corresponding contrast in the final look of the finished fabric. This savage's sword, I thought, which in the end shapes and fashions both warp and woof — this easy, indifferent sword must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity, in no way incompatible, all working together, interwoven. The straight warp of necessity, not to be swerved from its ultimate course — its every alternating vibration, indeed, only tending toward that; free will, still free to ply her shuttle between given threads; and chance, though restrained in its play within the straight lines of necessity, and directed sideways in its motions by free will — though thus hemmed in by both, chance rules each of them by turns, and strikes the last, shaping blow at events.

Thus we were weaving and weaving away when I started at a sound so strange, long-drawn, and musically wild and unearthly that the ball of free will dropped from my hand, and I stood gazing up at the clouds from which that voice dropped like a wing. High aloft in the crosstrees was that mad Gay-Header, Tashtego. His body was reaching eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and at brief, sudden intervals he continued his cries. To be sure, the same sound was perhaps at that very moment being heard all over the seas, from hundreds of whalemen's lookouts perched just as high in the air; but from few of those lungs could that familiar old cry have drawn such a marvelous cadence as from Tashtego the Indian's.

As he stood hovering over you, half-suspended in air, peering so wildly and eagerly toward the horizon, you would have thought him some prophet or seer beholding the shadows of Fate, and announcing their coming with those wild cries.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"Where away?"
"On the lee beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
Instantly all was commotion.
The Sperm Whale blows as a clock ticks, with the same unwavering and reliable regularity. And by this the whalemen distinguish this fish from other species of his kind.
"There go flukes!" was now the cry from Tashtego, and the whales disappeared.
"Quick, steward!" cried Ahab. "Time! Time!"
Dough-Boy hurried below, glanced at the watch, and reported the exact minute to Ahab.

The ship was now kept away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Since Tashtego reported that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bows. For that singular cunning the Sperm Whale at times shows — when, sounding (diving deep) with his head in one direction, he nevertheless mills round while hidden beneath the surface and swiftly swims off the opposite way — this deceitfulness of his could not be at work now; for there was no reason to suppose that the fish Tashtego had seen had been alarmed in any way, or indeed knew we were anywhere near. One of the men chosen as shipkeepers — that is, those not assigned to the boats — had by this time relieved the Indian at the mainmast head. The sailors at the fore and mizzen had come down; the line tubs were fixed in their places; the cranes were thrust out; the mainyard was backed; and the three boats swung over the sea like three samphire baskets over high cliffs. Outside the bulwarks their eager crews clung to the rail with one hand, while one foot was poised expectantly on the gunwale. That is how the long line of a man-of-war's men looks when they are about to throw themselves aboard an enemy's ship.

But at this critical instant a sudden exclamation was heard that drew every eye from the whale. With a start, all stared at dark Ahab, who was surrounded by five dusky phantoms that seemed freshly formed out of thin air.

chapters.title: Chapter 48 — The First Lowering
paragraphs: The phantoms, for so they seemed at the time, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and with a noiseless swiftness were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat that hung there. This boat had always been considered one of the spare boats, though technically it was called the captain's, because it hung from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bow was tall and dark, with one white tooth evilly protruding from his steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton clothed him funereally, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning all this blackness was a glistening white plaited turban — his own living hair, braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less dark in appearance, the companions of this figure had that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manillas — a race notorious for a certain devilish subtlety, and supposed by some honest white sailors to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents, here on the water, of their lord the devil, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.
While the wondering ship's company were still staring at these strangers, Ahab cried out to the white-turbaned old man at their head, "All ready there, Fedallah?"
"Ready," was the half-hissed reply.
"Lower away then, do you hear?" he shouted across the deck. "Lower away there, I say."

Such was the thunder of his voice that, despite their amazement, the men sprang over the rail. The pulleys whirled round in the blocks. With a lurch, the three boats dropped into the sea. And with a deft, offhand daring unknown in any other profession, the sailors leaped like goats down the rolling ship's side into the tossing boats below.

They had hardly pulled out from under the ship's shelter when a fourth boat, coming from the windward side, pulled around under the stern and revealed the five strangers rowing Ahab, who stood erect in the stern and loudly ordered Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask to spread themselves widely so as to cover a large stretch of water. But with all their eyes riveted upon the dark Fedallah and his crew, the men in the other boats did not obey the command.
"Captain Ahab? —" said Starbuck.
"Spread yourselves," cried Ahab. "Give way, all four boats. You, Flask, pull out more to leeward!"

"Aye, aye, sir," cheerily cried little King-Post, sweeping his great steering oar around. "Lay back!" he called to his crew. "There! — there! — there again! There she blows right ahead, boys! — lay back!"
"Never mind those yellow fellows, Archy."
"Oh, I don't mind them, sir," said Archy. "I knew it all before. Didn't I hear them in the hold? And didn't I tell Cabaco here about it? What do you say, Cabaco? They are stowaways, Mr. Flask."

"Pull, pull, my fine hearts-alive; pull, my children; pull, my little ones," Stubb sighed to his crew in a slow, soothing drawl, some of them still showing signs of uneasiness. "Why don't you break your backbones, my boys? What is it you're staring at? Those chaps in that boat over there? Tut! They are only five more hands come to help us — never mind from where — the more the merrier. Pull, then, do pull; never mind the brimstone — devils are good enough fellows. So, so; there you are now; that's the stroke for a thousand pounds; that's the stroke to sweep the stakes! Hurrah for the gold cup of sperm oil, my heroes! Three cheers, men — all hearts alive! Easy, easy; don't be in a hurry — don't be in a hurry. Why don't you snap your oars, you rascals? Bite something, you dogs! So, so, so, then — softly, softly! That's it — that's it! Long and strong. Give way there, give way! The devil take you, you ragamuffin rapscallions; you're all asleep. Stop snoring, you sleepers, and pull. Pull, will you? Pull, can't you? Pull, won't you? Why in the name of gudgeons and ginger-cakes don't you pull? — pull and break something! Pull, till your eyes start out of your head! Here!" — whipping the sharp knife out of his belt — "every mother's son of you draw his knife, and pull with the blade between his teeth. That's it — that's it. Now you're doing something; that looks like it, my steel-bits. Start her — start her, my silver-spoons! Start her, marling-spikes!"

Stubb's opening address to his crew is given here in full because he had rather a peculiar way of talking to them in general, and especially in preaching the religion of rowing. But you must not suppose from this sample of his sermons that he ever flew into real rages with his congregation. Not at all — and that was his chief peculiarity. He would say the most terrible things to his crew in a tone so strangely mixed of fun and fury, with the fury seeming so calculated merely as a spice to the fun, that no oarsman could hear such odd invocations without pulling for dear life, and yet pulling for the mere joke of the thing. Besides, all the while he himself looked so easy and lazy, handled his steering-oar so loungingly, and yawned so broadly — open-mouthed at times — that the mere sight of such a yawning commander, by sheer force of contrast, worked like a charm upon the crew. Then again, Stubb was one of those odd sorts of humorists whose jollity is sometimes so curiously ambiguous as to put all their subordinates on guard when it comes to obeying them.
In obedience to a signal from Ahab, Starbuck was now pulling diagonally across Stubb's bow. When for a minute or so the two boats were fairly near each other, Stubb hailed the mate.
"Mr. Starbuck! Portside boat there, ahoy! A word with you, sir, if you please!"
"Hello!" returned Starbuck, turning not a single inch as he spoke, still earnestly but in whispers urging his crew, his face set like flint away from Stubb's.
"What do you think of those yellow fellows, sir?"

"Smuggled on board, somehow, before the ship sailed. (Strong, strong, boys!)" in a whisper to his crew, then speaking out loud again: "A sad business, Mr. Stubb! (Drive her, drive her, my lads!) But never mind, Mr. Stubb, all for the best. Let all your crew pull strong, come what may. (Spring, my men, spring!) There's hogsheads of sperm ahead, Mr. Stubb, and that's what you came for. (Pull, my boys!) Sperm, sperm's the game! This at least is duty — duty and profit hand in hand."

"Aye, aye, I thought as much," Stubb said to himself when the boats diverged. "As soon as I clapped eyes on them, I thought so. Aye, and that's what he went into the after-hold for so often, as Dough-Boy long suspected. They were hidden down there. The White Whale's at the bottom of it. Well, well, so be it! Can't be helped! All right! Give way, men! It isn't the White Whale today! Give way!"

Now, the arrival of these outlandish strangers at such a critical moment as the lowering of the boats had, not unreasonably, stirred a kind of superstitious amazement in some of the ship's company. But Archy's supposed discovery had got around among them some time before, and though nobody had believed it then, it had in some small measure prepared them for the event. It took the sharpest edge off their wonder; and so, what with all this and Stubb's confident way of accounting for the strangers' appearance, they were for the time freed from superstitious guessing — though the affair still left plenty of room for all kinds of wild conjectures about dark Ahab's exact part in the matter from the beginning. As for me, I silently recalled the mysterious shadows I had seen creeping on board the Pequod in the dim Nantucket dawn, as well as the cryptic hints of the unaccountable Elijah.

Meanwhile Ahab, out of hearing of his officers, having edged farthest to windward, was still ranging ahead of the other boats — a sign of how powerful a crew was pulling him. Those tiger-yellow creatures of his seemed all steel and whalebone. Like five trip-hammers they rose and fell with regular strokes of strength, which every so often shot the boat along the water like a horizontal burst boiler out of a Mississippi steamer. As for Fedallah, who was seen pulling the harpooner's oar, he had thrown aside his black jacket and bared his chest, the whole of his body above the gunwale sharply outlined against the alternating dips of the watery horizon; while at the other end of the boat Ahab, one arm thrown half backward into the air like a fencer's, as if to counterbalance any tendency to trip, was seen steadily managing his steering oar as he had in a thousand boat-lowerings before the White Whale tore him. All at once the outstretched arm made a peculiar motion and then stayed fixed, while the boat's five oars were seen peaked all at once. Boat and crew sat motionless on the sea. Instantly the three spread-out boats behind paused on their way. The whales had irregularly sunk bodily down into the blue, giving no sign of the movement that could be seen from a distance, though Ahab, being closer, had observed it.
"Every man look out along his oars!" cried Starbuck. "You, Queequeg, stand up!"

Nimbly springing up on the triangular raised box in the bow, the savage stood erect there, and with intensely eager eyes gazed off toward the spot where the chase had last been sighted. Likewise, on the extreme stern of the boat, where it was also built up into a triangular platform level with the gunwale, Starbuck himself was seen coolly and skillfully balancing himself against the jerking tosses of his chip of a craft, silently scanning the vast blue eye of the sea.

Not very far off, Flask's boat was also lying breathlessly still. Its commander was recklessly standing on top of the loggerhead, a stout sort of post rooted in the keel and rising some two feet above the level of the stern platform. It is used for catching turns with the whale line. Its top is no bigger than the palm of a man's hand, and standing on such a base as that, Flask seemed perched at the masthead of some ship that had sunk to all but her trucks, the caps at the very tops of her masts. But little King-Post was small and short, and at the same time little King-Post was full of a large and tall ambition, so that this loggerhead standpoint of his by no means satisfied King-Post.
"I can't see three waves off. Tip us up an oar there and let me climb on that."
Upon this, Daggoo, with either hand on the gunwale to steady himself, swiftly slid to the stern, and then straightening up, volunteered his lofty shoulders as a pedestal.
"Good a masthead as any, sir. Will you mount?"
"That I will, and thank you very much, my fine fellow. Only I wish you were fifty feet taller."

Whereupon, planting his feet firmly against two opposite planks of the boat, the gigantic negro stooped a little and offered his flat palm to Flask's foot; then, putting Flask's hand on his hearse-plumed head and telling him to spring just as he himself should toss, with one skillful fling he landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders. And here now stood Flask, Daggoo with one lifted arm giving him a breastband to lean against and steady himself by.

At any time it is a strange sight to the novice to see with what wonderful, unconscious habit of skill the whaleman will keep upright in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Stranger still to see him giddily perched on the loggerhead itself in such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was more curious yet; for, holding himself up with a cool, indifferent, easy, unstudied, barbaric majesty, the noble negro rolled his fine form in harmony with every roll of the sea. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snowflake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. True, lively, tumultuous, showy little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but he did not add a single heave to the negro's lordly chest by it. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping on the living, magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

Meanwhile Stubb, the third mate, showed no such far-gazing anxieties. The whales might have made one of their regular soundings (their long, deep dives), not a temporary dive from mere fright; and if that were the case, Stubb, as was apparently his habit in such cases, was determined to while away the dragging interval with his pipe. He drew it from his hatband, where he always wore it at a slant like a feather. He loaded it and rammed the tobacco home with the end of his thumb; but he had barely struck his match across the rough sandpaper of his hand when Tashtego, his harpooner, whose eyes had been turned to windward like two fixed stars, suddenly dropped like light from his upright stance to his seat, crying out in a quick frenzy of hurry, "Down, down all, and give way! — there they are!"

To a landsman, no whale, nor any sign of a herring, would have been visible at that moment — nothing but a troubled patch of greenish-white water, with thin, scattered puffs of vapor hovering over it and drifting diffusely off to leeward, like the confused spray blown from white rolling breakers. The air around suddenly vibrated and tingled, as it were, like the air over intensely heated plates of iron. Beneath this atmospheric waving and curling, and partly beneath a thin layer of water as well, the whales were swimming. Seen ahead of all the other signs, the puffs of vapor they spouted seemed their couriers running before them, their detached outriders flying ahead.

All four boats were now in keen pursuit of that one spot of troubled water and air. But it seemed ready to outrun them. It flew on and on, like a mass of merging bubbles swept down a swift stream from the hills.

"Pull, pull, my good boys," said Starbuck, in the lowest possible but most intensely concentrated whisper to his men. The sharp fixed glance from his eyes, aimed straight ahead of the bow, seemed almost like two visible needles in two unerring binnacle compasses. He did not say much to his crew, nor did they say anything to him. Only the silence of the boat was at intervals piercingly broken by one of his peculiar whispers — now harsh with command, now soft with pleading.

How different the loud little King-Post. "Sing out and say something, my hearties! Roar and pull, my thunderbolts! Beach me, beach me on their black backs, boys! Only do that for me, and I'll sign over my Martha's Vineyard plantation to you, boys — including wife and children, boys! Lay me on — lay me on! Oh Lord, Lord! I'll go stark, staring mad! See! See that white water!" And shouting like this, he pulled his hat from his head and stamped up and down on it; then, picking it up, he flicked it far off over the sea; and finally he took to rearing and plunging in the boat's stern like a crazed colt from the prairie.

"Look at that fellow now," Stubb drawled philosophically, following along at a short distance with his unlit pipe still mechanically clamped between his teeth. "He's got fits, that Flask has. Fits? Yes, give him fits — that's the very word — pitch fits into them. Merrily, merrily, hearts alive! Pudding for supper, you know — merry's the word. Pull, babes — pull, sucklings — pull, all. But what the devil are you hurrying about? Softly, softly, and steadily, my men. Only pull, and keep pulling. Nothing more. Crack all your backbones, and bite your knives in two — that's all. Take it easy — why don't you take it easy, I say, and burst all your livers and lungs!"

But what it was that inscrutable Ahab said to that tiger-yellow crew of his — those are words best left out here, for you live under the blessed light of the evangelical land. Only the infidel sharks in the audacious seas may listen to such words, when, with a tornado brow and eyes of red murder and foam-glued lips, Ahab leaped after his prey.

Meanwhile, all the boats tore on. Flask's repeated, specific references to "that whale," as he called the imaginary monster that he declared was constantly teasing his boat's bow with its tail — these references of his were at times so vivid and lifelike that they would make one or two of his men snatch a fearful look over their shoulders. But this was against all rules; for the oarsmen must put out their eyes and ram a skewer through their necks, custom declaring that in these critical moments they must have no organs but ears and no limbs but arms.

It was a sight full of quick wonder and awe! The vast swells of the all-powerful sea; the surging, hollow roar they made as they rolled along the eight gunwales, like gigantic bowls on a boundless bowling green; the brief, suspended agony of the boat as it tipped for an instant on the knife-like edge of the sharper waves, which almost seemed to threaten to cut it in two; the sudden deep plunge into the watery glens and hollows; the keen spurring and goading to reach the top of the opposite hill; the headlong, sled-like slide down its other side — all these, with the cries of the headsmen and harpooners and the shuddering gasps of the oarsmen, and the wondrous sight of the ivory Pequod bearing down on her boats with outstretched sails, like a wild hen after her screaming brood — all this was thrilling.

Not the raw recruit, marching from the arms of his wife into the fever heat of his first battle — not the dead man's ghost encountering the first unknown phantom in the other world — neither of these can feel stranger and stronger emotions than the man who for the first time finds himself pulling into the charmed, churning circle of the hunted sperm whale.

The dancing white water made by the chase was now becoming more and more visible, owing to the deepening darkness of the dusky cloud-shadows cast on the sea. The jets of vapor no longer blended, but tilted everywhere to right and left; the whales seemed to be separating their wakes. The boats were pulled farther apart, Starbuck giving chase to three whales running dead to leeward. Our sail was now set, and with the still-rising wind we rushed along — the boat going with such madness through the water that the lee oars could barely be worked fast enough to escape being torn from the row-locks.
Soon we were running through a wide, drifting veil of mist. Neither ship nor boat to be seen.
"Give way, men," whispered Starbuck, drawing the sheet of his sail still further aft. "There is time to kill a fish yet before the squall comes. There's white water again! — close by! Spring!"

Soon after, two cries in quick succession on each side of us told us the other boats had struck fast. But they were hardly heard when, with a lightning-fast hissing whisper, Starbuck said: "Stand up!" and Queequeg, harpoon in hand, sprang to his feet.

Though not one of the oarsmen was facing the life-and-death danger so close ahead, yet with their eyes on the intense face of the mate in the stern of the boat, they knew the critical instant had come. They heard, too, an enormous wallowing sound, as of fifty elephants stirring in their bedding. Meanwhile the boat was still racing through the mist, the waves curling and hissing around us like the raised crests of enraged serpents.
"That's his hump. There, there, give it to him!" whispered Starbuck.

A short rushing sound leaped out of the boat — it was the darted iron of Queequeg. Then all in one welded commotion came an invisible push from behind, while forward the boat seemed to strike a ledge. The sail collapsed and exploded. A gush of scalding vapor shot up nearby. Something rolled and tumbled like an earthquake beneath us. The whole crew was half-suffocated as they were tossed helter-skelter into the white curdling cream of the squall. Squall, whale, and harpoon had all blended together. And the whale, merely grazed by the iron, escaped.

Though completely swamped, the boat was nearly unharmed. Swimming around it, we picked up the floating oars, and lashing them across the gunwale, tumbled back to our places. There we sat up to our knees in the sea, the water covering every rib and plank, so that to our downward-gazing eyes the suspended craft seemed a coral boat grown up to us from the ocean floor.

The wind increased to a howl; the waves clashed their shields together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire on the prairie, in which we were burning without being consumed — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; you might as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, flying cloud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea ruled out any attempt to bail out the boat. The oars were useless for rowing, and now served as life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, Starbuck, after many failures, managed to light the lamp in the lantern; then, fixing it on a waif pole (the flagged pole used to mark a killed whale), he handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that feeble candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

Wet, drenched through, and shivering with cold, despairing of ship or boat, we lifted our eyes as dawn came on. The mist still spread over the sea; the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg started to his feet, cupping his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, as of ropes and yards that the storm had muffled until then. The sound came nearer and nearer; the thick mists were dimly parted by a huge, vague form. Terrified, we all sprang into the sea as the ship at last loomed into view, bearing right down upon us at a distance of not much more than her own length.

Floating on the waves, we saw the abandoned boat as for one instant it tossed and gaped beneath the ship's bows like a chip at the foot of a waterfall; then the vast hull rolled over it, and it was seen no more until it came up wallowing astern. Again we swam for it, were dashed against it by the seas, and were at last taken up and safely landed on board. Before the squall came close, the other boats had cut loose from their fish and returned to the ship in good time. The ship had given us up, but was still cruising, in the hope that it might chance upon some token of our perishing — an oar or a lance pole.

chapters.title: Chapter 49 — The Hyena
paragraphs: There are certain queer times and occasions in this strange, mixed affair we call life when a man takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke, though he only dimly sees the wit of it, and more than suspects that the joke is at nobody's expense but his own. Still, nothing gets him down, and nothing seems worth arguing about. He bolts down all events, all creeds and beliefs and persuasions, all hard things visible and invisible, no matter how knobby, as an ostrich with a powerful digestion gobbles down bullets and gun flints. And as for small difficulties and worries, prospects of sudden disaster, danger to life and limb — all these, and death itself, seem to him only sly, good-natured hits and jolly punches in the ribs from the unseen and unaccountable old joker. That odd, wayward sort of mood I am speaking of comes over a man only in some time of extreme trouble; it comes in the very midst of his earnestness, so that what a moment before might have seemed to him a thing of the greatest importance now seems only part of the general joke. There is nothing like the perils of whaling to breed this free-and-easy sort of genial, desperado philosophy; and it was with this that I now regarded the whole voyage of the Pequod, and the great White Whale that was its object.

"Queequeg," I said, when they had dragged me — the last man — to the deck, and I was still shaking myself in my jacket to fling off the water, "Queequeg, my fine friend, does this sort of thing happen often?" Without much emotion, though soaked through just like me, he gave me to understand that such things did often happen.

"Mr. Stubb," I said, turning to that worthy, who, buttoned up in his oil jacket, was now calmly smoking his pipe in the rain, "Mr. Stubb, I think I have heard you say that of all whalemen you ever met, our chief mate, Mr. Starbuck, is by far the most careful and prudent. I suppose, then, that going headlong at a running whale with your sail set in a foggy squall is the height of a whaleman's discretion?"
"Certainly. I've lowered for whales from a leaking ship in a gale off Cape Horn."

"Mr. Flask," I said, turning to little King-Post, who was standing close by, "you are experienced in these things, and I am not. Will you tell me whether it is an unbreakable law in this fishery, Mr. Flask, for an oarsman to break his own back pulling himself backward into death's jaws?"

"Can't you put it more simply?" said Flask. "Yes, that's the law. I'd like to see a boat's crew backing water up to a whale face-first. Ha, ha! The whale would give them squint for squint, mind that!"

Here, then, from three impartial witnesses, I had a deliberate statement of the whole case. Considering, therefore, that squalls, capsizings in the water, and the bivouacs on the deep that follow were matters of common occurrence in this kind of life; considering that at the supremely critical instant of going on to the whale I must hand my life over to the man who steered the boat — often a fellow who, at that very moment, in his impetuousness, is on the point of sinking the craft with his own frantic stamping; considering that the particular disaster to our own particular boat was chiefly to be blamed on Starbuck's driving on to his whale almost in the teeth of a squall, and considering that Starbuck, for all that, was famous for his great caution in the fishery; considering that I belonged to this uncommonly prudent Starbuck's boat; and finally, considering what a devil's chase I was caught up in, concerning the White Whale — taking all things together, I say, I thought I might as well go below and make a rough draft of my will. "Queequeg," I said, "come along; you shall be my lawyer, executor, and legatee."

It may seem strange that sailors of all men should be tinkering with their last wills and testaments, but there are no people in the world fonder of that pastime. This was the fourth time in my nautical life that I had done the same thing. After the ceremony was over on this occasion, I felt all the easier; a stone was rolled away from my heart. Besides, all the days I should now live would be as good as the days that Lazarus lived after his resurrection — a supplementary clean gain of so many months or weeks, as the case might be. I survived myself; my death and burial were locked up in my chest. I looked around me calmly and contentedly, like a quiet ghost with a clean conscience sitting inside the bars of a snug family vault.
Now then, I thought, unconsciously rolling up my sleeves — here goes for a cool, collected dive at death and destruction, and the devil take the hindmost.

chapters.title: Chapter 50 — Ahab’s Boat and Crew. Fedallah
paragraphs: "Who would have thought it, Flask!" cried Stubb. "If I had only one leg, you wouldn't catch me in a boat — unless maybe to plug the drain-hole with my wooden toe. Oh! He's a wonderful old man!"

"I don't think it so strange, on that account," said Flask. "If his leg were off at the hip, now, that would be a different thing. That would disable him. But he has one knee, and a good part of the other left, you know."
"I don't know about that, little man. I've never yet seen him kneel."

Among whale-wise people it has often been debated whether, considering the supreme importance of his life to the success of the voyage, it is right for a whaling captain to risk that life in the active dangers of the chase. So Tamerlane's soldiers often argued, with tears in their eyes, whether that invaluable life of his ought to be carried into the thickest of the fight.

But with Ahab the question took on a different angle. Considering that even with two legs a man is but a hobbling creature in times of danger — considering that the pursuit of whales is always conducted under great and extraordinary difficulties, and that every individual moment involves peril — under these circumstances, is it wise for any maimed man to enter a whale-boat in the hunt? As a general rule, the joint-owners of the Pequod must plainly have thought not.

Ahab knew well that although his friends at home would think little of his getting into a boat during certain comparatively harmless turns of the chase, for the sake of being near the action and giving his orders in person, yet for Captain Ahab to have a boat actually assigned to him as a regular headsman in the hunt — above all, for Captain Ahab to be supplied with five extra men as that boat's crew — he knew well that such generous notions never entered the heads of the owners of the Pequod. So he had not asked them for a boat's crew, nor had he in any way hinted at his wishes on that score. Nevertheless, he had taken private measures of his own in the whole matter. Until Cabaco's discovery was made public, the sailors had little foreseen it. To be sure, once they had been a little while out of port and all hands had finished the customary business of fitting out the whaleboats for service, Ahab was, some time after this, now and then found busying himself with making thole-pins (the pegs that hold the oars in place) with his own hands for what was thought to be one of the spare boats, and even carefully cutting the small wooden skewers that are pinned over the groove in the bow when the line is running out; when all this was noticed in him, and particularly his concern to have an extra layer of sheathing in the bottom of the boat, as if to make it better withstand the pointed pressure of his ivory limb; and also the anxiety he showed in shaping exactly the thigh-board, or clumsy cleat, as it is sometimes called — the horizontal piece in the boat's bow for bracing the knee against when darting or stabbing at the whale; when it was noticed how often he stood up in that boat with his single knee fixed in the semicircular hollow in the cleat, and with the carpenter's chisel gouged out a little here and straightened it a little there — all these things, I say, had stirred much interest and curiosity at the time. But almost everybody supposed that this particular care in preparation on Ahab's part could only be with a view to the final chase of Moby Dick, for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. But such a supposition by no means involved the faintest suspicion that any boat's crew would be assigned to that boat.

Now, as for the subordinate phantoms, whatever wonder remained soon faded away, for in a whaler wonders soon fade. Besides, now and then such unaccountable odds and ends of strange nations come up from the unknown nooks and ash-holes of the earth to man these floating outlaws, the whalers; and the ships themselves often pick up such queer castaway creatures, found tossing about the open sea on planks, bits of wreck, oars, whaleboats, canoes, blown-off Japanese junks, and what not, that Beelzebub himself might climb up the side and step down into the cabin to chat with the captain, and it would not cause any uncontrollable excitement in the forecastle.

But be all this as it may, it is certain that while the subordinate phantoms soon found their place among the crew — though still, as it were, somehow distinct from them — that hair-turbaned Fedallah remained a muffled mystery to the last. Where he came from, in a well-mannered world like this; by what unaccountable sort of tie he soon showed himself to be linked with Ahab's peculiar fortunes — indeed, so far as to have some sort of half-hinted influence; Heaven knows, it might even have been authority over him — all this nobody knew. But no one can keep up an air of indifference about Fedallah. He was such a creature as civilized, domestic people in the temperate zone see only in their dreams, and even then only dimly; but the like of him now and then glide among the unchanging Asiatic communities, especially the Oriental islands to the east of the continent — those isolated, immemorial, unalterable countries which even in these modern days still keep much of the ghostly aboriginal quality of earth's first generations, when the memory of the first man was a distinct recollection, and all men, his descendants, not knowing where he came from, eyed each other as real phantoms, and asked the sun and the moon why they were created and to what end; when, though according to Genesis the angels indeed consorted with the daughters of men, the devils also, add the uncanonical rabbis, indulged in earthly love affairs.

chapters.title: Chapter 51 — The Spirit-Spout
paragraphs: Days, weeks passed, and under easy sail, the ivory Pequod had slowly swept across four separate cruising-grounds: the one off the Azores, the one off the Cape Verdes, the Plate — so called because it lies off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata — and the Carrol Ground, an unmarked watery expanse south of St. Helena.

It was while gliding through these last waters, one serene and moonlit night, when all the waves rolled by like scrolls of silver and, with their soft, spreading seethings, made what seemed a silvery silence rather than a solitude — on such a silent night a silvery jet was seen far ahead of the white bubbles at the bow. Lit up by the moon, it looked celestial; it seemed some plumed and glittering god rising from the sea. Fedallah first sighted this jet. For on these moonlit nights it was his habit to climb to the main masthead and stand lookout there, with the same precision as if it had been day. And yet, though herds of whales were seen by night, not one whaleman in a hundred would venture to lower for them. You can imagine, then, with what feelings the seamen watched this old Oriental perched aloft at such unusual hours, his turban and the moon companions in one sky. But when, after he had spent his regular stint up there for several nights in a row without uttering a single sound — when, after all this silence, his unearthly voice was heard announcing that silvery, moonlit jet, every reclining sailor started to his feet as if some winged spirit had landed in the rigging and hailed the mortal crew. "There she blows!" Had the trumpet of Judgment blown, they could not have quivered more; and yet they felt no terror — rather pleasure. For though it was a most unusual hour, so impressive was the cry, and so deliriously exciting, that almost every soul on board instinctively wanted to lower.

Walking the deck with quick, side-lunging strides, Ahab ordered the topgallant sails and royals set, and every studding-sail spread. The best man in the ship must take the helm. Then, with every masthead manned, the ship, piled high with sail, rolled down before the wind. The strange, upheaving, lifting pull of the breeze from astern, filling the hollows of so many sails, made the buoyant, hovering deck feel like air beneath the feet, while still she rushed along, as if two opposing forces were struggling in her — one to climb straight to heaven, the other to drive, yawing, toward some horizontal goal. And had you watched Ahab's face that night, you would have thought that in him too two different things were at war. While his one live leg made lively echoes along the deck, every stroke of his dead limb sounded like a coffin-tap. On life and death this old man walked. But though the ship sped so swiftly, and though eager glances shot like arrows from every eye, the silvery jet was seen no more that night. Every sailor swore he saw it once, but not a second time.

This midnight spout had almost become a forgotten thing when, some days later — there it was again: at the same silent hour, announced again, spotted by all. But when we set sail to overtake it, it once more vanished as if it had never existed. And so it served us night after night, until no one paid it any attention except to marvel at it. Mysteriously thrown into the clear moonlight or starlight, disappearing again for one, two, or three whole days, and somehow seeming at every new appearance to be advancing still further ahead of us — this solitary jet seemed forever beckoning us on.

Nor, given the ancient superstition of their race and the supernatural aura that seemed in many ways to surround the Pequod, were there lacking some seamen who swore that whenever and wherever it was sighted — at however remote times, or in however far-apart latitudes and longitudes — that unnearable spout was cast by one and the same whale, and that whale was Moby Dick. For a time, there also reigned a sense of peculiar dread at this flitting apparition, as if it were treacherously beckoning us on and on so that the monster might turn around upon us and tear us apart at last in the remotest and most savage seas.

These temporary fears, so vague but so awful, drew a strange power from the contrasting calm of the weather. Beneath all its blue gentleness, some thought there lurked a devilish charm, as for days upon days we voyaged through seas so wearily, so lonesomely mild that all of space, repelled by our vengeful mission, seemed to be emptying itself of life before our funeral-urn prow.

But at last, when we turned eastward, the Cape winds began howling around us, and we rose and fell upon the long, troubled seas that lie there. When the ivory-tusked Pequod bowed sharply to the blast and gored the dark waves in her fury, until showers of silver chips — the foam-flakes — flew over her bulwarks, then all this desolate emptiness of life went away, but gave place to sights more dismal than before.

Close to our bow, strange shapes darted back and forth in the water before us, while thick behind us flew inscrutable sea-ravens. Every morning, perched on our rigging, rows of these birds were seen. Despite our shouting, they stubbornly clung to the ropes for a long time, as though they considered our ship some drifting, uninhabited craft — a thing fated for desolation, and therefore a fitting roosting-place for their homeless selves. And the black sea heaved and heaved, still relentlessly heaving, as if its vast tides were a conscience, and the great soul of the world were in anguish and remorse for the long sin and suffering it had caused.

Cape of Good Hope, do they call you? Rather Cape Tormentoso, as they named you long ago. For, long deceived by the treacherous silences that had attended us before, we found ourselves launched into this tormented sea, where guilty beings transformed into those birds and those fish seemed condemned to swim forever without any harbor in store, or to beat that black air without any horizon. But calm, snow-white, and unchanging — still directing its fountain of feathers toward the sky — still beckoning us on from ahead — the solitary jet would at times appear.

Through all this blackness of the elements, Ahab, though taking almost continual command of the drenched and dangerous deck for the time, showed the gloomiest reserve, and spoke to his mates more seldom than ever. In stormy times like these, after everything above and aloft has been secured, nothing more can be done but wait passively for the outcome of the gale. Then captain and crew become practical fatalists. So, with his ivory leg inserted into its usual hole, and with one hand firmly gripping a shroud, Ahab would stand for hours and hours gazing dead to windward, while an occasional squall of sleet or snow would all but freeze his very eyelashes together. Meanwhile the crew, driven from the forward part of the ship by the dangerous seas that broke bursting over her bows, stood in a line along the bulwarks in the waist; and the better to guard against the leaping waves, each man had slipped himself into a sort of bowline, a loop of rope secured to the rail, in which he swung as in a loosened belt. Few or no words were spoken; and the silent ship, as if manned by painted sailors in wax, tore on day after day through all the swift madness and gladness of the demonic waves. By night the same muteness of humanity before the shrieks of the ocean prevailed; still in silence the men swung in the bowlines; still wordless Ahab stood up to the blast. Even when his worn-out body seemed to be demanding rest, he would not seek that rest in his hammock. Starbuck could never forget the old man's look when, going down into the cabin one night to note how the barometer stood, he saw him sitting bolt upright in his floor-screwed chair with his eyes closed, the rain and half-melted sleet of the storm from which he had come in some time before still slowly dripping from the hat and coat he had not taken off. On the table beside him lay unrolled one of those charts of tides and currents that have been spoken of before. His lantern swung from his tightly clenched hand. Though the body was upright, the head was thrown back so that the closed eyes were pointed toward the needle of the tell-tale that swung from a beam in the ceiling.*
*The cabin-compass is called the tell-tale because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course.
Terrible old man! thought Starbuck with a shudder. Sleeping through this gale, still you steadfastly keep your eye on your purpose.

chapters.title: Chapter 52 — The Albatross
paragraphs: Southeastward from the Cape, off the distant Crozetts — a good cruising ground for Right Whalemen — a sail appeared ahead: the Goney, or Albatross by name. As she slowly drew near, from my lofty perch at the foremast-head I had a good view of that sight so remarkable to a newcomer in the far ocean fisheries: a whaler at sea, long absent from home.

As if the waves had been fullers bleaching cloth, this craft was whitened like the skeleton of a stranded walrus. All down her sides this ghostly appearance was streaked with long channels of reddened rust, while all her spars and her rigging were like the thick branches of trees furred over with hoarfrost. Only her lower sails were set. It was a wild sight to see her long-bearded lookouts at those three mastheads. They seemed clad in the skins of beasts, so torn and patched were the clothes that had survived nearly four years of cruising. Standing in iron hoops nailed to the mast, they swayed and swung over a fathomless sea; and though, when the ship glided slowly close under our stern, we six men in the air came so near each other that we might almost have leaped from the mastheads of one ship to those of the other, yet those forlorn-looking fishermen, eyeing us mildly as they passed, said not one word to our own lookouts, while the hail from the quarter-deck was being heard below.
"Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"

But as the strange captain, leaning over the pale bulwarks, was in the act of putting his trumpet to his mouth, it somehow fell from his hand into the sea; and with the wind now rising hard, he tried in vain to make himself heard without it. Meanwhile his ship was still widening the distance between us. While the seamen of the Pequod were showing in various silent ways that they had marked this ominous incident at the very first mention of the White Whale's name to another ship, Ahab paused for a moment; it almost seemed as though he would have lowered a boat to board the stranger, had not the threatening wind forbidden it. But taking advantage of his windward position, he seized his trumpet again, and, knowing by her look that the stranger was a Nantucketer and shortly bound home, he hailed loudly — "Ahoy there! This is the Pequod, bound round the world! Tell them to address all future letters to the Pacific Ocean! And this time three years, if I am not at home, tell them to address them to ——"

At that moment the two ships' wakes were fairly crossed, and instantly — as was their strange custom — schools of small harmless fish that had been peacefully swimming alongside us for some days darted away with what seemed shuddering fins, and ranged themselves fore and aft along the stranger's flanks. Though in the course of his continual voyaging Ahab must often have noticed a similar sight before, to any monomaniac man the merest trifles capriciously carry meanings.

"Swim away from me, do you?" murmured Ahab, gazing over into the water. There seemed little in the words, but the tone conveyed more deep helpless sadness than the mad old man had ever before shown. But turning to the helmsman, who had been holding the ship into the wind to slow her progress, he cried out in his old lion's voice — "Up helm! Keep her off round the world!"

Round the world! There is much in that sound to inspire proud feelings. But where does all that circumnavigation lead? Only through numberless dangers to the very point where we started, where those we left behind — safe and secure — were all the time ahead of us.

Were this world an endless plain, and by sailing eastward we could forever reach new distances and discover sights more sweet and strange than any Cyclades or Islands of King Solomon, then there would be promise in the voyage. But in pursuit of those far mysteries we dream of, or in tormented chase of that demon phantom that at some time or other swims before all human hearts — while chasing such things over this round globe, they either lead us on through barren mazes or midway leave us overwhelmed.

chapters.title: Chapter 53 — The Gam
paragraphs: The ostensible reason why Ahab did not go on board the whaler we had spoken — that is, hailed at sea — was this: the wind and sea signaled storms. But even had this not been the case, he would not, perhaps, have boarded her after all — judging by his later conduct on similar occasions — if it had turned out that by hailing he had got a negative answer to the question he put. For, as it eventually turned out, he did not care to keep company, even for five minutes, with any stranger captain unless that captain could contribute some of the information he so absorbingly sought. But all this might not be properly appreciated unless something were said here about the peculiar customs of whaling vessels when they meet each other in foreign seas, and especially on a common cruising-ground.

If two strangers crossing the Pine Barrens in New York State, or the equally desolate Salisbury Plain in England — if, meeting each other by chance in such inhospitable wilds, these two cannot for the life of them avoid a mutual greeting, stopping for a moment to exchange the news, and perhaps sitting down for a while to rest together — then how much more natural that on the boundless Pine Barrens and Salisbury Plains of the sea, two whaling vessels sighting each other at the ends of the earth — off lonely Fanning's Island, or the faraway King's Mills — how much more natural, I say, that in such circumstances these ships should not only exchange hails, but come into still closer, more friendly and sociable contact. And this would seem especially a matter of course in the case of vessels owned in the same seaport, whose captains, officers, and not a few of the men know each other personally, and consequently have all sorts of dear domestic things to talk about.

For the long-absent ship, the outward-bound one perhaps has letters on board; at any rate, she will be sure to let her have some newspapers dated a year or two later than the last one in her blurred and thumb-worn files. And in return for that courtesy, the outward-bound ship would receive the latest whaling news from the cruising-ground she may be headed for, a thing of the utmost importance to her. And to some degree all this holds true of whaling vessels crossing each other's track on the cruising-ground itself, even though they are equally long absent from home. For one of them may have received a transfer of letters from some third vessel, now far away, and some of those letters may be for the people of the ship she now meets. Besides, they would exchange the whaling news and have a pleasant chat. For not only would they meet with all the sympathies of sailors, but also with all the special fellow-feeling that comes from a common pursuit and from hardships and dangers shared together.

Nor would difference of country make any very essential difference — that is, so long as both parties speak one language, as is the case with Americans and English. Though, to be sure, since there are so few English whalers, such meetings do not happen very often, and when they do, there is all too likely to be a sort of shyness between them; for your Englishman is rather reserved, and your Yankee doesn't care for that sort of thing in anybody but himself. Besides, the English whalers sometimes put on a kind of metropolitan superiority over the American whalers, regarding the long, lean Nantucketer, with his nondescript provincialisms, as a sort of sea-peasant. But just where this superiority of the English whalemen really lies would be hard to say, seeing that the Yankees, collectively, kill more whales in one day than all the English, collectively, in ten years. But this is a harmless little foible in the English whale-hunters, which the Nantucketer does not take much to heart — probably because he knows that he has a few foibles himself.

So, then, we see that of all ships sailing the sea separately, the whalers have the most reason to be sociable — and they are. Some merchant ships, on the other hand, crossing each other's wake in the mid-Atlantic, will often pass on without so much as a single word of recognition, cutting each other dead on the high seas like a pair of dandies on Broadway, and all the while indulging, perhaps, in fussy criticism of each other's rig. As for men-of-war, when they happen to meet at sea, they first go through such a string of silly bowings and scrapings, such a dipping of flags, that there does not seem to be much downright hearty goodwill and brotherly love about it at all. As for slave-ships meeting — why, they are in such a tremendous hurry that they run away from each other as soon as possible. And as for pirates, when they happen to cross each other's cross-bones, the first hail is "How many skulls?" — the same way whalers hail "How many barrels?" And once that question is answered, pirates steer apart at once, for they are infernal villains on both sides and don't like to see too much of each other's villainous likenesses.

But look at the godly, honest, unpretentious, hospitable, sociable, free-and-easy whaler! What does the whaler do when she meets another whaler in any sort of decent weather? She has a "Gam," a thing so utterly unknown to all other ships that they have never even heard the name; and if by chance they should hear of it, they only grin at it and repeat gamesome stuff about "spouters" and "blubber-boilers," and such pretty exclamations. Why all merchant seamen, and also all pirates and man-of-war's men and slave-ship sailors, should cherish such a scornful feeling toward whale-ships is a question it would be hard to answer. Because, in the case of pirates, say, I should like to know whether that profession of theirs has any special glory about it. It sometimes ends in uncommon elevation, it's true — but only at the gallows. And besides, when a man is elevated in that odd fashion, he has no proper foundation for his superior altitude. Hence I conclude that in boasting of being lifted high above a whaleman, the pirate has no solid basis to stand on.

But what is a Gam? You might wear out your index finger running up and down the columns of dictionaries and never find the word. Dr. Johnson never attained that much learning; Noah Webster's ark does not hold it. Nevertheless, this same expressive word has now been in constant use for many years among some fifteen thousand true-born Yankees. Certainly it needs a definition, and should be entered in the Lexicon. With that in view, let me learnedly define it.

GAM. Noun — A social meeting of two (or more) whale-ships, generally on a cruising-ground; when, after exchanging hails, they exchange visits by boats' crews: the two captains remaining, for the time, on board of one ship, and the two chief mates on the other.

There is another little item about gamming that must not be forgotten here. All professions have their own little peculiarities of detail; so has the whale fishery. In a pirate, man-of-war, or slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern sheets on a comfortable, sometimes cushioned seat there, and often steers himself with a pretty little milliner's tiller decorated with gay cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no seat astern, no sofa of that sort whatever, and no tiller at all. High times indeed, if whaling captains were wheeled about the water on casters like gouty old aldermen in patent chairs. And as for a tiller, the whale-boat never allows any such effeminacy; and therefore, since in gamming a complete boat's crew must leave the ship, and since the boat-steerer or harpooner is one of that number, that subordinate is the steersman on the occasion, and the captain, having no place to sit, is rowed off to his visit standing bolt upright like a pine tree. And you will often notice that, conscious of the eyes of the whole visible world resting on him from the sides of the two ships, this standing captain is keenly alive to the importance of keeping up his dignity by keeping on his legs. Nor is this any very easy matter; for behind him is the immense projecting steering oar, hitting him now and then in the small of his back, while the after-oar returns the favor by rapping his knees in front. He is thus completely wedged in front and behind, and can only spread himself sideways by settling down on his outstretched legs; but a sudden, violent pitch of the boat will often go far toward toppling him, because length of foundation is nothing without corresponding breadth. Simply make a spread angle of two poles, and you cannot stand them up. Then again, it would never do, in plain sight of the world's riveted eyes — it would never do, I say — for this straddling captain to be seen steadying himself the slightest bit by catching hold of anything with his hands; indeed, as a token of his entire, buoyant self-command, he generally carries his hands in his trouser pockets; but perhaps, as they are generally very large, heavy hands, he carries them there for ballast. Nevertheless there have been cases, well-authenticated ones too, where the captain has been known, for an uncommonly critical moment or two — in a sudden squall, say — to seize hold of the nearest oarsman's hair and hold on there like grim death.

chapters.title: Chapter 54 — The Town-Ho’s Story
paragraphs: (As told at the Golden Inn.)
The Cape of Good Hope, and all the watery region around it, is much like some notable crossroads of a great highway, where you meet more travelers than in any other part.

It was not very long after speaking the Goney that another homeward-bound whaleman, the Town-Ho,* was encountered. She was manned almost entirely by Polynesians. In the short gam that followed, she gave us strong news of Moby Dick. For some of us, the general interest in the White Whale was now wildly heightened by a circumstance of the Town-Ho's story, which seemed obscurely to involve the whale in a certain wondrous, inverted visitation of one of those so-called judgments of God that are sometimes said to overtake certain men. This circumstance, with its own particular accompaniments, forming what may be called the secret part of the tragedy about to be told, never reached the ears of Captain Ahab or his mates. For that secret part of the story was unknown even to the captain of the Town-Ho himself. It was the private property of three white seamen of that ship who were in league together, one of whom, it seems, passed it on to Tashtego under Romish injunctions of secrecy; but the following night Tashtego rambled in his sleep, and revealed so much of it that way that, when he was woken, he could not well hold back the rest. Nevertheless, so powerful an influence did this thing have on those seamen in the Pequod who came to know it fully, and by such a strange delicacy, so to call it, were they governed in this matter, that they kept the secret among themselves, so that it never traveled aft of the Pequod's mainmast. Weaving this darker thread into its proper place in the story as publicly told on the ship, I now set the whole of this strange affair down on lasting record.
*The ancient whale-cry upon first sighting a whale from the masthead, still used by whalemen in hunting the famous Galapagos terrapin.

For my humor's sake, I shall preserve the style in which I once narrated it at Lima, to a lounging circle of my Spanish friends, one saint's eve, smoking upon the thick gold-tiled terrace of the Golden Inn. Of those fine gentlemen, the young Dons, Pedro and Sebastian, were on the closest terms with me, and hence the occasional questions they put, which are duly answered at the time.

"Some two years before I first learned of the events I am about to recount to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the north of the Line. One morning, when the pumps were worked, as was the daily custom, it was noticed that she was taking more water into her hold than usual. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain had some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and was therefore very unwilling to leave them; and since the leak was not then considered at all dangerous (though, in fact, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather), the ship went on with her cruising, the sailors working at the pumps at long and easy intervals. But no good luck came. More days went by, and not only was the leak still undiscovered, but it noticeably increased. So much so that the captain, now taking some alarm, made all sail and headed for the nearest harbor among the islands, to have his hull hove out and repaired there."

"Though no short passage lay ahead of her, yet if the commonest luck held, he did not at all fear that his ship would founder on the way, because his pumps were of the best, and, taking turns at them, his thirty-six men could easily keep the ship free of water, never mind if the leak should double. In truth, since nearly the whole of this passage was attended by very favorable breezes, the Town-Ho would all but certainly have reached her port in perfect safety, without the least fatality, had it not been for the brutal overbearing of Radney, the mate, a Vineyarder from Martha's Vineyard, and the bitterly provoked vengeance of Steelkilt, a Lakeman and desperado from Buffalo."
"'Lakeman! — Buffalo! Pray, what is a Lakeman, and where is Buffalo?' said Don Sebastian, rising in his swinging grass hammock."

"On the eastern shore of our Lake Erie, Don; but — I beg your patience — perhaps you shall soon hear more of all that. Now, gentlemen, in square-sail brigs and three-masted ships, nearly as large and sturdy as any that ever sailed out of your old Callao to far Manila, this Lakeman, in the landlocked heart of our America, had nonetheless been raised on all those agrarian, freebooting impressions popularly connected with the open ocean. For taken all together, those grand freshwater seas of ours — Erie, and Ontario, and Huron, and Superior, and Michigan — have an ocean-like expanse, with many of the ocean's noblest traits, and with many of its varieties of races and climates around their rims. They contain round archipelagoes of romantic islands, just as the Polynesian waters do; for much of their length they are bordered by two great contrasting nations, as the Atlantic is; they provide long sea approaches to our many territorial colonies from the East, dotted all around their banks; here and there they are frowned upon by batteries, and by the goat-like, craggy guns of lofty Mackinaw; they have heard the swift thunder of naval victories; at intervals they yield their beaches to wild barbarians, whose red-painted faces flash out from their fur-hide wigwams; for leagues and leagues they are flanked by ancient, untrodden forests, where the gaunt pines stand like serried lines of kings in Gothic family trees, those same woods sheltering wild African beasts of prey, and silky-coated creatures whose exported furs make robes for Tartar Emperors; they mirror the paved capitals of Buffalo and Cleveland, as well as Winnebago villages; they float alike the full-rigged merchant ship, the armed cruiser of the State, the steamer, and the beech canoe; they are swept by north winds and dismasting blasts as terrible as any that lash the salt sea; they know what shipwrecks are, for out of sight of land, however inland, they have drowned many a ship at midnight with all its shrieking crew. So, gentlemen, though an inlander, Steelkilt was born to the wild ocean and raised on the wild ocean — as bold a mariner as any. And as for Radney: though as an infant he may have lain down on the lonely Nantucket beach to nurse at his mother the sea; though in later life he had long followed our austere Atlantic and your contemplative Pacific — he was still quite as vengeful and quarrelsome as the backwoods seaman fresh from the latitudes of buckhorn-handled Bowie knives. Yet this Nantucketer was a man with some good-hearted traits; and this Lakeman was a mariner who, though a sort of devil indeed, could still be handled by unbending firmness, tempered only by that common decency of human recognition which is the right of the lowliest slave; treated that way, this Steelkilt had long been kept harmless and docile. At any rate, he had proved so up to then; but Radney was doomed and driven mad, and Steelkilt — but, gentlemen, you shall hear."

"It was not more than a day or two at most after she had pointed her bow toward her island harbor that the Town-Ho's leak seemed to be increasing again, though only enough to require an hour or more at the pumps every day. You must know that in a settled and civilized ocean like our Atlantic, for example, some captains think little of pumping their whole way across it — though on a still, sleepy night, should the officer of the deck happen to forget his duty in that respect, the likelihood is that he and his shipmates would never remember it again, because all hands would be gently settling to the bottom. Nor in the lonely and savage seas far to the west of you, gentlemen, is it altogether unusual for ships to keep clanging at their pump-handles in full chorus even over a voyage of considerable length; that is, if it runs along a fairly accessible coast, or if some other reasonable refuge is open to them. It is only when a leaky vessel is in some very out-of-the-way part of those waters, some truly landless latitude, that her captain begins to feel a little anxious."

"Much this way it had been with the Town-Ho. So when her leak was found gaining once more, there was in truth some small concern shown by several of her company, especially by Radney the mate. He ordered the upper sails to be well hoisted, sheeted home anew, and every way spread to the breeze. Now this Radney, I suppose, was as little of a coward, and as little inclined to any sort of nervous fear for his own person, as any fearless, unthinking creature on land or on sea that you can conveniently imagine, gentlemen. So when he showed this anxiety about the safety of the ship, some of the seamen declared that it was only because he was a part owner in her. And so, when they were working at the pumps that evening, there was no small amount of sly joking going on among them on this point, as they stood with their feet continually washed over by the rippling clear water — clear as any mountain spring, gentlemen — that bubbled from the pumps, ran across the deck, and poured itself out in steady spouts at the lee scupper-holes."
