"Now, as you well know, it is not seldom the case in this conventional world of ours — watery or otherwise — that when a person placed in command over his fellow men finds one of them to be very significantly his superior in general pride of manhood, he immediately conceives an unconquerable dislike and bitterness toward that man; and if he has a chance, he will pull down and pulverize that subordinate's tower, and make a little heap of dust of it. Be this notion of mine as it may, gentlemen, at all events Steelkilt was a tall and noble animal with a head like a Roman's, and a flowing golden beard like the tasseled trappings of your last viceroy's snorting charger; and a brain, and a heart, and a soul in him, gentlemen, that would have made Steelkilt Charlemagne, had he been born son to Charlemagne's father. But Radney, the mate, was as ugly as a mule, and as hardy, as stubborn, as malicious. He did not love Steelkilt, and Steelkilt knew it."
"Spotting the mate drawing near as he was toiling at the pump with the rest, the Lakeman pretended not to notice him, but, not in the least intimidated, went on with his cheerful banter."

"'Aye, aye, my merry lads, it's a lively leak this! Hold a cup, one of you, and let's have a taste. By the Lord, it's worth bottling! I tell you what, men, old Rad's investment must go for it! He'd best cut away his part of the hull and tow it home. The fact is, boys, that swordfish only started the job. He's come back again with a gang of ship-carpenters, sawfish, and filefish, and what not; and the whole posse of them are now hard at work cutting and slashing at the bottom — making improvements, I suppose. If old Rad were here now, I'd tell him to jump overboard and scatter them. They're playing the devil with his estate, I can tell him. But he's a simple old soul, Rad, and a beauty too. Boys, they say the rest of his property is invested in looking-glasses. I wonder if he'd give a poor devil like me the model of his nose.'"
"'Damn your eyes! What's that pump stopping for?' roared Radney, pretending not to have heard the sailors' talk. 'Thunder away at it!'"

"'Aye, aye, sir,' said Steelkilt, merry as a cricket. 'Lively, boys, lively, now!' And with that the pump clanged like fifty fire-engines. The men tossed their hats off to it, and before long that peculiar gasping of the lungs was heard that marks the fullest strain of life's utmost energies."

"Leaving the pump at last with the rest of his gang, the Lakeman went forward all panting and sat himself down on the windlass, his face fiery red, his eyes bloodshot, wiping the heavy sweat from his brow. Now what deceiving fiend it was, gentlemen, that possessed Radney to meddle with such a man in that physically inflamed state, I don't know; but so it happened. Striding intolerably along the deck, the mate ordered him to get a broom and sweep down the planks, and also a shovel, and clear away some offensive matter left from letting a pig run loose."

"Now, gentlemen, sweeping a ship's deck at sea is a piece of housework that, in all weather but raging gales, is regularly attended to every evening; it has been known to be done on ships that were actually sinking at the time. Such, gentlemen, is the inflexibility of sea customs and the instinctive love of neatness in seamen, some of whom would not willingly drown without first washing their faces. But in all vessels this broom business is, by long-established right, the province of the boys, if there are boys aboard. Besides, it was the stronger men in the Town-Ho who had been divided into gangs, taking turns at the pumps; and being the most athletic seaman of them all, Steelkilt had been regularly appointed captain of one of the gangs. So he should have been excused from any trivial business not connected with truly nautical duties, as his comrades were. I mention all these details so that you may understand exactly how this affair stood between the two men."

"But there was more than this: the order about the shovel was almost as plainly meant to sting and insult Steelkilt as if Radney had spat in his face. Any man who has gone to sea as a sailor in a whale-ship will understand this; and all this, and doubtless much more, the Lakeman fully grasped when the mate gave his command. But as he sat still for a moment, and as he steadily looked into the mate's malignant eye and saw the stacks of powder-casks heaped up inside him and the slow-match silently burning along toward them — as he instinctively saw all this, that strange forbearance, that unwillingness to stir up the deeper passions of any already angry being — a reluctance felt most, when it is felt at all, by truly brave men even when they have been wronged — this nameless phantom feeling, gentlemen, stole over Steelkilt."

"Therefore, in his ordinary tone, only a little broken by the physical exhaustion he was in for the moment, he answered that sweeping the deck was not his business, and he would not do it. And then, without mentioning the shovel at all, he pointed to three lads as the usual sweepers, who, not being assigned to the pumps, had done little or nothing all day. To this Radney replied with an oath, repeating his command without condition in a most domineering and outrageous manner, and meanwhile advancing on the still-seated Lakeman with a raised cooper's club hammer, which he had snatched from a cask nearby."

"Heated and irritated as he was by his convulsive labor at the pumps, for all his initial nameless impulse to hold back, the sweating Steelkilt could barely stand this behavior from the mate. But somehow still smothering the fire within him, without speaking he remained stubbornly rooted to his seat, until at last the enraged Radney shook the hammer within a few inches of his face, furiously commanding him to obey."

"Steelkilt rose, and slowly retreating around the windlass, steadily followed by the mate with his threatening hammer, deliberately repeated his intention not to obey. Seeing, however, that his forbearance had not the slightest effect, he warned off the foolish, infatuated man with an awful and unspeakable signal of his twisted hand; but it was no use. And in this way the two went slowly once around the windlass; then, resolved at last to retreat no further, and reflecting that he had now put up with as much as suited his temper, the Lakeman stopped on the hatches and spoke to the officer as follows:"

"'Mr. Radney, I will not obey you. Take that hammer away, or look out for yourself.' But the predestined mate, coming still closer to where the Lakeman stood fixed, now shook the heavy hammer within an inch of his teeth, meanwhile repeating a string of unbearable curses. Not retreating the thousandth part of an inch, stabbing him in the eye with the unflinching dagger of his glance, Steelkilt, clenching his right hand behind him and stealthily drawing it back, told his persecutor that if the hammer so much as grazed his cheek, he (Steelkilt) would murder him. But, gentlemen, the fool had been branded for the slaughter by the gods. Immediately the hammer touched the cheek; the next instant the mate's lower jaw was smashed in against his head; he fell on the hatch spouting blood like a whale."
"Before the cry could reach the stern, Steelkilt was shaking one of the backstays leading far aloft to where two of his comrades were standing their mastheads. They were both Canallers."
"'Canallers!' cried Don Pedro. 'We have seen many whale-ships in our harbors, but never heard of your Canallers. Pardon — who and what are they?'"
"'Canallers, Don, are the boatmen of our great Erie Canal. You must have heard of it.'"
"'No, Senor. Hereabouts in this dull, warm, most lazy, and hereditary land, we know but little of your vigorous North.'"
"'Is that so? Well then, Don, refill my cup. Your chicha is very fine. And before going further I will tell you what our Canallers are, for such information may shed light on my story.'"

"For three hundred and sixty miles, gentlemen, through the entire breadth of the state of New York; through numerous populous cities and most thriving villages; through long, dismal, uninhabited swamps, and rich cultivated fields unrivaled for fertility; by billiard-room and bar-room; through the holy of holies of great forests; on Roman arches over Indian rivers; through sun and shade; by happy hearts or broken; through all the wide, contrasting scenery of those noble Mohawk counties; and especially by rows of snow-white chapels, whose spires stand almost like milestones — there flows one continuous stream of life as corrupt as Venice's and often lawless. There's your true Ashantee, gentlemen; there your pagans howl; where you always find them, next door to you, under the long-cast shadow and the snug, patronizing shelter of churches. For by some curious fatality, just as it is often noted that your big-city robbers always camp around the halls of justice, so sinners, gentlemen, most abound in the holiest neighborhoods."
"'Is that a friar passing?' said Don Pedro, looking down into the crowded plaza with humorous concern."
"'Well for our northern friend that Dame Isabella's Inquisition is waning in Lima,' laughed Don Sebastian. 'Proceed, Senor.'"

"'A moment! Pardon!' cried another of the company. 'In the name of all us Limeese, I only wish to say to you, sir sailor, that we have by no means overlooked your delicacy in not substituting present-day Lima for distant Venice in your comparison of corruption. Oh! Do not bow and look surprised; you know the proverb all along this coast: "Corrupt as Lima." It only bears out your saying, too: churches more plentiful than billiard-tables, and forever open — and "Corrupt as Lima." So too with Venice; I have been there — the holy city of the blessed evangelist, St. Mark! — St. Dominic, purge it! Your cup! Thanks — here I refill; now, you pour out again.'"

"Freely portrayed in his own calling, gentlemen, the Canaller would make a fine dramatic hero, so abundantly and picturesquely wicked is he. Like Mark Antony, for days and days along his green-turfed, flowery Nile, he lazily floats, openly toying with his red-cheeked Cleopatra, ripening his apricot thigh on the sunny deck. But ashore, all this softness is dashed away. The brigand-like getup the Canaller so proudly sports, and his slouched and gaily ribboned hat, proclaim his grand features. A terror to the smiling innocence of the villages he floats through, his swarthy face and bold swagger are shunned in the cities too. Once, when I was a vagabond on his own canal, I received good turns from one of these Canallers; I thank him heartily, and would not wish to be ungrateful; but it is often one of the chief redeeming qualities of your man of violence that at times he has as stiff an arm to back a poor stranger in a tight spot as to rob a wealthy one. In sum, gentlemen, how wild this canal life is, is emphatically shown by this: that our wild whale-fishery contains so many of its most finished graduates, and that hardly any breed of men, except Sydney men, are so much distrusted by our whaling captains. Nor does it at all lessen the curiousness of this matter that, for many thousands of our country boys and young men born along its route, the probationary life of the Grand Canal furnishes the only transition between quietly reaping in a Christian cornfield and recklessly plowing the waters of the most barbaric seas."

"'I see! I see!' exclaimed Don Pedro eagerly, spilling his chicha on his silver ruffles. 'No need to travel! The world's one Lima. I had thought, now, that in your temperate North the generations were cold and holy as the hills. — But the story.'"

"I left off, gentlemen, where the Lakeman shook the backstay. Hardly had he done so when he was surrounded by the three junior mates and the four harpooners, who all crowded him to the deck. But sliding down the ropes like baleful comets, the two Canallers rushed into the uproar and tried to drag their man out of it toward the forecastle. Others of the sailors joined them in this attempt, and a tangled melee followed; while, standing well out of harm's way, the valiant captain danced up and down with a whale-pike, calling on his officers to manhandle that atrocious scoundrel and smoke him out and along to the quarter-deck. Now and then he ran close up to the whirling edge of the confusion, and, prying into the heart of it with his pike, tried to prick out the object of his resentment. But Steelkilt and his desperadoes were too much for them all; they succeeded in reaching the forecastle deck, where, hastily swinging three or four large casks around into a line with the windlass, these sea-Parisians entrenched themselves behind the barricade."
"'Come out of that, you pirates!' roared the captain, now threatening them with a pistol in each hand, just brought to him by the steward. 'Come out of that, you cutthroats!'"

"Steelkilt leaped on the barricade, and striding up and down there, defied the worst the pistols could do. But he gave the captain to understand clearly that his — Steelkilt's — death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny from all hands. Fearing in his heart that this might prove all too true, the captain backed off a little, but still commanded the rebels to return immediately to their duty."
"'Will you promise not to touch us if we do?' demanded their ringleader."
"'Turn to! Turn to! — I make no promise — to your duty! Do you want to sink the ship by knocking off at a time like this? Turn to!' And he once more raised a pistol."

"'Sink the ship?' cried Steelkilt. 'Aye, let her sink. Not a man of us turns to unless you swear not to raise so much as a rope-yarn against us. What say you, men?' turning to his comrades. A fierce cheer was their response."

"The Lakeman now patrolled the barricade, all the while keeping his eye on the Captain, and jerking out sentences like these: 'It's not our fault; we didn't want it; I told him to take his hammer away; it was boys' work; he might have known me before this; I told him not to prod the buffalo; I believe I've broken a finger here against his cursed jaw; aren't those mincing knives down in the forecastle there, men? Look to those handspikes, my hearties. Captain, by God, look to yourself; say the word; don't be a fool; forget it all; we are ready to turn to; treat us decently, and we're your men; but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to! I make no promises. Turn to, I say!'"

"'Look here, now,' cried the Lakeman, flinging out his arm toward him, 'there are a few of us here — and I am one of them — who have shipped for the cruise, do you see? Now as you well know, sir, we can claim our discharge as soon as the anchor is down. So we don't want a fight. It's not in our interest. We want to be peaceable. We are ready to work, but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to!' roared the Captain."

"Steelkilt glanced around him a moment, and then said: 'I tell you what it is now, Captain — rather than kill you, and be hanged for such a shabby rascal, we won't lift a hand against you unless you attack us. But until you give us the word about not flogging us, we don't do a hand's turn.'"
"'Down into the forecastle, then. Down with you! I'll keep you there till you're sick of it. Down you go.'"

"'Shall we?' cried the ringleader to his men. Most of them were against it. But at length, in obedience to Steelkilt, they preceded him down into their dark den, disappearing with growls, like bears into a cave."

"As the Lakeman's bare head was just level with the planks, the Captain and his posse leaped the barricade, and, rapidly drawing the slide of the scuttle over, planted their group of hands on it and loudly called for the steward to bring the heavy brass padlock belonging to the companionway. Then, opening the slide a little, the Captain whispered something down the crack, closed it, and turned the key on them — ten in number — leaving on deck some twenty or more, who so far had remained neutral."

"All night a wide-awake watch was kept by all the officers, fore and aft, especially about the forecastle scuttle and the fore hatchway, where it was feared the rebels might come out after breaking through the bulkhead below. But the hours of darkness passed in peace, the men who still remained at their duty toiling hard at the pumps, whose clinking and clanking, at intervals through the dreary night, echoed dismally through the ship."

"At sunrise the Captain went forward, and, knocking on the deck, summoned the prisoners to work; but with a yell they refused. Water was then lowered down to them, and a couple of handfuls of biscuit were tossed after it; then, locking them in again and pocketing the key, the Captain returned to the quarter-deck. Twice a day for three days this was repeated; but on the fourth morning, as the usual summons was delivered, a confused wrangling and then a scuffling was heard, and suddenly four men burst up from the forecastle, saying they were ready to turn to. The stifling, foul air and a starvation diet, together perhaps with some fear of final punishment, had forced them to surrender unconditionally. Emboldened by this, the Captain repeated his demand to the rest, but Steelkilt shouted up to him a terrific hint to stop his babbling and take himself off where he belonged. On the fifth morning three others of the mutineers bolted up into the air, breaking free from the desperate arms below that tried to hold them back. Only three were left."
"'Better turn to, now?' said the Captain with a heartless jeer."
"'Shut us up again, will you!' cried Steelkilt."
"'Oh certainly,' said the Captain, and the key clicked."

"It was at this point, gentlemen, that — enraged by the defection of seven of his former comrades, stung by the mocking voice that had last hailed him, and maddened by his long entombment in a place as black as the bowels of despair — it was then that Steelkilt proposed to the two Canallers, who so far had seemed to be of one mind with him, that they burst out of their hole at the next summons from the garrison and, armed with their keen mincing knives (long, crescent-shaped, heavy implements with a handle at each end), run amok from the bowsprit to the taffrail, and, if any devilish desperation could make it possible, seize the ship. For himself, he said, he would do this whether they joined him or not. That was the last night he would spend in that den. But the scheme met no opposition from the other two; they swore they were ready for that, or for any other mad thing — for anything, in short, but surrender. And what was more, each of them insisted on being the first man on deck when the time came to make the rush. But to this their leader objected just as fiercely, reserving that place for himself, especially as his two comrades would not give way to each other on the matter, and both of them could not be first, for the ladder would admit only one man at a time. And here, gentlemen, the foul play of these villains must come out."

"On hearing their leader's frantic plan, each of them, in his own separate soul, had suddenly hit, it would seem, on the same piece of treachery: namely, to be foremost in breaking out, so as to be the first of the three, though the last of the ten, to surrender, and thereby secure whatever small chance of pardon such conduct might earn. But when Steelkilt made known his determination still to lead them to the last, they somehow, by some subtle chemistry of villainy, mixed their until then secret treacheries together; and when their leader fell into a doze, they opened their souls to each other in three sentences, and bound the sleeper with cords, and gagged him with cords, and shrieked out for the Captain at midnight."

"Thinking murder was at hand, and smelling in the dark for the blood, he and all his armed mates and harpooners rushed for the forecastle. In a few minutes the scuttle was opened, and, bound hand and foot, the still-struggling ringleader was shoved up into the air by his treacherous allies, who at once claimed the honor of securing a man who had been fully ripe for murder. But all of them were collared and dragged along the deck like dead cattle; and, side by side, they were lashed up in the mizzen rigging like three quarters of meat, and there they hung till morning. 'Damn you,' cried the Captain, pacing back and forth in front of them, 'the vultures wouldn't touch you, you villains!'"

"At sunrise he summoned all hands, and, separating those who had rebelled from those who had taken no part in the mutiny, he told the former that he had a good mind to flog them all round — thought, on the whole, he would do so — he ought to — justice demanded it; but for the present, considering their timely surrender, he would let them go with a reprimand, which he duly delivered in the plain vernacular."

"'But as for you, you carrion rogues,' turning to the three men in the rigging, 'for you, I mean to mince you up for the try-pots.' And, seizing a rope, he applied it with all his might to the backs of the two traitors, until they yelled no more, but hung their heads lifelessly sideways, as the two crucified thieves are drawn."

"'My wrist is sprained with you!' he cried at last. 'But there is still rope enough left for you, my fine bantam, who wouldn't give up. Take that gag from his mouth, and let us hear what he can say for himself.'"

"For a moment the exhausted mutineer made a trembling motion of his cramped jaws, and then painfully twisting his head around, said in a sort of hiss, 'What I say is this — and mind it well — if you flog me, I murder you!'"
"'You say so? Then see how you frighten me' — and the Captain drew back with the rope to strike."
"'Best not,' hissed the Lakeman."
"'But I must' — and the rope was once more drawn back for the stroke."

"Steelkilt here hissed out something inaudible to all but the Captain, who, to the amazement of all hands, started back, paced the deck rapidly two or three times, and then suddenly throwing down his rope, said, 'I won't do it — let him go — cut him down, do you hear?'"

"But as the junior mates were hurrying to carry out the order, a pale man with a bandaged head stopped them — Radney, the chief mate. Ever since the blow, he had lain in his berth; but that morning, hearing the commotion on deck, he had crept out, and so far had watched the whole scene. His mouth was in such a state that he could hardly speak; but mumbling something about how he, for one, was willing and able to do what the captain dared not attempt, he snatched the rope and advanced on his bound enemy."
"'You are a coward!' hissed the Lakeman."

"'So I am, but take that.' The mate was in the very act of striking when another hiss stayed his raised arm. He paused — and then pausing no more, made good on his word, in spite of Steelkilt's threat, whatever that might have been. The three men were then cut down, all hands were turned to, and sullenly worked by the moody seamen, the iron pumps clanged as before."

"Just after dark that day, when one watch had gone below, a commotion was heard in the forecastle; and the two trembling traitors came running up and besieged the cabin door, saying they dared not stay among the crew. Pleas, cuffs, and kicks could not drive them back, so at their own request they were put down in the ship's run, the narrow afterpart of her hold, for their salvation. Still, no sign of mutiny reappeared among the rest. On the contrary, it seemed that, mainly at Steelkilt's urging, they had resolved to keep the strictest peace, obey all orders to the last, and, when the ship reached port, desert her in a body. But in order to ensure the quickest end to the voyage, they all agreed to one thing more — namely, not to sing out for whales if any should be discovered. For in spite of her leak, and in spite of all her other dangers, the Town-Ho still kept men at her mastheads, and her captain was just as willing to lower for a whale at that moment as on the day his ship first reached the cruising ground; and Radney the mate was quite as ready to trade his berth for a boat, and with his bandaged mouth try to gag the whale's living jaw in death."

"But though the Lakeman had persuaded the seamen to adopt this sort of passiveness in their conduct, he kept his own counsel (at least till all was over) about his own proper and private revenge on the man who had stung him in the very ventricles of his heart. He was in Radney the chief mate's watch; and, as if the infatuated man were trying to run more than halfway to meet his doom, after the scene at the rigging he insisted, against the captain's express advice, on resuming the command of his watch at night. On this, and on one or two other circumstances, Steelkilt systematically built the plan of his revenge."

"During the night, Radney had an unseamanlike way of sitting on the bulwarks of the quarter-deck and leaning his arm on the gunwale of the boat that was hoisted up there, a little above the ship's side. In this position, it was well known, he sometimes dozed. There was a considerable gap between the boat and the ship, and down through it lay the sea. Steelkilt calculated his time, and found that his next trick at the helm would come round at two o'clock in the morning of the third day from the one on which he had been betrayed. At his leisure, he spent the interval braiding something very carefully during his watches below."
"'What are you making there?' said a shipmate."
"'What do you think? What does it look like?'"
"'Like a lanyard for your bag. But it's an odd one, seems to me.'"
"'Yes, rather odd,' said the Lakeman, holding it at arm's length before him. 'But I think it will do. Shipmate, I haven't enough twine — have you any?'"
"But there was none in the forecastle."
"'Then I must get some from old Rad.' And he rose to go aft."
"'You don't mean to go begging to him, of all people!' said a sailor."

"'Why not? Do you think he won't do me a turn, when it's to help himself in the end, shipmate?' And going to the mate, he looked at him quietly and asked him for some twine to mend his hammock. It was given him — neither twine nor lanyard was ever seen again; but the next night an iron ball, closely netted, partly rolled out of the pocket of the Lakeman's monkey jacket as he was tucking the coat into his hammock for a pillow. Twenty-four hours later, his trick at the silent helm — close beside the man who was apt to doze over the grave always dug ready to the seaman's hand — that fatal hour was then to come; and in the foreordaining soul of Steelkilt, the mate already lay stark and stretched out as a corpse, with his forehead crushed in."

"But, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned. Yet complete revenge he had, and without being the avenger. For by a mysterious fate, Heaven itself seemed to step in to take out of his hands into its own the damning thing he would have done."

"It was just between daybreak and sunrise on the morning of the second day, when they were washing down the decks, that a stupid Teneriffe man, drawing water in the main-chains, all at once shouted out, 'There she rolls! There she rolls!' Jesu, what a whale! It was Moby Dick."
"'Moby Dick!' cried Don Sebastian. 'St. Dominic! Sir sailor, but do whales have christenings? Whom do you call Moby Dick?'"
"'A very white, and famous, and most deadly immortal monster, Don — but that would be too long a story.'"
"'How? How?' cried all the young Spaniards, crowding around."
"'No, Dons, Dons — no, no! I cannot tell that now. Let me get more into the air, Sirs.'"
"'The chicha! The chicha!' cried Don Pedro. 'Our vigorous friend looks faint — fill up his empty glass!'"

"No need, gentlemen; one moment, and I'll go on. — Now, gentlemen, suddenly seeing the snowy whale within fifty yards of the ship — forgetting the pact among the crew — in the excitement of the moment the Teneriffe man had instinctively and involuntarily raised his voice for the monster, though for some little time past it had been plainly visible from the three sullen mastheads. Everything was now a frenzy. 'The White Whale — the White Whale!' was the cry from captain, mates, and harpooners, who, undeterred by fearful rumors, were all eager to capture so famous and precious a fish; while the sullen crew eyed sideways, and with curses, the appalling beauty of the vast milky mass that, lit up by the level, spangling rays of the sun, shifted and glistened like a living opal in the blue morning sea. Gentlemen, a strange fatality runs through the whole course of these events, as if truly mapped out before the world itself was charted. The mutineer was the mate's bowsman, and when they were fast to a whale, it was his duty to sit next to him, while Radney stood up with his lance in the bow, and to haul in or slacken the line at the word of command. Moreover, when the four boats were lowered, the mate's got the start; and no one howled more fiercely with delight than Steelkilt as he strained at his oar. After a hard pull, their harpooner got fast, and, spear in hand, Radney sprang to the bow. He was always a furious man in a boat, it seems. And now his bandaged cry was to beach him on the whale's topmost back. Only too willing, his bowsman hauled him up and up, through a blinding foam that blended two whitenesses together, until suddenly the boat struck as if against a sunken ledge, and, tipping over, spilled out the standing mate. At that instant, as he fell on the whale's slippery back, the boat righted and was dashed aside by the swell, while Radney was tossed over into the sea on the other flank of the whale. He struck out through the spray, and for an instant was dimly seen through that veil, wildly trying to get himself out of the eye of Moby Dick. But the whale rushed around in a sudden maelstrom, seized the swimmer between his jaws, and, rearing high up with him, plunged headlong again and went down."

"Meanwhile, at the first bump of the boat's bottom, the Lakeman had slackened the line so as to drop astern out of the whirlpool; calmly looking on, he thought his own thoughts. But a sudden, terrific, downward jerk of the boat quickly brought his knife to the line. He cut it, and the whale was free. But at some distance Moby Dick rose again, with some tatters of Radney's red woolen shirt caught in the teeth that had destroyed him. All four boats gave chase again; but the whale eluded them, and finally disappeared altogether."

"In good time, the Town-Ho reached her port — a savage, solitary place where no civilized creature lived. There, led by the Lakeman, all but five or six of the foremast hands deliberately deserted among the palms, eventually, as it turned out, seizing a large double war-canoe of the savages and setting sail for some other harbor."

"With the ship's company reduced to just a handful, the captain called on the Islanders to help him in the laborious business of heaving down the ship to stop the leak. But this small band of whites was forced to keep such unresting watch over their dangerous allies, both by night and by day, and the hard work they went through was so extreme, that when the vessel was ready for sea again they were so weakened that the captain dared not set out with them in so heavy a vessel. After consulting with his officers, he anchored the ship as far offshore as possible, loaded and ran out his two cannon from the bows, stacked his muskets on the poop, and, warning the Islanders not to approach the ship at their peril, took one man with him, set the sail of his best whaleboat, and steered straight before the wind for Tahiti, five hundred miles away, to get reinforcements for his crew."

"On the fourth day of the voyage, a large canoe was sighted, which seemed to have stopped at a low coral island. He steered away from it; but the savage craft bore down on him, and soon the voice of Steelkilt hailed him to heave to, or he would run him under water. The captain presented a pistol. With one foot on each prow of the yoked war-canoes, the Lakeman laughed him to scorn, assuring him that if the pistol so much as clicked in the lock, he would bury him in bubbles and foam."
"'What do you want of me?' cried the captain."
"'Where are you bound? And for what are you bound?' demanded Steelkilt. 'No lies.'"
"'I am bound to Tahiti for more men.'"
"'Very good. Let me board you a moment — I come in peace.' With that he leaped from the canoe, swam to the boat, and climbing the gunwale, stood face to face with the captain."

"'Cross your arms, sir. Throw back your head. Now, repeat after me. As soon as Steelkilt leaves me, I swear to beach this boat on that island and remain there six days. If I do not, may lightning strike me!'"
"'A pretty scholar,' laughed the Lakeman. 'Adios, Senor!' And leaping into the sea, he swam back to his comrades."

"Watching the boat until it was fairly beached and drawn up to the roots of the coconut trees, Steelkilt set sail again, and in due time arrived at Tahiti, his own destination. There luck befriended him. Two ships were about to sail for France and were providentially in need of precisely the number of men the sailor led. They embarked, and so forever got the start of their former captain, had he been at all inclined to bring legal retribution on them."

"Some ten days after the French ships sailed, the whale-boat arrived, and the captain was forced to enlist some of the more civilized Tahitians, who had been somewhat used to the sea. Chartering a small native schooner, he returned with them to his vessel, and finding all well there, again resumed his cruising."

"Where Steelkilt now is, gentlemen, no one knows; but on the island of Nantucket, the widow of Radney still turns to the sea that refuses to give up its dead, and still in dreams sees the awful white whale that destroyed him. * * * *"
"'Are you through?' said Don Sebastian quietly."
"'I am, Don.'"

"'Then I beg you, tell me if, to the best of your own convictions, this story of yours is in substance really true? It is so exceedingly wonderful! Did you get it from an unquestionable source? Bear with me if I seem to press.'"
"'Also bear with all of us, sir sailor, for we all join in Don Sebastian's request,' cried the company, with great interest."
"'Is there a copy of the Holy Evangelists, the Gospels, in the Golden Inn, gentlemen?'"
"'No,' said Don Sebastian, 'but I know a worthy priest nearby who will quickly get one for me. I go for it — but are you sure about this? This may grow too serious.'"
"'Will you be so good as to bring the priest also, Don?'"

"'Though there are no Auto-da-Fés in Lima now,' said one of the company to another, 'I fear our sailor friend runs the risk of the archbishop's attention. Let us move farther out of the moonlight. I see no need for this.'"
"'Excuse me for running after you, Don Sebastian; but may I also ask that you will be particular in getting the largest-sized Evangelists you can.'"
"'This is the priest; he brings you the Evangelists,' said Don Sebastian gravely, returning with a tall and solemn figure."
"'Let me remove my hat. Now, venerable priest, further into the light, and hold the Holy Book before me that I may touch it.'"

"'So help me Heaven, and on my honor the story I have told you, gentlemen, is in substance and its great items, true. I know it to be true. It happened on this earth. I walked that ship. I knew the crew. I have seen and talked with Steelkilt since the death of Radney.'"

chapters.title: Chapter 55 — Of the Monstrous Pictures of Whales
paragraphs: Before long I shall paint for you, as well as one can without canvas, something like the true form of the whale as he actually appears to the eye of the whaleman when, in his own whole body, the whale is moored alongside the whale-ship so that he can fairly be stepped upon there. It may be worthwhile, therefore, to look first at those curious imaginary portraits of him which, even down to the present day, confidently challenge the faith of the landsman. It is time to set the world right in this matter, by proving such pictures of the whale all wrong.

It may be that the original source of all those pictorial delusions will be found among the oldest Hindu, Egyptian, and Greek sculptures. For ever since those inventive but unscrupulous times when, on the marble panels of temples, the pedestals of statues, and on shields, medallions, cups, and coins, the dolphin was drawn in scales of chain-armor like Saladin's, and with a helmeted head like St. George's — ever since then, something of the same sort of license has prevailed, not only in most popular pictures of the whale, but in many scientific presentations of him.

Now, by far the most ancient surviving portrait that in any way claims to be the whale's is to be found in the famous cave-temple of Elephanta, in India. The Brahmins maintain that in the almost endless sculptures of that immemorial temple, all the trades and pursuits, every conceivable occupation of man, were prefigured ages before any of them actually came into being. No wonder, then, that our noble profession of whaling should in some way have been foreshadowed there. The Hindu whale referred to occurs in a separate section of the wall, depicting the incarnation of Vishnu in the form of leviathan, known to scholars as the Matse Avatar. But though this sculpture is half man and half whale, so as to show only the tail of the latter, even that small section of him is all wrong. It looks more like the tapering tail of an anaconda than the broad palms of the true whale's majestic flukes.

But go to the old galleries, and look now at a great Christian painter's portrait of this fish; for he succeeds no better than the antediluvian Hindu. It is Guido's picture of Perseus rescuing Andromeda from the sea-monster or whale. Where did Guido get the model for such a strange creature as that? Nor does Hogarth, in painting the same scene in his own "Perseus Descending," make out one bit better. The huge bulk of that Hogarthian monster undulates on the surface, scarcely drawing one inch of water. It has a sort of howdah (the canopied seat carried on an elephant's back) on its back, and its gaping, tusked mouth, into which the waves are rolling, might be taken for the Traitors' Gate that leads by water from the Thames into the Tower. Then there are the Prodromus whales of old Scotch Sibbald, and Jonah's whale as depicted in the prints of old Bibles and the woodcuts of old primers. What shall be said of these? As for the bookbinder's whale winding like a vine-stalk round the stock of a descending anchor — as stamped and gilded on the spines and title-pages of many books both old and new — that is a very picturesque but purely fabulous creature, copied, I take it, from similar figures on antique vases. Though it is universally called a dolphin, I nevertheless call this bookbinder's fish an attempt at a whale, because that is what it was meant to be when the device was first introduced. It was introduced by an old Italian publisher somewhere around the 15th century, during the Revival of Learning; and in those days, and even down to a comparatively late period, dolphins were popularly supposed to be a species of the Leviathan.

In the vignettes and other decorations of some ancient books you will at times meet with very curious attempts at the whale, where all manner of spouts, fountains, hot springs and cold, Saratoga and Baden-Baden, come bubbling up from his inexhaustible brain. On the title-page of the original edition of the "Advancement of Learning" you will find some curious whales.

But leaving all these unprofessional attempts, let us glance at those pictures of leviathan that claim to be sober, scientific drawings, by those who know. In old Harris's collection of voyages there are some plates of whales taken from a Dutch book of voyages, A.D. 1671, entitled "A Whaling Voyage to Spitzbergen in the ship Jonas in the Whale, Peter Peterson of Friesland, master." In one of those plates the whales, like great rafts of logs, are shown lying among ice-islands, with white bears running over their living backs. In another plate, the prodigious blunder is made of representing the whale with vertical flukes.

Then again, there is an imposing quarto volume written by one Captain Colnett, a Post Captain in the English navy, entitled "A Voyage round Cape Horn into the South Seas, for the purpose of extending the Spermaceti Whale Fisheries." In this book is an outline claiming to be a "Picture of a Physeter or Spermaceti whale, drawn by scale from one killed on the coast of Mexico, August, 1793, and hoisted on deck." I have no doubt the captain had this truthful picture made for the benefit of his marines. To mention just one thing about it, let me say that it has an eye which, applied according to the accompanying scale to a full-grown sperm whale, would make the eye of that whale a bow-window some five feet long. Ah, my gallant captain, why didn't you give us Jonah looking out of that eye!

Nor are the most conscientious compilations of Natural History for the benefit of the young and tender free from the same outrageous kind of mistake. Look at that popular work "Goldsmith's Animated Nature." In the abridged London edition of 1807, there are plates of an alleged "whale" and a "narwhal." I do not wish to seem inelegant, but this unsightly whale looks much like an amputated sow; and as for the narwhal, one glimpse of it is enough to amaze anyone that in this nineteenth century such a hippogriff could be passed off as genuine on any intelligent public of schoolboys.

Then again, in 1825, Bernard Germain, Count de Lacépède, a great naturalist, published a scientific, systematic book on whales, in which there are several pictures of the different species of the Leviathan. All of these are incorrect; and as for the picture of the Mysticetus or Greenland whale (that is to say, the Right whale), even Scoresby, a man of long experience with that species, declares that it has no counterpart in nature.

But the crowning touch to all this blundering business was reserved for the scientific Frederick Cuvier, brother of the famous Baron. In 1836 he published a Natural History of Whales, in which he gives what he calls a picture of the Sperm Whale. Before showing that picture to any Nantucketer, you had better arrange for your speedy retreat from Nantucket. In a word, Frederick Cuvier's Sperm Whale is not a Sperm Whale, but a squash. Of course, he never had the benefit of a whaling voyage (such men seldom have), but where he got that picture, who can tell? Perhaps he got it the way his scientific predecessor in the same field, Desmarest, got one of his authentic abortions — that is, from a Chinese drawing. And what lively lads with the pencil those Chinese are, many odd cups and saucers inform us.

As for the sign-painters' whales seen in the streets, hanging over the shops of oil-dealers, what shall be said of them? They are generally Richard III whales, with dromedary humps, and very savage, breakfasting on three or four sailor tarts — that is, whaleboats full of sailors — their deformities floundering in seas of blood and blue paint.

But these many mistakes in depicting the whale are not so very surprising after all. Consider! Most of the scientific drawings have been taken from the stranded fish; and these are about as accurate as a drawing of a wrecked ship with a broken back would be in representing the noble animal itself in all its unbattered pride of hull and spars. Though elephants have stood for their full-length portraits, the living Leviathan has never yet fairly floated himself for his. The living whale, in his full majesty and significance, is only to be seen at sea in unfathomable waters; and afloat, the vast bulk of him is out of sight, like a launched ship-of-the-line; and out of that element it is eternally impossible for mortal man to hoist him bodily into the air so as to preserve all his mighty swells and undulations. And, not to speak of the highly probable difference in outline between a young suckling whale and a full-grown Platonic Leviathan — even in the case of one of those young suckling whales hoisted to a ship's deck, his shape is then so outlandish, eel-like, limp and changeable that the devil himself could not catch his precise expression.

But it may be supposed that from the naked skeleton of the stranded whale, accurate hints may be gathered about his true form. Not at all. For it is one of the more curious things about this Leviathan that his skeleton gives very little idea of his general shape. Though Jeremy Bentham's skeleton, which hangs as a candelabrum in the library of one of his executors, correctly conveys the idea of a burly-browed utilitarian old gentleman, with all of Jeremy's other leading personal characteristics, nothing of this kind could be inferred from any leviathan's articulated bones. In fact, as the great anatomist Hunter says, the mere skeleton of the whale bears the same relation to the fully clothed and padded animal as the insect does to the chrysalis that so roundly envelops it. This peculiarity is strikingly evident in the head, as will be incidentally shown in some part of this book. It is also very curiously displayed in the side fin, the bones of which correspond almost exactly to the bones of the human hand, minus only the thumb. This fin has four regular bone-fingers: the index, middle, ring, and little finger. But all these are permanently lodged in their fleshy covering, as human fingers are in an artificial covering. "However recklessly the whale may sometimes serve us," said humorous Stubb one day, "he can never truly be said to handle us without mittens."

For all these reasons, then, whichever way you look at it, you must conclude that the great Leviathan is that one creature in the world which must remain unpainted to the last. True, one portrait may hit the mark much nearer than another, but none can hit it with any very considerable degree of exactness. So there is no earthly way of finding out precisely what the whale really looks like. And the only way you can get even a tolerable idea of his living outline is by going whaling yourself; but by doing so, you run no small risk of being stove in and sunk by him for good. So it seems to me you had best not be too particular in your curiosity about this Leviathan.

chapters.title: Chapter 56 — Of the Less Erroneous Pictures of Whales, and the True
paragraphs: Pictures of Whaling Scenes.

In connection with the monstrous pictures of whales, I am strongly tempted here to take up those still more monstrous stories about them which are found in certain books, both ancient and modern, especially in Pliny, Purchas, Hackluyt, Harris, Cuvier, and so forth. But I will let that matter pass.

I know of only four published outlines of the great Sperm Whale: Colnett's, Huggins's, Frederick Cuvier's, and Beale's. In the previous chapter Colnett and Cuvier were referred to. Huggins's is far better than theirs; but Beale's is by far the best. All of Beale's drawings of this whale are good, except the middle figure in the picture of three whales in various attitudes that heads his second chapter. His frontispiece, boats attacking Sperm Whales, though no doubt likely to provoke the polite skepticism of some parlor men, is admirably correct and lifelike in its general effect. Some of the Sperm Whale drawings in J. Ross Browne are pretty correct in outline; but they are wretchedly engraved. That is not his fault, though.

Of the Right Whale, the best outline pictures are in Scoresby. But they are drawn on too small a scale to give the impression one would want. He has only one picture of whaling scenes, and this is a sad deficiency, because it is only through such pictures, when done well, that you can get anything like a truthful idea of the living whale as seen by his living hunters.

But taken all in all, by far the finest — though in some details not the most correct — presentations of whales and whaling scenes to be found anywhere are two large French engravings, well executed, and taken from paintings by one Garnery. They represent attacks on the Sperm and the Right Whale respectively. In the first engraving a noble Sperm Whale is shown in the full majesty of his might, just risen beneath the boat from the depths of the ocean, and bearing high in the air upon his back the terrible wreck of the smashed planks. The prow of the boat is partly unbroken, and is drawn just balancing upon the monster's spine; and standing in that prow, for that one single immeasurable flash of time, you see an oarsman, half shrouded by the angry, boiling spout of the whale, and in the act of leaping, as if from a cliff. The action of the whole thing is wonderfully good and true. The half-emptied line-tub floats on the whitened sea; the wooden poles of the spilled harpoons bob in it at a slant; the heads of the swimming crew are scattered about the whale in contrasting expressions of fright; while in the black, stormy distance the ship is bearing down upon the scene. Serious fault might be found with the anatomical details of this whale, but let that pass; since, for the life of me, I could not draw so good a one.

In the second engraving, the boat is in the act of drawing alongside the barnacled flank of a large running Right Whale, which rolls his black weedy bulk in the sea like some mossy rock-slide from the Patagonian cliffs. His jets are upright, full, and black like soot, so that from so abundant a smoke in the chimney, you would think there must be a fine supper cooking in the great bowels below. Sea birds are pecking at the small crabs, shellfish, and other sea candies and macaroni which the Right Whale sometimes carries on his pestilent back. And all the while the thick-lipped leviathan is rushing through the deep, leaving tons of tumultuous white curds in his wake, and causing the light boat to rock in the swells like a skiff caught near the paddle-wheels of an ocean steamer. Thus the foreground is all raging commotion; but behind, in admirable artistic contrast, is the glassy level of a becalmed sea, the drooping, unstarched sails of the powerless ship, and the inert mass of a dead whale, a conquered fortress, with the flag of capture hanging lazily from the whale-pole stuck into his spout-hole.

Who Garnery the painter is, or was, I do not know. But I would stake my life that he was either practically familiar with his subject, or else marvelously tutored by some experienced whaleman. The French are the lads for painting action. Go and gaze at all the paintings of Europe, and where will you find such a gallery of living and breathing commotion on canvas as in that triumphal hall at Versailles, where the viewer fights his way, pell-mell, through the successive great battles of France; where every sword seems a flash of the Northern Lights, and the successive armed kings and Emperors dash by like a charge of crowned centaurs? Not wholly unworthy of a place in that gallery are these sea battle-pieces of Garnery.

The natural talent of the French for seizing the picturesqueness of things seems to be especially evident in the paintings and engravings they have of their whaling scenes. With not one tenth of England's experience in the fishery, and not a thousandth part of that of the Americans, they have nevertheless furnished both nations with the only finished sketches at all capable of conveying the real spirit of the whale hunt. For the most part, the English and American whale draftsmen seem entirely content with presenting the mechanical outline of things, such as the vacant profile of the whale — which, so far as picturesque effect is concerned, is about equivalent to sketching the profile of a pyramid. Even Scoresby, the justly renowned Right whaleman, after giving us a stiff full-length of the Greenland whale and three or four delicate miniatures of narwhals and porpoises, treats us to a series of classical engravings of boat hooks, chopping knives, and grapnels; and with the microscopic diligence of a Leuwenhoeck (the pioneer of the microscope) submits to the inspection of a shivering world ninety-six facsimiles of magnified Arctic snow crystals. I mean no disrespect to the excellent voyager (I honor him as a veteran), but in so important a matter it was certainly an oversight not to have obtained for every crystal a sworn affidavit taken before a Greenland Justice of the Peace.

In addition to those fine engravings from Garnery, there are two other French engravings worthy of note, by someone who signs himself "H. Durand." One of them, though not exactly suited to our present purpose, nevertheless deserves mention on other grounds. It is a quiet noon scene among the islands of the Pacific: a French whaler anchored inshore in a calm, lazily taking water on board; the loosened sails of the ship and the long leaves of the palms in the background both drooping together in the breezeless air. The effect is very fine, when you consider that it presents the hardy fishermen in one of their few moments of oriental repose. The other engraving is quite a different affair: the ship hove-to on the open sea, in the very heart of leviathan life, with a Right Whale alongside; the vessel (in the act of cutting-in) hove over toward the monster as if to a quay; and a boat, hurriedly pushing off from this scene of activity, is about to give chase to whales in the distance. The harpoons and lances lie leveled for use; three oarsmen are just setting the mast in its hole; while from a sudden roll of the sea, the little craft stands half-upright out of the water, like a rearing horse. From the ship, the smoke of the torments of the boiling whale is going up like the smoke over a village of blacksmiths; and to windward, a black cloud, rising up with the promise of squalls and rain, seems to quicken the activity of the excited seamen.

chapters.title: Chapter 57 — Of Whales in Paint; in Teeth; in Wood; in Sheet-Iron; in
paragraphs: Stone; in Mountains; in Stars.

On Tower Hill, as you go down to the London docks, you may have seen a crippled beggar (or kedger, as the sailors say) holding a painted board before him, representing the tragic scene in which he lost his leg. There are three whales and three boats; and one of the boats (presumed to contain the missing leg in all its original wholeness) is being crunched by the jaws of the foremost whale. For these ten years, they tell me, that man has held up that picture and exhibited that stump to an incredulous world. But the time of his vindication has now come. His three whales are as good whales as were ever published in Wapping, at any rate; and his stump as unquestionable a stump as any you will find in the western clearings. But though forever mounted on that stump, the poor whaleman never makes a stump-speech; instead, with downcast eyes, he stands ruefully contemplating his own amputation.

Throughout the Pacific, and also in Nantucket, and New Bedford, and Sag Harbor, you will come across lively sketches of whales and whaling scenes, engraved by the fishermen themselves on Sperm Whale teeth, or on ladies' busks (corset stays) worked out of Right Whale bone, and other such skrimshander (scrimshaw) articles, as the whalemen call the numerous ingenious little objects they elaborately carve out of the rough material in their hours of ocean leisure. Some of them have little boxes of dentist-like tools, specially intended for the skrimshandering business. But in general they toil with their jackknives alone; and with that almost all-powerful tool of the sailor, they will turn out for you anything you please in the way of a mariner's fancy.

Long exile from Christendom and civilization inevitably restores a man to that condition in which God placed him — that is, what is called savagery. Your true whale-hunter is as much a savage as an Iroquois. I myself am a savage, owing allegiance to no one but the King of the Cannibals — and ready at any moment to rebel against him.

Now, one of the peculiar characteristics of the savage in his domestic hours is his wonderful patience and industry. An ancient Hawaiian war-club or spear-paddle, in its full complexity and elaboration of carving, is as great a testament to human perseverance as a Latin dictionary. For with nothing but a bit of broken sea-shell or a shark's tooth, that miraculous intricacy of wooden net-work has been achieved. And it has cost steady years of steady work.

As with the Hawaiian savage, so with the white sailor-savage. With the same marvelous patience, and with the same single shark's tooth of his one poor jackknife, he will carve you a bit of bone sculpture — not quite as expertly made, but as densely packed in its maze-like design as the Greek savage Achilles's shield, and full of barbaric spirit and suggestion, as the prints of that fine old Dutch savage, Albert Durer.

Wooden whales, or whales cut in profile out of the small dark slabs of the noble South Sea war-wood, are frequently found in the forecastles of American whalers. Some of them are carved with considerable accuracy.

At some old gable-roofed country houses you will see brass whales hung by the tail as knockers on the roadside door. When the porter is sleepy, the anvil-headed whale would work best. But these knocking whales are seldom noteworthy as faithful likenesses. On the steeples of some old-fashioned churches you will see sheet-iron whales placed there as weather-vanes. But they are so high up, and besides are to all intents and purposes labeled "Hands off!" — so you cannot examine them closely enough to judge their merit.

In bony, ribbed regions of the earth, where at the base of high broken cliffs masses of rock lie strewn in fantastic groupings upon the plain, you will often discover shapes like the petrified forms of the Leviathan partly merged in grass, which on a windy day breaks against them in a surf of green waves.

Then again, in mountainous countries where the traveler is continually ringed by amphitheater-like heights, here and there from some lucky vantage point you will catch passing glimpses of the profiles of whales outlined along the undulating ridges. But you must be a thorough whaleman to see these sights; and not only that, but if you wish to return to such a sight again, you must be sure to take the exact intersecting latitude and longitude of your first standpoint; otherwise, so much a matter of chance are such observations of the hills, your precise earlier standpoint would require laborious rediscovery — like the Soloma Islands, which still remain unknown, though high-ruffed Mendanna once walked them and old Figuera chronicled them.

Nor, when your imagination is expanded and lifted by your subject, can you fail to trace out great whales in the starry heavens, and boats in pursuit of them — as when, long filled with thoughts of war, the Eastern nations saw armies locked in battle among the clouds. Thus in the North I have chased Leviathan round and round the Pole with the revolutions of the bright points that first outlined him for me. And beneath the brilliant Antarctic skies I have boarded the Argo-Navis and joined the chase against the starry Cetus far beyond the utmost reach of Hydrus and the Flying Fish.

With a frigate's anchors for my bridle-bits and bundles of harpoons for spurs, I wish I could mount that whale and leap the topmost skies, to see whether the fabled heavens with all their countless tents really lie encamped beyond my mortal sight!

chapters.title: Chapter 58 — Brit
paragraphs: Steering northeast from the Crozetts, we fell in with vast meadows of brit, the minute, yellow substance upon which the Right Whale largely feeds. For league upon league it undulated around us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe, golden wheat.

On the second day, numbers of Right Whales were seen, who — safe from the attack of a Sperm Whaler like the Pequod — with open jaws sluggishly swam through the brit. It clung to the fringing fibers of that wondrous Venetian blind in their mouths, and was in this way separated from the water that escaped at the lip.

As morning mowers, who side by side slowly and seethingly advance their scythes through the long wet grass of marshy meadows — even so these monsters swam, making a strange, grassy, cutting sound and leaving behind them endless swaths of blue upon the yellow sea.*

*That part of the sea known among whalemen as the "Brazil Banks" does not bear that name because of shallows and soundings there, as the Banks of Newfoundland do, but because of this remarkable meadow-like appearance, caused by the vast drifts of brit continually floating in those latitudes, where the Right Whale is often hunted.

But it was only the sound they made as they parted the brit that reminded one of mowers at all. Seen from the mastheads, especially when they paused and were still for a while, their vast black forms looked more like lifeless masses of rock than anything else. And as in the great hunting countries of India the stranger at a distance will sometimes pass elephants lying on the plains without knowing them for what they are, taking them for bare, blackened rises of the ground, so it often is with anyone who sees this species of the leviathans of the sea for the first time. And even when they are recognized at last, their immense size makes it very hard really to believe that such bulky masses of overgrowth can possibly be alive, in every part, with the same sort of life that lives in a dog or a horse.

Indeed, in other respects, you can hardly regard any creatures of the deep with the same feelings that you do those of the shore. For though some old naturalists have maintained that all creatures of the land have their kind in the sea — and though, taking a broad general view of the thing, this may very well be — yet when it comes to particulars, where, for example, does the ocean furnish any fish that in disposition matches the wise kindness of the dog? The accursed shark alone can in any general respect be said to bear some comparable likeness to him.

But though, to landsmen in general, the native inhabitants of the seas have always been regarded with feelings unspeakably unsociable and repellent; though we know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so that Columbus sailed over numberless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one; though by far the most terrible of all mortal disasters have, from time immemorial and without distinction, befallen tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone upon the waters; though a moment's consideration will teach that, however much baby man may brag of his science and skill, and however much, in a flattering future, that science and skill may increase, yet forever and forever, to the crack of doom, the sea will insult and murder him, and pulverize the stateliest, stiffest frigate he can make — nevertheless, by the continual repetition of these very impressions, man has lost that sense of the full awfulness of the sea which originally belongs to it.

The first boat we read of floated on an ocean that with Portuguese vengeance had drowned a whole world without leaving so much as a widow. That same ocean rolls now. That same ocean destroyed the wrecked ships of last year. Yes, foolish mortals — Noah's flood has not yet subsided. Two thirds of the fair world it still covers.

How do the sea and the land differ, that a miracle upon one is not a miracle upon the other? Supernatural terrors seized the Hebrews when under the feet of Korah and his company the living ground opened and swallowed them up forever. Yet not a modern sun ever sets without the living sea swallowing up ships and crews in precisely the same manner.

But not only is the sea such a foe to man, who is alien to it — it is also a fiend to its own offspring. Worse than the Persian host who murdered his own guests, it does not spare the creatures it has itself produced. Like a savage tigress that, tossing in the jungle, crushes her own cubs, so the sea dashes even the mightiest whales against the rocks, and leaves them there side by side with the split wrecks of ships. No mercy, no power but its own controls it. Panting and snorting like a mad battle horse that has lost its rider, the masterless ocean overruns the globe.

Consider the subtlety of the sea — how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, invisible for the most part, treacherously hidden beneath the loveliest shades of blue. Consider also the devilish brilliance and beauty of many of its most merciless species, like the elegantly shaped bodies of many kinds of sharks. Consider, once more, the universal cannibalism of the sea, all of whose creatures prey upon each other, waging eternal war since the world began.

Consider all this, and then turn to this green, gentle, and most docile earth. Consider them both — the sea and the land — and do you not find a strange parallel to something in yourself? For as this appalling ocean surrounds the green land, so in the soul of man there lies one island Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but surrounded by all the horrors of the half-known life. God keep you! Do not push off from that island — you can never return!

chapters.title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — though with no stagnant calm about it — when the long burnished path of sunlight on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the negro yelled out, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

Upon this, the seamen rushed to the yardarms, as in swarming-time the bees rush to the branches. Bareheaded in the sultry sun, Ahab stood on the bowsprit, and with one hand pushed far behind him in readiness to wave orders to the helmsman, he cast his eager glance in the direction indicated aloft by the outstretched, motionless arm of Daggoo.

Whether the fleeting attendance of that one still and solitary jet had gradually worked upon Ahab, so that he was now prepared to connect the ideas of gentleness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he hunted, or whether his eagerness misled him — whichever way it might have been, no sooner did he clearly perceive the white mass than with fierce intensity he instantly gave orders for lowering.

The four boats were soon on the water, Ahab's in advance, all swiftly pulling toward their prey. Soon it went down. And while, with oars suspended, we were awaiting its reappearance — look! — in the same spot where it sank, once more it slowly rose. Almost forgetting for the moment all thoughts of Moby Dick, we now gazed at the most wondrous phenomenon which the secret seas have ever revealed to mankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs in length and breadth, of a gleaming cream-color, lay floating on the water, with innumerable long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as if blindly to clutch at any unlucky object within reach. It had no perceptible face or front; no conceivable sign of either sensation or instinct; but it undulated there on the waves, an unearthly, formless, chance-like apparition of life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I would almost rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him than have seen you, white ghost!"
"What was it, sir?" said Flask.
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions the sperm whalemen in general have connected with the sight of this object, it is certain that the very rarity of a glimpse of it has gone far to invest it with ominous significance. So rarely is it seen that, though one and all of them declare it to be the largest living thing in the ocean, very few of them have any but the vaguest ideas about its true nature and form; nevertheless, they believe it furnishes the sperm whale with his only food. For though other species of whales find their food above water, and may be seen by man in the act of feeding, the spermaceti whale obtains his whole food in unknown zones below the surface; and only by inference can anyone tell what, precisely, that food consists of. At times, when closely pursued, he will vomit up what are supposed to be the detached arms of the squid, some of those thus brought up exceeding twenty and thirty feet in length. They imagine that the monster to which these arms belonged ordinarily clings by them to the bed of the ocean; and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, is supplied with teeth in order to attack and tear it.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppodan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classed among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward respects it would seem to belong — but only as the Anak of the tribe — its biblical giant.

chapters.title: Chapter 60 — The Line
paragraphs: With reference to the whaling scene soon to be described, as well as for the better understanding of all similar scenes presented elsewhere, I must speak here of the magical, sometimes horrible whale-line.

The line originally used in the fishery was of the best hemp, only lightly treated with tar vapor, not saturated with tar as ordinary ropes are. For while tar, as ordinarily used, makes the hemp more pliable for the ropemaker, and also makes the rope itself more convenient for the sailor in common ship use, not only would the ordinary quantity stiffen the whale-line too much for the close coiling it must undergo; but, as most seamen are beginning to learn, tar in general by no means adds to a rope's durability or strength, however much compactness and gloss it may give it.

In recent years, Manilla rope has in the American fishery almost entirely replaced hemp as a material for whale-lines. Though not as durable as hemp, it is stronger and far more soft and elastic. And I will add — since there is an aesthetics in all things — it is much more handsome and becoming to the boat than hemp. Hemp is a dusky, dark fellow, a sort of Indian; but Manilla is like a golden-haired Circassian to look at.

The whale-line is only two-thirds of an inch thick. At first sight you would not think it as strong as it really is. By experiment, each of its fifty-one yarns will suspend a weight of one hundred and twenty pounds, so that the whole rope will bear a strain nearly equal to three tons. In length, the common sperm whale-line measures something over two hundred fathoms. Toward the stern of the boat it is spirally coiled away in the tub — not like the worm-pipe (the coiled tube) of a still, though, but so as to form one round, cheese-shaped mass of densely bedded "sheaves," or layers of concentric spirals, without any hollow except the "heart," the tiny vertical tube formed at the axis of the cheese. Since the least tangle or kink in the coiling would, as the line ran out, infallibly take off somebody's arm, leg, or entire body, the utmost care is taken in stowing the line in its tub. Some harpooners will spend almost an entire morning at this business, carrying the line high aloft and then reeving it downward through a block toward the tub, so as to free it of every possible wrinkle and twist in the act of coiling.

In the English boats two tubs are used instead of one, the same line being continuously coiled in both tubs. There is some advantage in this, because these twin tubs, being so small, fit more readily into the boat and do not strain it so much; whereas the American tub, nearly three feet in diameter and of proportionate depth, makes rather bulky freight for a craft whose planks are only half an inch thick; for the bottom of the whale-boat is like ice at the critical point, which will bear up a considerable weight if it is spread out, but not very much if it is concentrated. When the painted canvas cover is clapped on the American line-tub, the boat looks as if it were pulling off with a prodigious great wedding-cake to present to the whales.

Both ends of the line are exposed; the lower end finishes in an eye-splice, or loop, which comes up from the bottom against the side of the tub and hangs over its edge, completely free of everything. This arrangement of the lower end is necessary for two reasons. First: to make it easier to fasten to it an additional line from a neighboring boat, in case the struck whale should sound (dive) so deep as to threaten to carry off the entire line originally attached to the harpoon. In these instances the whale is, of course, passed like a mug of ale, as it were, from the one boat to the other; though the first boat always hovers close by to assist its partner. Second: this arrangement is indispensable for common safety's sake; for if the lower end of the line were in any way attached to the boat, and the whale were then to run the line out to the end almost in a single smoking minute, as he sometimes does, he would not stop there, for the doomed boat would infallibly be dragged down after him into the depths of the sea; and in that case no town-crier would ever find her again.

Before lowering the boat for the chase, the upper end of the line is taken aft from the tub, and, passing round the loggerhead there (a stout wooden post in the stern), is carried forward again the entire length of the boat, resting crosswise upon the loom, or handle, of every man's oar, so that it jogs against his wrist in rowing; and it also passes between the men, as they sit alternately at the opposite gunwales, to the leaded chocks, or grooves, in the extreme pointed prow of the boat, where a wooden pin or skewer the size of a common quill keeps it from slipping out. From the chocks it hangs in a slight festoon over the bows, and is then passed inside the boat again; and after some ten or twenty fathoms of it (called box-line) have been coiled upon the box in the bows, it continues on its way to the gunwale still a little further aft, and is then attached to the short-warp — the rope which is directly connected with the harpoon; but before that connection is made, the short-warp goes through various mystifications too tedious to detail.

Thus the whale-line folds the whole boat in its complicated coils, twisting and writhing around it in almost every direction. All the oarsmen are caught up in its perilous contortions, so that to the timid eye of the landsman they seem like Indian jugglers, with the deadliest snakes playfully draped around their limbs. No son of mortal woman can seat himself for the first time amid those hempen intricacies and, while straining his utmost at the oar, reflect that at any unknown instant the harpoon may be darted and all these horrible contortions be set in play like ringed lightning — no one can be placed like that without a shudder that makes the very marrow in his bones quiver like a shaken jelly. Yet habit — strange thing! what can habit not accomplish? — livelier sallies, merrier mirth, better jokes, and brighter repartee you never heard over your mahogany dinner table than you will hear over the half-inch white cedar of the whale-boat, when it is hung with hangman's nooses like this; and, like the six burghers of Calais before King Edward, the six men who make up the crew pull into the jaws of death with a halter around every neck, as you might say.

Perhaps a very little thought will now enable you to account for those repeated whaling disasters — some few of which are casually recorded — of this man or that man being taken out of the boat by the line and lost. For when the line is darting out, to be seated in the boat then is like being seated in the midst of the manifold whizzings of a steam-engine in full play, when every flying beam and shaft and wheel is grazing you. It is worse; for you cannot sit motionless in the heart of these perils, because the boat is rocking like a cradle, and you are pitched one way and the other without the slightest warning; and only by a certain self-adjusting buoyancy, and by willing and acting in the same instant, can you escape being made a Mazeppa of (like Byron's hero, lashed to a runaway horse) and carried off where the all-seeing sun himself could never pick you out.

Again: as the profound calm which only seems to precede and foretell the storm is perhaps more dreadful than the storm itself — for, indeed, the calm is only the wrapper and envelope of the storm, and contains it within itself, as the seemingly harmless rifle holds the fatal powder, and the ball, and the explosion — so the graceful repose of the line, as it silently snakes about the oarsmen before being brought into actual play, is a thing which carries more true terror than any other aspect of this dangerous affair. But why say more? All men live enveloped in whale-lines. All are born with halters round their necks; but it is only when caught in the swift, sudden turn of death that mortals realize the silent, subtle, ever-present perils of life. And if you are a philosopher, then even seated in the whale-boat you would not at heart feel one bit more terror than if you were seated before your evening fire with a poker, and not a harpoon, by your side.

chapters.title: Chapter 61 — Stubb Kills a Whale
paragraphs: If to Starbuck the apparition of the Squid was a thing of omens, to Queequeg it was quite a different matter.
"When you see him squid," said the savage, honing his harpoon in the bow of his hoisted boat, "then you quick see him sperm whale."

The next day was exceedingly still and sultry, and with nothing special to occupy them, the Pequod's crew could hardly resist the spell of sleep brought on by such an empty sea. For this part of the Indian Ocean through which we were then voyaging is not what whalemen call a lively ground; that is, it offers fewer glimpses of porpoises, dolphins, flying fish, and other lively inhabitants of busier waters than the grounds off the Rio de la Plata, or the in-shore ground off Peru.
