It was my turn to stand at the foremast-head; and with my shoulders leaning against the slackened royal shrouds, I swayed idly back and forth in what seemed an enchanted air. No resolution could withstand it; in that dreamy mood, losing all consciousness, at last my soul went out of my body, though my body still continued to sway, as a pendulum will long after the power that first moved it is withdrawn.

Before forgetfulness came over me altogether, I had noticed that the seamen at the main and mizzen mastheads were already drowsy. So at last all three of us swung lifelessly from the spars, and for every swing we made there was a nod from below from the slumbering helmsman. The waves, too, nodded their lazy crests; and across the wide trance of the sea, east nodded to west, and the sun over all.

Suddenly bubbles seemed to be bursting beneath my closed eyes; my hands gripped the shrouds like vises; some invisible, gracious power preserved me; with a shock I came back to life. And look! Close under our lee, not forty fathoms off, a gigantic Sperm Whale lay rolling in the water like the capsized hull of a frigate, his broad, glossy back, of an Ethiopian hue, glistening in the sun's rays like a mirror. But lazily undulating in the trough of the sea, and every now and then calmly spouting his vapory jet, the whale looked like a portly burgher smoking his pipe on a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was your last. As if struck by some enchanter's wand, the sleepy ship and every sleeper in it all at once started awake; and more than a score of voices from all parts of the vessel, together with the three notes from aloft, shouted out the usual cry, as the great fish slowly and regularly spouted the sparkling brine into the air.
"Clear away the boats! Luff!" cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he slammed the helm down before the helmsman could reach the spokes.

The sudden shouts of the crew must have alarmed the whale; and before the boats were down, majestically turning, he swam away to leeward, but with such steady tranquility, and making so few ripples as he swam, that Ahab, thinking that after all he might not yet be alarmed, gave orders that not an oar should be used and no man must speak except in whispers. So, seated like Ontario Indians on the gunwales of the boats, we swiftly but silently paddled along, since the calm would not allow the noiseless sails to be set. Presently, as we glided along in chase, the monster flicked his tail straight up forty feet into the air, and then sank out of sight like a tower swallowed up.

"There go flukes!" was the cry — an announcement immediately followed by Stubb's producing his match and lighting his pipe, for now a breathing space was granted. After the full interval of his sounding (his deep dive) had passed, the whale rose again, and being now ahead of the smoker's boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted on the honor of the capture. It was obvious now that the whale had at last become aware of his pursuers. All cautious silence was therefore no longer of any use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered his crew on to the attack.
Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. Fully alive to his danger, he was going "head out" — that part projecting at a slant from the mad yeast he was brewing.*

*It will be seen elsewhere what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale's enormous head consists of. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part of him. So he raises it into the air with ease, and invariably does so when going at his utmost speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of the front of his head, and such the tapering, cutwater shape of the lower part, that by raising his head at a slant he may be said to transform himself from a bluff-bowed, sluggish galliot (a broad Dutch cargo boat) into a sharp-pointed New York pilot-boat.

"Start her, start her, my men! Don't hurry yourselves — take plenty of time — but start her; start her like thunderclaps, that's all," cried Stubb, sputtering out smoke as he spoke. "Start her, now; give them the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy — start her, all; but keep cool, keep cool — cucumbers is the word — easy, easy — only start her like grim death and grinning devils, and raise the buried dead straight up out of their graves, boys — that's all. Start her!"

"Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!" screamed the Gay-Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies, as every oarsman in the straining boat involuntarily lurched forward with the one tremendous leading stroke the eager Indian gave.
But his wild screams were answered by others equally wild. "Kee-hee! Kee-hee!" yelled Daggoo, straining forward and backward on his seat like a pacing tiger in his cage.

"Ka-la! Koo-loo!" howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of grenadier's steak. And so with oars and yells the keels cut the sea. Meanwhile, Stubb, keeping his place in the lead, still urged his men on to the attack, all the while puffing smoke from his mouth. Like desperadoes they tugged and strained, until the welcome cry was heard — "Stand up, Tashtego! — give it to him!" The harpoon was hurled. "Stern all!" The oarsmen backed water; at the same moment something went hot and hissing along every one of their wrists. It was the magical line. An instant before, Stubb had swiftly taken two extra turns with it around the loggerhead (the post in the stern around which the line is snubbed), from which, because of its increasingly rapid circling, a blue smoke of hemp now jetted up and mingled with the steady fumes from his pipe. As the line passed round and round the loggerhead, so also, just before reaching that point, it passed blisteringly through and through both of Stubb's hands, from which the hand-cloths — squares of quilted canvas sometimes worn at such times — had accidentally dropped. It was like holding an enemy's sharp two-edged sword by the blade, with that enemy all the time struggling to wrench it out of your grip.

"Wet the line! Wet the line!" cried Stubb to the tub oarsman (the one seated by the tub), who, snatching off his hat, dashed seawater into it.* More turns were taken, so that the line began to hold its place. The boat now flew through the boiling water like a shark all fins. Stubb and Tashtego here changed places — stem for stern — a staggering business indeed in that rocking commotion.

*Partly to show how indispensable this act is, it may be stated here that in the old Dutch fishery a mop was used to dash the running line with water; in many other ships, a wooden piggin, or bailer, is set aside for that purpose. Your hat, however, is the most convenient.

From the vibrating line stretching the entire length of the upper part of the boat, and from its now being tighter than a harpstring, you would have thought the craft had two keels — one cleaving the water, the other the air — as the boat churned on through both opposing elements at once. A continual cascade played at the bows; a ceaseless whirling eddy in her wake; and at the slightest motion from within, even of just a little finger, the vibrating, cracking craft tipped her spasmodic gunwale over into the sea. So they rushed on, each man clinging to his seat with all his might to keep from being tossed into the foam, and the tall form of Tashtego at the steering oar crouching almost double to bring down his center of gravity. Whole Atlantics and Pacifics seemed to pass as they shot on their way, until at last the whale somewhat slackened his flight.

"Haul in — haul in!" cried Stubb to the bowsman; and, facing round toward the whale, all hands began pulling the boat up to him while the boat was still being towed along. Soon drawing up alongside his flank, Stubb, firmly planting his knee in the clumsy cleat, darted dart after dart into the fleeing fish; at the word of command, the boat alternately backed away out of reach of the whale's horrible wallowing, and then drew up again for another throw.

The red tide now poured from all sides of the monster like brooks down a hill. His tormented body rolled not in brine but in blood, which bubbled and seethed for furlongs behind in their wake. The slanting sun, playing on this crimson pond in the sea, sent its reflection back into every face, so that they all glowed to each other like red men. And all the while, jet after jet of white smoke was shot in agony from the whale's spout-hole, and puff after vehement puff from the mouth of the excited headsman; as after every dart, hauling in his bent lance (by the line attached to it), Stubb straightened it again and again with a few rapid blows against the gunwale, and then again and again sent it into the whale.

"Pull up — pull up!" he now cried to the bowsman, as the waning whale slackened in his wrath. "Pull up! — close to!" And the boat drew up along the fish's flank. Then, reaching far over the bow, Stubb slowly churned his long sharp lance into the fish, and kept it there, carefully churning and churning, as if cautiously feeling for some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was afraid of breaking before he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his "flurry," the monster wallowed horribly in his blood and wrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the endangered boat, instantly dropping astern, had a hard time struggling blindly out of that frenzied twilight into the clear air of the day.

And now, his flurry subsiding, the whale once more rolled into view, surging from side to side, spasmodically expanding and contracting his spout-hole with sharp, cracking, agonized breaths. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it were the purple dregs of red wine, shot into the frightened air, and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!
"He's dead, Mr. Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes — both pipes smoked out!" And withdrawing his own pipe from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water, and for a moment stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.

chapters.title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the invariable custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman, or whale-killer, as temporary steersman, and the harpooner, or whale-fastener, pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, nervy arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung a distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however long and exhausting the chase, the harpooner is expected to pull his oar to the utmost all the while; indeed, he is expected to set the rest an example of superhuman activity, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and fearless shouts; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of your voice while every other muscle is strained and half wrenched out of place — that no one knows but those who have tried it. For my part, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, the exhausted harpooner all at once hears the exciting cry — "Stand up, and give it to him!" He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn halfway round on his center, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, try to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen together, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many luckless harpooners are madly cursed and demoted; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are gone four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many shipowners whaling is nothing but a losing business; for it is the harpooner who makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body, how can you expect to find it there when it is most wanted!

Again, if the dart is successful, then at the second critical instant — that is, when the whale starts to run — the boatheader and harpooner likewise start running fore and aft, to the imminent danger of themselves and everyone else. It is then that they change places; and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper station in the bow of the boat.

Now, I don't care who maintains otherwise, but all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from first to last; he should dart both the harpoon and the lance, and no rowing whatever should be expected of him, except under circumstances obvious to any fisherman. I know that this would sometimes mean a slight loss of speed in the chase; but the long experience of various whalemen of more than one nation has convinced me that in the great majority of failures in the fishery, it has by no means been so much the speed of the whale as the exhaustion of the harpooner, described above, that has caused them.
To ensure the greatest efficiency in the dart, the harpooners of this world must start to their feet out of idleness, and not out of toil.

chapters.title: Chapter 63 — The Crotch
paragraphs: Out of the trunk, the branches grow. Out of them, the twigs. So, in productive subjects, grow the chapters.

The crotch mentioned on a previous page deserves a mention of its own. It is a notched stick of a peculiar shape, some two feet long, which is inserted upright into the starboard gunwale near the bow, to provide a rest for the wooden end of the harpoon, whose other, naked, barbed end projects at a slant from the prow. In this way the weapon is instantly at hand for its thrower, who snatches it up from its rest as readily as a backwoodsman swings his rifle down from the wall. It is customary to have two harpoons resting in the crotch, called respectively the first and second irons.

But these two harpoons, each by its own cord, are both connected with the line; the object being this: to dart them both, if possible, one instantly after the other into the same whale, so that if, in the coming drag, one should pull out, the other may still keep its hold. It is a doubling of the chances. But it very often happens that, owing to the instantaneous, violent, convulsive running of the whale on receiving the first iron, it becomes impossible for the harpooner, however lightning-quick his movements, to pitch the second iron into him. Nevertheless, since the second iron is already connected with the line, and the line is running, that weapon must at all events be tossed out of the boat in advance, somehow and somewhere; otherwise all hands would be in the most terrible danger. So in such cases it is tumbled into the water, the spare coils of box line (mentioned in a preceding chapter) making this feat, in most instances, prudently possible. But this critical act is not always free of the saddest and most fatal accidents.

Furthermore, you must know that when the second iron is thrown overboard, it becomes from then on a dangling, sharp-edged terror, skittishly prancing about both boat and whale, tangling the lines or cutting them, and making a prodigious commotion in all directions. Nor, in general, is it possible to secure it again until the whale is fairly captured and a corpse.

Consider, now, how it must be when four boats are all engaging one unusually strong, active, and knowing whale; when, owing to these qualities in him, as well as to the thousand coinciding accidents of such a daring enterprise, eight or ten loose second irons may be dangling about him at once. For, of course, each boat is supplied with several harpoons to bend on to the line should the first one be darted without effect and not recovered. All these particulars are faithfully set down here, as they will not fail to shed light on several most important, however intricate, passages in scenes to be painted later.

chapters.title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some distance from the ship. It was a calm; so, forming a tandem of three boats, we began the slow business of towing the trophy to the Pequod. And now, as we eighteen men, with our thirty-six arms and one hundred and eighty thumbs and fingers, slowly toiled hour after hour at that inert, sluggish corpse in the sea, and it seemed hardly to budge at all except at long intervals, we had good evidence of the enormousness of the mass we were moving. For on the great canal of Hang-Ho, or whatever they call it, in China, four or five laborers on the towpath will pull a bulky loaded junk at the rate of a mile an hour; but this grand argosy we towed forged heavily along, as if loaded with pig-lead in bulk.

Darkness came on; but three lights up and down in the Pequod's main-rigging dimly guided our way, until, drawing nearer, we saw Ahab dropping one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. Gazing blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, he gave the usual orders for securing it for the night, and then, handing his lantern to a seaman, went his way into the cabin and did not come forward again until morning.

Though, in overseeing the pursuit of this whale, Captain Ahab had shown his customary activity, to call it that, yet now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, or impatience, or despair, seemed to be working in him; as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be slain; and though a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, all that would not advance his grand, monomaniac object one jot. Very soon, from the sound on the Pequod's decks, you would have thought that all hands were preparing to cast anchor in the deep; for heavy chains are being dragged along the deck and thrust rattling out of the portholes. But by those clanking links, the vast corpse itself, not the ship, is to be moored. Tied by the head to the stern and by the tail to the bows, the whale now lies with its black hull close to the vessel's; and seen through the darkness of the night, which hid the spars and rigging aloft, the two — ship and whale — seemed yoked together like colossal bullocks, one lying down while the other remains standing.*

*A little item may as well be told here. The strongest and most reliable hold the ship has on the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes, or tail; and since that part, from its greater density, is relatively heavier than any other (except the side-fins), its flexibility, even in death, makes it sink low beneath the surface, so that you cannot reach it by hand from the boat to put the chain around it. But this difficulty is ingeniously overcome: a small, strong line is prepared with a wooden float at its outer end and a weight in its middle, while the other end is made fast to the ship. By skillful management the wooden float is made to rise on the other side of the mass, so that, the line having now girdled the whale, the chain is easily made to follow; and being slipped along the body, it is at last locked fast around the smallest part of the tail, where it joins the broad flukes or lobes.

If moody Ahab was now all stillness, at least as far as could be known on deck, Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such an unaccustomed bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly left the sole management of affairs to him for the time being. One small contributing cause of all this liveliness in Stubb was soon made strangely plain. Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a thing flavorful to his palate.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his small!"

It should be known here that although these wild fishermen do not, as a general rule, follow the great military maxim of making the enemy pay the running expenses of the war (at least not before realizing the proceeds of the voyage), yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine relish for that particular part of the Sperm Whale that Stubb named, which takes in the tapering end of the body.

About midnight that steak was cut and cooked; and, lit by two lanterns of sperm oil, Stubb stoutly stood up to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as if that capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only one banqueting on whale's flesh that night. Mingling their mumblings with his own chewing, thousands on thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead leviathan, smackingly feasted on its fatness. The few sleepers below in their bunks were often startled by the sharp slapping of the sharks' tails against the hull, within a few inches of the sleepers' hearts. Peering over the side, you could just see them (as you had heard them before) wallowing in the sullen black waters, and turning over on their backs as they scooped out huge round pieces of the whale the size of a human head. This particular feat of the shark seems all but miraculous. How, from such an apparently unassailable surface, they manage to gouge out such symmetrical mouthfuls remains part of the universal problem of all things. The mark they leave on the whale can best be compared to the hollow a carpenter makes when countersinking for a screw.

Though amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks will be seen longingly gazing up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to bolt down every killed man that is tossed to them; and though, while the valiant butchers over the deck-table are thus cannibally carving each other's live meat with carving-knives all gilded and tasseled, the sharks, too, with their jewel-hilted mouths, are quarrelsomely carving away under the table at the dead meat; and though, if you turned the whole affair upside down, it would still be pretty much the same thing — that is to say, a shocking, sharkish business enough for all parties; and though sharks are also the invariable outriders of all slave ships crossing the Atlantic, systematically trotting alongside, to be handy in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere, or a dead slave to be decently buried; and though one or two other such instances might be set down, touching the set terms, places, and occasions when sharks most sociably gather and most hilariously feast; yet there is no conceivable time or occasion when you will find them in such countless numbers, and in gayer or more jovial spirits, than around a dead sperm whale moored by night to a whaleship at sea. If you have never seen that sight, then suspend your judgment on the propriety of devil-worship and the wisdom of conciliating the devil.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the mumblings of the banquet going on so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black, not in any very high spirits at having been roused from his warm hammock at a most unseasonable hour, came shambling along from his galley; for, like many old blacks, he had something the matter with his knee-pans, which he did not keep well scoured like his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shuffling and limping along, helping his step with his tongs, which, in a clumsy fashion, were made of straightened iron hoops. This old Ebony floundered along, and, obeying the word of command, came to a dead stop on the opposite side of Stubb's sideboard; then, with both hands folded before him and resting on his two-legged cane, he bowed his arched back still further over, at the same time tilting his head sideways so as to bring his best ear into play.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish morsel to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook; it's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're kicking up! Cook, go and talk to them; tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. Here, take this lantern," snatching one from his sideboard; "now then, go and preach to them!"

Sullenly taking the offered lantern, old Fleece limped across the deck to the bulwarks; and then, with one hand dropping his light low over the sea to get a good view of his congregation, with the other he solemnly flourished his tongs, and leaning far over the side, began addressing the sharks in a mumbling voice, while Stubb, softly crawling up behind, overheard all that was said.

"Fellow-critters: I'se ordered here to say dat you must stop dat damn noise dere. You hear? Stop dat damn smackin' of de lip! Massa Stubb say dat you can fill your damn bellies up to de hatches, but by Gor! you must stop dat damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in here, with a sudden slap on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who dat? Den preach to him yourself," sullenly turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, den, beloved fellow-critters:" —
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"Though you is all sharks, and by natur' very voracious, yet I say to you, fellow-critters, dat dat voraciousness — 'top dat damn slappin' of de tail! How you tink to hear, s'pose you keep up such a damn slappin' and bitin' dere?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like a gentleman."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame you so much for; dat is natur', and can't be helped; but to govern dat wicked natur', dat is de point. You is sharks, certain; but if you govern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is nothin' more dan de shark well governed. Now, look here, brethren, just try once to be civil, a-helpin' yourselves from dat whale. Don't be tearin' de blubber out of your neighbor's mouth, I say. Ain't one shark got as good a right as de other to dat whale? And, by Gor, none of you has de right to dat whale; dat whale belong to somebody else. I know some of you has very big mouth, bigger dan others; but den de big mouths sometimes has de small bellies; so dat de bigness of de mouth is not to swallow wid, but to bite off de blubber for de small fry of sharks, dat can't get into de crush to help demselves."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use goin' on; de damn villains will keep a-jostlin' and slappin' each other, Massa Stubb; dey don't hear one word; no use a-preachin' to such damn gluttons as you call 'em, till dere bellies is full, and dere bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey won't hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear nothin' at all, no more, for ever and ever."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damnedest row as ever you can; fill your damn bellies till dey bust — and den die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All 'tention," said Fleece, again stooping over his tongs in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What dat do wid de steak?" said the old black, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"'Bout ninety, dey say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' over de Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say de Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bress my soul if I cook anoder one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old negro muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever taste; joosy, very joosy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape-Down," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When dis old black man dies," said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and manner, "he hisself won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up dere," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So then, you expect to go up into our main-top, do you, cook, when you are dead? But don't you know the higher you climb, the colder it gets? Main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say dat at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look for yourself and see where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole, cook; but no, no, cook, you don't get there unless you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a ticklish business, but it must be done, or else it's no go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook, and hear my orders. Do you hear? Hold your hat in one hand, and clap the other on top of your heart when I'm giving my orders, cook. What! That your heart, there? — that's your gizzard! Aloft! Aloft! — that's it — now you have it. Hold it there now, and pay attention."
"All 'tention," said the old black, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears in front at one and the same time.

"Well then, cook, you see this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I have put it out of sight as soon as possible; you see that, don't you? Well, for the future, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here, the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other; that done, dish it; do you hear? And now tomorrow, cook, when we are cutting in the fish, be sure you stand by to get the tips of his fins; have them put in pickle. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. There, now you may go."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Make a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."

"Wish, by Gor, whale eat him, 'stead of him eat whale. I'm bressed if he ain't more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself," muttered the old man, limping away; and with this sage outburst he went to his hammock.

chapters.title: Chapter 65 — The Whale as a Dish
paragraphs: That mortal man should feed upon the creature that feeds his lamp, and, like Stubb, eat him by his own light, as you might say — this seems so outlandish a thing that one must go a little into the history and philosophy of it.

It is on record that three centuries ago the tongue of the Right Whale was considered a great delicacy in France, and commanded high prices there. Also, that in Henry VIII's time, a certain cook of the court obtained a handsome reward for inventing an admirable sauce to be eaten with barbecued porpoises, which, you remember, are a species of whale. Porpoises, indeed, are to this day considered fine eating. The meat is made into balls about the size of billiard balls, and being well seasoned and spiced, might be taken for turtle-balls or veal-balls. The old monks of Dunfermline were very fond of them. They had a great porpoise grant from the crown.

The fact is that, among his hunters at least, the whale would be considered a noble dish by all hands, were there not so much of him; but when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite. Only the most unprejudiced of men, like Stubb, eat cooked whale nowadays; but the Eskimos are not so fastidious. We all know how they live on whales, and keep rare old vintages of prime old train oil. Zogranda, one of their most famous doctors, recommends strips of blubber for infants, as being exceedingly juicy and nourishing. And this reminds me that certain Englishmen, who long ago were accidentally left behind in Greenland by a whaling vessel — that these men actually lived for several months on the moldy scraps of whales that had been left ashore after the blubber was tried out (boiled down for oil). Among the Dutch whalemen these scraps are called "fritters," which, indeed, they greatly resemble, being brown and crisp, and smelling something like old Amsterdam housewives' doughnuts, or oly-cooks, when fresh. They look so edible that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off them.

But what further lowers the whale as a civilized dish is his exceeding richness. He is the great prize ox of the sea, too fat to be delicately good. Look at his hump, which would be as fine eating as the buffalo's (which is prized as a rare dish), were it not such a solid pyramid of fat. But the spermaceti itself — how bland and creamy that is, like the transparent, half-jellied white meat of a coconut in the third month of its growth; yet far too rich to serve as a substitute for butter. Nevertheless, many whalemen have a way of absorbing it into some other substance and then eating it. In the long try-watches of the night it is a common thing for the seamen to dip their ship's biscuit into the huge oil-pots and let it fry there a while. I have made many a good supper that way.

With a small Sperm Whale, the brains are considered a fine dish. The casket of the skull is broken into with an axe, and the two plump, whitish lobes are drawn out (looking exactly like two large puddings); they are then mixed with flour and cooked into a most delectable mess, in flavor somewhat like calves' head, which is quite a dish among some epicures; and everyone knows that some young bucks among the epicures, by continually dining on calves' brains, by and by come to have a little brains of their own, enough to tell a calf's head from their own heads — which, indeed, takes uncommon discrimination. And that is why a young buck with an intelligent-looking calf's head before him is somehow one of the saddest sights you can see. The head looks at him in a sort of reproachful way, with an "Et tu, Brute!" expression.

It is not, perhaps, entirely because the whale is so excessively oily that landsmen seem to regard eating him with abhorrence; that seems to come, in some way, from the consideration mentioned before: that is, that a man should eat a newly murdered thing of the sea, and eat it by its own light too. But no doubt the first man who ever murdered an ox was regarded as a murderer; perhaps he was hanged; and if he had been put on trial by oxen, he certainly would have been; and he certainly deserved it, if any murderer does. Go to the meat-market on a Saturday night and see the crowds of live bipeds staring up at the long rows of dead quadrupeds. Doesn't that sight take a tooth out of the cannibal's jaw? Cannibals? Who is not a cannibal? I tell you it will be more tolerable for the Fijian who salted down a lean missionary in his cellar against a coming famine — it will be more tolerable for that provident Fijian, I say, in the day of judgment, than for you, civilized and enlightened gourmand, who nail geese to the ground and feast on their bloated livers in your pâté de foie gras.

But Stubb — he eats the whale by its own light, does he? And that is adding insult to injury, is it? Look at your knife-handle there, my civilized and enlightened gourmand, dining on that roast beef — what is that handle made of? What but the bones of the brother of the very ox you are eating? And what do you pick your teeth with after devouring that fat goose? With a feather of the same fowl. And with what quill did the Secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Ganders formally write his circulars? It is only within the last month or two that that society passed a resolution to patronize nothing but steel pens.

chapters.title: Chapter 66 — The Shark Massacre
paragraphs: When, in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale is brought alongside late at night after long and weary toil, it is not, as a general rule at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; it is not very soon completed, and it requires all hands to set about it. Therefore the common practice is to take in all sail, lash the helm alee, and then send everyone below to his hammock until daylight — with the provision that until then anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, the crew in rotation, two by two, each pair for an hour, shall come up on deck to see that all goes well.

But sometimes, especially on the Line in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for, say, six hours at a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish are not so abundant, their wondrous voracity can at times be considerably reduced by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades — a procedure which, nevertheless, in some instances only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not so in the present case with the Pequod's sharks; though, to be sure, any man unused to such sights who had looked over her side that night would almost have thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.

Nevertheless, when Stubb set the anchor-watch after his supper was over, and Queequeg and a forecastle seaman accordingly came on deck, no small excitement was stirred up among the sharks; for, immediately hanging the cutting stages over the side and lowering three lanterns so that they cast long gleams of light over the murky sea, these two mariners, darting their long whaling-spades, kept up an incessant murdering of the sharks,* striking the keen steel deep into their skulls, seemingly their only vital part. But in the foamy confusion of their mixed and struggling hosts, the marksmen could not always hit their mark; and this brought about new revelations of the incredible ferocity of the foe. They viciously snapped not only at each other's spilled entrails, but, bending round like flexible bows, bit at their own; until those entrails seemed swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, only to be voided out the opposite way through the gaping wound. Nor was this all. It was unsafe to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to lurk in their very joints and bones after what might be called the individual life had departed. One of these sharks, killed and hoisted on deck for the sake of his skin, almost took poor Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut down the dead lid of its murderous jaw.

*The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; it is about the size of a man's spread hand, and in general shape corresponds to the garden tool it is named after, except that its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible, and when in use it is honed now and then, just like a razor. A stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is fitted into its socket as a handle.
"Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."

chapters.title: Chapter 67 — Cutting In
paragraphs: It was a Saturday night, and such a Sabbath as followed! By their very profession, all whalemen are breakers of the Sabbath. The ivory Pequod was turned into what seemed a slaughterhouse. Every sailor was a butcher. You would have thought we were sacrificing ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods.

In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles — among other ponderous things, a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift — this vast bunch of grapes was hoisted up to the main-top and firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended in stages over the side, Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

One of the attending harpooners now advances with a long, keen weapon called a boarding-sword, and, watching his chance, he deftly slices a sizable hole in the lower part of the swaying mass. Into this hole the end of the second, alternating great tackle is then hooked, so as to keep a hold on the blubber in preparation for what follows. Then this accomplished swordsman, warning all hands to stand clear, once more makes a scientific dash at the mass, and with a few sidelong, desperate, lunging slices cuts it completely in two; so that while the short lower part is still fast, the long upper strip, called a blanket-piece, swings clear and is all ready for lowering. The heavers forward now take up their song again, and while the one tackle is peeling and hoisting a second strip from the whale, the other is slowly slackened away, and down goes the first strip through the main hatchway right beneath, into an unfurnished parlor called the blubber-room. Into this twilight apartment a number of nimble hands keep coiling away the long blanket-piece as if it were a great live mass of plaited serpents. And so the work goes on: the two tackles hoisting and lowering at the same time; both whale and windlass heaving, the heavers singing, the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and all hands swearing now and then, by way of easing the general friction.

chapters.title: Chapter 68 — The Blanket
paragraphs: I have given no small attention to that much-vexed subject, the skin of the whale. I have had arguments about it with experienced whalemen at sea and learned naturalists ashore. My original opinion remains unchanged, but it is only an opinion.

The question is: what and where is the skin of the whale? You already know what his blubber is. That blubber is something with the consistency of firm, close-grained beef, but tougher, more elastic and compact, and ranges from eight or ten to twelve and fifteen inches in thickness.

Now, however absurd it may seem at first to speak of any creature's skin as being of that sort of consistency and thickness, in point of fact these are no arguments against such a presumption; because you cannot raise any other dense enveloping layer from the whale's body except that same blubber; and the outermost enveloping layer of any animal, if reasonably dense, what can that be but the skin? True, from the unmarred dead body of the whale you may scrape off with your hand an infinitely thin, transparent substance, somewhat like the thinnest shreds of isinglass (a clear gelatin made from fish bladders), only it is almost as flexible and soft as satin — that is, before it is dried, when it not only contracts and thickens but becomes rather hard and brittle. I have several such dried bits, which I use as bookmarks in my whale-books. It is transparent, as I said before; and laying it on the printed page, I have sometimes amused myself by imagining that it had a magnifying effect. At any rate, it is pleasant to read about whales through their own spectacles, as you might say. But what I am driving at here is this. That same infinitely thin, isinglass substance, which, I admit, covers the entire body of the whale, is not so much to be regarded as the skin of the creature as the skin of the skin, so to speak; for it would be simply ridiculous to say that the proper skin of the tremendous whale is thinner and more tender than the skin of a newborn child. But no more of this.

Assuming the blubber to be the skin of the whale: when this skin, as in the case of a very large Sperm Whale, will yield the bulk of one hundred barrels of oil; and when you consider that, in quantity, or rather weight, that oil in its pressed-out state is only three-quarters, and not the entire substance, of the coat — you may get some idea from this of the enormousness of that living mass, a mere part of whose mere covering yields such a lake of liquid as that. Reckoning ten barrels to the ton, you have ten tons for the net weight of only three-quarters of the stuff of the whale's skin.

In life, the visible surface of the Sperm Whale is not the least among the many marvels he presents. Almost invariably it is obliquely crossed and re-crossed all over with countless straight marks in thick array, something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be impressed upon the isinglass substance mentioned above; rather, they seem to be seen through it, as if they were engraved upon the body itself. Nor is this all. In some instances, to the quick, observant eye, those linear marks, as in a real engraving, only provide the ground for quite other drawings. These are hieroglyphical; that is, if you call those mysterious ciphers on the walls of pyramids hieroglyphics, then that is the proper word to use here. From my retentive memory of the hieroglyphics on one Sperm Whale in particular, I was much struck by a plate showing the old Indian characters chiseled on the famous hieroglyphic palisades on the banks of the Upper Mississippi. Like those mystic rocks, too, the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable. This allusion to the Indian rocks reminds me of another thing. Besides all the other phenomena that the exterior of the Sperm Whale presents, he quite often shows his back, and more especially his flanks, with the regular linear pattern largely effaced by numerous rough scratches, altogether irregular and random in appearance. I should say that those New England rocks on the sea-coast which Agassiz imagines to bear the marks of violent scraping contact with vast floating icebergs — I should say that those rocks must resemble the Sperm Whale not a little in this respect. It also seems to me that such scratches in the whale are probably made by hostile contact with other whales; for I have noticed them most in the large, full-grown bulls of the species.

A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces, called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is very apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better still, an Indian poncho slipped over his head and hanging down around his extremity. It is because of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is able to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of the North, if he were not supplied with his cozy overcoat? True, other fish are found to be exceedingly lively in those Hyperborean waters; but these, mind you, are your cold-blooded, lungless fish, whose very bellies are refrigerators; creatures that warm themselves in the lee of an iceberg, as a traveler in winter would bask before an inn fire; whereas, like man, the whale has lungs and warm blood. Freeze his blood, and he dies. How wonderful it is, then — except after explanation — that this great monster, to whom bodily warmth is as indispensable as it is to man; how wonderful that he should be found at home, immersed to his lips for life in those Arctic waters! — where, when seamen fall overboard, they are sometimes found months afterward, frozen upright into the hearts of fields of ice, as a fly is found glued in amber. But it is more surprising still to know, as has been proved by experiment, that the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.

It does seem to me that herein we see the rare virtue of a strong individual vitality, and the rare virtue of thick walls, and the rare virtue of interior spaciousness. Oh, man! Admire and model yourself after the whale! You, too, remain warm among ice. You, too, live in this world without being of it. Be cool at the equator; keep your blood fluid at the Pole. Like the great dome of St. Peter's, and like the great whale, keep, O man, in all seasons a temperature of your own.
But how easy and how hopeless to teach these fine things! Of buildings, how few are domed like St. Peter's! Of creatures, how few are vast as the whale!

chapters.title: Chapter 69 — The Funeral
paragraphs: "Haul in the chains! Let the carcass go astern!"

The vast tackles have now done their duty. The peeled white body of the beheaded whale gleams like a marble tomb; though changed in color, it has not visibly lost anything in bulk. It is still colossal. Slowly it floats farther and farther away, the water around it torn and splashed by the insatiable sharks, and the air above harassed by rapacious flights of screaming birds, whose beaks are like so many insulting daggers in the whale. The vast white headless phantom floats farther and farther from the ship, and with every rod that it floats, what seem square roods of sharks and cubic roods of birds swell the murderous din. For hours and hours that hideous sight can be seen from the almost motionless ship. Beneath the unclouded, mild blue sky, upon the fair face of the pleasant sea, carried along by the joyous breezes, that great mass of death floats on and on, till it is lost in infinite perspectives.

Here is a most doleful and most mocking funeral! The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all punctiliously dressed in black or speckled. In life, few of them would have helped the whale, I think, if by chance he had needed it. But upon the banquet of his funeral they most piously pounce. Oh, horrible vultureism of earth! From which not even the mightiest whale is free.

Nor is this the end. Desecrated as the body is, a vengeful ghost survives and hovers over it to frighten. Sighted from afar by some timid warship or blundering discovery-vessel — when the distance hides the swarming birds but still shows the white mass floating in the sun, and the white spray heaving high against it — straightaway the whale's harmless corpse is set down in the log with trembling fingers: "Shoals, rocks, and breakers hereabouts: beware!" And for years afterward, perhaps, ships avoid the place, leaping over it as silly sheep leap over empty air, because their leader originally leaped there when a stick was held up. There's your law of precedents; there's your usefulness of traditions; there's the story of your stubborn survival of old beliefs never grounded on the earth, and now not even hovering in the air! There's orthodoxy!
Thus, while in life the great whale's body may have been a real terror to his enemies, in his death his ghost becomes a powerless panic to a world.
Are you a believer in ghosts, my friend? There are other ghosts than the Cock-Lane one, and far deeper men than Doctor Johnson who believe in them.

chapters.title: Chapter 70 — The Sphynx
paragraphs: It should not have been omitted that before completely stripping the body of the leviathan, he was beheaded. Now, the beheading of the Sperm Whale is a scientific anatomical feat upon which experienced whale surgeons very much pride themselves — and not without reason.

Consider that the whale has nothing that can properly be called a neck; on the contrary, where his head and body seem to join, there, in that very place, is the thickest part of him. Remember, too, that the surgeon must operate from above, with some eight or ten feet between him and his subject, and that subject almost hidden in a discolored, rolling, and often tumultuous and bursting sea. Bear in mind also that under these unfavorable circumstances he has to cut many feet deep into the flesh; and in that underground fashion, without getting so much as a single peep into the ever-contracting gash he is making, he must skillfully steer clear of all the neighboring, forbidden parts, and divide the spine exactly at a critical point close to where it enters the skull. Don't you marvel, then, at Stubb's boast that he needed only ten minutes to behead a sperm whale?

When first severed, the head is dropped astern and held there by a cable until the body is stripped. That done, if it belongs to a small whale, it is hoisted on deck to be dealt with at leisure. But with a full-grown leviathan this is impossible; for the sperm whale's head makes up nearly one third of his entire bulk, and to suspend such a burden completely, even by the immense tackles of a whaler, would be as futile as trying to weigh a Dutch barn in jewelers' scales.

The Pequod's whale having been beheaded and the body stripped, the head was hoisted against the ship's side — about halfway out of the sea, so that it might still be largely buoyed up by its native element. And there, with the strained vessel leaning steeply over toward it because of the enormous downward drag from the lower masthead, and every yard-arm on that side sticking out like a crane over the waves — there that blood-dripping head hung at the Pequod's waist like the giant Holofernes's from the girdle of Judith.

When this last task was done, it was noon, and the seamen went below to their dinner. Silence reigned over the previously tumultuous but now deserted deck. An intense copper calm, like a universal yellow lotus, was more and more unfolding its noiseless, measureless leaves upon the sea.

A short time passed, and up into this silence came Ahab, alone, from his cabin. Taking a few turns on the quarterdeck, he paused to gaze over the side; then, slowly climbing into the main-chains, he took Stubb's long spade — still lying there after the whale's beheading — and, striking it into the lower part of the half-suspended mass, he placed its other end like a crutch under one arm, and so stood leaning over, his eyes intently fixed on this head.

It was a black and hooded head; and hanging there in the midst of so intense a calm, it seemed like the Sphynx's in the desert. "Speak, you vast and venerable head," muttered Ahab, "you who, though you have no beard, yet here and there look hoary with mosses; speak, mighty head, and tell us the secret thing that is in you. Of all divers, you have dived the deepest. That head upon which the upper sun now gleams has moved among this world's foundations. Where unrecorded names and navies rust, and untold hopes and anchors rot; where in her murderous hold this frigate earth is ballasted with the bones of millions of the drowned; there, in that awful water-land, there was your most familiar home. You have been where diving-bell or diver never went; you have slept by many a sailor's side, where sleepless mothers would give their lives to lay them down. You saw the locked lovers when they leaped from their flaming ship; heart to heart they sank beneath the exulting wave; true to each other, when heaven seemed false to them. You saw the murdered mate when pirates tossed him from the midnight deck; for hours he fell into the deeper midnight of the insatiable maw; and his murderers still sailed on unharmed — while swift lightning shattered the neighboring ship that would have carried a righteous husband to outstretched, longing arms. O head! you have seen enough to split the planets and make an infidel of Abraham, and not one syllable is yours!"
"Sail ho!" cried a triumphant voice from the main-masthead.

"Aye? Well now, that's cheering," cried Ahab, suddenly straightening up, while whole thunderclouds swept aside from his brow. "That lively cry upon this deadly calm might almost convert a better man. — Where away?"
"Three points on the starboard bow, sir, and bringing down her breeze to us!"

"Better and better, man. If only St. Paul would come along that way now, and bring his breeze to my breezelessness! O Nature, and O soul of man! how far beyond all words are your linked analogies! Not the smallest atom stirs or lives on matter but has its cunning duplicate in mind."

chapters.title: Chapter 71 — The Jeroboam’s Story
paragraphs: Hand in hand, ship and breeze blew on. But the breeze came faster than the ship, and soon the Pequod began to rock.

By and by, through the spyglass, the stranger's boats and manned mastheads proved her a whale-ship. But as she was so far to windward and shooting past, apparently making a passage to some other ground, the Pequod could not hope to reach her. So the signal flag was hoisted to see what response would be made.

It should be said here that, like the vessels of navies, the ships of the American Whale Fleet each have a private signal; all these signals are collected in a book, with the names of the respective vessels attached, and every captain is provided with it. By this means the whale captains are able to recognize each other on the ocean, even at considerable distances and with no small ease.

The Pequod's signal was at last answered by the stranger's hoisting her own, which proved the ship to be the Jeroboam of Nantucket. Squaring her yards, she bore down, came up abeam under the Pequod's lee, and lowered a boat. It soon drew near; but as the side-ladder was being rigged by Starbuck's order to accommodate the visiting captain, the stranger in question waved his hand from his boat's stern to show that this was entirely unnecessary. It turned out that the Jeroboam had a malignant epidemic on board, and that Mayhew, her captain, was afraid of infecting the Pequod's company. For although he himself and his boat's crew remained uninfected, and although his ship was half a rifle-shot away, with an incorruptible sea and air rolling and flowing between, he nevertheless conscientiously kept to the timid quarantine of the land, and flatly refused to come into direct contact with the Pequod.

But this by no means prevented all communication. Keeping a gap of a few yards between itself and the ship, the Jeroboam's boat, by occasional use of its oars, managed to keep parallel to the Pequod as she heavily forged through the sea (for by this time it was blowing very fresh), with her main-topsail aback; though, indeed, at times the sudden onset of a large rolling wave would push the boat some way ahead, but it would soon be skillfully brought back to its proper position. Subject to this and other such interruptions now and then, a conversation was kept up between the two parties — though at intervals it was broken by still another interruption of a very different sort.

Pulling an oar in the Jeroboam's boat was a man of singular appearance, even in that wild whaling life where the whole is made up of nothing but remarkable individuals. He was a small, short, youngish man, sprinkled all over his face with freckles, and wearing an abundance of yellow hair. A long-skirted coat of cabalistic cut, of a faded walnut color, enveloped him; its overlapping sleeves were rolled up at his wrists. A deep, settled, fanatic delirium was in his eyes.

As soon as this figure had first been sighted, Stubb had exclaimed — "That's him! that's him! — the long-togged scaramouch the Town-Ho's company told us of!" Stubb was referring here to a strange story told about the Jeroboam, and a certain man among her crew, some time before, when the Pequod spoke the Town-Ho. According to this account, and what was learned afterward, it seemed that the scaramouch in question had gained a remarkable hold over almost everybody in the Jeroboam. His story was this:

He had originally been raised among the crazy society of Neskyeuna Shakers, where he had been a great prophet; in their cracked, secret meetings he had several times descended from heaven by way of a trap-door, announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket — but which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum. A strange, apostolic whim having seized him, he had left Neskyeuna for Nantucket, where, with that cunning peculiar to craziness, he put on a steady, common-sense exterior and offered himself as a green-hand candidate for the Jeroboam's whaling voyage. They took him on; but the moment the ship was out of sight of land, his insanity broke out in a flood. He announced himself as the archangel Gabriel, and ordered the captain to jump overboard. He published his manifesto, in which he proclaimed himself the deliverer of the isles of the sea and vicar-general of all Oceanica. The unflinching earnestness with which he declared these things — the dark, daring play of his sleepless, excited imagination, and all the preternatural terrors of real delirium — combined to invest this Gabriel, in the minds of most of the ignorant crew, with an atmosphere of sacredness. Moreover, they were afraid of him. As such a man, however, was not of much practical use in the ship, especially as he refused to work except when he pleased, the unbelieving captain would gladly have been rid of him; but on learning that the captain intended to land him at the first convenient port, the archangel at once opened all his seals and vials — devoting the ship and all hands to unconditional damnation if this intention was carried out. So strongly did he work upon his disciples among the crew that at last they went to the captain in a body and told him that if Gabriel was sent from the ship, not a man of them would remain. He was therefore forced to give up his plan. Nor would they allow Gabriel to be mistreated in any way, whatever he might say or do; so that it came about that Gabriel had the complete freedom of the ship. The consequence of all this was that the archangel cared little or nothing for the captain and mates; and since the epidemic had broken out, he was more high-handed than ever, declaring that the plague, as he called it, was at his sole command, and that it would not be stopped except at his good pleasure. The sailors, mostly poor devils, cringed, and some of them fawned before him; following his instructions, they sometimes paid him personal homage, as to a god. Such things may seem incredible; but, however astonishing, they are true. Nor is the history of fanatics half so striking for the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself as for his measureless power of deceiving and bedeviling so many others. But it is time to return to the Pequod.
"I'm not afraid of your epidemic, man," said Ahab from the bulwarks to Captain Mayhew, who stood in the boat's stern. "Come on board."
But now Gabriel started to his feet.
"Think, think of the fevers, yellow and bilious! Beware of the horrible plague!"
"Gabriel! Gabriel!" cried Captain Mayhew. "You must either —" But that instant a headlong wave shot the boat far ahead, and its noise drowned all speech.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" demanded Ahab, when the boat drifted back.
"Think, think of your whale-boat, stoven and sunk! Beware of the horrible tail!"

"I tell you again, Gabriel, that —" But again the boat tore ahead as if dragged by fiends. Nothing was said for some moments, while a succession of riotous waves rolled by, which, by one of those occasional whims of the sea, were tumbling it, not heaving it. Meanwhile, the hoisted sperm whale's head jogged about very violently, and Gabriel was seen eyeing it with rather more apprehension than his archangel nature seemed to warrant.

When this interlude was over, Captain Mayhew began a dark story about Moby Dick — not, however, without frequent interruptions from Gabriel whenever his name was mentioned, and from the crazy sea that seemed to be in league with him.

It seemed that the Jeroboam had not long left home when, on speaking a whale-ship, her people were reliably informed of the existence of Moby Dick and the havoc he had made. Greedily drinking in this news, Gabriel solemnly warned the captain against attacking the White Whale in case the monster should be seen; in his gibbering insanity he declared the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnate, the Shakers accepting the Bible. But when, a year or two afterward, Moby Dick was fairly sighted from the mastheads, Macey, the chief mate, burned with eagerness to encounter him; and the captain himself being not unwilling to give him the chance, despite all the archangel's denunciations and warnings, Macey succeeded in persuading five men to man his boat. With them he pushed off; and after much weary pulling, and many perilous, unsuccessful attacks, he at last succeeded in getting one iron fast. Meanwhile Gabriel, climbing to the main-royal masthead, was tossing one arm in frantic gestures and hurling forth prophecies of swift doom upon the sacrilegious attackers of his divinity. Now, while Macey the mate was standing up in his boat's bow, and with all the reckless energy of his tribe was venting his wild exclamations at the whale and trying to get a fair chance for his poised lance — look! a broad white shadow rose from the sea, and by its quick, fanning motion for the moment knocked the breath out of the oarsmen's bodies. The next instant the luckless mate, so full of furious life, was struck bodily into the air, and, making a long arc in his descent, fell into the sea about fifty yards away. Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman's head; but the mate sank forever.

It is well to parenthesize here that of the fatal accidents in the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps almost as frequent as any. Sometimes, nothing is injured but the man who is thus annihilated; oftener the boat's bow is knocked off, or the thigh-board, in which the headsman stands, is torn from its place and accompanies the body. But strangest of all is the circumstance that, in more instances than one, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence is discernible; the man being stark dead.

The whole calamity, with the falling figure of Macey, was plainly seen from the ship. Raising a piercing shriek — "The vial! the vial!" — Gabriel called the terror-stricken crew off from any further hunting of the whale. This terrible event invested the archangel with added influence, because his credulous disciples believed that he had specifically foretold it, instead of only making a general prophecy, which anyone might have done, and so have happened to hit one of many marks in the wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship.

When Mayhew had finished his story, Ahab put such questions to him that the stranger captain could not help asking whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if the opportunity came. To which Ahab answered — "Aye." Immediately, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring at the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward-pointing finger — "Think, think of the blasphemer — dead, and down there! — beware of the blasphemer's end!"
Ahab stolidly turned aside, then said to Mayhew, "Captain, I have just remembered my letter-bag. There is a letter for one of your officers, if I'm not mistaken. Starbuck, look through the bag."

Every whale-ship takes out a goodly number of letters for various ships, whose delivery to the persons to whom they may be addressed depends upon the mere chance of encountering them in the four oceans. Thus, most letters never reach their mark; and many are only received after attaining an age of two or three years or more.

Soon Starbuck returned with a letter in his hand. It was badly creased, damp, and covered with a dull, spotted green mold from being kept in a dark locker in the cabin. Of such a letter, Death himself might well have been the postman.

"Can't you read it?" cried Ahab. "Give it to me, man. Aye, aye, it's but a dim scrawl — what's this?" As he was studying it out, Starbuck took a long cutting-spade pole, and with his knife slightly split the end, to insert the letter there, and in that way hand it to the boat without its having to come any closer to the ship.
Meanwhile, Ahab holding the letter, muttered, "Mr. Har — yes, Mr. Harry — a woman's handwriting — the man's wife, I'll wager — aye — Mr. Harry Macey, Ship Jeroboam — why, it's Macey, and he's dead!"
"Poor fellow! Poor fellow! And from his wife," sighed Mayhew. "But let me have it."
"No, keep it yourself," cried Gabriel to Ahab. "You are soon going that way."

"Curses strangle you!" yelled Ahab. "Captain Mayhew, stand by now to receive it." And taking the fatal letter from Starbuck's hands, he caught it in the slit of the pole and reached it out toward the boat. But as he did so, the oarsmen, expecting it, stopped rowing; the boat drifted a little toward the ship's stern; so that, as if by magic, the letter suddenly came level with Gabriel's eager hand. He clutched it in an instant, seized the boat-knife, and, impaling the letter on it, sent it, thus loaded, back into the ship. It fell at Ahab's feet. Then Gabriel shrieked out to his comrades to pull hard on their oars, and in that manner the mutinous boat rapidly shot away from the Pequod.
As, after this interlude, the seamen resumed their work upon the jacket of the whale, many strange things were hinted in reference to this wild affair.

chapters.title: Chapter 72 — The Monkey-Rope
paragraphs: In the tumultuous business of cutting-in and attending to a whale, there is much running back and forth among the crew. Now hands are wanted here, and then again hands are wanted there. There is no staying in any one place; for at one and the same time everything has to be done everywhere. It is much the same with anyone who tries to describe the scene. We must now retrace our steps a little. It was mentioned that, on first breaking ground in the whale's back, the blubber-hook was inserted into the original hole cut there by the spades of the mates. But how did so clumsy and weighty a mass as that hook get fixed in that hole? It was put there by my particular friend Queequeg, whose duty it was, as harpooner, to go down onto the monster's back for that special purpose. But in very many cases circumstances require the harpooner to remain on the whale until the whole flensing, or stripping, operation is finished. The whale, mind you, lies almost entirely submerged, except for the parts being worked on. So down there, some ten feet below the level of the deck, the poor harpooner flounders about, half on the whale and half in the water, as the vast mass revolves like a treadmill beneath him. On the occasion in question, Queequeg appeared in Highland costume — a shirt and socks — in which, to my eyes at least, he looked uncommonly well; and no one had a better chance to observe him, as will soon be seen.

Being the savage's bowsman — that is, the person who pulled the bow-oar in his boat (the second one from forward) — it was my cheerful duty to attend to him while he made that hard-scrabble scramble on the dead whale's back. You have seen Italian organ-boys holding a dancing-ape by a long cord. Just so, from the ship's steep side, I held Queequeg down there in the sea, by what is technically called in the fishery a monkey-rope, attached to a strong strip of canvas belted around his waist.

It was a humorously perilous business for both of us. For, before we go further, it must be said that the monkey-rope was fast at both ends — fast to Queequeg's broad canvas belt, and fast to my narrow leather one. So that for better or for worse, we two, for the time being, were wedded; and should poor Queequeg sink to rise no more, then both custom and honor demanded that, instead of the cord being cut, it should drag me down in his wake. So, then, an elongated Siamese ligature united us. Queequeg was my own inseparable twin brother; nor could I in any way get rid of the dangerous liabilities that the hempen bond entailed.

So strongly and metaphysically did I conceive of my situation then that, while earnestly watching his motions, I seemed distinctly to perceive that my own individuality was now merged in a joint-stock company of two; that my free will had received a mortal wound; and that another's mistake or misfortune might plunge innocent me into undeserved disaster and death. Therefore, I saw that here was a sort of interregnum in Providence; for its even-handed fairness never could have allowed so gross an injustice. And yet, still further pondering — while I jerked him now and then from between the whale and the ship, which threatened to jam him — still further pondering, I say, I saw that this situation of mine was the precise situation of every mortal that breathes; only, in most cases, he, one way or another, has this Siamese connection with a plurality of other mortals. If your banker breaks, you snap; if your apothecary by mistake sends you poison in your pills, you die. True, you may say that by exceeding caution you may possibly escape these and the countless other evil chances of life. But however carefully I handled Queequeg's monkey-rope, sometimes he jerked it so that I came very near sliding overboard. Nor could I possibly forget that, whatever I did, I had the management of only one end of it.*

*The monkey-rope is found in all whalers; but it was only in the Pequod that the monkey and his holder were ever tied together. This improvement upon the original practice was introduced by no less a man than Stubb, in order to give the imperiled harpooner the strongest possible guarantee of the faithfulness and vigilance of his monkey-rope holder.

I have hinted that I would often jerk poor Queequeg from between the whale and the ship — where he would occasionally fall, from the incessant rolling and swaying of both. But this was not the only jamming danger he was exposed to. Undaunted by the massacre made among them during the night, the sharks — now freshly and more keenly lured by the previously pent-up blood that began to flow from the carcass — the rabid creatures swarmed around it like bees in a beehive.

And right in among those sharks was Queequeg, who often pushed them aside with his floundering feet. A thing altogether incredible were it not that, attracted by such prey as a dead whale, the otherwise indiscriminately carnivorous shark will seldom touch a man.

Nevertheless, it may well be believed that since they have such a ravenous finger in the pie, it is thought only wise to keep a sharp eye on them. Accordingly, besides the monkey-rope, with which I now and then jerked the poor fellow away from too close a neighborhood to the jaws of what seemed a peculiarly ferocious shark, he was provided with yet another protection. Suspended over the side in one of the stages, Tashtego and Daggoo continually flourished a couple of keen whale-spades over his head, with which they slaughtered as many sharks as they could reach. This procedure of theirs, to be sure, was very disinterested and benevolent of them. They meant Queequeg's best happiness, I admit; but in their hasty zeal to befriend him, and because both he and the sharks were at times half hidden by the blood-muddied water, those indiscreet spades of theirs would come nearer to amputating a leg than a tail. But poor Queequeg, I suppose, straining and gasping there with that great iron hook — poor Queequeg, I suppose, only prayed to his Yojo, and gave up his life into the hands of his gods.

Well, well, my dear comrade and twin brother, thought I, as I drew in and then slacked off the rope with every swell of the sea — what does it matter, after all? Are you not the precious image of each and all of us men in this whaling world? That unsounded ocean you gasp in is Life; those sharks, your foes; those spades, your friends; and what with sharks and spades, you are in a sad pickle and peril, poor lad.
