But courage! There is good cheer in store for you, Queequeg. For now, as with blue lips and bloodshot eyes the exhausted savage at last climbs up the chains and stands all dripping and involuntarily trembling over the side, the steward comes forward and, with a kindly, consoling glance, hands him — what? Some hot cognac? No! He hands him — ye gods! — he hands him a cup of lukewarm ginger and water!

"Ginger? Do I smell ginger?" Stubb asked suspiciously, coming near. "Yes, this must be ginger," peering into the as yet untasted cup. Then, standing as if in disbelief for a while, he calmly walked toward the astonished steward, slowly saying, "Ginger? ginger? And will you have the goodness to tell me, Mr. Dough-Boy, where the virtue of ginger lies? Ginger! Is ginger the sort of fuel you use, Dough-Boy, to kindle a fire in this shivering cannibal? Ginger! — what the devil is ginger? Sea-coal? Firewood? — lucifer matches? — tinder? — gunpowder? — what the devil is ginger, I say, that you offer this cup to our poor Queequeg here?"

"There is some sneaking Temperance Society movement behind this business," he suddenly added, now approaching Starbuck, who had just come from forward. "Will you look at that little can, sir? Smell it, if you please." Then, watching the mate's face, he added, "The steward, Mr. Starbuck, had the nerve to offer that calomel and jalap to Queequeg there, just this instant off the whale. Is the steward an apothecary, sir? And may I ask whether this is the sort of bitters with which he blows the life back into a half-drowned man?"
"I trust not," said Starbuck. "It is poor stuff enough."

"Aye, aye, steward," cried Stubb. "We'll teach you to drug a harpooner! None of your apothecary's medicine here! You want to poison us, do you? You've got life insurance on us and want to murder us all and pocket the money, do you?"
"It was not me," cried Dough-Boy. "It was Aunt Charity that brought the ginger on board, and told me never to give the harpooners any spirits, but only this ginger-jub — so she called it."

"Ginger-jub! You gingerly rascal! Take that! And run along with you to the lockers, and get something better. I hope I do no wrong, Mr. Starbuck. It is the captain's orders — grog for the harpooner on a whale."
"Enough," replied Starbuck. "Only don't hit him again, but —"
"Oh, I never hurt when I hit, except when I hit a whale or something of that sort. And this fellow's a weasel. What were you about to say, sir?"
"Only this: go down with him, and get what you want yourself."

When Stubb reappeared, he came with a dark flask in one hand and a sort of tea-caddy in the other. The first contained strong spirits and was handed to Queequeg. The second was Aunt Charity's gift, and that was freely given to the waves.

chapters.title: Chapter 73 — Stubb and Flask kill a Right Whale; and Then Have a Talk
paragraphs: over Him.

It must be remembered that all this time we have a Sperm Whale's enormous head hanging from the Pequod's side. But we must let it continue hanging there a while till we can get a chance to attend to it. For the present, other matters press, and the best we can do now for the head is to pray heaven the tackles may hold.

Now, during the past night and morning, the Pequod had gradually drifted into a sea which, by its occasional patches of yellow brit, gave unusual signs that Right Whales were near — a species of the Leviathan that few supposed to be lurking anywhere nearby at this particular time. And though all hands commonly disdained the capture of those inferior creatures; and though the Pequod was not commissioned to cruise for them at all; and though she had passed numbers of them near the Crozetts without lowering a boat — yet now that a Sperm Whale had been brought alongside and beheaded, to everyone's surprise the announcement was made that a Right Whale should be captured that day, if the opportunity arose.

Nor was it long in coming. Tall spouts were seen to leeward, and two boats, Stubb's and Flask's, were sent off in pursuit. Pulling farther and farther away, they at last became almost invisible to the men at the masthead. But suddenly, in the distance, they saw a great heap of tumultuous white water, and soon after word came from aloft that one or both of the boats must be fast. An interval passed, and the boats were in plain sight, in the act of being dragged straight toward the ship by the towing whale. So close did the monster come to the hull that at first it seemed as if he meant it harm; but suddenly going down in a maelstrom within three rods of the planks, he wholly disappeared from view, as if diving under the keel. "Cut, cut!" was the cry from the ship to the boats, which for one instant seemed on the point of being dashed fatally against the vessel's side. But having plenty of line still in the tubs, and the whale not sounding very rapidly, they paid out plenty of rope, and at the same time pulled with all their might so as to get ahead of the ship. For a few minutes the struggle was intensely critical; for while they still slacked out the tightened line in one direction and still plied their oars in another, the opposing strain threatened to take them under. But it was only a few feet's advance they were trying to gain. And they stuck to it till they did gain it; when instantly a swift tremor was felt running like lightning along the keel, as the strained line, scraping beneath the ship, suddenly rose into view under her bows, snapping and quivering, and flinging off its drippings so that the drops fell like bits of broken glass on the water, while the whale beyond also rose into sight, and once more the boats were free to fly. But the exhausted whale slackened his speed, and, blindly changing his course, went around the stern of the ship, towing the two boats after him, so that they made a complete circuit.

Meanwhile, they hauled more and more on their lines, till, closely flanking him on both sides, Stubb answered Flask lance for lance; and so round and round the Pequod the battle went, while the multitudes of sharks that had been swimming around the Sperm Whale's body rushed to the fresh blood that was spilled, thirstily drinking at every new gash, as the eager Israelites drank at the new fountains that burst from the smitten rock.
At last his spout grew thick, and with a frightful roll and vomit, he turned upon his back — a corpse.
While the two headsmen were engaged in making fast cords to his flukes, and otherwise getting the mass ready for towing, some conversation ensued between them.
"I wonder what the old man wants with this lump of foul lard," said Stubb, not without some disgust at the thought of having to deal with so ignoble a leviathan.

"Wants with it?" said Flask, coiling some spare line in the boat's bow. "Did you never hear that the ship which even once has a Sperm Whale's head hoisted on her starboard side, and at the same time a Right Whale's on the port side — did you never hear, Stubb, that that ship can never afterward capsize?"
"Why not?"

"I don't know, but I heard that yellowish ghost of a Fedallah saying so, and he seems to know all about ships' charms. But I sometimes think he'll charm the ship to no good in the end. I don't half like that fellow, Stubb. Did you ever notice how that tusk of his is a sort of carved into a snake's head, Stubb?"

"Sink him! I never look at him at all; but if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks, and no one by — look down there, Flask" — pointing into the sea with a peculiar motion of both hands — "Aye, will I! Flask, I take that Fedallah to be the devil in disguise. Do you believe that cock and bull story about his having been stowed away on board ship? He's the devil, I say. The reason why you don't see his tail is because he tucks it up out of sight; he carries it coiled away in his pocket, I guess. Blast him! now that I think of it, he's always wanting oakum to stuff into the toes of his boots."
"He sleeps in his boots, doesn't he? He hasn't got any hammock, but I've seen him lie at night in a coil of rigging."
"No doubt — and it's because of his cursed tail. He coils it down, do you see, in the eye of the rigging."
"What's the old man have so much to do with him for?"
"Striking up a swap or a bargain, I suppose."
"Bargain? — about what?"

"Why, do you see, the old man is dead set on that White Whale, and the devil there is trying to come around him and get him to swap away his silver watch, or his soul, or something of that sort, and then he'll deliver Moby Dick."
"Nonsense! Stubb, you are joking. How can Fedallah do that?"

"I don't know, Flask, but the devil is a curious fellow, and a wicked one, I tell you. Why, they say he went sauntering into the old flagship once, switching his tail about, devilish easy and gentlemanlike, and asking if the old governor was at home. Well, he was at home, and asked the devil what he wanted. The devil, switching his hoofs, up and says, 'I want John.' 'What for?' says the old governor. 'What business is that of yours?' says the devil, getting mad — 'I want to use him.' 'Take him,' says the governor — and by the Lord, Flask, if the devil didn't give John the Asiatic cholera before he was through with him, I'll eat this whale in one mouthful. But look sharp — aren't you all ready there? Well, then, pull ahead, and let's get the whale alongside."
"I think I remember some story like the one you were telling," said Flask, when at last the two boats were slowly advancing with their burden toward the ship. "But I can't remember where I heard it."
"Three Spaniards? Adventures of those three bloody-minded soldiers? Did you read it there, Flask? I guess you did?"
"No — never saw such a book. Heard of it, though. But now, tell me, Stubb — do you suppose that devil you were speaking of just now was the same you say is now on board the Pequod?"

"Am I the same man that helped kill this whale? Doesn't the devil live forever? Who ever heard that the devil was dead? Did you ever see any parson wearing mourning for the devil? And if the devil has a latchkey to get into the admiral's cabin, don't you suppose he can crawl into a porthole? Tell me that, Mr. Flask?"
"How old do you suppose Fedallah is, Stubb?"

"Do you see that mainmast there?" pointing to the ship. "Well, that's the figure one. Now take all the hoops in the Pequod's hold, and string them along in a row with that mast, for zeros, do you see? Well, that wouldn't even begin to be Fedallah's age. Not all the coopers in creation could show hoops enough to make zeros enough."

"But see here, Stubb, I thought you boasted a little just now that you meant to give Fedallah a toss in the sea if you got a good chance. Now, if he's as old as all those hoops of yours come to, and if he's going to live forever, what good will it do to pitch him overboard — tell me that?"
"Give him a good ducking, anyway."
"But he'd crawl back."
"Duck him again, and keep ducking him."
"Suppose he should take it into his head to duck you, though — yes, and drown you — what then?"

"I should like to see him try it; I'd give him such a pair of black eyes that he wouldn't dare to show his face in the admiral's cabin again for a long while, let alone down in the orlop there, where he lives, and hereabouts on the upper decks where he sneaks so much. Damn the devil, Flask; so you suppose I'm afraid of the devil? Who's afraid of him, except the old governor who daresn't catch him and put him in double-darbies, as he deserves, but lets him go about kidnapping people; aye, and signed a bond with him that all the people the devil kidnapped, he'd roast for him? There's a governor!"
"Do you suppose Fedallah wants to kidnap Captain Ahab?"

"Do I suppose it? You'll know it before long, Flask. But I am going now to keep a sharp look-out on him; and if I see anything very suspicious going on, I'll just take him by the nape of his neck, and say — Look here, Beelzebub, you don't do it; and if he makes any fuss, by the Lord I'll make a grab into his pocket for his tail, take it to the capstan, and give him such a wrenching and heaving that his tail will come short off at the stump — do you see? And then, I rather guess when he finds himself docked in that queer fashion, he'll sneak off without the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs."
"And what will you do with the tail, Stubb?"
"Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home — what else?"
"Now, do you mean what you say, and have been saying all along, Stubb?"
"Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship."
The boats were now hailed to tow the whale on the port side, where fluke chains and other gear were already prepared for securing him.
"Didn't I tell you so?" said Flask. "Yes, you'll soon see this right whale's head hoisted up opposite that sperm whale's."

In good time, Flask's saying proved true. As before, the Pequod had leaned steeply over toward the sperm whale's head; now, by the counterweight of both heads, she regained her even keel — though sorely strained, you may well believe. So, when on one side you hoist in Locke's head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant's and you come back again — but in very poor shape. Thus some minds forever keep trimming boat. Oh, you foolish ones! Throw all these thunder-heads overboard, and then you will float light and right.

In disposing of the body of a right whale, when brought alongside the ship, the same preliminary proceedings commonly take place as in the case of a sperm whale; only, in the latter instance, the head is cut off whole, but in the former the lips and tongue are separately removed and hoisted on deck, with all the well-known black bone attached to what is called the crown-piece. But nothing like this, in the present case, had been done. The carcasses of both whales had dropped astern; and the head-laden ship not a little resembled a mule carrying a pair of overburdening panniers.

Meanwhile, Fedallah was calmly eyeing the right whale's head, and every now and then glancing from the deep wrinkles there to the lines in his own hand. And Ahab happened to stand so that the Parsee occupied his shadow; while, if the Parsee's shadow was there at all, it seemed only to blend with and lengthen Ahab's. As the crew toiled on, Laplandish speculations were bandied about among them concerning all these passing things.

chapters.title: Chapter 74 — The Sperm Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Here, now, are two great whales, laying their heads together. Let us join them and lay our own together.

Of the grand order of folio leviathans, the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale are by far the most noteworthy. They are the only whales regularly hunted by man. To the Nantucketer, they present the two extremes of all the known varieties of the whale. As the external difference between them is mainly observable in their heads; and as a head of each is this moment hanging from the Pequod's side; and as we may freely go from one to the other, by merely stepping across the deck — where, I should like to know, will you obtain a better chance to study practical cetology than here?

In the first place, you are struck by the general contrast between these heads. Both are massive enough, heaven knows; but there is a certain mathematical symmetry in the Sperm Whale's that the Right Whale's sadly lacks. There is more character in the Sperm Whale's head. As you look at it, you find yourself involuntarily granting him an immense superiority in pervading dignity. In the present instance, too, this dignity is heightened by the pepper-and-salt color of his head at the summit, a sign of advanced age and long experience. In short, he is what the fishermen technically call a "gray-headed whale."

Let us now note what is least dissimilar in these heads — namely, the two most important organs: the eye and the ear. Far back on the side of the head, and low down, near the angle of either whale's jaw, if you search carefully, you will at last see a lashless eye, which you would think belonged to a young colt — it is so disproportionately small.

Now, from this peculiar sideways position of the whale's eyes, it is plain that he can never see an object that is exactly ahead, any more than one that is exactly astern. In a word, the position of the whale's eyes corresponds to that of a man's ears; and you may imagine for yourself how it would go with you if you surveyed objects sideways through your ears. You would find that you could command only some thirty degrees of vision forward of the straight side-line of sight, and about thirty more behind it. If your bitterest enemy were walking straight toward you in broad daylight with a dagger raised, you would not be able to see him, any more than if he were creeping up on you from behind. In a word, you would have two backs, so to speak; but at the same time also two fronts (side fronts): for what is it that makes the front of a man — what, indeed, but his eyes?

Moreover, in most other animals that I can now think of, the eyes are so placed as to blend their visual power imperceptibly, producing one picture for the brain and not two. But the peculiar position of the whale's eyes, effectively divided as they are by many cubic feet of solid head, which towers between them like a great mountain separating two lakes in valleys, must of course wholly separate the impressions that each independent organ conveys. The whale, therefore, must see one distinct picture on this side and another distinct picture on that side, while all between must be profound darkness and nothingness to him. Man, in effect, may be said to look out on the world from a sentry-box with two joined sashes for his window. But in the whale these two sashes are set in separately, making two distinct windows, but sadly impairing the view. This peculiarity of the whale's eyes is something always to be borne in mind in the fishery, and to be remembered by the reader in some later scenes.

A curious and most puzzling question might be raised about this matter of the Leviathan's vision. But I must be content with a hint. So long as a man's eyes are open in the light, the act of seeing is involuntary; that is, he cannot help mechanically seeing whatever objects are in front of him. Nevertheless, anyone's experience will teach him that, though he can take in an undiscriminating sweep of things at one glance, it is quite impossible for him to examine any two things attentively and completely — however large or however small — at one and the same instant of time, even if they lie side by side and touch each other. But if you now separate these two objects and surround each with a circle of profound darkness, then, in order to see one of them in such a way as to bring your mind to bear on it, you will utterly shut the other out of your consciousness at that moment. How is it, then, with the whale? True, both his eyes, in themselves, must act simultaneously; but is his brain so much more comprehensive, combining and subtle than man's that he can at the same moment attentively examine two distinct prospects, one on one side of him and the other in exactly the opposite direction? If he can, then it is as marvelous a thing in him as if a man were able to work through the proofs of two distinct problems in Euclid simultaneously. Nor, strictly investigated, is there anything incongruous in this comparison.

It may be only an idle whim, but it has always seemed to me that the extraordinary wavering movements some whales display when beset by three or four boats, and the timidity and liability to odd frights so common in such whales — that all this, I think, comes indirectly from the helpless perplexity of will in which their divided and diametrically opposite powers of vision must involve them.

But the ear of the whale is fully as curious as the eye. If you are a complete stranger to their race, you might hunt over these two heads for hours and never discover that organ. The ear has no external flap whatever; and into the hole itself you can hardly insert a quill, it is so wondrously tiny. It is lodged a little behind the eye. As to their ears, this important difference is to be observed between the sperm whale and the right: while the ear of the former has an external opening, that of the latter is entirely and evenly covered over with a membrane, so that it is quite imperceptible from outside.

Is it not curious that so vast a being as the whale should see the world through so small an eye, and hear the thunder through an ear smaller than a hare's? But if his eyes were as broad as the lens of Herschel's great telescope, and his ears as capacious as the porches of cathedrals, would that make him any longer of sight, or any sharper of hearing? Not at all. Why, then, do you try to "enlarge" your mind? Make it subtler.

Let us now, with whatever levers and steam-engines we have at hand, tip the sperm whale's head over so that it lies bottom up; then, climbing a ladder to the summit, take a peep down the mouth; and if the body were not now completely separated from it, we might go down with a lantern into the great Kentucky Mammoth Cave of his stomach. But let us hold on here by this tooth and look about us where we are. What a really beautiful and chaste-looking mouth! From floor to ceiling it is lined, or rather papered, with a glistening white membrane, glossy as bridal satin.

But come out now and look at this portentous lower jaw, which seems like the long narrow lid of an immense snuff-box, with the hinge at one end instead of one side. If you pry it up, so as to get it overhead, and expose its rows of teeth, it looks like a terrific portcullis; and such, alas, it proves to be for many a poor fellow in the fishery, on whom these spikes fall with impaling force. But far more terrible is the sight when, fathoms down in the sea, you see some sulky whale floating there suspended, with his prodigious jaw, some fifteen feet long, hanging straight down at right angles to his body, for all the world like a ship's jib-boom. This whale is not dead; he is only dispirited; out of sorts, perhaps; hypochondriac; and so listless that the hinges of his jaw have relaxed, leaving him there in that ungainly sort of plight, a reproach to all his tribe, who must, no doubt, be calling down lockjaw on him.

In most cases this lower jaw — being easily unhinged by a practiced hand — is detached and hoisted on deck for the purpose of extracting the ivory teeth and furnishing a supply of that hard white whalebone with which the fishermen fashion all sorts of curious articles, including canes, umbrella-sticks, and handles for riding-whips.

With a long, weary hoist the jaw is dragged on board, as if it were an anchor; and when the proper time comes — some few days after the other work — Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, being all accomplished dentists, are set to drawing teeth. With a keen cutting-spade, Queequeg lances the gums; then the jaw is lashed down to ringbolts, and a tackle being rigged from aloft, they drag out these teeth, as Michigan oxen drag stumps of old oaks out of wild woodlands. There are generally forty-two teeth in all; in old whales, much worn down, but undecayed, and not filled in our artificial fashion. The jaw is afterwards sawn into slabs, and piled away like joists for building houses.

chapters.title: Chapter 75 — The Right Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Crossing the deck, let us now have a good long look at the Right Whale's head.

As in general shape the noble Sperm Whale's head may be compared to a Roman war-chariot (especially in front, where it is so broadly rounded), so, seen broadly, the Right Whale's head bears a rather inelegant resemblance to a gigantic galliot-toed shoe, its toe rounded like the bow of a Dutch galliot. Two hundred years ago an old Dutch voyager likened its shape to that of a shoemaker's last. And in this same last or shoe, that old woman of the nursery tale, with her swarming brood, might very comfortably be housed, she and all her children.

But as you come nearer to this great head, it begins to take on different aspects, according to your point of view. If you stand on its summit and look at these two F-shaped spout-holes, you would take the whole head for an enormous bass-viol, and these spiracles for the openings in its sounding-board. Then again, if you fix your eye on this strange, crested, comb-like encrustation on the top of the mass — this green, barnacled thing, which the Greenlanders call the "crown," and the Southern fishermen the "bonnet" of the Right Whale — fixing your eyes solely on this, you would take the head for the trunk of some huge oak, with a bird's nest in its fork. At any rate, when you watch those live crabs that nestle here on this bonnet, such an idea will be almost sure to occur to you; unless, indeed, your fancy has been fixed by the technical term "crown" also given to it; in which case you will take great interest in thinking how this mighty monster is actually a diademed king of the sea, whose green crown has been put together for him in this marvelous way. But if this whale is a king, he is a very sulky-looking fellow to grace a diadem. Look at that hanging lower lip! What a huge sulk and pout is there! A sulk and pout, by carpenter's measurement, about twenty feet long and five feet deep; a sulk and pout that will yield you some 500 gallons of oil and more.

A great pity, now, that this unfortunate whale should be hare-lipped. The cleft is about a foot across. Probably the mother, during an important interval, was sailing down the Peruvian coast when earthquakes made the beach gape. Over this lip, as over a slippery threshold, we now slide into the mouth. Upon my word, if I were at Mackinaw, I should take this for the inside of an Indian wigwam. Good Lord! Is this the road that Jonah went? The roof is about twelve feet high, and runs up to a pretty sharp angle, as if there were a regular ridge-pole there; while these ribbed, arched, hairy sides present us with those wondrous, half-vertical, scimitar-shaped slats of whalebone, say three hundred on a side, which, hanging down from the upper part of the head or crown bone, form those Venetian blinds that have been briefly mentioned elsewhere. The edges of these bones are fringed with hairy fibers, through which the Right Whale strains the water, and in whose tangles he keeps back the small fish when he goes open-mouthed through the seas of brit at feeding time. In the central blinds of bone, as they stand in their natural order, there are certain curious marks, curves, hollows and ridges, by which some whalemen calculate the creature's age, as the age of an oak is reckoned by its circular rings. Though the certainty of this test is far from demonstrable, it has the flavor of probability by analogy. At any rate, if we accept it, we must grant the Right Whale a far greater age than will seem reasonable at first glance.

In old times, the most curious fancies seem to have prevailed about these blinds. One voyager in Purchas calls them the wondrous "whiskers" inside the whale's mouth;* another, "hogs' bristles"; a third old gentleman in Hackluyt uses the following elegant language, with "chop" for jaw: "There are about two hundred and fifty fins growing on each side of his upper chop, which arch over his tongue on each side of his mouth."

*This reminds us that the Right Whale really does have a sort of whisker, or rather a mustache, consisting of a few scattered white hairs on the upper part of the outer end of the lower jaw. Sometimes these tufts give a rather piratical expression to his otherwise solemn face.

As everyone knows, these same "hogs' bristles," "fins," "whiskers," "blinds," or whatever you please, supply the ladies with their busks and other stiffening contrivances. But in this respect the demand has long been declining. It was in Queen Anne's time that the bone was in its glory, the farthingale (a hooped petticoat) being then all the fashion. And as those ancient ladies moved about gaily, though in the jaws of the whale, as you might say, so, in a shower, with the same thoughtlessness, do we nowadays run under the same jaws for protection; the umbrella being a tent spread over the same bone.

But now forget all about blinds and whiskers for a moment and, standing in the Right Whale's mouth, look around you afresh. Seeing all these colonnades of bone so methodically ranged about, would you not think you were inside the great Haarlem organ, gazing upon its thousand pipes? For a carpet to the organ we have the softest of Turkey rugs — the tongue, which is glued, as it were, to the floor of the mouth. It is very fat and tender, and apt to tear to pieces when it is hoisted on deck. This particular tongue now before us — at a passing glance I should say it was a six-barreler; that is, it will yield you about that amount of oil.

By now you must have plainly seen the truth of what I started with — that the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale have almost entirely different heads. To sum up, then: in the Right Whale's there is no great well of sperm; no ivory teeth at all; no long, slender mandible of a lower jaw, like the Sperm Whale's. Nor in the Sperm Whale are there any of those blinds of bone; no huge lower lip; and scarcely anything of a tongue. Again, the Right Whale has two external spout-holes, the Sperm Whale only one.
Look your last, now, on these venerable hooded heads, while they yet lie together. For one will soon sink, unrecorded, in the sea. The other will not be very long in following.

Can you catch the expression of the Sperm Whale's head there? It is the same he died with, only some of the longer wrinkles in the forehead now seem to have faded away. I think his broad brow is full of a prairie-like placidity, born of a speculative indifference to death. But notice the other head's expression. See that amazing lower lip, pressed by accident against the ship's side, so as to clasp the jaw firmly. Does not this whole head seem to speak of an enormous practical resolution in facing death? This Right Whale I take to have been a Stoic; the Sperm Whale, a Platonist, who might have taken up Spinoza in his later years.

chapters.title: Chapter 76 — The Battering-Ram
paragraphs: Before leaving the Sperm Whale's head for now, I would have you, as a sensible physiologist, simply — and particularly — take note of its front, in all its compact concentration. I would have you examine it now with the single aim of forming for yourself some unexaggerated, intelligent estimate of whatever battering-ram power may be lodged there. This is a vital point, for you must either settle this matter to your own satisfaction, or remain forever an unbeliever about one of the most appalling, but no less true, events to be found perhaps anywhere in all recorded history.

You observe that in the ordinary swimming position of the Sperm Whale, the front of his head presents an almost entirely vertical surface to the water. You observe that the lower part of that front slopes considerably backward, so as to leave more room for the long socket that receives the boom-like lower jaw. You observe that the mouth is entirely under the head, much as though your own mouth were entirely under your chin. Moreover, you observe that the whale has no external nose, and that what nose he has — his spout hole — is on the top of his head; you observe that his eyes and ears are at the sides of his head, nearly one third of his entire length back from the front. So you must by now have realized that the front of the Sperm Whale's head is a dead, blind wall, without a single organ or tender projection of any kind whatsoever. Furthermore, you must now consider that only in the extreme, lower, backward-sloping part of the front of the head is there the slightest trace of bone, and that not until you get nearly twenty feet back from the forehead do you come to the full development of the skull. So this whole enormous boneless mass is like one wad. Finally, although, as will soon be revealed, its contents partly consist of the most delicate oil, you must now be told the nature of the substance that so impregnably encases all that apparent delicacy. Earlier I described to you how the blubber wraps the body of the whale as the rind wraps an orange. It is just the same with the head, but with this difference: around the head this envelope, though not so thick, has a boneless toughness that no one who has not handled it can imagine. The most sharply pointed harpoon, the keenest lance thrown by the strongest human arm, bounces off it powerlessly. It is as though the forehead of the Sperm Whale were paved with horses' hoofs. I do not think that any sensation lurks in it.

Think of another thing, too. When two large, loaded Indiamen — big merchant ships of the India trade — happen to crowd and crush toward each other in the docks, what do the sailors do? They do not hang between them, at the point where they will touch, any merely hard substance, like iron or wood. No, they hold there a large, round wad of tow (coarse flax or hemp fiber) and cork, wrapped in the thickest and toughest of ox-hide. That wad bravely and without injury takes the squeeze that would have snapped all their oak handspikes and iron crowbars. By itself this is enough to illustrate the obvious fact I am driving at. But in addition to this, it has occurred to me as a hypothesis that, since ordinary fish have what is called a swimming bladder, which they can swell or shrink at will; and since the Sperm Whale, as far as I know, has no such equipment; considering, too, the otherwise unaccountable way in which he sometimes sinks his head completely beneath the surface, and at other times swims with it raised high out of the water; considering the unobstructed elasticity of its envelope; considering the unique interior of his head — it has occurred to me as a hypothesis, I say, that those mystical, lung-celled honeycombs in there may possibly have some hitherto unknown and unsuspected connection with the outer air, so that they can be swelled and shrunk by the atmosphere. If this is so, imagine the irresistible force of that might, when the most impalpable and destructive of all the elements contributes to it.

Now, notice this. Driving this dead, impregnable, uninjurable wall unerringly forward, and this most buoyant thing inside it, there swims behind it all a mass of tremendous life, which can only be properly measured the way piled wood is — by the cord; and all of it obeys a single will, as the smallest insect does. So when I later describe to you in detail all the special powers and concentrations of force lurking everywhere in this vast monster, and show you some of his lesser feats of head-smashing, I trust you will have given up all ignorant disbelief and be ready to stand by this: that even if the Sperm Whale smashed a passage through the Isthmus of Darien, in Panama, and mixed the Atlantic with the Pacific, you would not raise one hair of your eyebrow. For unless you acknowledge the whale, you are only a provincial and a sentimentalist in Truth. But clear Truth is something only salamander giants can face; how small, then, are the chances for the provincials? What happened to the feeble youth who lifted the veil of the dread goddess at Lais?

chapters.title: Chapter 77 — The Great Heidelburgh Tun
paragraphs: Now comes the baling of the case. But to understand it properly, you must know something of the curious internal structure of the thing being operated upon.

Regarding the Sperm Whale's head as a solid oblong, you may divide it sideways, along an inclined plane, into two quoins,* of which the lower is the bony structure forming the skull and jaws, and the upper an oily mass entirely free of bones, its broad forward end forming the expanded, vertical, apparent forehead of the whale. At the middle of the forehead, subdivide this upper quoin horizontally, and you then have two almost equal parts, which were already naturally divided by an internal wall of a thick, tendinous substance.

*Quoin is not a Euclidean term. It belongs to pure nautical mathematics. I am not aware that it has been defined before. A quoin is a solid which differs from a wedge in having its sharp end formed by the steep slant of one side, instead of by both sides tapering toward each other.

The lower subdivided part, called the junk, is one immense honeycomb of oil, formed throughout its whole extent by tough, elastic white fibers crossing and recrossing into ten thousand infiltrated cells. The upper part, known as the Case, may be regarded as the great Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale, after the famous giant wine-cask of that name. And as that famous great cask is mystically carved in front, so the whale's vast pleated forehead forms countless strange devices for the emblematic adornment of his wondrous tun. Moreover, as the Tun of Heidelburgh was always kept filled with the most excellent of the wines of the Rhine valleys, so the tun of the whale contains by far the most precious of all his oily vintages; namely, the highly prized spermaceti, in its absolutely pure, limpid and fragrant state. Nor is this precious substance found unmixed in any other part of the creature. Though in life it remains perfectly fluid, yet on exposure to the air after death it soon begins to solidify, sending out beautiful crystalline shoots, as when the first thin, delicate ice is just forming in water. A large whale's case generally yields about five hundred gallons of sperm, though, owing to unavoidable circumstances, a good deal of it is spilled, leaks and dribbles away, or is otherwise irretrievably lost in the ticklish business of securing what you can.

I do not know with what fine and costly material the Heidelburgh Tun was coated within, but in supreme richness that coating could not possibly have compared with the silken, pearl-colored membrane, like the lining of a fine fur coat, forming the inner surface of the Sperm Whale's case.

It will have been seen that the Heidelburgh Tun of the Sperm Whale takes in the whole length of the entire top of the head; and since — as has been set out elsewhere — the head takes up one third of the whole length of the creature, then, putting that length at eighty feet for a good-sized whale, you have more than twenty-six feet for the depth of the tun when it is hoisted lengthwise, up and down, against a ship's side.

Since, in beheading the whale, the operator's instrument is brought close to the spot where an entrance is later forced into the spermaceti magazine, he has to be uncommonly careful, lest a careless, untimely stroke should invade the sanctuary and wastefully let out its invaluable contents. It is this beheaded end of the head, too, that is at last raised out of the water and held in that position by the enormous cutting tackles, whose hempen combinations, on one side, make quite a wilderness of ropes in that quarter.
Thus much being said, attend now, I ask you, to that marvelous and — in this particular instance — almost fatal operation whereby the Sperm Whale's great Heidelburgh Tun is tapped.

chapters.title: Chapter 78 — Cistern and Buckets
paragraphs: Nimble as a cat, Tashtego climbs aloft and, without changing his upright posture, runs straight out along the overhanging main-yard-arm to the point where it projects exactly over the hoisted Tun. He has taken with him a light tackle called a whip, consisting of only two parts running through a single-sheaved block (a pulley with a single wheel). Securing this block so that it hangs down from the yard-arm, he swings one end of the rope until it is caught and firmly held by a hand on deck. Then, hand over hand, down the other part, the Indian drops through the air until he deftly lands on the summit of the head. There — still raised high above the rest of the company, to whom he calls out in lively fashion — he seems some Turkish Muezzin calling the good people to prayer from the top of a tower. A short-handled sharp spade is sent up to him, and he diligently searches for the proper place to begin breaking into the Tun. In this business he goes very carefully, like a treasure-hunter in some old house, sounding the walls to find where the gold is walled in. By the time this cautious search is over, a stout iron-bound bucket, exactly like a well-bucket, has been attached to one end of the whip, while the other end, stretched across the deck, is held there by two or three alert hands. These now hoist the bucket within reach of the Indian, to whom someone else has handed up a very long pole. Inserting this pole into the bucket, Tashtego guides the bucket down into the Tun until it entirely disappears; then, when he gives the word to the seamen at the whip, up comes the bucket again, all bubbling like a dairymaid's pail of new milk. Carefully lowered from its height, the brimming bucket is caught by a hand appointed for the purpose and quickly emptied into a large tub. Then it goes back up aloft and through the same round again, until the deep cistern will yield no more. Toward the end, Tashtego has to ram his long pole harder and harder, and deeper and deeper into the Tun, until some twenty feet of the pole have gone down.

Now, the people of the Pequod had been baling for some time in this way, and several tubs had been filled with the fragrant sperm, when all at once a strange accident happened. Whether it was that Tashtego, that wild Indian, was so heedless and reckless as to let go for a moment his one-handed hold on the great cabled tackles holding up the head; or whether the place where he stood was so treacherous and oozy; or whether the Evil One himself would have it happen so, without stating his particular reasons — how exactly it was, there is no telling now; but suddenly, as the eightieth or ninetieth bucket came suckingly up — my God! poor Tashtego — like the twin bucket that goes down as the other comes up in a real well, dropped head first down into this great Tun of Heidelburgh, and with a horrible oily gurgling went clean out of sight!

"Man overboard!" cried Daggoo, who, amid the general dismay, was the first to come to his senses. "Swing the bucket this way!" And he put one foot into it, the better to secure his slippery handhold on the whip itself, and the hoisters ran him high up to the top of the head, almost before Tashtego could have reached its bottom inside. Meanwhile, there was a terrible tumult. Looking over the side, they saw the head, lifeless until then, throbbing and heaving just below the surface of the sea, as if at that moment seized by some momentous idea; whereas it was only the poor Indian unconsciously revealing by those struggles the perilous depth to which he had sunk.

At this instant, while Daggoo, on the summit of the head, was clearing the whip — which had somehow got fouled in the great cutting tackles — a sharp cracking noise was heard; and to the unspeakable horror of all, one of the two enormous hooks holding up the head tore out, and with a vast vibration the enormous mass swung sideways, until the drunken ship reeled and shook as if struck by an iceberg. The one remaining hook, on which the entire strain now depended, seemed every instant on the point of giving way — an event made still more likely by the violent motions of the head.

"Come down, come down!" yelled the seamen to Daggoo. But with one hand holding on to the heavy tackles, so that if the head should drop he would still remain suspended, the negro, having cleared the foul line, rammed the bucket down into the now collapsed well, meaning that the buried harpooner should grasp it and so be hauled out.
"In heaven's name, man," cried Stubb, "are you ramming home a cartridge there? — Stop! How will that help him — jamming that iron-bound bucket on top of his head? Stop, will you!"
"Stand clear of the tackle!" cried a voice like the bursting of a rocket.

Almost in the same instant, with a thunder-boom, the enormous mass dropped into the sea, like Niagara's Table Rock into the whirlpool; the suddenly relieved hull rolled away from it so far that the glittering copper sheathing far down her side came into view; and all caught their breath as Daggoo, half swinging — now over the sailors' heads, and now over the water — was dimly seen through a thick mist of spray, clinging to the dangling tackles, while poor, buried-alive Tashtego was sinking utterly down to the bottom of the sea! But hardly had the blinding vapor cleared away when a naked figure with a boarding-sword in his hand was seen for one swift moment hovering over the bulwarks. The next, a loud splash announced that my brave Queequeg had dived to the rescue. Everyone rushed together to the side, and every eye counted every ripple, as moment followed moment and no sign of either the sinker or the diver could be seen. Some hands now jumped into a boat alongside and pushed a little way off from the ship.

"Ha! Ha!" cried Daggoo all at once, from his now quiet, swinging perch overhead. And looking further off from the side, we saw an arm thrust upright from the blue waves — a sight as strange as an arm thrust forth from the grass over a grave.

"Both! Both! — it is both!" cried Daggoo again with a joyful shout. And soon after, Queequeg was seen boldly striking out with one hand, and with the other clutching the long hair of the Indian. Drawn into the waiting boat, they were quickly brought to the deck. But Tashtego was long in coming to, and Queequeg did not look very well either.

Now, how had this noble rescue been accomplished? Why, diving after the slowly descending head, Queequeg, with his keen sword, had made side lunges near its bottom, so as to cut a large hole there; then, dropping his sword, he had thrust his long arm far inward and upward, and so hauled out poor Tash by the head. He declared that when he first reached in for him, a leg was presented; but, knowing well that that was not as it ought to be, and might cause great trouble, he had thrust back the leg, and by a deft heave and toss had turned the Indian a somersault; so that at the next try he came out in the good old way — head first. As for the great head itself, that was doing as well as could be expected.

And thus, through the courage and great skill in obstetrics of Queequeg, the deliverance — or rather, delivery — of Tashtego was successfully accomplished, in the teeth, too, of the most untoward and apparently hopeless impediments; which is a lesson by no means to be forgotten. Midwifery should be taught in the same course with fencing and boxing, riding and rowing.

I know that this strange adventure of the Gay-Header's will be sure to seem incredible to some landsmen, though they themselves may have seen or heard of someone falling into a cistern ashore — an accident which happens not infrequently, and with much less reason, too, than the Indian's, considering the extreme slipperiness of the rim of the Sperm Whale's well.

But perhaps it may be shrewdly objected: how is this? We thought the tissued, infiltrated head of the Sperm Whale was the lightest and most corklike part of him; and yet you make it sink in an element of far greater specific gravity than itself. We have you there. Not at all — I have you; for at the time poor Tash fell in, the case had been nearly emptied of its lighter contents, leaving little but the dense tendinous wall of the well — a double-welded, hammered substance, as I have said before, much heavier than sea water, a lump of which sinks in it almost like lead. But in this instance the tendency of this substance to sink rapidly was materially counteracted by the other parts of the head that remained attached to it, so that it sank very slowly and deliberately indeed, giving Queequeg a fair chance to perform his agile obstetrics on the run, as you might say. Yes, it was a running delivery, so it was.

Now, had Tashtego perished in that head, it would have been a very precious perishing: smothered in the very whitest and daintiest of fragrant spermaceti; coffined, hearsed and entombed in the secret inner chamber and sanctum sanctorum of the whale. Only one sweeter end comes readily to mind — the delicious death of an Ohio honey-hunter, who, seeking honey in the fork of a hollow tree, found such a great store of it that, as he leaned too far over, it sucked him in, so that he died embalmed. How many, do you think, have likewise fallen into Plato's honey head, and sweetly perished there?

chapters.title: Chapter 79 — The Prairie
paragraphs: To scan the lines of his face, or feel the bumps on the head of this Leviathan — this is something no physiognomist or phrenologist, no reader of character from the face or from the skull, has yet undertaken. Such an enterprise would seem about as hopeful as for Lavater to have scrutinized the wrinkles on the Rock of Gibraltar, or for Gall to have climbed a ladder and felt over the Dome of the Pantheon. Still, in that famous work of his, Lavater not only treats of the various faces of men, but also attentively studies the faces of horses, birds, serpents and fish, and dwells in detail on the changes of expression to be seen in them. Nor have Gall and his disciple Spurzheim failed to throw out some hints about the phrenological characteristics of beings other than man. Therefore, though I am poorly qualified to be a pioneer in applying these two semi-sciences to the whale, I will do my best. I try all things; I achieve what I can.

Regarded physiognomically, the Sperm Whale is an anomalous creature. He has no proper nose. And since the nose is the central and most conspicuous of the features, and since it perhaps most modifies and finally controls their combined expression, it would seem that its entire absence, as an external appendage, must very largely affect the whale's countenance. For as in landscape gardening a spire, cupola, monument or tower of some sort is thought almost indispensable to complete the scene, so no face can be physiognomically in keeping without the raised, open-work belfry of the nose. Knock the nose off Phidias's marble Jove, and what a sorry remainder! Nevertheless, Leviathan is of so mighty a magnitude, and all his proportions are so stately, that the same deficiency which would be hideous in the sculptured Jove is no blemish at all in him. No, it is an added grandeur. A nose on the whale would have been impertinent. As you sail round his vast head in your jolly-boat on your physiognomical voyage, your noble conceptions of him are never insulted by the reflection that he has a nose to be pulled — a pestilent notion that so often insists on intruding even when you look at the mightiest royal beadle on his throne.
In some respects, perhaps the most imposing physiognomical view to be had of the Sperm Whale is that of the full front of his head. This aspect is sublime.

In thought, a fine human brow is like the East when troubled with the morning. In the repose of the pasture, the curled brow of the bull has a touch of the grand in it. When the elephant pushes heavy cannon up mountain passes, his brow is majestic. Human or animal, the mystical brow is like that great golden seal affixed by the German emperors to their decrees. It signifies — "God: done this day by my hand." But in most creatures, and even in man himself, the brow is very often a mere strip of alpine land lying along the snow line. Few are the foreheads which, like Shakespeare's or Melancthon's, rise so high and come down so low that the eyes themselves seem clear, eternal, tideless mountain lakes; and in the forehead's wrinkles above them you seem to track the antlered thoughts coming down there to drink, as Highland hunters track the deer's prints in the snow. But in the great Sperm Whale, this high and mighty godlike dignity inherent in the brow is so immensely amplified that, gazing on it in that full front view, you feel the Deity and the dread powers more forcibly than in looking at any other object in living nature. For you see no one point precisely; not one distinct feature is revealed; no nose, eyes, ears or mouth; no face — he has none, properly speaking; nothing but that one broad firmament of a forehead, pleated with riddles, dumbly lowering with the doom of boats, and ships, and men. Nor does this wondrous brow diminish in profile, though viewed that way its grandeur does not overpower you so much. In profile you plainly see that horizontal, half-moon-shaped hollow in the middle of the forehead which, in man, is Lavater's mark of genius.

But how? Genius in the Sperm Whale? Has the Sperm Whale ever written a book or made a speech? No, his great genius is declared in his doing nothing in particular to prove it. It is declared, moreover, in his pyramid-like silence. And this reminds me that had the great Sperm Whale been known to the young Orient World, he would have been deified by the childlike thoughts of its magi. They deified the crocodile of the Nile because the crocodile is tongueless; and the Sperm Whale has no tongue, or at least it is so exceedingly small that it cannot be thrust out. If hereafter any highly cultured, poetical nation shall lure back to their birthright the merry May-day gods of old, and enthrone them, living, once more in the now egotistical sky, on the now unhaunted hill, then be sure that, raised to Jove's high seat, the great Sperm Whale shall lord it there.

Champollion deciphered the wrinkled granite hieroglyphics. But there is no Champollion to decipher the Egypt of every man's and every being's face. Physiognomy, like every other human science, is only a passing fable. If, then, Sir William Jones, who read thirty languages, could not read the simplest peasant's face in its deeper and subtler meanings, how can unlettered Ishmael hope to read the awful Chaldee of the Sperm Whale's brow? I only put that brow before you. Read it if you can.

chapters.title: Chapter 80 — The Nut
paragraphs: If the Sperm Whale is physiognomically a Sphinx, to the phrenologist his brain seems that geometrical circle which it is impossible to square.

In the full-grown creature the skull will measure at least twenty feet in length. Unhinge the lower jaw, and the side view of this skull is like the side of a moderately inclined plane resting throughout on a level base. But in life — as we have seen elsewhere — this inclined plane is filled up at an angle, and almost squared off, by the enormous mass of the junk and sperm lying on top of it. At the high end the skull forms a crater to bed that part of the mass; while under the long floor of this crater — in another cavity seldom more than ten inches long and as many deep — lies the mere handful of this monster's brain. In life the brain is at least twenty feet from his apparent forehead; it is hidden away behind its vast outworks, like the innermost citadel within the enlarged fortifications of Quebec. It is secreted in him like a choice casket, so much so that I have known some whalemen who flatly deny that the Sperm Whale has any other brain than that palpable semblance of one formed by the cubic yards of his sperm magazine. Given its strange folds, courses and convolutions, they think it more in keeping with the idea of his general might to regard that mystic part of him as the seat of his intelligence.

It is plain, then, that phrenologically the head of this Leviathan, in the creature's living, intact state, is an entire delusion. As for his true brain, you can then see no indication of it, nor feel any. The whale, like all things that are mighty, wears a false brow before the common world.

If you unload his skull of its spermy heaps and then take a rear view of its rear end, which is the high end, you will be struck by its resemblance to the human skull seen in the same position and from the same point of view. Indeed, place this reversed skull (scaled down to human size) among a plate of men's skulls, and you would involuntarily mistake it for one of them; and noticing the depressions on one part of its summit, you would say, in phrenological language — This man had no self-esteem, and no veneration. And by those negations, taken together with the positive fact of his prodigious bulk and power, you can best form for yourself the truest, though not the most exhilarating, conception of what the most exalted potency is.

But if, from the comparative dimensions of the whale's actual brain, you think it incapable of being adequately charted, then I have another idea for you. If you look attentively at almost any quadruped's spine, you will be struck by the resemblance of its vertebrae to a strung necklace of dwarfed skulls, all bearing a rudimentary resemblance to the skull proper. It is a German notion that the vertebrae are absolutely undeveloped skulls. But I take it that the Germans were not the first men to perceive the curious external resemblance. A foreign friend once pointed it out to me in the skeleton of an enemy he had killed, with whose vertebrae he was inlaying the beaked prow of his canoe in a sort of bas-relief. Now, I consider that the phrenologists have left out an important thing in not pushing their investigations from the cerebellum through the spinal canal. For I believe that much of a man's character will be found indicated in his backbone. I would rather feel your spine than your skull, whoever you are. A thin joist of a spine never yet held up a full and noble soul. I rejoice in my spine, as in the firm, audacious staff of that flag which I fling half out to the world.

Apply this spinal branch of phrenology to the Sperm Whale. His cranial cavity is continuous with the first neck-vertebra; and in that vertebra the bottom of the spinal canal will measure ten inches across and eight in height, and is triangular in shape, with the base downward. As it passes through the remaining vertebrae the canal tapers in size, but for a considerable distance it remains of large capacity. Now, of course, this canal is filled with much the same strangely fibrous substance — the spinal cord — as the brain, and communicates directly with the brain. And what is more, for many feet after emerging from the brain's cavity, the spinal cord keeps an undiminished girth, almost equal to that of the brain. Under all these circumstances, would it be unreasonable to survey and map out the whale's spine phrenologically? For, seen in this light, the wonderful comparative smallness of his brain proper is more than made up for by the wonderful comparative magnitude of his spinal cord.

But leaving this hint to work as it may with the phrenologists, I would merely assume the spinal theory for a moment, in reference to the Sperm Whale's hump. This august hump, if I am not mistaken, rises over one of the larger vertebrae, and is therefore, in some sense, the outer convex mold of it. From its relative position, then, I should call this high hump the organ of firmness or indomitableness in the Sperm Whale. And that the great monster is indomitable, you will yet have reason to know.

chapters.title: Chapter 81 — The Pequod Meets The Virgin
paragraphs: The fated day arrived, and we duly met the ship Jungfrau, captained by Derick De Deer, out of Bremen.

Once the greatest whaling people in the world, the Dutch and Germans are now among the least. But here and there, at very wide intervals of latitude and longitude, you still occasionally meet their flag in the Pacific.

For some reason, the Jungfrau seemed quite eager to pay her respects. While still some distance from the Pequod, she rounded to and dropped a boat, and her captain was rowed toward us, standing impatiently in the bow instead of the stern.
"What has he got in his hand there?" cried Starbuck, pointing to something the German was waving. "Impossible! A lamp-feeder!"

"Not that," said Stubb. "No, no, it's a coffee-pot, Mr. Starbuck. He's coming over to make us our coffee, that German. Don't you see that big tin can beside him? That's his boiling water. Oh, he's all right, that German."
"Go on with you," cried Flask. "It's a lamp-feeder and an oil-can. He's out of oil and has come begging."

However curious it may seem for an oil-ship to be borrowing oil on the whaling-ground, and however much it may turn on its head the old proverb about carrying coals to Newcastle, sometimes such a thing really happens. And in the present case, Captain Derick De Deer was indeed carrying a lamp-feeder, just as Flask had said.

As he climbed onto the deck, Ahab abruptly confronted him, paying no attention to what he held. But in his broken English, the German quickly showed his complete ignorance of the White Whale. He immediately turned the conversation to his lamp-feeder and oil-can, remarking that he had to turn into his hammock at night in total darkness. His last drop of Bremen oil was gone, and not a single flying-fish had been captured to make up the difference. He finished by hinting that his ship was indeed what the Fishery technically calls a clean one — that is, an empty one — well deserving the name of Jungfrau, or the Virgin.

His needs supplied, Derick departed. But he had not yet reached his ship when whales were spotted almost simultaneously from the mastheads of both vessels. Derick was so eager for the chase that without pausing to put his oil-can and lamp-feeder aboard, he swung his boat around and went after the great lamp-feeders themselves.

Now, since the whales had surfaced to leeward, Derick and the other three German boats that soon followed him had a considerable head start on the Pequod's boats. There were eight whales, an average pod. Aware of their danger, they were swimming abreast at great speed straight before the wind, rubbing their flanks as closely as a team of horses in harness. They left a great, wide wake behind them, as though continually unrolling a vast parchment upon the sea.

Far behind in this rapid wake swam a huge, humped old bull. His comparatively slow progress and the unusual yellowish growths covering him made him seem afflicted with jaundice or some other infirmity. Whether this whale belonged to the pod ahead was questionable, for it is not customary for such ancient leviathans to be social. Nevertheless, he stuck to their wake, though their backwater must have slowed him, because the white foam at his broad muzzle was broken and choppy, like the swell formed when two opposing currents meet. His spout was short, slow, and labored — coming forth with a choking sort of gush and spending itself in torn shreds, followed by strange subterranean rumblings inside him that seemed to find their exit at his other buried end, causing the waters behind him to bubble up.

"Who's got some paregoric?" said Stubb. "He has the stomach-ache, I'm afraid. Lord, think of having half an acre of stomach-ache! Contrary winds are holding a mad Christmas inside him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern. But look — did a whale ever yaw like that before? He must have lost his tiller."

As an overloaded East Indiaman bearing down the Hindostan coast with a deck-load of frightened horses careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way, so did this old whale heave his aged bulk. Now and then, partly turning over on his cumbersome rib-ends, he exposed the cause of his unsteady wake: the unnatural stump of his starboard fin. Whether he had lost that fin in battle or had been born without it was hard to say.
"Only wait a bit, old chap, and I'll give you a sling for that wounded arm," cried cruel Flask, pointing to the whale-line near him.
"Watch he doesn't sling you with it," cried Starbuck. "Give way, or the German will have him."

With single purpose, all the rival boats were pointed toward this one whale. Not only was he the largest and therefore the most valuable, but he was nearest to them. The other whales were swimming with such great speed as to almost defy pursuit for the time being. At this point, the Pequod's boats had shot past the three German boats that launched last. But from the great head start he had, Derick's boat still led the chase, though his foreign rivals closed in with every moment. The only thing they feared was that, being already so close to the whale, he would manage to dart his iron before they could completely overtake and pass him. As for Derick, he seemed quite confident this would be the case, and occasionally shook his lamp-feeder at the other boats with a mocking gesture.

"The ungracious and ungrateful dog!" cried Starbuck. "He mocks and taunts me with the very charity box I filled for him not five minutes ago!" Then in his old intense whisper: "Give way, greyhounds! Dog to it!"

"I tell you what it is, men," cried Stubb to his crew. "It's against my religion to get mad. But I'd like to eat that villainous German. Pull — won't you? Are you going to let that rascal beat you? Do you love brandy? A hogshead of brandy, then, to the best man. Come, why don't some of you burst a blood-vessel? Who's been dropping an anchor overboard? We don't budge an inch — we're dead in the water. Look, there's grass growing on the boat's bottom, and by the Lord, the mast is budding. This won't do, boys. Look at that German! The short and long of it is, men — will you spit fire or not?"

"Oh, see the foam he makes!" cried Flask, dancing up and down. "What a hump! Oh, do pile on the muscle — he lies like a log! Oh, my lads, do spring! Flapjacks and clams for supper, you know, my lads — baked clams and muffins! Oh, do, do spring! He's a hundred-barrel whale! Don't lose him now — don't, oh, don't! See that German! Oh, won't you pull for your pudding, my lads? Such a prize! Such a beauty! Don't you love spermaceti? There goes three thousand dollars, men! A bank! A whole bank! The Bank of England! Oh, do, do, do! What's that German about now?"

At this moment Derick was in the act of pitching his lamp-feeder at the advancing boats, and also his oil-can — perhaps with the double purpose of slowing his rivals' progress while accelerating his own through the backward momentum of the throw.

"The unmannerly Dutch dogger!" cried Stubb. "Pull now, men, like fifty thousand battleship-loads of red-haired devils. What do you say, Tashtego — are you the man to snap your spine in twenty-two pieces for the honor of old Gayhead? What do you say?"
"I say, pull like god-damn," cried the Indian.

Fiercely but evenly spurred on by the German's taunts, the Pequod's three boats now began ranging almost abreast, and in that formation they steadily closed the gap. In that fine, loose, gallant stance of the headsman drawing near to his prey, the three mates stood up proudly, occasionally urging on the rear oarsman with an exhilarating cry: "There she slides now! Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the German! Sail over him!"

But Derick had such a decisive head start that despite all their courage, he would have won this race — had not righteous judgment descended upon him in the form of a crab that caught the blade of his middle oarsman. While this clumsy fellow was struggling to free his oar, and while Derick's boat was nearly capsizing as he thundered at his men in a mighty rage — that was the moment for Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask. With a shout, they surged forward and ranged up diagonally on the German's quarter. An instant more, and all four boats were in the whale's immediate wake, while stretching from them on both sides was the foaming swell the whale created.

It was a terrific, most pitiable, and maddening sight. The whale was now going head out, sending his spout before him in a continual tormented jet, while his one poor fin beat his side in an agony of fright. Now to this side, now to that, he swerved in his faltering flight. At every wave he broke, he either spasmodically sank into the sea or sideways rolled toward the sky his one beating fin. I have seen a bird with a clipped wing making frightened broken circles in the air, vainly trying to escape piratical hawks. But the bird has a voice, and with plaintive cries makes known her fear. But the fear of this vast dumb creature of the sea was chained up and enchanted in him. He had no voice save that choking respiration through his blowhole, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable — while still, in his amazing bulk, his portcullis jaw, and his omnipotent tail, there was enough to terrify the bravest man who pitied him.

Seeing now that only a few more moments would give the Pequod's boats the advantage, and rather than be cheated of his prey, Derick chose to risk what must have seemed to him an unusually long throw before his last chance escaped forever.

But no sooner did his harpooner stand up for the strike than all three tigers — Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo — instinctively sprang to their feet. Standing in a diagonal row, they simultaneously aimed their barbs and darted over the head of the German harpooner. Their three Nantucket irons entered the whale. Blinding vapors of foam and white fire! The three boats, in the first fury of the whale's headlong rush, bumped the German's aside with such force that both Derick and his baffled harpooner were spilled out and sailed over by the three flying keels.

"Don't be afraid, my butter-boxes," cried Stubb, casting a passing glance at them as he shot by. "You'll be picked up presently — all right. I saw some sharks astern — St. Bernard's dogs, you know — they relieve distressed travelers. Hurrah! This is the way to sail now. Every keel a sunbeam! Hurrah! Here we go like three tin kettles at the tail of a mad cougar! This puts me in mind of being fastened to an elephant in a carriage on a plain — makes the wheel-spokes fly, boys, when you fasten to him that way. And there's danger of being pitched out, too, when you hit a hill. Hurrah! This is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones — all a rush down an endless slope! Hurrah! This whale carries the everlasting mail!"

But the monster's run was brief. Giving a sudden gasp, he plunged straight down. With a grating rush, the three lines flew around the loggerheads with such force as to gouge deep grooves into them. The harpooners were so afraid this rapid sounding would soon exhaust the lines that they used all their skill to catch repeated smoking turns with the rope to hold on. At last — owing to the perpendicular strain from the lead-lined chocks of the boats, where the three ropes went straight down into the blue — the gunwales of the bows were almost level with the water, while the three sterns tilted high in the air. When the whale stopped sounding, they remained in that position for a time, afraid to let out more line, though the situation was precarious. Boats have been pulled down and lost this way, yet it is this "holding on" — this hooking up of the whale from the back by the sharp barbs in his living flesh — that often torments the Leviathan into rising again to meet the sharp lance of his enemies. Yet the peril aside, it is doubtful whether this is always the best course. It is reasonable to assume that the longer the wounded whale stays underwater, the more he is exhausted. Because of the enormous surface area of a full-grown sperm whale — something less than two thousand square feet — the pressure of the water is immense. We all know what an astonishing atmospheric weight we ourselves bear, even here above ground in the air. How vast, then, the burden of a whale, bearing on his back a column of two hundred fathoms of ocean! It must at least equal the weight of fifty atmospheres. One whaleman has estimated it at the weight of twenty warships, with all their guns, stores, and men on board.

As the three boats lay there on that gently rolling sea, gazing down into its eternal blue noon — and as not a single groan or cry, not so much as a ripple or a bubble, came up from its depths — what landsman would have thought that beneath all that silence and peace, the greatest monster of the seas was writhing and wrenching in agony! Not eight inches of perpendicular rope were visible at the bows. Can it be believed that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the weight of an eight-day clock? Suspended? And from what? From three bits of board. Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said: "Can you fill his skin with barbed irons? Or his head with fish-spears? The sword of him that strikes at him cannot hold; the spear, the dart, nor the coat of mail. He regards iron as straw; the arrow cannot make him flee; darts are counted as stubble; he laughs at the shaking of a spear!" This the creature? This he? Oh, that prophecies should go unfulfilled! For with the strength of a thousand thighs in his tail, Leviathan had run his head under the mountains of the sea to hide from the Pequod's fish-spears!

In that sloping afternoon sunlight, the shadows that the three boats cast beneath the surface must have been long enough and broad enough to shade half of Xerxes' army. Who can tell how terrifying those huge phantoms must have been, flitting over the wounded whale's head!

"Stand by, men — he stirs," cried Starbuck, as the three lines suddenly vibrated in the water, conducting upward to them like magnetic wires the life-and-death throbs of the whale. Every oarsman felt them in his seat. The next moment, largely relieved from the downward strain at the bows, the boats gave a sudden bounce upward, like a small ice field when a dense herd of polar bears is scared off it into the sea.
"Haul in! Haul in!" cried Starbuck again. "He's rising."

The lines, of which hardly an instant before not a hand's breadth could have been gained, were now flung back in long, quick coils, dripping, into the boats. Soon the whale broke the surface within two ship-lengths of the hunters.

His movements clearly showed his extreme exhaustion. In most land animals, there are certain valves in their veins that, when the animal is wounded, at least partly shut off the blood flow in certain directions. Not so with the whale. One of his peculiarities is a completely non-valvular blood-vessel structure, so that when pierced by even so small a point as a harpoon, a deadly drain begins at once upon his whole arterial system. When this is worsened by the extraordinary water pressure at great depth below the surface, his life may be said to pour from him in constant streams. Yet so vast is the quantity of blood in him, and so distant and numerous its interior sources, that he will keep bleeding for a considerable period — even as a river will flow during a drought whose source lies in the hidden springs of far-off hills. Even now, when the boats closed on this whale and dangerously drew over his swaying flukes, and the lances were thrust into him, they were followed by steady jets from the new wounds, which kept continually playing, while the natural spout-hole in his head only sent its frightened moisture into the air at intervals, however rapid. From this last vent no blood yet came, because no vital part had been struck. His life, as they significantly call it, was untouched.

As the boats now more closely surrounded him, the whole upper part of his body, including much that is normally submerged, was plainly revealed. His eyes — or rather the places where his eyes had been — were visible. As strange, misshapen growths gather in the knotholes of the noblest oaks when they lie fallen, so from the spots where the whale's eyes had once been, there now protruded blind bulbs, horribly pitiable to see. But pity there was none. For all his old age, his one arm, and his blind eyes, he must die and be murdered — in order to light the gay weddings and other celebrations of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional harmlessness of all toward all. Still rolling in his blood, at last he partly revealed a strangely discolored lump or swelling, the size of a bushel, low on his flank.
"A nice spot," cried Flask. "Just let me prick him there once."
"Hold off!" cried Starbuck. "There's no need of that!"

But humane Starbuck was too late. The instant the dart struck, an ulcerous jet shot from that cruel wound. Goaded by it into more than bearable agony, the whale — now spouting thick blood — blindly charged the boats with savage fury, spattering them and their exulting crews all over with showers of gore, capsizing Flask's boat and damaging the bows. It was his death stroke. For by this time, so drained was he from blood loss that he helplessly rolled away from the wreck he had made, lay panting on his side, and impotently flapped his stumped fin. Then over and over he slowly revolved like a dying world, turned up the white secrets of his belly, lay like a log, and died. It was most pitiable, that last expiring spout. As when unseen hands gradually draw the water from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled, melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground — so fell the last long dying spout of the whale.

Soon, while the crews waited for the ship to arrive, the body showed signs of sinking with all its treasures untouched. Immediately, by Starbuck's orders, lines were secured to it at different points, so that before long every boat served as a buoy, with the sunken whale suspended a few inches beneath them by the ropes. By very careful management, when the ship drew near, the whale was transferred to her side and strongly secured there by the stiffest fluke-chains. For it was clear that unless artificially held up, the body would sink at once to the bottom.

It happened that almost upon the first cut into him with the spade, the entire length of a corroded harpoon was found embedded in his flesh, on the lower part of the lump described before. But since the stumps of harpoons are frequently found in the dead bodies of captured whales, with the flesh perfectly healed around them and no sign of their location, there must have been some other unknown reason to explain the ulceration. But still more curious was the fact that a stone lance-head was found in him, not far from the buried iron, with the flesh perfectly firm around it. Who had thrown that stone lance? And when? It might have been hurled by some Northwest Indian long before America was discovered.

What other marvels might have been dug out of this monstrous cabinet there is no telling. But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries when the ship was unprecedentedly dragged sideways toward the sea, owing to the body's rapidly increasing tendency to sink. However, Starbuck, who was in charge, hung on to it to the last — hung on so stubbornly, in fact, that when at length the ship would have capsized if she had kept locking arms with the body, and the command was given to break clear, the strain upon the timber-heads to which the fluke-chains and cables were fastened was so immense that it was impossible to cast them off. Meanwhile, everything in the Pequod was tilted at an angle. To cross to the other side of the deck was like walking up the steep gabled roof of a house. The ship groaned and gasped. Many of the ivory inlays in her bulwarks and cabins were popped from their places by the unnatural dislocation. In vain, handspikes and crowbars were brought to bear upon the immovable fluke-chains to pry them loose from the timber-heads. And the whale had now settled so low that the submerged ends could not be reached at all, while every moment whole tons of weight seemed to be added to the sinking mass, and the ship seemed on the point of going over.
