"Hold on, hold on, won't you?" cried Stubb to the body. "Don't be in such a devil of a hurry to sink! By thunder, men, we must do something or we're done for. No use prying there. Stop it, I say, with your handspikes, and one of you run for a prayer book and a pen-knife and cut the big chains."

"Knife? Aye, aye," cried Queequeg, and seizing the carpenter's heavy hatchet, he leaned out of a porthole and, steel against iron, began slashing at the largest fluke-chains. But only a few strokes, full of sparks, were needed before the tremendous strain did the rest. With a terrific snap, every fastening broke loose. The ship righted. The carcass sank.

Now, this occasional inevitable sinking of the recently killed sperm whale is a very curious thing. No fisherman has yet adequately explained it. Usually the dead sperm whale floats with great buoyancy, its side or belly considerably elevated above the surface. If the only whales that sank this way were old, meager, broken-hearted creatures, with their pads of fat diminished and all their bones heavy and rheumatic, then you might reasonably argue that this sinking is caused by an uncommon density in the whale, resulting from this lack of buoyant matter in him. But it is not so. For young whales in the peak of health, swelling with noble aspirations, prematurely cut off in the warm flush and springtime of life with all their panting fat about them — even these strong, buoyant heroes sometimes sink.

It should be said, however, that the Sperm Whale is far less prone to this than any other species. Where one Sperm Whale goes down, twenty Right Whales do. This difference is no doubt largely due to the greater quantity of bone in the Right Whale. His Venetian blinds alone — the slatted baleen in his mouth — sometimes weigh more than a ton, and from this burden the Sperm Whale is wholly free. But there are instances where, after many hours or several days, the sunken whale rises again, more buoyant than in life. The reason is obvious. Gases are generated inside him. He swells to prodigious size and becomes a sort of animal balloon. A warship could hardly keep him under then. In the shore whaling, in the shallows among the bays of New Zealand, when a Right Whale shows signs of sinking, they fasten buoys to him with plenty of rope, so that when the body has gone down, they know where to look for it when it rises again.

It was not long after the sinking of the body that a cry was heard from the Pequod's mastheads, announcing that the Jungfrau was again lowering her boats — though the only spout in sight was that of a fin-back, a species of whale that is virtually impossible to capture because of its incredible swimming speed. Nevertheless, the fin-back's spout is so similar to the sperm whale's that unskilled fishermen often mistake it. And so Derick and all his men were now in valiant chase of this uncatchable brute. The Virgin, crowding on all sail, followed after her four young boats, and they all disappeared far to leeward, still in bold, hopeful pursuit.
Oh! Many are the fin-backs, and many are the Dericks, my friend.

chapters.title: Chapter 82 — The Honor and Glory of Whaling
paragraphs: There are some enterprises in which a careful disorderliness is the true method.

The more I dive into this matter of whaling, and the further I push my research up to its very source, the more I am impressed by its great honor and antiquity. And especially when I find so many great demigods and heroes, and prophets of every sort, who one way or another have brought it distinction, I am carried away by the thought that I myself belong, even if only in a humble rank, to a brotherhood so emblazoned with glory.

The gallant Perseus, a son of Jupiter, was the first whaleman; and to the eternal honor of our calling, let it be said that the first whale our brotherhood ever attacked was not killed for any sordid motive. Those were the knightly days of our profession, when we took up arms only to rescue the distressed, and not to fill men's lamp-feeders. Everyone knows the fine story of Perseus and Andromeda: how the lovely Andromeda, a king's daughter, was tied to a rock on the seacoast, and just as Leviathan was in the very act of carrying her off, Perseus, the prince of whalemen, fearlessly advanced, harpooned the monster, and rescued and married the maiden. It was an admirable, artful feat, and one the best harpooners of today rarely achieve, since this Leviathan was killed with the very first throw. And let no one doubt this Arkite story; for in ancient Joppa, now Jaffa, on the Syrian coast, there stood for many ages, in one of the pagan temples, the vast skeleton of a whale, which the city's legends and all its inhabitants declared to be the very bones of the monster Perseus killed. When the Romans took Joppa, that same skeleton was carried to Italy in triumph. What seems most remarkable and suggestively important in this story is this: it was from Joppa that Jonah set sail.

Related to the adventure of Perseus and Andromeda — indeed, some suppose it was indirectly derived from it — is the famous story of St. George and the Dragon. That dragon, I maintain, was a whale; for in many old chronicles whales and dragons are strangely jumbled together and often stand in for each other. "You are like a lion of the waters, and like a dragon of the sea," says Ezekiel — plainly meaning a whale; in fact, some versions of the Bible use that very word. Besides, it would take a great deal from the glory of the exploit if St. George had merely met a crawling reptile of the land, instead of doing battle with the great monster of the deep. Any man can kill a snake, but only a Perseus, a St. George, a Nantucket Coffin has the heart to march boldly up to a whale.

Don't let the modern paintings of this scene mislead us. It is true that the creature this valiant whaleman of old fought is vaguely shown in a griffin-like shape, and that the battle is pictured on land, with the saint on horseback. But consider the great ignorance of those times, when artists did not know the true form of the whale; consider that, as in Perseus's case, St. George's whale may have crawled up out of the sea onto the beach; and consider that the animal St. George rode might have been only a large seal, or sea-horse. With all this in mind, it will not seem altogether inconsistent with the sacred legend and the most ancient drawings of the scene to hold that this so-called dragon was none other than the great Leviathan himself. In fact, set before the strict and piercing truth, this whole story will fare like Dagon, that fish, flesh, and fowl idol of the Philistines: when he was set up before the ark of Israel, his horse's head and both the palms of his hands fell off him, and only the stump, the fishy part of him, remained. So, then, one of our own noble stamp — a whaleman, no less — is the guardian patron of England; and by rights, we Nantucket harpooners should be enrolled in the most noble Order of St. George. And therefore let the knights of that honorable company (none of whom, I venture to say, has ever had anything to do with a whale, as their great patron did) — let them never look down on a Nantucketer, since even in our woolen frocks and tarred trousers we are far better entitled to St. George's decoration than they are.

Whether to admit Hercules among us or not was something I long remained doubtful about. For although, according to the Greek myths, that ancient Crockett and Kit Carson — that brawny doer of joyful good deeds — was swallowed down and thrown up again by a whale, it is still debatable whether that strictly makes him a whaleman. Nowhere does it appear that he ever actually harpooned his fish, unless, indeed, from the inside. Nevertheless, he may be considered a sort of involuntary whaleman; at any rate, the whale caught him, even if he didn't catch the whale. I claim him as one of our clan.

But by the best contradictory authorities, this Greek story of Hercules and the whale is considered to derive from the still more ancient Hebrew story of Jonah and the whale, and vice versa. Certainly they are very similar. If I claim the demigod, then why not the prophet?

Nor do heroes, saints, demigods, and prophets alone make up the whole roll of our order. Our grand master is still to be named; for like the royal kings of old, we trace the headwaters of our brotherhood to nothing less than the great gods themselves. That wondrous Eastern story must now be retold from the Shaster, the Hindu scriptures, which give us the dread Vishnoo, one of the three persons in the godhead of the Hindus — give us this divine Vishnoo himself for our Lord; Vishnoo, who, by the first of his ten earthly incarnations, has forever set apart and sanctified the whale. When Brahma, or the God of Gods, says the Shaster, resolved to re-create the world after one of its periodic dissolutions, he gave birth to Vishnoo to preside over the work. But the Vedas, or mystical books — which Vishnoo apparently had to read before beginning the creation, and which therefore must have contained something in the way of practical hints to young architects — these Vedas were lying at the bottom of the waters. So Vishnoo became incarnate in a whale, and, sounding down in him to the uttermost depths, rescued the sacred volumes. Wasn't this Vishnoo a whaleman, then, just as a man who rides a horse is called a horseman?
Perseus, St. George, Hercules, Jonah, and Vishnoo! There's a membership roll for you! What club but the whaleman's can be headed like that?

chapters.title: Chapter 83 — Jonah Historically Regarded
paragraphs: Reference was made in the preceding chapter to the historical story of Jonah and the whale. Now, some Nantucketers rather distrust this historical story of Jonah and the whale. But then there were some skeptical Greeks and Romans who, standing apart from the orthodox pagans of their times, equally doubted the story of Hercules and the whale, and of Arion and the dolphin; and yet their doubting those traditions did not make those traditions one bit less factual, for all that.

One old Sag-Harbor whaleman's chief reason for questioning the Hebrew story was this. He had one of those quaint old-fashioned Bibles decorated with curious, unscientific engravings, one of which showed Jonah's whale with two spouts in his head — a peculiarity true only of one species of Leviathan (the Right Whale and the varieties of that order), of which the fishermen have this saying: "A penny roll would choke him"; his swallow is so very small. But Bishop Jebb has an answer to this ready in advance. It is not necessary, the Bishop hints, to think of Jonah as entombed in the whale's belly, but rather as temporarily lodged in some part of his mouth. And this seems reasonable enough of the good Bishop. For truly, the Right Whale's mouth would hold a couple of whist-tables and comfortably seat all the players. Possibly, too, Jonah might have tucked himself away in a hollow tooth; but, on second thought, the Right Whale has no teeth.

Another reason Sag-Harbor (he went by that name) gave for his lack of faith in this matter of the prophet was something vaguely to do with the imprisoned body and the whale's gastric juices. But this objection likewise falls to the ground, because a German biblical interpreter supposes that Jonah must have taken refuge in the floating body of a whale that was already dead — just as the French soldiers in the Russian campaign turned their dead horses into tents and crawled inside them. Besides, other continental commentators have guessed that when Jonah was thrown overboard from the Joppa ship, he promptly escaped to another vessel close by, some vessel with a whale for a figurehead; and, I would add, possibly called "The Whale," just as some craft nowadays are christened the "Shark," the "Gull," or the "Eagle." Nor has there been any shortage of learned interpreters who have held that the whale mentioned in the book of Jonah simply meant a life-preserver — an inflated bag of wind — which the endangered prophet swam to, and so was saved from a watery death. Poor Sag-Harbor, then, seems beaten on every side. But he had still another reason for his lack of faith. It was this, if I remember right: Jonah was swallowed by the whale in the Mediterranean Sea, and after three days he was vomited up somewhere within three days' journey of Nineveh, a city on the Tigris, which is very much more than three days' journey from the nearest point of the Mediterranean coast. How is that?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet within that short distance of Nineveh? Yes. He might have carried him around by way of the Cape of Good Hope. But, to say nothing of the passage through the whole length of the Mediterranean, and another passage up the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, such a supposition would involve sailing completely around all of Africa in three days — to say nothing of the Tigris waters near the site of Nineveh being too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, this idea of Jonah's rounding the Cape of Good Hope at so early a date would snatch the honor of discovering that great headland from Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, and so make modern history a liar.

But all these foolish arguments of old Sag-Harbor only showed his foolish pride of reason — a thing all the more blameworthy in him, since he had little learning beyond what he had picked up from the sun and the sea. I say it only shows his foolish, impious pride, and his abominable, devilish rebellion against the reverend clergy. For a Portuguese Catholic priest put forward this very idea of Jonah's going to Nineveh by way of the Cape of Good Hope as a remarkable magnifying of the general miracle. And so it was. Besides, to this day the highly enlightened Turks devoutly believe in the historical story of Jonah. And some three centuries ago, an English traveler in old Harris's Voyages tells of a Turkish mosque built in honor of Jonah, in which there was a miraculous lamp that burned without any oil.

chapters.title: Chapter 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform a similar operation on their boats — they grease the bottom. Nor can it be doubted that, since such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no small advantage, considering that oil and water are hostile, that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely along. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning, not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, he took more than his usual pains over it, crawling under its bottom where it hung over the side and rubbing in the grease as though he were diligently trying to raise a crop of hair on the craft's bald keel. He seemed to be acting on some particular premonition. Nor did what followed prove it unfounded.
Toward noon whales were sighted; but as soon as the ship sailed down on them, they turned and fled in headlong haste — a disordered flight, like that of Cleopatra's barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats gave chase, and Stubb's was in the lead. With great effort, Tashtego at last managed to plant one iron; but the stricken whale, without sounding at all, kept up his horizontal flight, even faster than before. Such unbroken strain on the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably pull it out. It became essential to lance the fleeing whale, or be content to lose him. But hauling the boat up to his flank was impossible; he swam so fast and furiously. What was left, then?

Of all the wondrous devices and skills, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties that the veteran whaleman is so often driven to, none surpass that fine maneuver with the lance called pitchpoling. Neither small sword nor broadsword, in all its drills, can boast anything like it. It is indispensable only with a whale that is a stubborn runner; its great feature and fact is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately thrown from a violently rocking, jerking boat racing ahead at full speed. Steel and wood included, the whole spear is some ten or twelve feet long; the shaft is much slighter than the harpoon's, and of a lighter material too — pine. It is fitted with a small rope of considerable length, called a warp, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after the throw.

But before going further, it is important to mention here that although the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way as the lance, it is seldom done; and when it is, it succeeds still less often, because of the harpoon's greater weight and shorter length compared with the lance, which in practice become serious drawbacks. As a general rule, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb — a man whose humorous, deliberate coolness and composure in the direst emergencies made him especially fit to excel at pitchpoling. Look at him: he stands upright in the tossing bow of the flying boat; wrapped in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing two or three times along its length to see that it is exactly straight, Stubb, whistling, gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to keep its free end in his grip and leave the rest unobstructed. Then, holding the lance squarely in front of the middle of his waistband, he levels it at the whale; and, keeping it trained on him, he steadily presses down the butt-end in his hand, thereby raising the point until the weapon stands neatly balanced on his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He reminds you a little of a juggler balancing a long staff on his chin. The next moment, with a rapid, nameless impulse, the bright steel spans the foaming distance in a superb, lofty arc and quivers in the whale's life-spot. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

"That drove the spigot out of him!" cried Stubb. "It's the immortal Fourth of July; all fountains must run wine today! If only it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I'd have you hold a mug to the jet, and we'd drink a round from it! Yes, truly, my hearties, we'd brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl drink down the living stuff."

Again and again, to such playful talk, the skillful throw is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held on a skillful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry, the convulsion of his death; the towline is slackened, and the pitchpoler, dropping astern, folds his hands and silently watches the monster die.

chapters.title: Chapter 85 — The Fountain
paragraphs: That for six thousand years — and no one knows how many millions of ages before — the great whales should have been spouting all over the sea, sprinkling and misting the gardens of the deep as if with so many watering-cans and misting-pots; and that for some centuries now, thousands of hunters should have been close by the whale's fountain, watching these sprinklings and spoutings — that all this should be so, and yet that down to this blessed minute (fifteen and a quarter minutes past one in the afternoon of this sixteenth day of December, A.D. 1851) it should still remain an open question whether these spoutings are, after all, really water or nothing but vapor — this is surely a remarkable thing.

Let us, then, look into this matter, along with some interesting related points. Everyone knows that, by the peculiar ingenuity of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air that is always mixed into the element they swim in; so a herring or a cod might live a century without once raising its head above the surface. But because of his distinctive internal structure, which gives him real lungs like a human being's, the whale can live only by breathing the free air of the open atmosphere. Hence his need to visit the upper world at regular intervals. But he cannot breathe through his mouth at all, for in his ordinary posture the Sperm Whale's mouth is buried at least eight feet below the surface; and, what is more, his windpipe has no connection with his mouth. No, he breathes through his spiracle, or blowhole, alone; and this is on the top of his head.

If I say that in any creature breathing is only a function indispensable to life, in that it draws from the air a certain element which, once brought into contact with the blood, gives the blood its life-giving principle, I don't think I shall be wrong — though I may be using some unnecessary scientific words. Assume it, and it follows that if all the blood in a man could be aerated with one breath, he might then seal up his nostrils and not take another for a considerable time. That is to say, he would then live without breathing. Strange as it may seem, this is exactly the case with the whale, who systematically lives, at intervals, his full hour and more (when at the bottom) without drawing a single breath or inhaling so much as a particle of air in any way; for remember, he has no gills. How is this? Between his ribs and on each side of his spine he is supplied with a remarkable, intricate Cretan labyrinth of vermicelli-like vessels, and when he leaves the surface these vessels are completely swollen with oxygenated blood. So for an hour or more, a thousand fathoms down in the sea, he carries a surplus stock of vitality in him, just as the camel crossing the waterless desert carries a surplus supply of drink for future use in its four supplementary stomachs. The anatomical fact of this labyrinth is indisputable; and that the supposition founded on it is reasonable and true seems all the more convincing to me when I consider that leviathan's otherwise inexplicable stubbornness in "having his spoutings out," as the fishermen put it. This is what I mean. If undisturbed, the Sperm Whale, on rising to the surface, will stay there for a length of time exactly the same as on all his other undisturbed risings. Say he stays eleven minutes and jets seventy times — that is, takes seventy breaths; then whenever he rises again, he is sure to take his seventy breaths over again, to the minute. Now, if after he has taken a few breaths you alarm him so that he sounds, he will keep dodging back up to make good his regular allowance of air. And not until those seventy breaths are counted out will he finally go down to stay out his full term below. Notice, however, that these rates differ from one whale to another; but in any one whale they are the same. Now, why should the whale insist like this on having his spoutings out, unless it is to refill his reservoir of air before descending for good? How obvious it is, too, that this necessity of rising exposes the whale to all the fatal hazards of the chase. For neither hook nor net could catch this vast leviathan when he is sailing a thousand fathoms beneath the sunlight. So it is not so much your skill, O hunter, as these great necessities that win you the victory!

In man, breathing goes on incessantly — one breath serving for only two or three heartbeats; so whatever other business he has to attend to, waking or sleeping, breathe he must, or die he will. But the Sperm Whale breathes only about one-seventh of his time — his Sunday, so to speak.

It has been said that the whale breathes only through his spout-hole. If it could truthfully be added that his spouts are mixed with water, then I think we would have the reason why his sense of smell seems wiped out in him; for the only thing about him that at all corresponds to a nose is that same spout-hole, and being so clogged with two elements, it could hardly be expected to have the power of smelling. But because of the mystery of the spout — whether it is water or whether it is vapor — no absolute certainty can yet be reached on this point. It is certain, nevertheless, that the Sperm Whale has no proper organs of smell. But what does he want them for? There are no roses, no violets, no cologne in the sea.

Furthermore, since his windpipe opens only into the tube of his spouting canal, and since that long canal — like the grand Erie Canal — is fitted with a sort of locks (which open and shut) to keep air in below or keep water out above, the whale has no voice; unless you insult him by saying that when he rumbles so strangely, he is talking through his nose. But then again, what has the whale to say? I have seldom known any profound being that had anything to say to this world, unless forced to stammer out something to earn a living. Oh, how lucky that the world is such an excellent listener!

Now, the Sperm Whale's spouting canal, meant chiefly as it is for carrying air, runs for several feet horizontally just beneath the upper surface of his head, and a little to one side; this curious canal is very much like a gas-pipe laid down on one side of a city street. But the question comes back whether this gas-pipe is also a water-pipe; in other words, whether the Sperm Whale's spout is merely the vapor of the exhaled breath, or whether that exhaled breath is mixed with water taken in at the mouth and discharged through the spiracle. It is certain that the mouth connects indirectly with the spouting canal; but it cannot be proved that this is for the purpose of discharging water through the spiracle. For the greatest need to do so would seem to arise when he accidentally takes in water while feeding. But the Sperm Whale's food is far beneath the surface, and there he cannot spout even if he wanted to. Besides, if you watch him very closely and time him with your watch, you will find that, when he is undisturbed, there is an unvarying rhythm between the timing of his jets and his ordinary periods of breathing.

But why pester anyone with all this reasoning on the subject? Speak out! You have seen him spout; then declare what the spout is. Can't you tell water from air? My dear sir, in this world it is not so easy to settle these plain things. I have always found your plain things the knottiest of all. And as for this whale spout, you might almost stand in it and still be undecided about what exactly it is.

The central body of it is hidden in the snowy, sparkling mist that envelops it; and how can you tell for certain whether any water falls from it, when, whenever you are close enough to a whale to get a close view of his spout, he is always in a tremendous commotion, with the water cascading all around him? And if at such times you thought you really saw drops of moisture in the spout, how do you know that they are not merely condensed from its vapor? Or how do you know that they are not those very drops lying on the surface of the spout-hole fissure, which is countersunk into the top of the whale's head? For even when he is swimming tranquilly through the midday sea in a calm, with his raised hump as sun-dried as a dromedary's in the desert — even then the whale always carries a small basin of water on his head, just as under a blazing sun you will sometimes see a hollow in a rock filled up with rain.

Nor is it at all wise for the hunter to be too curious about the precise nature of the whale's spout. It won't do for him to go peering into it and putting his face in it. You cannot go to this fountain with your pitcher, fill it, and carry it away. For even slight contact with the outer, vapory shreds of the jet, which will often happen, makes your skin smart feverishly from the acrid sting of the stuff that touches it. And I know a man who came into still closer contact with the spout — whether with some scientific object in view or otherwise, I cannot say — and the skin peeled off his cheek and arm. So among whalemen the spout is considered poisonous; they try to avoid it. Another thing: I have heard it said, and I don't much doubt it, that if the jet is spouted straight into your eyes, it will blind you. The wisest thing the investigator can do, then, it seems to me, is to leave this deadly spout alone.

Still, we can form a hypothesis, even if we cannot prove and establish it. My hypothesis is this: that the spout is nothing but mist. And besides other reasons, I am driven to this conclusion by considerations of the great inherent dignity and sublimity of the Sperm Whale. I consider him no common, shallow being, since it is an undisputed fact that he is never found on soundings — in water shallow enough to reach bottom with a lead line — or near shores; all other whales sometimes are. He is both ponderous and profound. And I am convinced that from the heads of all ponderous, profound beings, such as Plato, Pyrrho, the Devil, Jupiter, Dante, and so on, there always rises a certain half-visible steam while they are thinking deep thoughts. While I was composing a little treatise on Eternity, I had the curiosity to set a mirror in front of me; and before long I saw reflected there a curious, intricate worming and rippling in the air over my head. The invariable dampness of my hair while I am plunged in deep thought, after six cups of hot tea in my thin-shingled attic on an August noon — this seems a further argument for the above supposition.

And how nobly it raises our idea of the mighty, misty monster to see him solemnly sailing through a calm tropical sea, his vast, mild head overhung by a canopy of vapor produced by his incommunicable contemplations — and that vapor, as you will sometimes see it, glorified by a rainbow, as if Heaven itself had put its seal upon his thoughts. For, you see, rainbows do not visit clear air; they only light up vapor. And so, through all the thick mists of the dim doubts in my mind, divine intuitions now and then shoot, kindling my fog with a heavenly ray. And for this I thank God; for all have doubts; many deny; but few, along with their doubts or denials, have intuitions. Doubts of all things earthly, and intuitions of some things heavenly — this combination makes neither believer nor infidel, but makes a man who regards them both with an equal eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 86 — The Tail
paragraphs: Other poets have sung the praises of the soft eye of the antelope and the lovely plumage of the bird that never lands. Less heavenly, I celebrate a tail.

If you reckon the largest sperm whale's tail to begin at the point of the trunk where it tapers to about the girth of a man, it covers an area on its upper surface alone of at least fifty square feet. The compact round root expands into two broad, firm, flat palms or flukes, gradually thinning to less than an inch in thickness. At the junction, these flukes slightly overlap, then recede sideways from each other like wings, leaving a wide gap between them. In no living thing are the lines of beauty more exquisitely defined than in the crescent borders of these flukes. At full expansion in a full-grown whale, the tail will considerably exceed twenty feet across.

The entire structure seems a dense, webbed bed of welded sinews. But cut into it and you find three distinct layers: upper, middle, and lower. The fibers in the upper and lower layers are long and horizontal. Those in the middle are very short, running crosswise between the outer layers. This three-part structure, as much as anything else, gives the tail its power. To the student of old Roman walls, the middle layer will offer a curious parallel to the thin course of tiles always alternating with stone in those wonderful ancient ruins, which undoubtedly contribute so much to the masonry's great strength.

But as if this vast local power in the sinewy tail were not enough, the whole bulk of the leviathan is knit over with a warp and woof of muscular fibers and filaments. These pass on either side of the loins and run down into the flukes, blending with them seamlessly and greatly adding to their might. So in the tail, the combined, measureless force of the whole whale seems concentrated to a point. If annihilation could occur to matter, this would be the thing to do it.

Nor does this amazing strength at all cripple the graceful flexibility of its motions, where an infantlike ease undulates through a titanic power. On the contrary, those motions derive their most fearsome beauty from it. Real strength never impairs beauty or harmony but often bestows it. In everything impressively beautiful, strength has much to do with the magic. Take away the tied tendons that everywhere seem bursting from the marble in the carved Hercules, and its charm would be gone. When devout Eckerman lifted the linen sheet from Goethe's naked corpse, he was overwhelmed by the massive chest, which seemed like a Roman triumphal arch. When Angelo — Michelangelo — paints even God the Father in human form, mark what robustness is there. And whatever they may reveal of divine love in the Son, those soft, curled, hermaphroditic Italian paintings in which his image has been most successfully embodied — so destitute of all brawniness — hint nothing of any power but the merely negative, feminine one of submission and endurance, which by all accounts form the peculiar practical virtues of his teachings.

Such is the subtle elasticity of the organ I describe that whether wielded in sport, in earnest, or in anger, whatever its mood, its movements are invariably marked by exceeding grace. No fairy's arm can surpass it.
Five great motions are peculiar to it. First, when used as a fin for propulsion. Second, when used as a club in battle. Third, in sweeping. Fourth, in lob-tailing. Fifth, in peaking flukes.

First: Being horizontal in position, the Leviathan's tail acts differently from the tails of all other sea creatures. It never wriggles. In man or fish, wriggling is a sign of inferiority. To the whale, his tail is his sole means of propulsion. Coiled forward like a scroll beneath the body and then rapidly sprung backward — this is what gives that singular darting, leaping motion to the monster when swimming furiously. His side fins serve only to steer.

Second: It is somewhat significant that while one sperm whale fights another only with his head and jaw, in his conflicts with man he chiefly and contemptuously uses his tail. In striking at a boat, he swiftly curves his flukes away from it, and the blow is delivered only by the recoil. If made in the unobstructed air, especially if it descends on its mark, the stroke is simply irresistible. No ribs of man or boat can withstand it. Your only salvation lies in dodging it. But if it comes sideways through the water, then partly owing to the light buoyancy of the whaleboat and the springiness of its materials, a cracked rib or a smashed plank or two — a sort of stitch in the side — is generally the worst of it. These underwater side-blows are so common in the fishery that they are considered child's play. Someone strips off a shirt, and the hole is plugged.

Third: I cannot prove it, but it seems to me that in the whale the sense of touch is concentrated in the tail. In this respect, there is a delicacy in it matched only by the daintiness of the elephant's trunk. This sensitivity is chiefly shown in the action of sweeping, when with maidenly gentleness the whale slowly moves his immense flukes from side to side upon the surface of the sea. And if he feels but a sailor's whisker — woe to that sailor, whiskers and all. What tenderness there is in that preliminary touch! Had this tail any grasping power, I should think of Darmonodes' elephant that so frequented the flower market and with low bows presented bouquets to young ladies, then caressed their waists. On more accounts than one, it is a pity the whale does not possess this grasping ability. For I have heard of yet another elephant that, when wounded in a fight, curved its trunk around and extracted the dart.

Fourth: Coming upon the whale unawares in the fancied security of the middle of solitary seas, you find him unbent from the vast dignity of his bulk, and kittenlike, he plays on the ocean as if it were a hearth. But still you see his power in his play. The broad palms of his tail are flipped high into the air, then brought smiting down upon the surface — the thunderous concussion resounding for miles. You would almost think a cannon had been fired. And if you noticed the light wreath of vapor from the blowhole at his other end, you would think that was the smoke from the touch-hole.

Fifth: In his normal floating posture, the leviathan's flukes lie considerably below the level of his back, completely out of sight beneath the surface. But when he is about to plunge into the depths, his entire flukes and at least thirty feet of his body are tossed erect in the air, remaining there vibrating a moment before they shoot downward out of view. Except for the sublime breach — to be described elsewhere — this peaking of the whale's flukes is perhaps the grandest sight in all of living nature. Out of the bottomless deep, the gigantic tail seems to be spasmodically grasping at the highest heaven. So in dreams, I have seen majestic Satan thrusting forth his tormented colossal claw from the flaming Baltic of Hell. But in gazing at such scenes, it all depends on your mood. If you are in the Dantean frame, devils will come to mind. If in that of Isaiah, archangels. Standing at the masthead of my ship during a sunrise that crimsoned sky and sea, I once saw a large herd of whales in the east, all heading toward the sun, and for a moment vibrating in concert with peaked flukes. As it seemed to me then, such a grand embodiment of adoration of the gods was never seen, even in Persia, the home of fire worshippers. As Ptolemy Philopater testified of the African elephant, I then testified of the whale, pronouncing him the most devout of all beings. For according to King Juba, the military elephants of antiquity often hailed the morning with their trunks uplifted in the most profound silence.

The casual comparison in this chapter between the whale and the elephant — so far as some aspects of the tail of the one and the trunk of the other are concerned — should not suggest those two opposite organs are equal, much less the creatures they belong to. For as the mightiest elephant is but a terrier to Leviathan, so compared with Leviathan's tail, his trunk is but the stalk of a lily. The most dreadful blow from the elephant's trunk would be as the playful tap of a fan compared with the measureless crush and crash of the sperm whale's ponderous flukes, which have repeatedly hurled entire boats with all their oars and crews into the air, much as an Indian juggler tosses his balls.*

*Though all comparison in general bulk between the whale and the elephant is absurd — inasmuch as in that regard the elephant stands in much the same relation to the whale as a dog does to the elephant — nevertheless, there are some points of curious similarity. Among these is the spout. It is well known that the elephant will often draw up water or dust in his trunk, and then, elevating it, jet it forth in a stream.

The more I consider this mighty tail, the more I deplore my inability to express it. At times there are gestures in it that, though they would well grace the hand of man, remain wholly inexplicable. In an extensive herd, so remarkable, at times, are these mystic gestures that I have heard hunters declare them akin to Freemason signs and symbols — that the whale, by these methods, was intelligently conversing with the world. Nor are there lacking other motions of the whale in his general body, full of strangeness and unaccountable to his most experienced pursuer. Dissect him how I may, then, I only go skin deep. I do not know him, and never will. But if I cannot even understand the tail of this whale, how can I understand his head? Much more, how can I comprehend his face, when he has none? You shall see my back parts, my tail, he seems to say, but my face shall not be seen. But I cannot fully make out his back parts either. And hint what he will about his face — I say again he has no face.

chapters.title: Chapter 87 — The Grand Armada
paragraphs: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast wall, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several passages for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

Those narrow Straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java. Standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory known to seamen as Java Head, they closely resemble the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire. And considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that eastern sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance — however ineffective — of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis. Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships that for centuries past, by night and day, have passed between Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive such ceremony, they by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.

Since time out of mind, the pirate boats of the Malays, lurking among the low, shaded coves and islets of Sumatra, have sailed out upon passing vessels, fiercely demanding tribute at spear-point. Though by repeated bloody punishments at the hands of European warships their boldness has of late been somewhat checked, even now we occasionally hear of English and American vessels that have been ruthlessly boarded and plundered in those waters.

With a fair, fresh wind, the Pequod was now drawing near to these straits. Ahab intended to pass through them into the Java Sea, and thence, cruising northward over waters known to be frequented by the sperm whale, sweep inshore by the Philippine Islands and reach the far coast of Japan in time for the great whaling season there. By this route, the circumnavigating Pequod would sweep almost all the known sperm whale cruising grounds of the world before descending upon the equator in the Pacific — where Ahab, though everywhere else frustrated in his pursuit, firmly counted on giving battle to Moby Dick in the sea he was most known to frequent, at a season when he might most reasonably be expected to haunt it.

But how now? In this far-ranging quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Mark this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that did you carry them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

Now, as many sperm whales had been captured off the western coast of Java, near the Straits of Sunda, and since most of the surrounding waters were generally recognized by fishermen as an excellent cruising ground, the Pequod's lookouts were repeatedly hailed and warned to stay wide awake as she gained upon Java Head. But though the green palmy cliffs of the land soon loomed on the starboard bow, and with delighted nostrils the fresh cinnamon was sniffed in the air, yet not a single spout was sighted. Almost giving up all thought of finding any whales in these parts, the ship had nearly entered the straits when the customary cheering cry was heard from aloft, and before long a spectacle of singular magnificence greeted us.

But here it must be noted that owing to the relentless activity with which sperm whales have lately been hunted over all four oceans, they now frequently gather in extensive herds, instead of almost invariably sailing in small, separate groups as in former times. Sometimes these herds embrace so great a multitude that it would almost seem as if numerous nations of them had sworn a solemn pact for mutual assistance and protection. To this massing of sperm whales may be attributed the fact that even in the best cruising grounds, you may now sometimes sail for weeks and months without being greeted by a single spout — and then be suddenly confronted by what seems thousands upon thousands.

Broad on both bows, at a distance of two or three miles, forming a great semicircle that embraced one half of the level horizon, a continuous chain of whale-spouts was playing and sparkling in the noonday air. Unlike the straight perpendicular twin-jets of the right whale, which divide at the top and fall over in two branches like the drooping boughs of a willow, the single forward-slanting spout of the sperm whale presents a thick curled bush of white mist, continually rising and falling away to leeward.

Seen from the Pequod's deck as she would rise on a high hill of the sea, this host of vapory spouts, individually curling up into the air and viewed through a blending atmosphere of bluish haze, looked like the thousand cheerful chimneys of some dense city, glimpsed on a balmy autumn morning by some horseman on a hill.

As marching armies approaching an unfriendly mountain pass accelerate their march, all eagerness to put that perilous passage behind them and once more expand in comparative safety upon the plain — even so did this vast fleet of whales now seem hurrying forward through the straits, gradually contracting the wings of their semicircle and swimming on in one solid but still crescent-shaped formation.

Crowding on all sail, the Pequod pressed after them. The harpooners handled their weapons and cheered loudly from the bows of their still-suspended boats. If the wind only held, they had little doubt that chased through these Straits of Sunda, the vast host would only spread out into the eastern seas to witness the capture of not a few of their number. And who could tell whether, in that gathered caravan, Moby Dick himself might not be temporarily swimming, like the worshipped white elephant in a Siamese coronation procession! So with every sail set, we drove these leviathans before us — when suddenly, the voice of Tashtego was heard, loudly directing attention to something in our wake.

Corresponding to the crescent ahead of us, we saw another behind us. It seemed formed of detached white vapors, rising and falling somewhat like whale-spouts, only they did not fully come and go but constantly hovered without quite disappearing. Leveling his glass at this sight, Ahab quickly spun in his pivot-hole, crying: "Aloft there, and rig whips and buckets to wet the sails! Malays, sir, and after us!"

As if lurking too long behind the headlands, waiting until the Pequod had fairly entered the straits, these rascally Asians were now in hot pursuit to make up for their overcautious delay. But when the swift Pequod, with a fresh leading wind, was herself in hot chase — how very kind of these tawny philanthropists to help speed her on to her own chosen pursuit, serving as mere riding-crops and spurs to her. As Ahab paced the deck with glass under arm, in his forward turn beholding the monsters he chased and in his backward turn the bloodthirsty pirates chasing him — some such thought seemed his. And when he glanced upon the green walls of the watery passage through which the ship was sailing, and considered that through that gate lay the route to his vengeance, and saw how through that same gate he was now both chasing and being chased to his deadly end — and not only that, but a herd of remorseless wild pirates and inhuman atheistical devils were infernally cheering him on with their curses — when all these thoughts had passed through his brain, Ahab's brow was left gaunt and furrowed, like a black sand beach after some stormy tide has been gnawing it without being able to drag the firm thing from its place.

But thoughts like these troubled very few of the reckless crew. When, after steadily dropping the pirates astern, the Pequod at last shot past the vivid green Cockatoo Point on the Sumatra side, emerging upon the broad waters beyond, the harpooners seemed more grieved that the swift whales had been gaining on the ship than glad that the ship had so victoriously gained upon the Malays. But still driving on in the whales' wake, at length they seemed to slow their speed. Gradually the ship neared them. The wind dying away, word was passed to launch the boats. But no sooner did the herd — by some wonderful instinct of the sperm whale — become aware of the three boats coming after them, though still a mile behind, than they rallied again. Forming in close ranks and battalions, so that their spouts all looked like flashing lines of stacked bayonets, they moved on with redoubled speed.

Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the battle against Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. Best, therefore, withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

Though many of the whales, as has been said, were in violent motion, as a whole the herd neither advanced nor retreated but collectively remained in one place. As is customary in such cases, the boats separated at once, each making for some lone whale on the outskirts of the shoal. In about three minutes, Queequeg's harpoon was flung. The stricken whale darted blinding spray in our faces, then ran away with us like light, steering straight for the heart of the herd. Though such a move by a harpooned whale is by no means unprecedented and indeed is almost always expected to some degree, it presents one of the more dangerous episodes of the fishery. For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid farewell to cautious living and exist only in a delirious rush.

As, blind and deaf, the whale plunged forward, as if by sheer speed to rid himself of the iron leech fastened to him — as we tore a white gash in the sea, menaced on all sides by the crazed creatures rushing to and fro around us — our beset boat was like a ship mobbed by icebergs in a tempest, striving to steer through their complicated channels and straits, not knowing at what moment it might be locked in and crushed.

But not a bit daunted, Queequeg steered us expertly — now sheering off from this monster directly across our route, now edging away from that one whose colossal flukes were suspended overhead — while all the time Starbuck stood in the bow, lance in hand, pricking aside whatever whales he could reach with short thrusts, for there was no time for long ones. Nor were the oarsmen quite idle, though their usual duty was now entirely suspended. They chiefly attended to the shouting part of the business. "Out of the way, Commodore!" cried one to a great whale that suddenly rose bodily to the surface and for an instant threatened to swamp us. "Hard down with your tail, there!" cried a second to another that, close to our gunwale, seemed calmly cooling himself with his own fan-like extremity.

All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called drags. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is attached to the middle of this block, and the other end, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drag is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so when you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence the drag comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drag. They were hampered like prisoners with chain and ball. But upon flinging the third, the clumsy wooden block caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three shirts in and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

It would have been nearly impossible to throw these drag-harpoons had our whale's pace not greatly slowed as we advanced into the herd. Moreover, as we went still further from the circumference of commotion, the chaos seemed to be waning. So when at last the jerking harpoon pulled free and the towing whale vanished sideways, we glided with the tapering force of his parting momentum between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal — as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake. Here the storms raging in the gaps between the outermost whales were heard but not felt. In this central expanse, the sea presented that smooth satin-like surface called a sleek, produced by the subtle moisture thrown off by the whale in his quieter moods. Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion. And still in the distracted distance we saw the tumults of the outer concentric circles — successive pods of whales, eight or ten in each, swiftly going round and round like multiplied teams of horses in a ring, so closely shoulder to shoulder that a titanic circus-rider might easily have arched over the middle ones and ridden round on their backs. Owing to the density of the whales reposing more immediately around the trapped center of the herd, no possible chance of escape was presently offered to us. We had to watch for a breach in the living wall that hemmed us in — the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up. Keeping to the center of the lake, we were occasionally visited by small, tame cows and calves: the women and children of this routed host.

Now, including the occasional wide intervals between the revolving outer circles and the spaces between the various pods in any one of those circles, the entire area at this point must have contained at least two or three square miles. At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because, as if the cows and calves had been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and as if the wide extent of the herd had prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping — or possibly, being so young, innocent, and inexperienced — however it may have been, these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at. Like household dogs, they came snuffling right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.

But far beneath this wondrous world upon the surface, another and still stranger world met our eyes as we gazed over the side. For suspended in those watery vaults floated the forms of nursing mother whales, and those that by their enormous girth seemed shortly to become mothers. The lake, as I have hinted, was to a considerable depth exceedingly transparent. And as human infants while suckling will calmly and fixedly gaze away from the breast, as if leading two different lives at the same time — while yet drawing mortal nourishment, still spiritually feasting upon some unearthly memory — even so did the young of these whales seem to look up toward us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of seaweed in their newborn sight. Floating on their sides, the mothers also seemed quietly eyeing us. One of these little infants, that from certain signs seemed hardly a day old, might have measured some fourteen feet in length and six feet around. He was a little frisky, though his body seemed scarcely recovered from the cramped position it had so recently occupied in the womb, where, tail to head and all ready for the final spring, the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar's bow. The delicate side-fins and the palms of his flukes still freshly retained the plaited, crumpled appearance of a baby's ears newly arrived from foreign parts.
"Line! Line!" cried Queequeg, looking over the gunwale. "Him fast! Him fast! Who line him? Who struck? Two whale — one big, one little!"
"What ails you, man?" cried Starbuck.
"Look here," said Queequeg, pointing down.

As when the struck whale that from the tub has reeled out hundreds of fathoms of rope — as, after deep sounding, he floats up again and shows the slackened curling line buoyantly rising and spiraling toward the air — so now Starbuck saw long coils of the umbilical cord of Madame Leviathan, by which the young cub seemed still tethered to its mother. Not seldom in the rapid turns of the chase, this natural line, with the maternal end loose, becomes entangled with the hemp one, so that the cub is trapped. Some of the subtlest secrets of the seas seemed revealed to us in this enchanted pond. We saw young Leviathan courtship in the deep.*

*The sperm whale, like all other species of Leviathan but unlike most other fish, breeds indiscriminately at all seasons. After a gestation that may probably be set at nine months, it produces but one at a time, though in some few known instances giving birth to twins — a contingency provided for in suckling by two teats, curiously situated one on each side of the anus, though the breasts themselves extend upward from that point. When by chance these parts in a nursing whale are cut by the hunter's lance, the mother's pouring milk and blood discolor the sea in rivaling streams for yards. The milk is very sweet and rich. It has been tasted by man, and it might go well with strawberries. When overflowing with mutual affection, the whales greet each other in human fashion.

And thus, though surrounded by circle upon circle of terrors and frights, did these inscrutable creatures at the center freely and fearlessly indulge in all peaceful pursuits — yea, serenely reveling in tenderness and delight. But even so, amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still forever centrally float in mute calm. And while ponderous planets of unceasing woe revolve around me, deep down and deep inland there I still bathe myself in an eternal mildness of joy.

Meanwhile, as we lay entranced, the occasional sudden frantic scenes in the distance showed the activity of the other boats, still engaged in dragging the whales on the frontier of the host, or possibly carrying on the war within the first circle, where there was room enough and some convenient retreats. But the sight of the enraged dragged whales now and then blindly darting to and fro across the circles was nothing to what at last met our eyes. It is sometimes the custom, when fast to a whale more than usually powerful and alert, to try to hamstring him by severing or maiming his gigantic tail-tendon. This is done by throwing a short-handled cutting-spade with a rope attached for hauling it back. A whale wounded in this way — as we afterward learned — but not effectively, had broken away from the boat, carrying along with him half of the harpoon line. In the extraordinary agony of the wound, he was now dashing among the revolving circles like the lone mounted desperado Arnold at the Battle of Saratoga, carrying dismay wherever he went.

But agonizing as this whale's wound was, and appalling a spectacle in itself, the peculiar horror he seemed to inspire in the rest of the herd was owing to a cause which at first the intervening distance hid from us. But at length we saw that by one of the unimaginable accidents of the fishery, this whale had become entangled in the harpoon line he towed. He had also run off with the cutting-spade in him. While the free end of the rope attached to that weapon had permanently caught in the coils of the harpoon line wound around his tail, the cutting-spade itself had worked loose from his flesh. So, tormented to madness, he was now churning through the water, violently flailing with his flexible tail and tossing the keen spade about him, wounding and killing his own companions.

This terrific sight seemed to rouse the whole herd from their frozen fright. First, the whales forming the margin of our lake began to crowd a little and jostle against each other, as if lifted by spent waves from afar. Then the lake itself began faintly to heave and swell. The submarine nurseries and bridal chambers vanished. In tighter and tighter orbits, the whales in the more central circles began to swim in thickening clusters. Yes, the long calm was departing. A low advancing hum was soon heard. And then, like the tumultuous masses of block-ice when the great river Hudson breaks up in spring, the entire host of whales came tumbling upon their inner center, as if to pile themselves up in one common mountain. Instantly Starbuck and Queequeg changed places, Starbuck taking the stern.

"Oars! Oars!" he intensely whispered, seizing the helm. "Grip your oars and clench your souls now! My God, men, stand by! Shove him off, Queequeg — the whale there! Prick him! Hit him! Stand up — stand up, and stay so! Spring, men — pull, men! Never mind their backs — scrape them! Scrape away!"

The boat was now all but jammed between two vast black hulks, leaving a narrow strait between their long bodies. But by desperate effort we at last shot into a temporary opening, then pulled hard, earnestly watching for another way out. After many similar narrow escapes, we at last swiftly glided into what had just been one of the outer circles but was now crossed by random whales, all violently making for the center. This lucky escape was cheaply purchased by the loss of Queequeg's hat, which, while he stood in the bow pricking the fleeing whales, was snatched clean from his head by the air-current made by the sudden tossing of a pair of broad flukes close by.

Riotous and disordered as the universal commotion now was, it soon resolved itself into what seemed a systematic movement. Having clumped together at last in one dense body, the whales renewed their forward flight with increased speed. Further pursuit was useless, but the boats still lingered in their wake to pick up whatever dragged whales might be dropped behind, and also to secure one that Flask had killed and marked. The mark is a pennanted pole, two or three of which are carried by every boat. When additional prey is at hand, these are inserted upright into the floating body of a dead whale, both to mark its place on the sea and as a token of prior possession, should the boats of any other ship draw near.

The result of this hunt was somewhat illustrative of that wise saying in the fishery: the more whales, the less fish. Of all the dragged whales, only one was captured. The rest managed to escape for the time, but only to be taken, as will later be seen, by some other vessel than the Pequod.

chapters.title: Chapter 88 — Schools and Schoolmasters
paragraphs: The previous chapter gave an account of an immense body or herd of sperm whales, and there was also given the probable cause behind those vast gatherings.

Now, though such great bodies are at times encountered, as has been seen, even today small separate bands are occasionally observed, ranging from twenty to fifty individuals each. Such bands are known as schools. They are generally of two sorts: those composed almost entirely of females, and those mustering none but young, vigorous males — or bulls, as they are familiarly called.

In gallant attendance upon the school of females, you invariably see a male of full-grown size, but not old, who upon any alarm shows his chivalry by falling to the rear and covering the flight of his ladies. In truth, this gentleman is a luxurious sultan, swimming about the watery world, surrounded by all the comforts and pleasures of the harem. The contrast between this sultan and his consorts is striking, because while he is always of the largest proportions, the ladies, even at full growth, are not more than one-third the bulk of an average-sized male. They are comparatively delicate, indeed — I daresay not exceeding half a dozen yards around the waist. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that on the whole they are hereditarily entitled to plumpness.

It is very curious to watch this harem and its lord in their indolent wanderings. Like fashionable society, they are forever on the move in leisurely search of variety. You meet them on the equator in time for the full bloom of the feeding season, having just returned perhaps from spending the summer in the northern seas, and so cheating summer of all its unpleasant weariness and warmth. By the time they have lounged up and down the equatorial promenade awhile, they start for the eastern waters in anticipation of the cool season there, and so evade the other excessive temperature of the year.

When serenely traveling on one of these journeys, if any strange suspicious sights are seen, the lord whale keeps a wary eye on his interesting family. Should any rudely bold young Leviathan happen that way and presume to draw confidentially close to one of the ladies — with what prodigious fury the lord assails him and chases him away! High times indeed, if unprincipled young rakes like him are to be permitted to invade the sanctity of domestic bliss. Though do what the lord will, he cannot keep the most notorious seducer out of his bed, for alas, all fish bed in common. As on shore, the ladies often cause the most terrible duels among their rival admirers. Just so with the whales, who sometimes come to deadly battle, and all for love. They fence with their long lower jaws, sometimes locking them together and striving for supremacy like elks that warring interweave their antlers. Not a few are captured bearing the deep scars of these encounters: furrowed heads, broken teeth, scalloped fins, and in some instances wrenched and dislocated mouths.

But suppose the invader of domestic bliss takes himself away at the first rush of the harem's lord. Then it is very amusing to watch that lord. Gently he insinuates his vast bulk among them again and revels there awhile, still in tantalizing proximity to young Lothario, like pious Solomon devoutly worshipping among his thousand concubines. Granting other whales to be in sight, the fishermen will seldom give chase to one of these grand sultans, for these grand sultans are too lavish with their strength, and hence their oil-yield is small. As for the sons and daughters they beget, those sons and daughters must take care of themselves — at least with only the mother's help. For like certain other roving lovers that might be named, the lord whale has no taste for the nursery, however much for the bower. And so, being a great traveler, he leaves his anonymous babies all over the world, every baby an exotic. In good time, nevertheless, as the ardor of youth declines — as years and gloom increase, as reflection lends her solemn pauses — in short, as a general weariness overtakes the sated sultan, a love of ease and virtue replaces the love of maidens. Our lord enters upon the impotent, repentant, lecturing stage of life, forswears and disbands the harem, and grown to an exemplary, sulky old soul, goes about all alone among the meridians and parallels saying his prayers and warning each young Leviathan from his amorous errors.

Now, as the harem of whales is called by the fishermen a school, so is the lord and master of that school technically known as the schoolmaster. It is therefore not in strict character — however admirably satirical — that after going to school himself, he should then go abroad teaching not what he learned there but the folly of it. His title of schoolmaster would very naturally seem derived from the name of the harem itself. But some have guessed that the man who first gave this name to this sort of sultan whale must have read the memoirs of Vidocq, and informed himself what sort of country schoolmaster that famous Frenchman was in his younger days, and what was the nature of those secret lessons he taught some of his pupils.

The same seclusion and isolation to which the schoolmaster whale retreats in his advancing years is true of all aged sperm whales. Almost universally, a lone whale — as a solitary Leviathan is called — proves to be an ancient one. Like the venerable moss-bearded Daniel Boone, he will have no one near him but Nature herself. And her he takes to wife in the wilderness of waters — and the best of wives she is, though she keeps so many moody secrets.

The schools composed of nothing but young, vigorous males, previously mentioned, offer a strong contrast to the harem schools. For while those female whales are characteristically timid, the young males — or forty-barrel-bulls, as they call them — are by far the most combative of all Leviathans and proverbially the most dangerous to encounter, excepting those wondrous gray-headed, grizzled whales sometimes met, who will fight you like grim fiends aggravated by gout.

The forty-barrel-bull schools are larger than the harem schools. Like a mob of young college men, they are full of fight, fun, and mischief, tumbling round the world at such a reckless, rollicking rate that no prudent insurance man would cover them any more than he would a riotous student at Yale or Harvard. They soon outgrow this wildness, though, and when about three-quarters grown, they break up and separately go about in quest of settlements — that is, harems.

Another difference between the male and female schools is still more characteristic of the sexes. Say you strike a forty-barrel-bull: poor devil! All his comrades abandon him. But strike a member of the harem school, and her companions swim around her with every sign of concern, sometimes lingering so near and so long as to fall prey themselves.

chapters.title: Chapter 89 — Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
paragraphs: The mention of the marker-pole in the chapter before last calls for some account of the laws and regulations of the whale fishery, of which the marker may be considered the grand symbol and badge.

It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would constantly arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

Perhaps the only formal whaling code authorized by legislation was that of Holland, decreed by the States-General in 1695. But though no other nation has ever had any written whaling law, the American fishermen have been their own legislators and lawyers in this matter. They have provided a system which for terse completeness surpasses Justinian's Pandects and the bylaws of the Chinese Society for the Suppression of Meddling with Other People's Business. Yes, these laws might be engraved on a Queen Anne's farthing, or the barb of a harpoon, and worn around the neck, so small are they.
I. A Fast-Fish belongs to the party fast to it.
II. A Loose-Fish is fair game for anybody who can soonest catch it.
But what causes trouble with this masterful code is the admirable brevity of it, which requires a vast volume of commentary to explain it.

First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a marker or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the marking party plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

These are the learned commentaries. But the commentaries of the whalemen themselves sometimes consist of hard words and harder knocks — the fists doing the arguing. True, among the more upright and honorable whalemen, allowances are always made for special cases where it would be an outrageous moral injustice for one party to claim possession of a whale previously chased or killed by another. But others are by no means so scrupulous.

Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when they had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally claimed it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of celebration, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. Wherefore the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

Mr. Erskine was counsel for the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine went on to illustrate his position by alluding to a recent adultery case, in which a gentleman, after in vain trying to curb his wife's unfaithfulness, had at last abandoned her upon the seas of life. But in the course of years, repenting of that step, he brought an action to recover possession of her. Erskine was on the other side and had then supported the case by saying that though the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and had once had her fast, and only by reason of the great force of her wayward plunging had at last abandoned her — yet abandon her he did, so that she became a Loose-Fish. And therefore when a subsequent gentleman re-harpooned her, the lady then became that subsequent gentleman's property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her.
Now in the present case Erskine argued that the examples of the whale and the lady were mutually illustrative of each other.

These arguments and counter-arguments being duly heard, the very learned judge officially decided as follows: As for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives. But with regard to the disputed whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants — the whale because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture, and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it acquired property in those articles, and hence anybody who afterward took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterward took the fish; therefore, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

An ordinary man looking at this decision of the very learned judge might possibly object to it. But plowed down to the bedrock of the matter, the two great principles laid down in the twin whaling laws previously quoted — applied and explained by Lord Ellenborough in the above-cited case — these two laws touching Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish will, on reflection, be found the fundamentals of all human law. For notwithstanding its complicated decorative sculpture, the Temple of the Law, like the Temple of the Philistines, has but two pillars to stand on.

Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and American slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last penny but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a nameplate for a marker — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish?
