So that — let us say it again — no dying Chaldee or Greek had higher and holier thoughts than those whose mysterious shadows you saw creeping over the face of poor Queequeg, as he lay quietly in his swaying hammock, and the rolling sea seemed to be gently rocking him to his final rest, and the ocean's invisible flood-tide lifted him higher and higher toward his destined heaven.

Every man in the crew gave him up for lost; and as for Queequeg himself, what he thought of his condition was forcibly shown by a curious favor he asked. He called one of the men to him in the gray morning watch, just as day was breaking, and, taking his hand, said that while in Nantucket he had happened to see certain little canoes of dark wood, like the rich war-wood of his native island; and on inquiring, he had learned that all whalemen who died in Nantucket were laid in those same dark canoes, and that the idea of being laid out that way had greatly pleased him. For it was not unlike the custom of his own people, who, after embalming a dead warrior, stretched him out in his canoe and so left him to be floated away to the starry archipelagoes; for not only do they believe that the stars are islands, but that far beyond all visible horizons their own mild, uncontinented seas flow together with the blue heavens, and so form the white breakers of the Milky Way. He added that he shuddered at the thought of being buried in his hammock, according to the usual custom at sea, tossed like something vile to the death-devouring sharks. No: he wanted a canoe like those of Nantucket, all the more congenial to him as a whaleman because, like a whaleboat, these coffin-canoes had no keel — though that meant uncertain steering, and a great deal of leeway down the dim ages.

Now, when this strange circumstance was made known aft, the carpenter was at once ordered to do Queequeg's bidding, whatever it might involve. There was some heathenish, coffin-colored old lumber aboard, which, on a long voyage some time before, had been cut from the aboriginal groves of the Lackaday islands, and it was recommended that the coffin be made from these dark planks. No sooner had the carpenter been told of the order than he took his rule and, with all the indifferent promptness of his character, went straight into the forecastle and took Queequeg's measure with great accuracy, regularly marking Queequeg's person with chalk as he shifted the rule.
"Ah! poor fellow! he'll have to die now," ejaculated the Long Island sailor.

Going to his vise-bench, the carpenter, for convenience' sake and general reference, now measured off on it, by transfer, the exact length the coffin was to be, and then made the record permanent by cutting two notches at its ends. This done, he marshaled the planks and his tools, and set to work.
When the last nail was driven, and the lid duly planed and fitted, he lightly shouldered the coffin and went forward with it, inquiring whether they were ready for it yet in that direction.

Overhearing the indignant but half-humorous cries with which the people on deck began to drive the coffin away, Queequeg, to everyone's consternation, commanded that the thing should be instantly brought to him. Nor was there any denying him; seeing that, of all mortals, some dying men are the most tyrannical; and certainly, since they will shortly trouble us so little for evermore, the poor fellows ought to be indulged.

Leaning over in his hammock, Queequeg regarded the coffin for a long time with an attentive eye. He then called for his harpoon, had the wooden stock drawn from it, and then had the iron part placed in the coffin along with one of the paddles of his boat. Also at his own request, biscuits were then arranged round the inside walls; a flask of fresh water was placed at the head, and a small bag of woody earth scraped up in the hold at the foot; and when a piece of sailcloth had been rolled up for a pillow, Queequeg now begged to be lifted into his final bed, so that he might try out its comforts, if it had any. He lay without moving for a few minutes, then told someone to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then, crossing his arms on his chest with Yojo between them, he called for the coffin lid (hatch, he called it) to be placed over him. The head part turned back on a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with little but his composed face in view. "Rarmai" (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signaled to be put back in his hammock.
But before this was done, Pip, who had been slyly hovering nearby all this while, came close to him where he lay and, with soft sobs, took him by the hand, holding his tambourine in the other.

"Poor rover! Will you never be done with all this weary roving? Where are you going now? But if the currents carry you to those sweet Antilles where the beaches are beaten only by water-lilies, will you do one little errand for me? Seek out one Pip, who's been missing a long time now: I think he's in those far Antilles. If you find him, then comfort him, for he must be very sad; for look! he's left his tambourine behind — I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die; and I'll beat you your dying march."

"I have heard," murmured Starbuck, gazing down the scuttle, "that in violent fevers men wholly without learning have talked in ancient languages; and that when the mystery is looked into, it always turns out that in their wholly forgotten childhood those ancient languages had really been spoken in their hearing by some lofty scholars. So, in my fond faith, poor Pip, in this strange sweetness of his lunacy, brings heavenly vouchers of all our heavenly homes. Where did he learn that, if not there? — Listen! He's speaking again: but more wildly now."

"Form up two by two! Let's make a General of him! Ho, where's his harpoon? Lay it across here. — Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Hurrah! Oh, for a gamecock now to sit on his head and crow! Queequeg dies game! — mind you that; Queequeg dies game! — take good note of that; Queequeg dies game! I say; game, game, game! But base little Pip, he died a coward; died all a-shiver — shame on Pip! Listen; if you find Pip, tell all the Antilles he's a runaway; a coward, a coward, a coward! Tell them he jumped from a whaleboat! I'd never beat my tambourine over base Pip, and hail him General, if he were dying here once more. No, no! Shame on all cowards — shame on them! Let them go drown like Pip, who jumped from a whaleboat. Shame! Shame!"
During all this, Queequeg lay with closed eyes, as if in a dream. Pip was led away, and the sick man was replaced in his hammock.

But now that he had apparently made every preparation for death, now that his coffin had proved a good fit, Queequeg suddenly rallied; soon there seemed no need for the carpenter's box. And then, when some expressed their delighted surprise, he said, in substance, that the cause of his sudden recovery was this: at a critical moment he had just remembered a little duty ashore that he was leaving undone, and so had changed his mind about dying; he could not die yet, he declared. They asked him, then, whether living or dying was a matter of his own sovereign will and pleasure. He answered, certainly. In a word, it was Queequeg's notion that if a man made up his mind to live, mere sickness could not kill him: nothing but a whale, or a gale, or some violent, ungovernable, unintelligent destroyer of that sort.

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized: while a sick civilized man may take six months to recover, generally speaking a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length, after sitting on the windlass for a few idle days (but eating with a vigorous appetite), he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretch, yawned a little, and then, springing into the head of his hoisted boat and poising a harpoon, declared himself fit for a fight.

With a wild whimsicality, he now used his coffin as a sea-chest; and emptying his canvas bag of clothes into it, he set them in order there. He spent many spare hours carving the lid with all kinds of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that in this way he was trying, in his rough fashion, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold, a wondrous work in one volume, but one whose mysteries not even he himself could read, though his own living heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to molder away with the living parchment on which they were inscribed, and so remain unsolved to the last. And it must have been this thought that prompted Ahab's wild exclamation when, one morning, he turned away from surveying poor Queequeg — "Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!"

chapters.title: Chapter 111 — The Pacific
paragraphs: When gliding by the Bashee isles we emerged at last upon the great South Sea. Were it not for other things, I could have greeted my dear Pacific with uncounted thanks, for now the long prayer of my youth was answered: that serene ocean rolled eastward from me a thousand leagues of blue.

There is, one knows not what sweet mystery about this sea, whose gently awesome stirrings seem to speak of some hidden soul beneath — like those fabled heavings of the Ephesian sod over the buried Evangelist St. John. And it is fitting that over these sea-pastures, wide-rolling watery prairies and Potters' Fields of all four continents, the waves should rise and fall, and ebb and flow unceasingly; for here millions of mixed shades and shadows, drowned dreams, sleepwalkings, reveries — all that we call lives and souls — lie dreaming, dreaming, still; tossing like sleepers in their beds; the ever-rolling waves made so only by their restlessness.

To any meditative Magian rover, this serene Pacific, once seen, must forever after be the sea of his adoption. It rolls the midmost waters of the world, the Indian Ocean and the Atlantic being only its arms. The same waves wash the breakwaters of the newly built Californian towns, planted only yesterday by the most recent race of men, and bathe the faded but still gorgeous skirts of Asiatic lands older than Abraham; while between them all float milky ways of coral islands, and low-lying, endless, unknown archipelagoes, and impenetrable Japans. Thus this mysterious, divine Pacific girdles the world's whole bulk; makes all coasts one bay to it; seems the tide-beating heart of the earth. Lifted by those eternal swells, you cannot help but acknowledge the seductive god, bowing your head to Pan.

But few thoughts of Pan stirred Ahab's brain as, standing like an iron statue at his accustomed place beside the mizzen rigging, with one nostril he unthinkingly sniffed the sugary musk from the Bashee isles (in whose sweet woods mild lovers must be walking), and with the other consciously breathed in the salt breath of the newfound sea — that sea in which the hated White Whale must even then be swimming. Launched at last upon these almost final waters, and gliding toward the Japanese cruising ground, the old man's purpose intensified. His firm lips met like the lips of a vise; the Delta of his forehead's veins swelled like overloaded brooks; even in his sleep, his ringing cry ran through the vaulted hull: "Stern all! The White Whale spouts thick blood!"

chapters.title: Chapter 112 — The Blacksmith
paragraphs: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather that now reigned in these latitudes, and in preparation for the especially active pursuits expected shortly, Perth, the begrimed, blistered old blacksmith, had not moved his portable forge back to the hold after finishing his share of the work on Ahab's leg, but kept it on deck, lashed fast to ringbolts by the foremast; for he was now almost constantly called on by the headsmen, and harpooners, and bowsmen to do some little job for them — altering, or repairing, or reshaping their various weapons and boat gear. Often he would be surrounded by an eager circle, all waiting to be served, holding boat-spades, pike-heads, harpoons and lances, and jealously watching his every sooty movement as he toiled. Nevertheless, this old man's was a patient hammer wielded by a patient arm. No murmur, no impatience, no petulance came from him. Silent, slow and solemn, bowing his chronically broken back still further, he toiled away as if toil were life itself, and the heavy beating of his hammer the heavy beating of his heart. And so it was. — Most miserable!

A peculiar walk in this old man, a certain slight but painful-looking yawing in his gait, had at an early period of the voyage excited the curiosity of the sailors. And to the persistence of their questions he had finally given in, and so it came about that everyone now knew the shameful story of his wretched fate.

Out late, and not innocently, one bitter winter midnight on the road between two country towns, the blacksmith, half-stupefied, felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and took refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The outcome was the loss of the ends of both his feet. Out of this revelation, piece by piece, there at last came out the four acts of gladness, and the one long fifth act of grief, its catastrophe not yet reached, of his life's drama.

He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing called, in the technical language of sorrow, ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, with plenty to do; he owned a house and garden, embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife and three merry, rosy-cheeked children, and every Sunday went to a cheerful-looking church planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness, and further concealed in a most cunning disguise, a desperate burglar slid into his happy home and robbed them all of everything. And darker still to tell, it was the blacksmith himself who unknowingly led this burglar into the heart of his family. It was the Bottle Conjuror! When that fatal cork was drawn, out flew the fiend and shriveled up his home. Now, for prudent, most wise and economical reasons, the blacksmith's shop was in the basement of his house, but with a separate entrance of its own; so the young, loving, healthy wife had always listened — with no unhappy nervousness, but with vigorous pleasure — to the stout ringing of her young-armed old husband's hammer, whose echoes, muffled by passing through the floors and walls, came up to her, not unsweetly, in her nursery; and so, to stout Labor's iron lullaby, the blacksmith's infants were rocked to sleep.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why can you not sometimes come in time? Had you taken this old blacksmith to yourself before his full ruin came upon him, then the young widow would have had a delicious grief, and her orphans a truly venerable, legendary father to dream of in their later years; and all of them a care-killing sufficiency to live on. But Death plucked down some virtuous elder brother, on whose whistling daily toil alone hung the responsibilities of some other family, and left the worse-than-useless old man standing, until the hideous rot of life should make him easier to harvest.

Why tell the whole? The blows of the basement hammer came further apart every day, and each blow every day was fainter than the last; the wife sat frozen at the window, with tearless eyes, glitteringly gazing into the weeping faces of her children; the bellows fell; the forge choked up with cinders; the house was sold; the mother dived down into the long churchyard grass; her children twice followed her there; and the houseless, familyless old man staggered off, a vagabond in mourning crape, his every woe unreverenced, his gray head a scorn to flaxen curls!

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is only the first greeting to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored. Therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men, who still have left in them some inward scruples against suicide, the all-contributed and all-receptive ocean alluringly spreads out his whole plain of unimaginable, captivating terrors and wonderful, new-life adventures; and from the hearts of infinite Pacifics the thousand mermaids sing to them: "Come to us, broken-hearted; here is another life without the guilt of dying in between; here are supernatural wonders, without dying for them. Come to us! Bury yourself in a life which, to your landed world, now equally abhorred and abhorring, is more oblivious than death. Come to us! You too, put up your gravestone within the churchyard, and come to us, till we marry you!"
Listening to these voices, East and West, at early sunrise and at nightfall, the blacksmith's soul answered: Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.

chapters.title: Chapter 113 — The Forge
paragraphs: With matted beard, and wrapped in a bristling sharkskin apron, Perth was standing about midday between his forge and anvil, the anvil set on an ironwood log, with one hand holding a pike-head in the coals and the other at his forge's lungs, the bellows, when Captain Ahab came along, carrying in his hand a small, rusty-looking leather bag. While still a little distance from the forge, moody Ahab paused; until at last Perth, drawing his iron out of the fire, began hammering it on the anvil — the red mass sending off sparks in thick hovering flights, some of which flew close to Ahab.
"Are these your Mother Carey's chickens, Perth? They are always flying in your wake; birds of good omen, too, but not to all — look here, they burn; but you — you live among them without a scorch."
"Because I am scorched all over, Captain Ahab," answered Perth, resting for a moment on his hammer; "I am past scorching; not easily can you scorch a scar."

"Well, well; no more. Your shrunken voice sounds too calmly, sanely woeful to me. In no Paradise myself, I am impatient of all misery in others that is not mad. You should go mad, blacksmith; say, why don't you go mad? How can you endure without being mad? Do the heavens yet hate you, that you cannot go mad? What were you making there?"
"Welding an old pike-head, sir; there were seams and dents in it."
"And can you make it all smooth again, blacksmith, after such hard usage as it had?"
"I think so, sir."
"And I suppose you can smooth almost any seams and dents; never mind how hard the metal, blacksmith?"
"Aye, sir, I think I can; all seams and dents but one."

"Look here, then," cried Ahab, passionately advancing, and leaning with both hands on Perth's shoulders; "look here — here — can you smooth out a seam like this, blacksmith?" sweeping one hand across his furrowed brow; "if you could, blacksmith, glad enough would I lay my head upon your anvil, and feel your heaviest hammer between my eyes. Answer! Can you smooth this seam?"
"Oh! That is the one, sir! Did I not say all seams and dents but one?"

"Aye, blacksmith, it is the one; aye, man, it is unsmoothable; for though you only see it here in my flesh, it has worked down into the bone of my skull — that is all wrinkles! But away with child's play; no more gaffs and pikes today. Look here!" jingling the leather bag as if it were full of gold coins. "I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand yoke of fiends could not pull apart, Perth; something that will stick in a whale like his own fin-bone. There's the stuff," flinging the pouch upon the anvil. "Look, blacksmith, these are the gathered nail-stubs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
"Horseshoe stubs, sir? Why, Captain Ahab, you have here, then, the best and stubbornest stuff we blacksmiths ever work."

"I know it, old man; these stubs will weld together like glue from the melted bones of murderers. Quick! Forge me the harpoon. And forge me first twelve rods for its shank; then wind and twist and hammer these twelve together like the yarns and strands of a tow-line. Quick! I'll blow the fire."

When at last the twelve rods were made, Ahab tried them, one by one, by spiraling them with his own hand round a long, heavy iron bolt. "A flaw!" rejecting the last one. "Work that over again, Perth."

This done, Perth was about to begin welding the twelve into one, when Ahab stayed his hand and said he would weld his own iron. As, then, with regular, gasping grunts, he hammered on the anvil, Perth passing him the glowing rods one after another, and the hard-pressed forge shooting up its intense straight flame, the Parsee passed silently, and bowing over his head toward the fire, seemed to be invoking some curse or some blessing upon the toil. But, as Ahab looked up, he slid aside.

"What's that bunch of lucifer matches dodging about there for?" muttered Stubb, looking on from the forecastle. "That Parsee smells fire like a fuse; and smells of it himself, like a hot musket's powder-pan."
At last the shank, in one complete rod, received its final heat; and as Perth, to temper it, plunged it all hissing into the cask of water near by, the scalding steam shot up into Ahab's bent face.
"Would you brand me, Perth?" wincing for a moment with the pain; "have I been but forging my own branding-iron, then?"
"Pray God, not that; yet I fear something, Captain Ahab. Is not this harpoon for the White Whale?"
"For the white fiend! But now for the barbs; you must make them yourself, man. Here are my razors — the best of steel; here, and make the barbs sharp as the needle-sleet of the Icy Sea."
For a moment, the old blacksmith eyed the razors as though he would rather not use them.
"Take them, man, I have no need for them; for I now neither shave, sup, nor pray till — but here — to work!"

Fashioned at last into an arrow-shape and welded by Perth to the shank, the steel soon pointed the end of the iron; and as the blacksmith was about to give the barbs their final heat, prior to tempering them, he cried to Ahab to place the water-cask near.

"No, no — no water for that; I want it of the true death-temper. Ahoy, there! Tashtego, Queequeg, Daggoo! What say you, pagans! Will you give me as much blood as will cover this barb?" holding it high up. A cluster of dark nods replied: Yes. Three punctures were made in the heathen flesh, and the White Whale's barbs were then tempered.
"Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!" deliriously howled Ahab, as the malignant iron scorchingly devoured the baptismal blood.

Now, mustering the spare poles from below and selecting one of hickory, with the bark still on it, Ahab fitted the end to the socket of the iron. A coil of new tow-line was then unwound, and some fathoms of it taken to the windlass and stretched to a great tension. Pressing his foot upon it, till the rope hummed like a harp-string, then eagerly bending over it and seeing no strandings, Ahab exclaimed: "Good! and now for the seizings."

At one end the rope was unstranded, and the separate spread yarns were all braided and woven round the socket of the harpoon; the pole was then driven hard up into the socket; from the lower end the rope was traced halfway along the pole's length and firmly secured there with intertwistings of twine. This done, pole, iron and rope — like the Three Fates — remained inseparable, and Ahab moodily stalked away with the weapon, the sound of his ivory leg and the sound of the hickory pole both ringing hollowly along every plank. But before he entered his cabin, a light, unnatural, half-bantering, yet most piteous sound was heard. Oh, Pip! Your wretched laugh, your idle but unresting eye, all your strange mummery, not without meaning blended with the black tragedy of the melancholy ship, and mocked it!

chapters.title: Chapter 114 — The Gilder
paragraphs: Penetrating further and further into the heart of the Japanese cruising ground, the Pequod was soon all astir in the fishery. Often, in mild, pleasant weather, for twelve, fifteen, eighteen, and twenty hours on end, they were engaged in the boats, steadily pulling, or sailing, or paddling after the whales, or, for an interval of sixty or seventy minutes, calmly waiting for them to rise — though with but small success for their pains.

At such times, under a softened sun, afloat all day upon smooth, slow-heaving swells, seated in his boat as light as a birch canoe, and so sociably mingling with the soft waves themselves that, like hearthstone cats, they purr against the gunwale — these are the times of dreamy quietude, when beholding the tranquil beauty and brilliance of the ocean's skin, one forgets the tiger heart that pants beneath it; and would not willingly remember that this velvet paw but conceals a merciless fang.

These are the times when in his whaleboat the rover softly feels a certain filial, confident, land-like feeling toward the sea; he regards it as so much flowery earth; and the distant ship, revealing only the tops of her masts, seems struggling forward not through high rolling waves but through the tall grass of a rolling prairie — as when the western emigrants' horses only show their erect ears, while their hidden bodies widely wade through the amazing verdure.

The long-drawn virgin valleys; the mild blue hillsides; as over these there steals the hush, the hum; you almost swear that play-weary children lie sleeping in these solitudes, in some glad springtime, when the flowers of the woods are plucked. And all this mixes with your most mystic mood; so that fact and fancy, half-way meeting, interpenetrate and form one seamless whole.

Nor did such soothing scenes, however temporary, fail to have at least an equally temporary effect on Ahab. But if these secret golden keys did seem to open his own secret golden treasuries within him, his breath upon them proved only tarnishing.

Oh, grassy glades! Oh, ever-vernal endless landscapes in the soul; in you, though long parched by the dead drought of the earthy life, in you, men yet may roll like young horses in new morning clover; and for some few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of the life immortal on them. Would to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled, mingling threads of life are woven by warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady unretracing progress in this life; we do not advance through fixed gradations, and at the last one pause — through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's thoughtless faith, adolescence's doubt (the common doom), then skepticism, then disbelief, resting at last in manhood's pondering repose of If. But once gone through, we trace the round again; and are infants, boys, and men, and Ifs eternally. Where lies the final harbor, from which we unmoor no more? In what rapt ether sails the world, of which the weariest will never weary? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unwedded mothers die in bearing them: the secret of our paternity lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.
And that same day, too, gazing far down from his boat's side into that same golden sea, Starbuck lowly murmured:

"Loveliness unfathomable, as ever lover saw in his young bride's eye! Tell me not of your teeth-tiered sharks and your kidnapping cannibal ways. Let faith oust fact; let fancy oust memory; I look deep down and do believe."
And Stubb, fish-like, with sparkling scales, leaped up in that same golden light:
"I am Stubb, and Stubb has his history; but here Stubb takes oaths that he has always been jolly!"

chapters.title: Chapter 115 — The Pequod Meets The Bachelor
paragraphs: And jolly enough were the sights and sounds that came bearing down before the wind, some few weeks after Ahab's harpoon had been welded.

It was a Nantucket ship, the Bachelor, which had just wedged in her last cask of oil and bolted down her bursting hatches; and now, in glad holiday dress, was joyously, though somewhat boastfully, sailing round among the widely separated ships on the ground, before turning her prow for home.

The three men at her mastheads wore long streamers of narrow red bunting on their hats; from the stern a whaleboat was hung, bottom down; and hanging captive from the bowsprit was the long lower jaw of the last whale they had killed. Signals, ensigns and jacks of all colors were flying from her rigging on every side. Lashed sideways in each of her three basketed tops were two barrels of sperm; above them, in her topmast crosstrees, you saw slender breakers (small casks) of the same precious fluid; and nailed to her main truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast, was a brass lamp.

As was learned afterward, the Bachelor had met with the most surprising success — all the more wonderful because, while cruising in the same seas, numerous other vessels had gone entire months without securing a single fish. Not only had barrels of beef and bread been given away to make room for the far more valuable sperm, but additional casks had been bartered for from the ships she had met; and these were stowed along the deck and in the captain's and officers' staterooms. Even the cabin table itself had been knocked into kindling; and the cabin mess dined off the broad head of an oil-butt, lashed down to the floor for a centerpiece. In the forecastle, the sailors had actually caulked and pitched their chests and filled them; it was humorously added that the cook had clapped a head on his largest boiler and filled it; that the steward had plugged his spare coffee-pot and filled it; that the harpooners had headed the sockets of their irons and filled them; that, indeed, everything was filled with sperm except the captain's trouser pockets, and those he reserved for thrusting his hands into, in self-satisfied testimony of his entire satisfaction.

As this glad ship of good luck bore down upon the moody Pequod, the barbaric sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle; and as she drew still nearer, a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge try-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like skin called the poke, the stomach-skin of the black fish, gave out a loud roar at every stroke of the crew's clenched hands. On the quarter-deck, the mates and harpooners were dancing with the olive-hued girls who had eloped with them from the Polynesian Isles; while, suspended in an ornamented boat firmly secured aloft between the foremast and mainmast, three Long Island negroes, with glittering fiddle-bows of whale ivory, were presiding over the hilarious jig. Meanwhile, others of the ship's company were tumultuously busy at the masonry of the try-works, from which the huge pots had been removed. You would almost have thought they were pulling down the cursed Bastille, such wild cries they raised as the now useless brick and mortar were being hurled into the sea.

Lord and master over all this scene, the captain stood erect on the ship's elevated quarter-deck, so that the whole rejoicing drama was full before him, and seemed merely staged for his own individual amusement.

And Ahab, he too was standing on his quarter-deck, shaggy and black, with a stubborn gloom; and as the two ships crossed each other's wakes — one all celebrations for things past, the other all forebodings for things to come — their two captains in themselves embodied the whole striking contrast of the scene.
"Come aboard, come aboard!" cried the gay Bachelor's commander, lifting a glass and a bottle in the air.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" gritted Ahab in reply.
"No; only heard of him; but don't believe in him at all," said the other good-humoredly. "Come aboard!"
"You are too damned jolly. Sail on. Have you lost any men?"

"Not enough to speak of — two islanders, that's all; but come aboard, old hearty, come along. I'll soon take that black from your brow. Come along, will you — merry's the play — a full ship and homeward-bound."

"How wondrous familiar is a fool!" muttered Ahab; then aloud: "You are a full ship and homeward-bound, you say; well, then, call me an empty ship, and outward-bound. So go your ways, and I will mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

And thus, while the one ship went cheerily before the breeze, the other stubbornly fought against it; and so the two vessels parted, the crew of the Pequod looking with grave, lingering glances toward the receding Bachelor, but the Bachelor's men never heeding their gaze for the lively revelry they were in. And as Ahab, leaning over the taffrail, eyed the homeward-bound craft, he took from his pocket a small vial of sand, and then, looking from the ship to the vial, seemed to be bringing two remote associations together, for that vial was filled with Nantucket soundings.

chapters.title: Chapter 116 — The Dying Whale
paragraphs: Not seldom in this life, when, on the right side, fortune's favorites sail close by us, we, though all drooping before, catch somewhat of the rushing breeze and joyfully feel our sagging sails fill out. So it seemed with the Pequod. For next day after encountering the gay Bachelor, whales were seen and four were slain; and one of them by Ahab.

It was far into the afternoon; and when all the spearings of the crimson fight were done, and, floating in the lovely sunset sea and sky, sun and whale both silently died together — then such sweetness and such plaintiveness, such wreathing prayers, curled up into that rosy air that it almost seemed as if, far over from the deep green convent valleys of the Manilla isles, the Spanish land-breeze, wantonly turned sailor, had gone to sea freighted with these vesper hymns.

Soothed again, but only soothed to deeper gloom, Ahab, who had backed off from the whale, sat intently watching its final wanings from the now tranquil boat. For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales dying — the turning sunward of the head, and so expiring — that strange spectacle, seen on such a placid evening, somehow conveyed to Ahab a wondrousness unknown before.

"He turns and turns himself to it — how slowly, but how steadfastly, his homage-rendering and invoking brow, with his last dying motions. He too worships fire; most faithful, broad, baronial vassal of the sun! Oh, that these too-favoring eyes should see these too-favoring sights. Look! Here, far water-locked; beyond all hum of human weal or woe; in these most candid and impartial seas; where to traditions no rocks furnish tablets; where for long Chinese ages the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, as stars that shine upon the Niger's unknown source — here, too, life dies sunward full of faith; but see! No sooner dead than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.

"Oh, you dark Hindu half of nature, who of drowned bones have built your separate throne somewhere in the heart of these unverdured seas; you are an infidel, you queen, and too truly you speak to me in the wide-slaughtering Typhoon, and the hushed burial of its after-calm. Nor has this whale of yours turned his dying head sunward, and then gone round again, without a lesson to me.

"Oh, trebly hooped and welded hip of power! Oh, high aspiring, rainbowed jet! The one strives, the other jets, all in vain! In vain, oh whale, do you seek intercession with the all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life but gives it not again. Yet you, darker half, rock me with a prouder, if a darker faith. All your unnamable inminglings float beneath me here; I am buoyed by breaths of once living things, exhaled as air, but water now.

"Then hail, forever hail, O sea, in whose eternal tossings the wild fowl finds his only rest. Born of earth, yet suckled by the sea; though hill and valley mothered me, you billows are my foster-brothers!"

chapters.title: Chapter 117 — The Whale Watch
paragraphs: The four whales killed that evening had died wide apart; one far to windward, one less distant to leeward, one ahead, one astern. These last three were brought alongside before nightfall; but the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night. And that boat was Ahab's.

The waif-pole, the pole planted to mark a dead whale, was thrust upright into the dead whale's spout-hole; and the lantern hanging from its top cast a troubled flickering glare upon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which gently chafed the whale's broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.

Ahab and all his boat's crew seemed asleep but the Parsee; who, crouching in the bow, sat watching the sharks that spectrally played round the whale and tapped the light cedar planks with their tails. A sound like the moaning in squadrons over Asphaltites of unforgiven ghosts of Gomorrah ran shuddering through the air.
Started from his slumbers, Ahab, face to face, saw the Parsee; and hooped round by the gloom of the night, they seemed the last men in a flooded world. "I have dreamed it again," said he.
"Of the hearses? Have I not said, old man, that neither hearse nor coffin can be yours?"
"And who are hearsed that die on the sea?"

"But I said, old man, that before you could die on this voyage, two hearses must truly be seen by you on the sea; the first not made by mortal hands; and the visible wood of the last one must be grown in America."
"Aye, aye! A strange sight that, Parsee: a hearse and its plumes floating over the ocean with the waves for the pallbearers. Ha! Such a sight we shall not soon see."
"Believe it or not, you cannot die till it be seen, old man."
"And what was that saying about yourself?"
"Though it come to the last, I shall still go before you, your pilot."

"And when you are so gone before — if that ever befall — then before I can follow, you must still appear to me, to pilot me still? Was it not so? Well, then, if I believed all you say, oh my pilot, I have here two pledges that I shall yet slay Moby Dick and survive it."
"Take another pledge, old man," said the Parsee, as his eyes lit up like fireflies in the gloom — "Hemp only can kill you."
"The gallows, you mean. I am immortal then, on land and on sea," cried Ahab, with a laugh of derision; "Immortal on land and on sea!"
Both were silent again, as one man. The gray dawn came on, and the slumbering crew arose from the boat's bottom, and before noon the dead whale was brought to the ship.

chapters.title: Chapter 118 — The Quadrant
paragraphs: The season for the Line, the equator, at length drew near; and every day, when Ahab, coming from his cabin, cast his eyes aloft, the vigilant helmsman would ostentatiously handle his spokes, and the eager sailors would quickly run to the braces and stand there with all their eyes centrally fixed on the nailed doubloon, impatient for the order to point the ship's prow for the equator. In good time the order came. It was close upon high noon; and Ahab, seated in the bows of his high-hoisted boat, was about to take his usual daily observation of the sun to determine his latitude.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, while his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! Level by nature to this earth's horizon are the glances of man's eyes; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," stepping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself — these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the sailors clustered together on the forecastle, until Ahab, pacing the deck in agitation, shouted out: "To the braces! Up helm! — square in!"

In an instant the yards swung round; and as the ship half-wheeled upon her heel, her three firm-seated, graceful masts, erectly poised upon her long, ribbed hull, seemed like the three Horatii pirouetting on one sufficient steed.
Standing between the knightheads (the timbers on either side of the bowsprit), Starbuck watched the Pequod's tumultuous way, and Ahab's also, as he went lurching along the deck.

"I have sat before the dense coal fire and watched it all aglow, full of its tormented flaming life; and I have seen it wane at last, down, down, to dumbest dust. Old man of oceans! Of all this fiery life of yours, what will at length remain but one little heap of ashes!"

"Aye," cried Stubb, "but sea-coal ashes — mind you that, Mr. Starbuck — sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, 'Here someone thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.' And damn me, Ahab, but you act right; live in the game, and die in it!"

chapters.title: Chapter 119 — The Candles
paragraphs: It is the warmest climates that nurse the cruelest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of never-fading green. It is the most dazzling skies that carry the deadliest thunders in their basket: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner meets the most terrible of all storms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst out of that cloudless sky like a bomb exploding on a dazed and sleepy town.

Toward evening of that day, the Pequod was torn of her canvas and, bare-poled, was left to fight a typhoon which had struck her directly ahead. When darkness came on, sky and sea roared and split with the thunder and blazed with the lightning that showed the disabled masts fluttering here and there with the rags which the first fury of the storm had left for its after-sport.

Holding on to a shroud, Starbuck was standing on the quarter-deck, glancing aloft at every flash of lightning to see what further disaster might have befallen the intricate rigging there, while Stubb and Flask were directing the men in hoisting the boats higher and lashing them more firmly. But all their efforts seemed in vain. Though hoisted to the very top of the cranes, the windward quarter boat (Ahab's) did not escape. A great rolling sea, dashing high against the reeling ship's tall, teetering side, stove in the boat's bottom at the stern, and left it again, dripping through like a sieve.

"Bad work, bad work, Mr. Starbuck," said Stubb, looking at the wreck, "but the sea will have its way. Stubb, for one, can't fight it. You see, Mr. Starbuck, a wave has such a great long start before it leaps — all round the world it runs, and then comes the spring! But as for me, all the start I have to meet it is just across the deck here. But never mind; it's all in fun, so the old song says —" (Sings.)
Oh! jolly is the gale, / And a joker is the whale, / A-flourishing his tail — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
The scud all a-flying, / That's his flip only foaming; / When he stirs in the spicing — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
Thunder splits the ships, / But he only smacks his lips, / A-tasting of this flip — / Such a funny, sporty, gamy, jesty, joky, hoky-poky lad, is the Ocean, oh!
"Enough, Stubb," cried Starbuck, "let the Typhoon sing, and strike his harp here in our rigging; but if you are a brave man you will hold your peace."

"But I am not a brave man; never said I was a brave man; I am a coward; and I sing to keep up my spirits. And I tell you what it is, Mr. Starbuck, there's no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I sing you the doxology for a wind-up."
"Madman! Look through my eyes if you have none of your own."
"What! How can you see better on a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"

"Here!" cried Starbuck, seizing Stubb by the shoulder and pointing his hand toward the weather bow. "Don't you see that the gale comes from the east, the very course Ahab is to run for Moby Dick? The very course he swung to at noon today? Now look at his boat there; where is it stove? In the stern-sheets, man, where he always stands — his stand-point is stove, man! Now jump overboard and sing away, if you must!"
"I don't half understand you; what's in the wind?"

"Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," mused Starbuck suddenly, paying no attention to Stubb's question. "The gale that now hammers at us to stave us, we can turn it into a fair wind that will drive us toward home. Over there, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward — I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
At that moment in one of the intervals of profound darkness following the flashes, a voice was heard at his side; and almost at the same instant a volley of thunder peals rolled overhead.
"Who's there?"
"Old Thunder!" said Ahab, groping his way along the bulwarks to his pivot-hole; but suddenly finding his path made plain by angled lances of fire.

Now, just as the lightning rod on a spire ashore is meant to carry the dangerous fluid off into the soil, so the similar rod that some ships at sea carry to each mast is meant to conduct it into the water. But this conductor must reach down to a considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and, moreover, if it were kept towing there all the time, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering more than a little with some of the rigging and more or less slowing the vessel's way through the water. Because of all this, the lower parts of a ship's lightning-rods are not always overboard; they are generally made in long slender links, so that they can more readily be hauled up into the chains (the ledges outside the hull where the shrouds are fastened), or thrown down into the sea, as occasion requires.

"The rods! The rods!" cried Starbuck to the crew, suddenly warned to vigilance by the vivid lightning that had just been darting like torches to light Ahab to his post. "Are they overboard? Drop them over, fore and aft. Quick!"

"Stop!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we be the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himalayas and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but away with privileges! Let them be, sir."
"Look aloft!" cried Starbuck. "The corpusants! The corpusants!"

All the yard-arms were tipped with a pallid fire — the corpusants, or St. Elmo's fire; and touched at each three-pointed lightning-rod-end with three tapering white flames, each of the three tall masts was silently burning in that sulfurous air, like three gigantic wax tapers before an altar.

"Blast the boat! Let it go!" cried Stubb at this instant, as a washing sea heaved up under his own little craft, so that its gunwale violently jammed his hand as he was passing a lashing. "Blast it!" But slipping backward on the deck, his uplifted eyes caught the flames; and immediately shifting his tone, he cried: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

To sailors, oaths are everyday words; they will swear in the trance of the calm and in the teeth of the tempest; they will hurl curses from the topsail-yard-arms when most they teeter over a seething sea; but in all my voyaging, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship — when His Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.

While this pallidness was burning aloft, few words were heard from the enchanted crew; who in one thick cluster stood on the forecastle, all their eyes gleaming in that pale phosphorescence, like a far-away constellation of stars. Set off against the ghostly light, the gigantic jet-black negro, Daggoo, loomed up to three times his real stature, and seemed the black cloud from which the thunder had come. The parted mouth of Tashtego revealed his shark-white teeth, which strangely gleamed as if they too had been tipped by corpusants; while lit up by the preternatural light, Queequeg's tattooing burned like Satanic blue flames on his body.

The tableau all waned at last with the pallidness aloft; and once more the Pequod and every soul on her decks were wrapped in a pall. A moment or two passed, when Starbuck, going forward, pushed against someone. It was Stubb. "What do you think now, man; I heard your cry; it was not the same in the song."

"No, no, it wasn't; I said the corpusants have mercy on us all; and I hope they will, still. But do they only have mercy on long faces? Have they no sympathy for a laugh? And look, Mr. Starbuck — but it's too dark to look. Hear me, then: I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck; for those masts are rooted in a hold that is going to be chock-full of sperm-oil, d'you see; and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three sperm candles — that's the good promise we saw."

At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into view. Glancing upward, he cried: "See! See!" And once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled otherworldliness in their pallor.
"The corpusants have mercy on us all," cried Stubb again.

At the base of the mainmast, directly beneath the doubloon and the flame, the Parsee was kneeling in front of Ahab, but with his head bowed away from him; while nearby, from the arched and overhanging rigging, where they had just been busy securing a spar, a number of the seamen, arrested by the glare, now clung together and hung there like a knot of numbed wasps from a drooping orchard twig. In various enchanted attitudes, like the standing or stepping or running skeletons in Herculaneum, others remained rooted to the deck; but all their eyes were turned upward.

"Aye, aye, men!" cried Ahab. "Look up at it; mark it well; the white flame only lights the way to the White Whale! Hand me those mainmast links there; I want to feel this pulse, and let mine beat against it — blood against fire! So."

Then turning — the last link held fast in his left hand, he put his foot upon the Parsee; and with fixed upward eye and high-flung right arm, he stood erect before the lofty three-pointed trinity of flames.

"Oh! You clear spirit of clear fire, whom I once worshipped on these seas as a Persian, until in the sacramental act I was so burned by you that to this hour I bear the scar — I know you now, you clear spirit, and I know now that the right way to worship you is defiance. You will be kind to neither love nor reverence; and even for hate you can only kill; and all are killed. It is no fearless fool who faces you now. I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; but to the last gasp of my earthquake life I will dispute its unconditional, unintegral mastery in me. In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here. Though only a point at best — wherever I came from, wherever I go — yet while I live on earth, the queenly personality lives in me and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in your lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss you; but at your highest, come as mere supernal power, and though you launch navies of fully laden worlds, there is something in here that still remains indifferent. Oh, you clear spirit, you made me out of your fire, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to you."
[Sudden, repeated flashes of lightning; the nine flames leap lengthwise to thrice their previous height; Ahab, with the rest, closes his eyes, his right hand pressed hard upon them.]

"I acknowledge your speechless, placeless power; didn't I say so? Nor was it wrung out of me; nor do I drop these links now. You can blind; but then I can grope. You can consume; but then I can be ashes. Take the homage of these poor eyes, and shutter-hands. I would not take it. The lightning flashes through my skull; my eyeballs ache and ache; my whole beaten brain seems beheaded, and rolling on some stunning ground. Oh, oh! Blindfolded, I will still talk to you. Light though you are, you leap out of darkness; but I am darkness leaping out of light, leaping out of you! The javelins stop; open, eyes; do you see, or not? There burn the flames! Oh, you magnanimous one! Now I do glory in my genealogy. But you are only my fiery father; my sweet mother I do not know. Oh, cruel! What have you done with her? There lies my puzzle; but yours is greater. You do not know how you came to be, and so you call yourself unbegotten; you certainly do not know your beginning, and so you call yourself unbegun. I know something of myself that you do not know of yourself, oh you omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond you, you clear spirit, to whom all your eternity is only time, all your creativeness mechanical. Through you, your flaming self, my scorched eyes dimly see it. Oh, you foundling fire, you hermit immemorial, you too have your incommunicable riddle, your unshared grief. Here again, with haughty agony, I read my sire. Leap! Leap up, and lick the sky! I leap with you; I burn with you; I long to be welded with you; defiantly I worship you!"
"The boat! The boat!" cried Starbuck, "look at your boat, old man!"

Ahab's harpoon, the one forged at Perth's fire, remained firmly lashed in its conspicuous crotch, so that it projected beyond his whale-boat's bow; but the sea that had stove its bottom had caused the loose leather sheath to drop off; and from the keen steel barb there now came a leveled flame of pale, forked fire. As the silent harpoon burned there like a serpent's tongue, Starbuck grasped Ahab by the arm: "God, God is against you, old man; forbear! It is an ill voyage! Ill begun, ill continued; let me square the yards while we may, old man, and make a fair wind of it homeward, to go on a better voyage than this."

Overhearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew instantly ran to the braces — though not a sail was left aloft. For the moment all the aghast mate's thoughts seemed theirs; they raised a half-mutinous cry. But dashing the rattling lightning links to the deck, and snatching the burning harpoon, Ahab waved it like a torch among them; swearing to impale with it the first sailor that but cast loose a rope's end. Petrified by his look, and shrinking still more from the fiery dart he held, the men fell back in dismay, and Ahab again spoke:

"All your oaths to hunt the White Whale are as binding as mine; and heart, soul, and body, lungs and life, old Ahab is bound. And that you may know to what tune this heart beats — look here; thus I blow out the last fear!" And with one blast of his breath he extinguished the flame.

As in the hurricane that sweeps the plain, men flee the neighborhood of some lone, gigantic elm, whose very height and strength but render it so much the more unsafe, because so much the more a mark for thunderbolts; so at those last words of Ahab's, many of the sailors did run from him in a terror of dismay.

chapters.title: Chapter 120 — The Deck Towards the End of the First Night Watch
paragraphs: Ahab standing by the helm. Starbuck approaching him.
"We must send down the main-top-sail yard, sir. The band is working loose and the lee lift is half-stranded. Shall I strike it, sir?"
"Strike nothing; lash it. If I had sky-sail poles, I'd sway them up now."
"Sir! — in God's name! — sir?"
"Well."
"The anchors are working, sir. Shall I get them inboard?"

"Strike nothing, and stir nothing, but lash everything. The wind rises, but it has not got up to my tablelands yet. Quick, and see to it. By masts and keels! He takes me for the hunchbacked skipper of some coasting vessel. Send down my main-top-sail yard! Ho, you gluepots! Loftiest trucks were made for wildest winds, and this brain-truck of mine now sails amid the cloud-scud. Shall I strike that? Oh, none but cowards send down their brain-trucks in tempest time. What a hooroosh aloft there! I would even take it for sublime, did I not know that the colic is a noisy malady. Oh, take medicine, take medicine!"

chapters.title: Chapter 121 — Midnight.—The Forecastle Bulwarks
paragraphs: Stubb and Flask mounted on them, and passing additional lashings over the anchors hanging there.

"No, Stubb; you may pound that knot there as much as you please, but you will never pound into me what you were just now saying. And how long ago is it since you said the very contrary? Didn't you once say that whatever ship Ahab sails in, that ship should pay something extra on its insurance policy, just as though it were loaded with powder barrels aft and boxes of lucifer matches forward? Stop, now; didn't you say so?"

"Well, suppose I did? What then? I've partly changed my flesh since that time; why not my mind? Besides, supposing we really are loaded with powder barrels aft and lucifer matches forward — how the devil could the matches catch fire in this drenching spray here? Why, my little man, you have pretty red hair, but you couldn't catch fire now. Shake yourself; you're Aquarius, the Water-bearer, Flask; a man might fill pitchers at your coat collar. Don't you see, then, that for these extra risks the Marine Insurance companies have extra guarantees? Here are hydrants, Flask. But listen again, and I'll answer you the other thing. First take your leg off the crown of the anchor here, though, so I can pass the rope; now listen. What's the mighty difference between holding a mast's lightning-rod in the storm and standing close by a mast that hasn't got any lightning-rod at all in a storm? Don't you see, you timber-head, that no harm can come to the holder of the rod unless the mast is struck first? What are you talking about, then? Not one ship in a hundred carries rods, and Ahab — yes, man, and all of us — were in no more danger then, in my poor opinion, than all the crews in ten thousand ships now sailing the seas. Why, you King-Post, you, I suppose you would have every man in the world go about with a small lightning-rod running up the corner of his hat, like a militia officer's skewered feather, and trailing behind like his sash. Why don't you be sensible, Flask? It's easy to be sensible; why don't you, then? Any man with half an eye can be sensible."
"I don't know that, Stubb. You sometimes find it rather hard."

"Yes, when a fellow's soaked through, it's hard to be sensible, that's a fact. And I'm about drenched with this spray. Never mind; catch the turn there, and pass it. Seems to me we're lashing down these anchors now as if they were never going to be used again. Tying these two anchors here, Flask, seems like tying a man's hands behind him. And what big generous hands they are, to be sure. These are your iron fists, hey? What a hold they have, too! I wonder, Flask, whether the world is anchored anywhere; if she is, she swings on an uncommonly long cable, though. There, hammer that knot down, and we're done. So; next to touching land, landing on deck is the most satisfying. I say, just wring out my jacket skirts, will you? Thank you. They laugh at long-togs so, Flask; but it seems to me a long-tailed coat ought always to be worn in all storms afloat. The tails, tapering down that way, serve to carry off the water, d'you see. Same with cocked hats; the cocks form gable-end eave-troughs, Flask. No more monkey-jackets and tarpaulins for me; I must put on a swallow-tail and jam down a beaver hat; so. Hallo! Whew! There goes my tarpaulin overboard; Lord, Lord, that the winds that come from heaven should be so unmannerly! This is a nasty night, lad."

chapters.title: Chapter 122 — Midnight Aloft.—Thunder and Lightning
paragraphs: The main-top-sail yard. Tashtego passing new lashings around it.
"Um, um, um. Stop that thunder! Plenty too much thunder up here. What's the use of thunder? Um, um, um. We don't want thunder; we want rum; give us a glass of rum. Um, um, um!"

chapters.title: Chapter 123 — The Musket
paragraphs: During the most violent shocks of the Typhoon, the man at the Pequod's jawbone tiller had several times been flung reeling to the deck by its spasmodic motions, even though preventer tackles had been attached to it — for they were slack — because some play in the tiller was indispensable.

In a severe gale like this, while the ship is only a shuttlecock tossed by the blast, it is by no means uncommon to see the needles in the compasses, at intervals, go round and round. It was so with the Pequod's; at almost every shock the helmsman had not failed to notice the whirling speed with which they spun round on the cards; it is a sight that hardly anyone can watch without some sort of unaccustomed emotion.

Some hours after midnight, the Typhoon abated so much that through the strenuous efforts of Starbuck and Stubb — one engaged forward and the other aft — the shattered remnants of the jib and fore and main-topsails were cut adrift from the spars, and went whirling away to leeward like the feathers of an albatross, which are sometimes cast to the winds when that storm-tossed bird is on the wing.

The three corresponding new sails were now bent and reefed, and a storm-trysail was set farther aft, so that the ship soon went through the water with some precision again; and the course — for the present, east-southeast — which he was to steer, if practicable, was once more given to the helmsman. For during the violence of the gale he had steered only according to its shifts. But as he was now bringing the ship as near her course as possible, watching the compass meanwhile — look! a good sign! — the wind seemed to be coming round astern; yes, the foul breeze had turned fair!

Instantly the yards were squared, to the lively song of "Ho! the fair wind! oh-ye-ho, cheerly men!" — the crew singing for joy that so promising an event should so soon have proven false the evil omens preceding it.

In compliance with the standing order of his commander — to report immediately, at any of the twenty-four hours, any decided change in the affairs of the deck — Starbuck had no sooner trimmed the yards to the breeze, however reluctantly and gloomily, than he mechanically went below to inform Captain Ahab of the circumstance.

Before knocking at his stateroom, he involuntarily paused in front of it for a moment. The cabin lamp — taking long swings this way and that — was burning fitfully, and casting fitful shadows on the old man's bolted door, a thin one, with fixed blinds set in it in place of upper panels. The isolated, underground seclusion of the cabin made a certain humming silence reign there, though it was hooped round by all the roar of the elements. The loaded muskets in the rack were shiningly revealed, standing upright against the forward bulkhead. Starbuck was an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck's heart, at the instant he saw the muskets, there strangely arose an evil thought — but so blended with its neutral or good accompaniments that for the moment he hardly recognized it for what it was.

"He would have shot me once," he murmured. "Yes, there's the very musket he pointed at me — that one with the studded stock. Let me touch it — lift it. Strange, that I, who have handled so many deadly lances, strange that I should shake so now. Loaded? I must see. Yes, yes; and powder in the pan — that's not good. Better spill it? Wait. I'll cure myself of this. I'll hold the musket boldly while I think. I come to report a fair wind to him. But fair how? Fair for death and doom — that's fair for Moby Dick. It's a fair wind that's only fair for that accursed fish. The very barrel he pointed at me! — the very one; this one — I hold it here; he would have killed me with the very thing I'm handling now. Yes, and he would gladly kill all his crew. Doesn't he say he will not strike his spars to any gale? Hasn't he smashed his heavenly quadrant? And in these same dangerous seas, doesn't he grope his way by mere dead reckoning of the error-ridden log? And in this very Typhoon, didn't he swear that he would have no lightning-rods? But shall this crazed old man be meekly allowed to drag a whole ship's company down to doom with him? Yes, it would make him the willful murderer of thirty men and more, if this ship comes to any deadly harm; and my soul swears this ship will come to deadly harm if Ahab has his way. If, then, he were this instant — put aside, that crime would not be his. Ha! Is he muttering in his sleep? Yes, just there — in there, he's sleeping. Sleeping? Yes, but still alive, and soon awake again. I can't stand against you, then, old man. Not reasoning, not protest, not pleading will you listen to; you scorn all this. Flat obedience to your own flat commands — that is all you breathe. Yes, and you say the men have vowed your vow; you say all of us are Ahabs. Great God forbid! But is there no other way? No lawful way? Make him a prisoner to be taken home? What! Hope to wrest this old man's living power from his own living hands? Only a fool would try it. Say he were even tied hand and foot; knotted all over with ropes and hawsers; chained down to ring-bolts on this cabin floor; he would be more hideous than a caged tiger then. I could not endure the sight; could not possibly escape his howlings; all comfort, sleep itself, priceless reason would leave me on the long, intolerable voyage. What, then, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked-up Japan the nearest. I stand alone here on an open sea, with two oceans and a whole continent between me and the law. Yes, yes, that's how it is. Is heaven a murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed, burning sheets and skin together like tinder? And would I be a murderer, then, if —" and slowly, stealthily, half looking sideways, he placed the loaded musket's end against the door.

"On this level, Ahab's hammock swings inside; his head this way. A touch, and Starbuck may survive to hug his wife and child again. Oh Mary! Mary! — boy! boy! boy! But if I don't wake you to death, old man, who can tell to what unsounded depths Starbuck's body may sink a week from today, with all the crew! Great God, where are You? Shall I? Shall I? — The wind has gone down and shifted, sir; the fore and main topsails are reefed and set; she heads her course."
"Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch your heart at last!"
Such were the sounds that now came hurtling from out the old man's tormented sleep, as if Starbuck's voice had caused the long dumb dream to speak.
The still-leveled musket shook like a drunkard's arm against the panel; Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; but turning from the door, he placed the death-tube in its rack, and left the place.
"He's too sound asleep, Mr. Stubb; go down, and wake him, and tell him. I must see to the deck here. You know what to say."

chapters.title: Chapter 124 — The Needle
paragraphs: Next morning the not-yet-subsided sea rolled in long, slow billows of mighty bulk, and, striving in the Pequod's gurgling track, pushed her on like giants' palms outspread. The strong, unstaggering breeze blew in such abundance that sky and air seemed vast outbellying sails; the whole world boomed before the wind. Muffled in the full morning light, the invisible sun could be known only by the spread intensity of his place, where his bayonet rays moved on in stacks. Emblazonings, as of crowned Babylonian kings and queens, reigned over everything. The sea was like a crucible of molten gold, bubbling and leaping with light and heat.

Long maintaining an enchanted silence, Ahab stood apart; and every time the pitching ship lowered her bowsprit, he turned to eye the bright sun's rays ahead; and when she profoundly settled by the stern, he turned behind and saw the sun's rearward place, and how the same yellow rays were blending with his undeviating wake.

"Ha, ha, my ship! You might well be taken now for the sea-chariot of the sun. Ho, ho! All you nations before my prow, I bring the sun to you! Yoke on the further billows; hallo! A tandem, I drive the sea!"
But suddenly reined back by some counter thought, he hurried toward the helm, huskily demanding how the ship was heading.
"East-southeast, sir," said the frightened steersman.
"You lie!" striking him with his clenched fist. "Heading east at this hour in the morning, and the sun astern?"
Upon this every soul was confounded; for the phenomenon just then observed by Ahab had unaccountably escaped everyone else; but its very blinding obviousness must have been the cause.

Thrusting his head halfway into the binnacle, Ahab caught one glimpse of the compasses; his uplifted arm slowly fell; for a moment he almost seemed to stagger. Standing behind him, Starbuck looked, and lo! The two compasses pointed east, and the Pequod was just as unerringly going west.

But before the first wild alarm could get out abroad among the crew, the old man with a rigid laugh exclaimed: "I have it! It has happened before. Mr. Starbuck, last night's thunder turned our compasses — that's all. You have before now heard of such a thing, I take it."
"Aye; but never before has it happened to me, sir," said the pale mate, gloomily.

Here it must be said that accidents like this have occurred in more than one case to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner's needle, is, as everyone knows, essentially one with the electricity seen in the heavens; so it is not much to be wondered at that such things should happen. In instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, so as to knock down some of the spars and rigging, the effect on the needle has at times been still more fatal: all its loadstone power has been destroyed, so that the formerly magnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife's knitting needle. But in either case, the needle never again recovers by itself the original power thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses are affected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship, even if the lowest one were set into the kelson, the timber running along the keel inside the hold.

Deliberately standing before the binnacle, and eyeing the reversed compasses, the old man, with the sharp of his extended hand, now took the precise bearing of the sun, and satisfied that the needles were exactly inverted, shouted out his orders for the ship's course to be changed accordingly. The yards were put hard up, and once more the Pequod thrust her undaunted bows into the opposing wind, for the supposed fair one had only been tricking her.

Meanwhile, whatever his own secret thoughts were, Starbuck said nothing, but quietly issued all the necessary orders; while Stubb and Flask — who in some small degree seemed then to be sharing his feelings — likewise went along without a murmur. As for the men, though some of them rumbled low, their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate. But as ever before, the pagan harpooners remained almost wholly unimpressed; or if impressed, it was only with a certain magnetism shot into their kindred hearts from inflexible Ahab's.
For a space the old man walked the deck in rolling reveries. But chancing to slip with his ivory heel, he saw the crushed copper sight-tubes of the quadrant he had the day before dashed to the deck.

"You poor, proud heaven-gazer and sun's pilot! Yesterday I wrecked you, and today the compasses would gladly have wrecked me. So, so. But Ahab is lord over the level loadstone yet. Mr. Starbuck — a lance without a pole; a top-maul, and the smallest of the sail-maker's needles. Quick!"

Contributing, perhaps, to the impulse behind what he was now about to do were certain prudent motives, whose object might have been to revive the spirits of his crew by a stroke of his subtle skill, in a matter so wondrous as that of the inverted compasses. Besides, the old man well knew that to steer by reversed needles, though clumsily workable, was not a thing superstitious sailors would let pass without some shuddering and forebodings of evil.

"Men," said he, steadily turning upon the crew, as the mate handed him the things he had demanded, "my men, the thunder turned old Ahab's needles; but out of this bit of steel Ahab can make one of his own, that will point as true as any."
Abashed glances of servile wonder were exchanged by the sailors, as this was said; and with fascinated eyes they awaited whatever magic might follow. But Starbuck looked away.

With a blow from the top-maul Ahab knocked off the steel head of the lance, and then, handing the mate the long iron rod that remained, told him to hold it upright without letting it touch the deck. Then, after repeatedly striking the upper end of this iron rod with the maul, he placed the blunted needle endwise on top of it and hammered that, less strongly, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then, going through some small strange motions with it — whether necessary to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely meant to increase the awe of the crew, is uncertain — he called for linen thread; and moving to the binnacle, he slipped out the two reversed needles there and hung the sail-needle horizontally by its middle over one of the compass-cards. At first the steel went round and round, quivering and vibrating at either end; but at last it settled into its place, and Ahab, who had been intently watching for this result, stepped openly back from the binnacle and, pointing his outstretched arm toward it, exclaimed: "Look for yourselves, and see if Ahab is not lord of the level loadstone! The sun is east, and that compass swears it!"
One after another they peered in, for nothing but their own eyes could persuade such ignorance as theirs, and one after another they slunk away.
In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.

chapters.title: Chapter 125 — The Log and Line
paragraphs: Though the fated Pequod had now been afloat so long on this voyage, the log and line — a wooden float paid out astern from a reel on a line, to measure the ship's speed — had very seldom been used. Owing to a confident reliance on other means of determining the vessel's position, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and often more for form's sake than anything else, they regularly put down on the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progress every hour. It had been so with the Pequod. The wooden reel and the angular log attached to it hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rain and spray had dampened it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But, heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab as he happened to glance at the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene; and he remembered that his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing with a plunging motion; astern, the billows rolled in riots.
"Forward, there! Heave the log!"
Two seamen came. The golden-hued Tahitian and the grizzly Manxman. "Take the reel, one of you; I'll heave."
They went toward the extreme stern, on the ship's lee side, where the deck, with the oblique energy of the wind, was now almost dipping into the creamy, sidelong-rushing sea.

The Manxman took the reel, and holding it high up by the projecting handle-ends of the spindle, round which the spool of line revolved, so stood with the angular log hanging downward, till Ahab advanced to him.

Ahab stood before him and was lightly unwinding some thirty or forty turns to form a preliminary hand-coil to toss overboard, when the old Manxman, who was intently eyeing both him and the line, made bold to speak.
"Sir, I mistrust it; this line looks far gone. Long heat and wet have spoiled it."
"It will hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet — have they spoiled you? You seem to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds you; not you it."
"I hold the spool, sir. But just as my captain says. With these gray hairs of mine, it's not worth while disputing, especially with a superior who'll never confess."
"What's that? There now's a patched professor in Queen Nature's granite-founded College; but I think he's too subservient. Where were you born?"
"In the little rocky Isle of Man, sir."
"Excellent! You've hit the world by that."
"I don't know, sir, but I was born there."

"In the Isle of Man, hey? Well, the other way, it's good. Here's a man from Man; a man born in once independent Man, and now unmanned of Man; which is sucked in — by what? Up with the reel! The dead, blind wall butts all inquiring heads at last. Up with it! So."
