The log was heaved. The loose coils rapidly straightened out in a long dragging line astern, and then instantly the reel began to whirl. In turn, jerkingly raised and lowered by the rolling waves, the towing resistance of the log caused the old reelman to stagger strangely.
"Hold hard!"
Snap! The overstrained line sagged down in one long loop; the tugging log was gone.

"I crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad sea parts the log-line. But Ahab can mend all. Haul in here, Tahitian; reel up, Manxman. And look, let the carpenter make another log, and mend the line. See to it."

"There he goes now; to him nothing's happened; but to me the skewer seems loosening out of the middle of the world. Haul in, haul in, Tahitian! These lines run whole and whirling out: come in broken, and dragging slow. Ha, Pip? Come to help; eh, Pip?"

"Pip? Who are you calling Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip's missing. Let's see now if you haven't fished him up here, fisherman. It drags hard; I guess he's holding on. Jerk him, Tahiti! Jerk him off; we haul in no cowards here. Ho! There's his arm just breaking water. A hatchet! A hatchet! Cut it off — we haul in no cowards here. Captain Ahab! Sir, sir! Here's Pip, trying to get on board again."
"Peace, you crazy loon," cried the Manxman, seizing him by the arm. "Away from the quarter-deck!"
"The greater idiot always scolds the lesser," muttered Ahab, advancing. "Hands off that holiness! Where did you say Pip was, boy?"
"Astern there, sir, astern! Look! Look!"
"And who are you, boy? I don't see my reflection in the vacant pupils of your eyes. Oh God! That man should be a thing for immortal souls to sieve through! Who are you, boy?"

"Bell-boy, sir; ship's crier; ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high — looks cowardly — quickest known by that! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip the coward?"

"There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, you frozen heavens! Look down here. You begot this luckless child, and have abandoned him, you creative libertines. Here, boy; Ahab's cabin shall be Pip's home henceforth, while Ahab lives. You touch my inmost center, boy; you are tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let's go down."

"What's this? Here's velvet shark-skin," intently gazing at Ahab's hand, and feeling it. "Ah, now, had poor Pip but felt so kind a thing as this, perhaps he would never have been lost! This seems to me, sir, like a man-rope; something that weak souls may hold by. Oh, sir, let old Perth now come and rivet these two hands together; the black one with the white, for I will not let this go."

"Oh, boy, nor will I let go of you, unless by holding on I should drag you to worse horrors than are here. Come, then, to my cabin. Look, you believers in gods all goodness and in man all ill — look, you! See the omniscient gods oblivious of suffering man; and man, though idiotic and not knowing what he does, yet full of the sweet things of love and gratitude. Come! I feel prouder leading you by your black hand than if I grasped an Emperor's!"

"There go two daft ones now," muttered the old Manxman. "One daft with strength, the other daft with weakness. But here's the end of the rotten line — all dripping, too. Mend it, eh? I think we had best have a new line altogether. I'll see Mr. Stubb about it."

chapters.title: Chapter 126 — The Life-Buoy
paragraphs: Steering now southeastward by Ahab's leveled steel, and with her progress determined solely by Ahab's level log and line, the Pequod held on her path toward the Equator. Making so long a passage through such unfrequented waters, sighting no ships, and before long pushed sideways by unvarying trade winds over monotonously mild waves — all these seemed the strange calm things that come before some riotous and desperate scene.

At last, when the ship drew near to the outskirts, as it were, of the Equatorial fishing-ground, and in the deep darkness that goes before the dawn was sailing by a cluster of rocky islets, the watch — then headed by Flask — was startled by a cry so plaintively wild and unearthly — like half-articulated wailings of the ghosts of all Herod's murdered Innocents — that one and all, they started from their reveries, and for the space of some moments stood, or sat, or leaned all transfixedly listening, like the carved Roman slave, while that wild cry remained within hearing. The Christian or civilized part of the crew said it was mermaids, and shuddered; but the pagan harpooners remained unappalled. Yet the gray Manxman — the oldest mariner of all — declared that the wild thrilling sounds that were heard were the voices of newly drowned men in the sea.

Below in his hammock, Ahab did not hear of this till gray dawn, when he came to the deck; it was then recounted to him by Flask, not without hinted dark meanings. He hollowly laughed, and thus explained the wonder.

Those rocky islands the ship had passed were the resort of great numbers of seals, and some young seals that had lost their dams, or some dams that had lost their cubs, must have risen near the ship and kept company with her, crying and sobbing with their human sort of wail. But this only the more affected some of them, because most mariners cherish a very superstitious feeling about seals, arising not only from their peculiar tones when in distress, but also from the human look of their round heads and semi-intelligent faces, seen peeringly uprising from the water alongside. In the sea, under certain circumstances, seals have more than once been mistaken for men.

But the crew's forebodings were destined to receive a most plausible confirmation in the fate of one of their number that morning. At sunrise this man went from his hammock to his masthead at the fore; and whether it was that he was not yet half awake (for sailors sometimes go aloft in a transition state) — whether it was so with the man, there is now no telling; but, be that as it may, he had not been long at his perch when a cry was heard — a cry and a rushing — and looking up, they saw a falling phantom in the air; and looking down, a little tossed heap of white bubbles in the blue of the sea.

The life-buoy — a long slender cask — was dropped from the stern, where it always hung obedient to a cunning spring; but no hand rose to seize it, and the sun had beaten on this cask so long that it had shrunk, so that it slowly filled, and the parched wood also filled at every pore; and the studded, iron-bound cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if to give him his pillow, though in truth only a hard one.

And thus the first man of the Pequod that mounted the mast to look out for the White Whale, on the White Whale's own peculiar ground — that man was swallowed up in the deep. But few, perhaps, thought of that at the time. Indeed, in some sort, they were not grieved at this event, at least as a portent; for they regarded it, not as a foreshadowing of evil in the future, but as the fulfillment of an evil already presaged. They declared that now they knew the reason of those wild shrieks they had heard the night before. But again the old Manxman said no.

The lost life-buoy was now to be replaced; Starbuck was directed to see to it; but as no cask of sufficient lightness could be found, and as in the feverish eagerness of what seemed the approaching crisis of the voyage all hands were impatient of any toil but what was directly connected with its final end, whatever that might prove to be, they were going to leave the ship's stern without a buoy, when by certain strange signs and innuendoes Queequeg hinted a hint concerning his coffin.
"A life-buoy of a coffin!" cried Starbuck, starting.
"Rather queer, that, I should say," said Stubb.
"It will make a good enough one," said Flask. "The carpenter here can arrange it easily."
"Bring it up; there's nothing else for it," said Starbuck, after a melancholy pause. "Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so — the coffin, I mean. Do you hear me? Rig it."
"And shall I nail down the lid, sir?" moving his hand as with a hammer.
"Aye."
"And shall I caulk the seams, sir?" moving his hand as with a caulking-iron.
"Aye."
"And shall I then pay over the same with pitch, sir?" moving his hand as with a pitch-pot.
"Away! What possesses you? Make a life-buoy of the coffin, and no more. Mr. Stubb, Mr. Flask, come forward with me."

"He goes off in a huff. The whole he can endure; at the parts he balks. Now I don't like this. I make a leg for Captain Ahab, and he wears it like a gentleman; but I make a bandbox for Queequeg, and he won't put his head into it. Are all my pains to go for nothing with that coffin? And now I'm ordered to make a life-buoy of it. It's like turning an old coat; going to bring the flesh on the other side now. I don't like this cobbling sort of business — I don't like it at all; it's undignified; it's not my place. Let tinkers' brats do tinkerings; we are their betters. I like to take in hand none but clean, virgin, fair-and-square mathematical jobs, something that regularly begins at the beginning, and is at the middle when midway, and comes to an end at the conclusion; not a cobbler's job, that's at an end in the middle, and at the beginning at the end. It's the old woman's tricks to be giving cobbling jobs. Lord! what an affection all old women have for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who ran away with a bald-headed young tinker once. And that's the reason I never would work for lonely widow old women ashore, when I kept my job-shop in the Vineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run off with me. But heigh-ho! there are no caps at sea but snow-caps. Let me see. Nail down the lid; caulk the seams; pay over the same with pitch; batten them down tight, and hang it with the snap-spring over the ship's stern. Were ever such things done before with a coffin? Some superstitious old carpenters, now, would be tied up in the rigging before they would do the job. But I'm made of knotty Aroostook hemlock; I don't budge. Cruppered with a coffin! Sailing about with a grave-yard tray! But never mind. We workers in woods make bridal-bedsteads and card-tables, as well as coffins and hearses. We work by the month, or by the job, or by the profit; not for us to ask the why and wherefore of our work, unless it be too confounded cobbling, and then we stash it if we can. Hem! I'll do the job, now, tenderly. I'll have me — let's see — how many in the ship's company, all told? But I've forgotten. Anyway, I'll have me thirty separate, Turk's-headed life-lines, each three feet long, hanging all round to the coffin. Then, if the hull goes down, there'll be thirty lively fellows all fighting for one coffin, a sight not seen very often beneath the sun! Come hammer, caulking-iron, pitch-pot, and marling-spike! Let's get to it."

chapters.title: Chapter 127 — The Deck
paragraphs: The coffin laid upon two line-tubs, between the vice-bench and the open hatchway; the Carpenter caulking its seams; the string of twisted oakum slowly unwinding from a large roll of it placed in the bosom of his frock. Ahab comes slowly from the cabin-gangway, and hears Pip following him.
"Back, lad; I'll be with you again soon. He goes! This hand of mine does not do my bidding more kindly than that boy does. — Middle aisle of a church! What's here?"
"Life-buoy, sir. Mr. Starbuck's orders. Oh, look, sir! Beware the hatchway!"
"Thank you, man. Your coffin lies handy to the vault."
"Sir? The hatchway? Oh! So it does, sir, so it does."
"Aren't you the leg-maker? Look, didn't this stump come from your shop?"
"I believe it did, sir; does the ferrule stand, sir?"
"Well enough. But aren't you also the undertaker?"
"Aye, sir; I patched up this thing here as a coffin for Queequeg; but they've set me now to turning it into something else."

"Then tell me: aren't you an arrant, all-grasping, intermeddling, monopolizing, heathenish old scamp, to be one day making legs, and the next day coffins to clap them in, and yet again life-buoys out of those same coffins? You are as unprincipled as the gods, and as much of a jack-of-all-trades."
"But I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do."

"The gods again. Listen, don't you ever sing while working on a coffin? The Titans, they say, hummed snatches of song when chipping out the craters for volcanoes; and the grave-digger in the play sings, spade in hand. Don't you ever?"

"Sing, sir? Do I sing? Oh, I'm indifferent enough, sir, for that; but the reason why the grave-digger made music must have been because there was none in his spade, sir. But the caulking mallet is full of it. Listen to it."

"Aye, and that's because the lid there is a sounding-board; and what makes the sounding-board in all things is this — there's nothing beneath. And yet a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same, carpenter. Have you ever helped carry a bier, and heard the coffin knock against the churchyard gate, going in?"
"Faith, sir, I've —"
"Faith? What's that?"
"Why, faith, sir, it's only a sort of exclamation-like — that's all, sir."
"Um, um; go on."
"I was about to say, sir, that —"
"Are you a silk-worm? Do you spin your own shroud out of yourself? Look at your bosom! Be quick! and get these traps out of sight."

"He goes aft. That was sudden, now; but squalls come sudden in hot latitudes. I've heard that the Isle of Albemarle, one of the Gallipagos, is cut by the Equator right in the middle. Seems to me some sort of Equator cuts that old man, too, right in his middle. He's always under the Line — fiery hot, I tell you! He's looking this way — come, oakum; quick. Here we go again. This wooden mallet is the cork, and I'm the professor of musical glasses — tap, tap!"
(Ahab to himself.)

"There's a sight! There's a sound! The gray-headed woodpecker tapping the hollow tree! Blind and dumb might well be envied now. See! that thing rests on two line-tubs, full of tow-lines. A most malicious wag, that fellow. Rat-tat! So man's seconds tick! Oh, how immaterial are all materials! What things real are there, but imponderable thoughts? Here now's the very dreaded symbol of grim death, by mere chance, made the expressive sign of the help and hope of most endangered life. A life-buoy of a coffin! Does it go further? Can it be that in some spiritual sense the coffin is, after all, but an immortality-preserver! I'll think of that. But no. So far gone am I in the dark side of earth, that its other side, the theoretic bright one, seems but uncertain twilight to me. Will you never be done, carpenter, with that accursed sound? I go below; don't let me see that thing here when I return again. Now, then, Pip, we'll talk this over; I do suck most wondrous philosophies from you! Some unknown conduits from the unknown worlds must empty into you!"

chapters.title: Chapter 128 — The Pequod Meets The Rachel
paragraphs: Next day, a large ship, the Rachel, was sighted bearing straight down on the Pequod, all her spars thickly clustered with men. At the time the Pequod was making good speed through the water; but as the broad-winged stranger shot close to her from windward, her boastful sails all fell slack together like empty bladders that have burst, and all life fled from the stricken hull.
"Bad news; she brings bad news," muttered the old Manxman. But before her commander, who stood up in his boat with his trumpet to his mouth — before he could hail hopefully, Ahab's voice was heard.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Aye, yesterday. Have you seen a whale-boat adrift?"

Throttling his joy, Ahab answered no to this unexpected question, and would then gladly have boarded the stranger, when the stranger's captain himself, having stopped his vessel, was seen climbing down her side. A few sharp pulls at the oars, and his boat-hook soon gripped the Pequod's main-chains, and he sprang onto the deck. Ahab immediately recognized him as a Nantucketer he knew. But no formal greeting was exchanged.
"Where was he? — not killed! — not killed!" cried Ahab, pressing close to him. "How did it happen?"

It seemed that rather late on the previous afternoon, three of the stranger's boats had been engaged with a shoal of whales that had led them some four or five miles from the ship; and while they were still in swift chase to windward, the white hump and head of Moby Dick had suddenly loomed up out of the water, not very far to leeward. At that, the fourth rigged boat — a reserve one — had been instantly lowered to give chase. After a keen sail before the wind, this fourth boat — the swiftest-keeled of all — seemed to have succeeded in fastening to him; at least, as far as the man at the mast-head could tell anything about it. In the distance he saw the boat shrunk to a dot; then a swift gleam of bubbling white water; and after that, nothing more. From this it was concluded that the stricken whale must have run away with his pursuers for some indefinite distance, as often happens. There was some apprehension, but as yet no real alarm. The recall signals were hoisted in the rigging; darkness came on; and since the ship had to pick up her three boats far to windward before going in search of the fourth in exactly the opposite direction, she had not only been forced to leave that boat to its fate until nearly midnight, but for the time being to increase her distance from it. But once the rest of her crew were at last safe aboard, she crowded on all sail — studding-sail on studding-sail — after the missing boat, lighting a fire in her try-pots as a beacon, with every other man aloft on the lookout. But though she then sailed far enough to reach the presumed spot where the missing men were last seen; though she then stopped to lower her spare boats to row all around her; and, finding nothing, had dashed on again, stopped again, and lowered her boats again; and though she had kept doing this until daylight — still not the least glimpse of the missing keel had been seen.

Having told the story, the stranger captain at once went on to reveal why he had boarded the Pequod. He wanted her to join his own ship in the search, the two of them sailing over the sea some four or five miles apart, on parallel lines, and so sweeping a double horizon, as it were.

"I will wager something now," whispered Stubb to Flask, "that someone in that missing boat went off wearing that captain's best coat; maybe his watch — he's so cursed anxious to get it back. Who ever heard of two pious whale-ships cruising after one missing whale-boat in the height of the whaling season? See, Flask, only see how pale he looks — pale in the very buttons of his eyes — look — it wasn't the coat — it must have been the —"

"My boy, my own boy is among them. For God's sake — I beg you, I implore you" — so the stranger captain now cried out to Ahab, who until then had received his plea with nothing but ice. "Let me charter your ship for forty-eight hours — I will gladly pay for it, and pay handsomely — if there is no other way — for forty-eight hours only — only that — you must, oh, you must, and you shall do this thing."
"His son!" cried Stubb, "oh, it's his son he's lost! I take back the coat and watch — what does Ahab say? We must save that boy."
"He's drowned with the rest of them, last night," said the old Manx sailor standing behind them. "I heard; all of you heard their spirits."

Now, as it soon turned out, what made this incident of the Rachel's all the more melancholy was that not only was one of the captain's sons among the missing boat's crew, but among the crews of the other boats — which had at the same time been separated from the ship in the other direction during the dark confusion of the chase — there had been yet another son. So for a time the wretched father was plunged to the very bottom of the cruelest perplexity, which was only resolved for him when his chief mate instinctively adopted a whale-ship's ordinary procedure in such emergencies: when caught between endangered but divided boats, always pick up the majority first. But the captain, for some unknown reason of temperament, had refrained from mentioning all this, and not until Ahab's iciness forced him to it did he speak of his one still-missing boy — a little lad, only twelve years old, whose father, with the earnest but untroubled boldness of a Nantucketer's paternal love, had sought this early to initiate him into the perils and wonders of a calling that had been, almost from time immemorial, the destiny of all his race. Nor is it uncommon for Nantucket captains to send a son of such tender age away from them, on a long three or four years' voyage in some ship other than their own, so that the boy's first knowledge of a whaleman's career will not be weakened by any chance display of a father's natural but ill-timed favoritism, or undue anxiety and concern.
Meanwhile the stranger was still begging his poor favor of Ahab; and Ahab still stood like an anvil, taking every blow without the least quiver of his own.

"I will not go," said the stranger, "until you say yes to me. Do to me as you would have me do to you in the same case. For you, too, have a boy, Captain Ahab — though only a child, and nestling safely at home now — a child of your old age, too. Yes, yes, you relent; I see it — run, run, men, now, and stand by to square in the yards."

"Avast," cried Ahab — "don't touch a rope-yarn"; then, in a voice that drew out and shaped every word — "Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I am losing time. Good-bye, good-bye. God bless you, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go. Mr. Starbuck, look at the binnacle watch, and three minutes from this very instant warn off all strangers; then brace forward again, and let the ship sail as before."

Turning hurriedly, with his face averted, he went down into his cabin, leaving the stranger captain transfixed at this unconditional and utter rejection of so earnest a plea. But starting out of his trance, Gardiner silently hurried to the side, more fell than stepped into his boat, and returned to his ship.

Soon the two ships' wakes parted; and as long as the strange vessel stayed in view, she was seen to yaw this way and that toward every dark spot on the sea, however small. This way and that her yards were swung round; to starboard and to larboard she kept tacking; now she beat against a head sea, and now it pushed her before it; while all the while her masts and yards were thickly clustered with men, like three tall cherry trees when the boys are up among the boughs picking cherries.

But by her still halting course and winding, woeful way, you plainly saw that this ship that so wept with spray still remained without comfort. She was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.

chapters.title: Chapter 129 — The Cabin
paragraphs: (Ahab moving to go on deck; Pip catches him by the hand to follow.)

"Lad, lad, I tell you that you must not follow Ahab now. The hour is coming when Ahab would not scare you from him, yet would not have you by him. There is something in you, poor lad, that I feel is too much of a cure for my malady. Like cures like; and for this hunt, my malady becomes my most desired health. Stay down here, where they will serve you as if you were the captain. Aye, lad, you shall sit here in my own screwed chair; you must be another screw to it."
"No, no, no! You don't have a whole body, sir; just use poor me for your one lost leg; only tread on me, sir; I ask no more, so long as I remain a part of you."
"Oh! in spite of a million villains, this makes me a bigot in the fadeless fidelity of man! — and a black! and crazy! — but I think like-cures-like applies to him too; he grows so sane again."

"They tell me, sir, that Stubb once deserted poor little Pip, whose drowned bones now show white, for all the blackness of his living skin. But I will never desert you, sir, as Stubb did him. Sir, I must go with you."
"If you talk to me like this much more, Ahab's purpose will turn keel-up in him. I tell you no; it cannot be."
"Oh good master, master, master!"

"Weep like that, and I will murder you! Take care, for Ahab too is mad. Listen, and you will often hear my ivory foot upon the deck, and still know that I am there. And now I leave you. Your hand! — Met! You are as true, lad, as the circumference to its center. So: God forever bless you; and if it comes to that — God forever save you, come what may."
(Ahab goes; Pip steps one step forward.)

"He stood here this very instant; I stand in his air — but I'm alone. Now if even poor Pip were here I could endure it, but he's missing. Pip! Pip! Ding, dong, ding! Who's seen Pip? He must be up here; let's try the door. What? Neither lock, nor bolt, nor bar; and yet there's no opening it. It must be the spell; he told me to stay here. Yes, and told me this screwed chair was mine. Here, then, I'll sit myself down, against the transom, in the ship's full middle, all her keel and her three masts before me. Here, our old sailors say, in their black seventy-fours (warships of seventy-four guns) great admirals sometimes sit at table and lord it over rows of captains and lieutenants. Ha! What's this? Epaulets! epaulets! The epaulets all come crowding! Pass round the decanters; glad to see you; fill up, monsieurs! What an odd feeling, now, when a black boy's host to white men with gold lace on their coats! — Monsieurs, have you seen one Pip? — a little negro lad, five feet high, hang-dog look, and cowardly! Jumped from a whale-boat once — seen him? No! Well then, fill up again, captains, and let's drink shame upon all cowards! I name no names. Shame upon them! Put one foot upon the table. Shame upon all cowards. — Hush! Up there, I hear ivory — Oh, master! master! I am down-hearted indeed when you walk over me. But here I'll stay, though this stern strikes rocks, and they bulge through, and oysters come to join me."

chapters.title: Chapter 130 — The Hat
paragraphs: And now that, at the proper time and place, after so long and wide a preliminary cruise, Ahab — all other whaling waters swept — seemed to have chased his foe into a fold of the ocean, to slay him there the more securely; now that he found himself close to the very latitude and longitude where his tormenting wound had been inflicted; now that a vessel had been hailed which, only the day before, had actually encountered Moby Dick; and now that all his successive meetings with various ships had, in their contrasting ways, combined to show the demonic indifference with which the white whale tore his hunters, whether sinning or sinned against — now there lurked something in the old man's eyes that feeble souls could hardly bear to see. Like the never-setting polar star, which through the long, six-month arctic night keeps up its piercing, steady, central gaze, Ahab's purpose now gleamed fixedly down upon the constant midnight of the gloomy crew. It so dominated them that all their forebodings, doubts, misgivings and fears were forced to hide beneath their souls, and not sprout a single blade or leaf.

In this foreshadowing interval, too, all humor, forced or natural, vanished. Stubb no longer tried to raise a smile; Starbuck no longer tried to check one. Joy and sorrow, hope and fear alike seemed ground to the finest dust, and powdered for the time in the clamped mortar of Ahab's iron soul. Like machines, they moved dumbly about the deck, always aware that the old man's despot eye was on them.

But had you studied him closely in his more secret, private hours, when he thought no eye but one was on him, you would have seen that just as Ahab's eyes awed the crew's, the inscrutable Parsee's glance awed his — or at least, somehow, in some wild way, affected it at times. Such an added, gliding strangeness now began to surround the thin Fedallah, and such ceaseless shudderings shook him, that the men eyed him doubtfully, half uncertain, it seemed, whether he really was a mortal substance or else a tremulous shadow cast upon the deck by some unseen being's body. And that shadow was always hovering there. For not even by night had Fedallah ever been known for certain to sleep or go below. He would stand still for hours, but he never sat or leaned; his wan but wondrous eyes said plainly — We two watchmen never rest.

Nor could the sailors now step onto the deck at any time, night or day, without finding Ahab there before them — either standing in his pivot-hole, or pacing the planks exactly between two unvarying limits, the main-mast and the mizen; or else they saw him standing in the cabin-scuttle, his living foot advanced upon the deck as if to take a step, his hat slouched heavily over his eyes. So however motionless he stood, and however many days and nights were added on in which he had not swung in his hammock, still, hidden beneath that slouching hat, they could never tell for certain whether, for all this, his eyes were actually closed at times, or whether he was still intently watching them — no matter that he stood like that in the scuttle for a whole hour at a stretch, and the unheeded night-damp gathered in beads of dew on that stone-carved coat and hat. The clothes the night had wet, the next day's sunshine dried on him; and so, day after day and night after night, he no longer went below the planks; whatever he wanted from the cabin, he sent for.

He ate in the same open air — that is, his only two meals, breakfast and dinner; supper he never touched. Nor did he reap his beard, which grew darkly, all gnarled, like the unearthed roots of blown-over trees, which still grow idly on at the naked base though they have perished in the green growth above. But though his whole life had now become one watch on deck, and though the Parsee's mystic watch was as unbroken as his own, these two never seemed to speak — one man to the other — except when, at long intervals, some passing, unimportant matter made it necessary. Though such a potent spell seemed secretly to join the two, openly, and to the awe-struck crew, they seemed as far apart as the poles. If by day they happened to speak one word, by night both were dumb men, as far as the slightest exchange of words went. At times, for the longest hours, without a single hail, they stood far apart in the starlight, Ahab in his scuttle, the Parsee by the mainmast, but still gazing fixedly at each other — as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, and in Ahab the Parsee saw his abandoned substance.

And yet, somehow, Ahab — in his own proper self, as he was daily, hourly and every instant commandingly revealed to his subordinates — Ahab seemed an independent lord, and the Parsee only his slave. Then again, both seemed yoked together, with an unseen tyrant driving them: the lean shadow alongside the solid rib. For whatever this Parsee might be, all rib and keel was solid Ahab.

At the first faintest glimmering of dawn, his iron voice was heard from aft — "Man the mast-heads!" — and all through the day, until after sunset and after twilight, the same voice was heard every hour, at the striking of the helmsman's bell — "What do you see? — sharp! sharp!"

But when three or four days had slipped by since meeting the children-seeking Rachel, and still no spout had been seen, the monomaniac old man seemed to distrust his crew's loyalty — at least, that of nearly all of them except the Pagan harpooners. He even seemed to suspect that Stubb and Flask might willingly overlook the sight he was seeking. But if these suspicions really were his, he shrewdly refrained from putting them into words, however much his actions might seem to hint at them.

"I will have the first sight of the whale myself," he said. "Aye! Ahab must have the doubloon!" And with his own hands he rigged a nest of basketed bowlines; and sending a man aloft with a single-sheaved block to fasten to the main-mast head, he took the two ends of the rope rove down through it; and attaching one to his basket, he prepared a belaying pin for the other end, so as to fasten it at the rail. This done, with that end still in his hand and standing beside the pin, he looked round at his crew, sweeping from one to another, letting his glance rest long on Daggoo, Queequeg and Tashtego, but avoiding Fedallah; and then, settling his firm, trusting eye on the chief mate, he said — "Take the rope, sir — I give it into your hands, Starbuck." Then, settling himself in the basket, he gave the word for them to hoist him to his perch, Starbuck being the one who finally made the rope fast, and who afterwards stood near it. And so, with one hand clinging round the royal mast, Ahab gazed out over the sea for miles and miles — ahead, astern, this side and that — within the wide, expanded circle commanded from so great a height.

When a sailor at sea, working with his hands at some high, almost isolated spot in the rigging that happens to offer no foothold, is hoisted up to that spot and held there by the rope, the rope's fastened end on deck is always given in strict charge to one particular man, who has the special watch of it. This is because, in such a wilderness of running rigging, whose various relations aloft cannot always be told with certainty from what can be seen of them on deck, and when the deck-ends of these ropes are being cast off from their fastenings every few minutes, it would be only a natural fatality if, without a constant watchman, the hoisted sailor were cast adrift through some carelessness of the crew and fell swooping down into the sea. So Ahab's proceedings in this matter were not unusual. The only strange thing about them seemed to be that Starbuck — almost the only man who had ever ventured to oppose him with anything even slightly approaching decisiveness, and one of those, too, whose faithfulness on the lookout he had seemed somewhat to doubt — it was strange that this was the very man he should choose as his watchman, freely placing his whole life in the hands of a man he otherwise distrusted.

Now, the first time Ahab was perched aloft, before he had been there ten minutes, one of those savage red-billed sea-hawks that so often fly annoyingly close around the manned mast-heads of whalemen in these latitudes — one of these birds came wheeling and screaming round his head in a maze of untrackably swift circlings. Then it shot a thousand feet straight up into the air, then spiraled downward, and went eddying round his head again.

But with his gaze fixed on the dim and distant horizon, Ahab seemed not to notice this wild bird; nor, indeed, would anyone else have noticed it much, since it was no uncommon occurrence; only now, almost the least heedful eye seemed to see some sort of cunning meaning in almost every sight.

"Your hat, your hat, sir!" suddenly cried the Sicilian seaman, who, being posted at the mizen-masthead, stood directly behind Ahab, though somewhat lower than his level, and with a deep gulf of air dividing them.
But already the sable wing was before the old man's eyes; the long hooked bill at his head — with a scream, the black hawk darted away with his prize.

An eagle flew three times around Tarquin's head, lifting off his cap and then putting it back, and at that Tanaquil, his wife, declared that Tarquin would be king of Rome. But it was only because the cap was put back that the omen was counted good. Ahab's hat was never restored; the wild hawk flew on and on with it, far ahead of the prow, and at last disappeared; while from the point where it disappeared, a tiny black spot was dimly seen falling from that vast height into the sea.

chapters.title: Chapter 131 — The Pequod Meets The Delight
paragraphs: The intense Pequod sailed on; the rolling waves and days went by; the life-buoy coffin still swung lightly; and another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, was sighted. As she drew near, all eyes were fixed on her broad beams, called shears, which in some whaling ships cross the quarter-deck at a height of eight or nine feet, serving to carry the spare, unrigged or disabled boats.

On the stranger's shears could be seen the shattered white ribs and a few splintered planks of what had once been a whale-boat; but you could now see through this wreck as plainly as you see through the peeled, half-unhinged, bleaching skeleton of a horse.
"Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Look!" replied the hollow-cheeked captain from his taffrail; and with his trumpet he pointed to the wreck.
"Have you killed him?"
"The harpoon that will ever do that is not yet forged," answered the other, glancing sadly at a rounded hammock on the deck, whose gathered sides some silent sailors were busy sewing together.

"Not forged!" — and snatching Perth's leveled iron from the crotch, Ahab held it out, exclaiming — "Look here, Nantucketer; here in this hand I hold his death! These barbs are tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning; and I swear to temper them a third time in that hot place behind the fin, where the White Whale most feels his accursed life!"

"Then God keep you, old man — do you see that?" — pointing to the hammock — "I am burying only one of five stout men who were alive only yesterday but were dead before night. Only that one do I bury; the rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb." Then, turning to his crew — "Are you ready there? Place the plank on the rail, then, and lift the body; so, then — Oh! God" — advancing toward the hammock with uplifted hands — "may the resurrection and the life —"
"Brace forward! Up helm!" cried Ahab like lightning to his men.

But the suddenly started Pequod was not quick enough to escape the sound of the splash the corpse soon made as it struck the sea; not quick enough, indeed, to keep some of the flying bubbles from perhaps sprinkling her hull with their ghostly baptism.
As Ahab now glided from the dejected Delight, the strange life-buoy hanging at the Pequod's stern came into conspicuous relief.
"Ha! Over there! Look over there, men!" cried a foreboding voice in her wake. "In vain, oh you strangers, do you flee our sad burial; you only turn your taffrail to us to show us your coffin!"

chapters.title: Chapter 132 — The Symphony
paragraphs: It was a clear steel-blue day. The firmaments of air and sea were hardly separable in that all-pervading azure; only the pensive air was transparently pure and soft, with a woman's look, and the robust and manlike sea heaved with long, strong, lingering swells, as Samson's chest in his sleep.

Here and there, on high, glided the snow-white wings of small, unspeckled birds; these were the gentle thoughts of the feminine air. But to and fro in the deeps, far down in the bottomless blue, rushed mighty leviathans, swordfish and sharks; and these were the strong, troubled, murderous thinkings of the masculine sea.
But though the two contrasted so within, without the contrast was only in shades and shadows; those two seemed one — it was only the sex, as it were, that distinguished them.

Aloft, like a royal czar and king, the sun seemed to be giving this gentle air to this bold and rolling sea, even as bride to groom. And at the girdling line of the horizon, a soft and tremulous motion — most seen here at the equator — denoted the fond, throbbing trust, the loving alarms, with which the poor bride gave her bosom away.

Tied up and twisted; gnarled and knotted with wrinkles; haggardly firm and unyielding; his eyes glowing like coals that still glow in the ashes of ruin — untottering Ahab stood forth in the clearness of the morning, lifting his splintered helmet of a brow to the fair girl's forehead of heaven.

Oh, immortal infancy and innocence of the azure! Invisible winged creatures that frolic all around us! Sweet childhood of air and sky! How oblivious you were of old Ahab's close-coiled woe! But just so have I seen little Miriam and Martha, laughing-eyed elves, heedlessly frolicking around their old father, playing with the circle of singed locks that grew on the edge of that burnt-out crater of his brain.

Slowly crossing the deck from the scuttle, Ahab leaned over the side and watched how his shadow in the water sank and sank to his gaze, the more he strove to pierce the depths. But the lovely aromas in that enchanted air seemed at last to dispel, for a moment, the cankerous thing in his soul. That glad, happy air, that winsome sky, at last stroked and caressed him; the stepmother world, so long cruel — forbidding — now threw affectionate arms round his stubborn neck, and seemed to sob joyously over him, as if over someone whom, however willful and erring, she could still find it in her heart to save and to bless. From beneath his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop.

Starbuck saw the old man — saw how heavily he leaned over the side; and he seemed to hear in his own true heart the measureless sobbing that stole out of the center of the serenity all around. Careful not to touch him or be noticed by him, he still drew near him, and stood there.
Ahab turned.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir."

"Oh, Starbuck! It is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky. On such a day — very much such a sweetness as this — I struck my first whale — a boy-harpooner of eighteen! Forty — forty — forty years ago! — ago! Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time! Forty years on the pitiless sea! For forty years Ahab has forsaken the peaceful land, for forty years to make war on the horrors of the deep! Aye and yes, Starbuck, out of those forty years I have not spent three ashore. When I think of this life I have led — the desolation of solitude it has been; the masoned, walled town of a captain's exclusiveness, which lets in so little sympathy from the green country outside — oh, weariness! heaviness! Guinea-coast slavery of solitary command! — when I think of all this, only half-suspected, not so keenly known to me before — and how for forty years I have fed on dry salted fare, fit emblem of the dry nourishment of my soil! — while the poorest landsman has had fresh fruit to his daily hand, and broken the world's fresh bread against my moldy crusts — away, whole oceans away, from that young girl-wife I married when I was past fifty, and sailed for Cape Horn the next day, leaving only one dent in my marriage pillow — wife? wife? — rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl when I married her, Starbuck; and then the madness, the frenzy, the boiling blood and the smoking brow with which, for a thousand lowerings, old Ahab has furiously, foamingly chased his prey — more a demon than a man! — aye, aye! what a forty years' fool — fool — old fool, old Ahab has been! Why this strife of the chase? Why weary and palsy the arm at the oar, and the iron, and the lance? How is Ahab the richer or better now? Look. Oh, Starbuck! is it not hard that, with this weary load I bear, one poor leg should have been snatched from under me? Here, brush this old hair aside; it blinds me, so that I seem to weep. Locks so gray never grew except out of some ashes! But do I look very old, so very, very old, Starbuck? I feel deadly faint, bowed and humped, as though I were Adam, staggering beneath the piled-up centuries since Paradise. God! God! God! — crack my heart! — stave in my brain! — mockery! mockery! bitter, biting mockery of gray hairs, have I lived enough joy to wear you, and to seem and feel so intolerably old? Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God. By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man; I see my wife and my child in your eye. No, no; stay on board, on board! — do not lower when I do, when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be yours. No, no! not with the far-away home I see in that eye!"

"Oh, my Captain! my Captain! noble soul! grand old heart, after all! Why should anyone give chase to that hated fish? Away with me! Let us fly these deadly waters! Let us go home! Wife and child, too, are Starbuck's — wife and child of his brotherly, sisterly, play-fellow youth; just as yours, sir, are the wife and child of your loving, longing, paternal old age! Away! Let us away! — let me alter the course this instant! How cheerily, how hilariously, O my Captain, we would bowl along on our way to see old Nantucket again! I think, sir, they have some such mild blue days, just like this one, in Nantucket."

"They have, they have. I have seen them — some summer days in the morning. About this time — yes, it is his noon nap now — the boy vivaciously wakes; sits up in bed; and his mother tells him of me, of cannibal old me; how I am abroad upon the deep, but will yet come back to dance him again."

"It is my Mary, my Mary herself! She promised that my boy, every morning, should be carried to the hill to catch the first glimpse of his father's sail! Yes, yes! no more! it is done! we head for Nantucket! Come, my Captain, study out the course, and let us away! See, see! the boy's face from the window! the boy's hand on the hill!"
But Ahab's glance was averted; like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil.

"What is it, what nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what deceiving, hidden lord and master, and cruel, remorseless emperor commands me; that against all natural lovings and longings, I keep on pushing, and crowding, and jamming myself on like this all the time; recklessly making me ready to do what in my own proper, natural heart I dared not so much as dare? Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm? But if the great sun does not move of himself, but is as an errand-boy in heaven; and not one single star can revolve except by some invisible power; how then can this one small heart beat, this one small brain think thoughts, unless God does that beating, does that thinking, does that living, and not I? By heaven, man, we are turned round and round in this world, like that windlass there, and Fate is the handspike. And all the while — there! — that smiling sky, and this unsounded sea! Look! see that Albicore there! Who put it into him to chase and fang that flying-fish? Where do murderers go, man? Who's to doom, when the judge himself is dragged to the bar? But it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky; and the air smells now as if it blew from a far-away meadow; they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping among the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, toil as we may, we all sleep at last on the field. Sleep? Aye, and rust amid greenness, like last year's scythes flung down and left in the half-cut swaths — Starbuck!"
But blanched to a corpse's hue with despair, the mate had stolen away.
Ahab crossed the deck to gaze over on the other side; but started at two reflected, fixed eyes in the water there. Fedallah was motionlessly leaning over the same rail.

chapters.title: Chapter 133 — The Chase—First Day
paragraphs: That night, during the middle watch, when the old man — as he did from time to time — stepped out of the scuttle where he had been leaning and went to his pivot-hole, he suddenly thrust his face out fiercely and sniffed the sea air, the way a clever ship's dog will when the ship draws near some savage island. He declared that a whale must be close. Soon the whole watch could smell that peculiar odor which the living sperm whale sometimes gives off to a great distance; and no sailor was surprised when Ahab, after checking the compass, then the dog-vane, and then fixing the exact bearing of the smell as nearly as he could, quickly ordered the ship's course altered slightly and the sail shortened.

The shrewd thinking behind these movements was sufficiently proved at daybreak by the sight of a long sleek on the sea directly and lengthwise ahead, smooth as oil, and resembling in its pleated watery wrinkles the polished metallic marks of some swift tidal rip at the mouth of a deep, rapid stream.
"Man the mastheads! Call all hands!"

Thundering on the forecastle deck with the butts of three clubbed handspikes, Daggoo woke the sleepers with such Judgment-Day claps that they seemed to be breathed out of the scuttle, so instantly did they appear, clothes in hand.
"What do you see?" cried Ahab, flattening his face to the sky.
"Nothing, nothing, sir!" was the sound hailing down in reply.
"Topgallant sails! Stunsails! Aloft and alow, and on both sides!"

All sail being set, he now cast loose the life-line, reserved for swaying him to the main royal-masthead; and in a few moments they were hoisting him up there, when, while but two-thirds of the way aloft, and while peering ahead through the horizontal vacancy between the main-topsail and topgallant-sail, he raised a gull-like cry in the air. "There she blows! — there she blows! A hump like a snow-hill! It is Moby Dick!"

Fired by the cry, which the three lookouts seemed to take up at the same moment, the men on deck rushed into the rigging to see the famous whale they had been pursuing so long. Ahab had now reached his final perch, some feet above the other lookouts, with Tashtego standing just below him on the cap of the topgallant-mast, so that the Indian's head was almost level with Ahab's heel. From this height the whale could now be seen a mile or so ahead, showing his high, sparkling hump at every roll of the sea and regularly jetting his silent spout into the air. To the credulous sailors it seemed the same silent spout they had seen so long ago in the moonlit Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
"And did none of you see it before?" cried Ahab, hailing the perched men all around him.
"I saw him almost that same instant, sir, that Captain Ahab did, and I cried out," said Tashtego.

"Not the same instant; not the same — no, the doubloon is mine; Fate kept the doubloon for me. Only I; none of you could have raised the White Whale first. There she blows! — there she blows! — there she blows! There again! — there again!" he cried, in long-drawn, lingering, measured tones, keeping time with the gradual lengthening of the whale's visible jets. "He's going to sound! In stunsails! Down topgallant-sails! Stand by three boats. Mr. Starbuck, remember, stay on board and keep the ship. Helm there! Luff, luff a point! So; steady, man, steady! There go flukes! No, no; only black water! All ready the boats there? Stand by, stand by! Lower me, Mr. Starbuck; lower, lower — quick, quicker!" And he slid through the air to the deck.
"He is heading straight to leeward, sir," cried Stubb, "right away from us; cannot have seen the ship yet."
"Be quiet, man! Stand by the braces! Hard down the helm! — brace up! Shiver her! — shiver her! So; well that! Boats, boats!"

Soon all the boats but Starbuck's were dropped; all the boat-sails set — all the paddles plying; with rippling swiftness, shooting to leeward; and Ahab heading the charge. A pale, death-glimmer lit up Fedallah's sunken eyes; a hideous grimace gnawed his mouth.

Like noiseless nautilus shells, their light prows sped through the sea; but they closed on the foe only slowly. As they came nearer, the ocean grew smoother still; it seemed to be drawing a carpet over its waves; it seemed a noon meadow, so serenely did it spread. At length the breathless hunter came so close to his seemingly unsuspecting prey that the whale's entire dazzling hump was plainly visible, sliding along the sea as if it were a thing apart, and ringed all the while by a revolving circle of the finest, fleecy, greenish foam. Beyond it he saw the vast, intricate wrinkles of the slightly projecting head. Ahead of the whale, far out on the soft waters patterned like a Turkish rug, went the glistening white shadow of his broad, milky forehead, with a musical rippling playfully keeping the shadow company; behind, the blue waters flowed in turn into the moving valley of his steady wake; and on either side bright bubbles rose and danced along beside him. But these were broken again by the light toes of hundreds of gay sea-birds softly feathering the sea between their fitful flights; and like some flagstaff rising from the painted hull of an argosy, the tall but shattered pole of a recent lance stuck up from the white whale's back; and every so often one of the cloud of soft-toed birds, hovering and skimming to and fro like a canopy over the fish, would silently perch and rock on this pole, its long tail feathers streaming like pennons.

A gentle joyousness — a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness — clothed the gliding whale. Not the white bull Jupiter, swimming away with the ravished Europa clinging to his graceful horns, his lovely, leering eyes turned sideways on the girl, rippling with smooth, bewitching speed straight for the bridal bower in Crete — not Jove, not that great majesty Supreme! — surpassed the glorified White Whale as he swam so divinely.

On each soft side — coincident with the parted swell that, but once leaving him, then flowed so wide away — on each bright side, the whale shed off enticings. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, namelessly transported and allured by all this serenity, had ventured to assail it; but had fatally found that quietude but the garment of tornadoes. Yet calm, enticing calm, oh whale! You glide on, to all who for the first time eye you, no matter how many in that same way you may have tricked and destroyed before.

And thus, through the serene tranquilities of the tropical sea, among waves whose hand-clappings were suspended by exceeding rapture, Moby Dick moved on, still withholding from sight the full terrors of his submerged trunk, entirely hiding the wrenched hideousness of his jaw. But soon the fore part of him slowly rose from the water; for an instant his whole marbleized body formed a high arch, like Virginia's Natural Bridge, and warningly waving his bannered flukes in the air, the grand god revealed himself, sounded, and went out of sight. Hoveringly halting and dipping on the wing, the white sea-fowls longingly lingered over the agitated pool that he left.
With oars at rest and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now silently floated, awaiting Moby Dick's reappearance.

"An hour," said Ahab, standing rooted in his boat's stern; and he gazed beyond the whale's place, toward the dim blue spaces and wide wooing vacancies to leeward. It was only an instant; for again his eyes seemed whirling round in his head as he swept the watery circle. The breeze now freshened; the sea began to swell.
"The birds! — the birds!" cried Tashtego.

In long Indian file, like herons taking wing, the white birds were now all flying toward Ahab's boat; and when they were within a few yards they began fluttering over the water there, wheeling round and round with joyous, expectant cries. Their vision was keener than man's; Ahab could find no sign in the sea. But suddenly, as he peered down and down into its depths, far down he saw a white living spot no bigger than a white weasel rising with wonderful speed and growing larger as it rose, until it turned, and then two long crooked rows of white, glistening teeth were plainly revealed, floating up from the unfathomable bottom. It was Moby Dick's open mouth and scrolled jaw, his vast, shadowed bulk still half blending with the blue of the sea. The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like a marble tomb with its door open; and with one sidelong sweep of his steering oar, Ahab whirled the boat aside from this tremendous apparition. Then, calling on Fedallah to change places with him, he went forward to the bow, seized Perth's harpoon, and ordered his crew to grip their oars and stand ready to back the boat astern.

Now, because the boat had been spun round on its axis in time, its bow was made to face the whale's head in advance, while the head was still under water. But as if he saw through this stratagem, Moby Dick, with that malicious intelligence ascribed to him, shifted himself sideways in an instant, as it were, shooting his pleated head lengthwise beneath the boat.

Through and through — through every plank and every rib — a thrill ran for an instant, as the whale, lying obliquely on his back in the manner of a biting shark, slowly and sensitively took the bows fully into his mouth, so that the long, narrow, scrolled lower jaw curled high up into the open air, and one of the teeth caught in a rowlock. The bluish pearl-white of the inside of the jaw was within six inches of Ahab's head, and reached higher than that. In this position the White Whale now shook the slight cedar boat as a mildly cruel cat shakes her mouse. Fedallah gazed with unastonished eyes and crossed his arms; but the tiger-yellow crew were tumbling over each other's heads to reach the farthest end of the stern.

And now the two springy gunwales were bending in and out as the whale toyed with the doomed boat in this devilish way; his body was submerged beneath the boat, so he could not be darted at from the bow, for the bow was almost inside him, as it were; and the other boats had involuntarily paused, as before a sudden crisis impossible to withstand. It was then that the monomaniac Ahab, furious at being so tantalizingly close to his foe — a closeness that put him, fully alive and helpless, in the very jaws he hated — frenzied by all this, seized the long bone with his bare hands and wildly strove to wrench it loose from its grip. As he strove in vain, the jaw slipped from him; the frail gunwales bent in, collapsed, and snapped, as both jaws, like enormous shears, slid further aft, bit the boat completely in two, and locked themselves shut again in the sea, midway between the two floating wrecks. These drifted apart, their broken ends drooping, the crew at the stern-wreck clinging to the gunwales and struggling to hold on to the oars in order to lash them across.

At that opening moment, before the boat was snapped, Ahab had been the first to see the whale's intent, from the crafty lifting of his head — a movement that loosened his hold for the time — and at that moment his hand made one final effort to push the boat out of the bite. But the boat, only slipping further into the whale's mouth and tilting sideways as it slipped, had shaken off his hold on the jaw and spilled him out as he leaned into the push; and so he fell flat on his face upon the sea.

Rippling away from his prey, Moby Dick now lay a little distance off, thrusting his oblong white head vertically up and down in the billows while slowly revolving his whole spindle-shaped body; so that whenever his vast wrinkled forehead rose — some twenty feet or more out of the water — the swells, now rising, broke dazzlingly against it with all their merging waves, vindictively tossing their shattered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the Channel billows, only half baffled, recoil from the base of the Eddystone lighthouse only to leap triumphantly over its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It receives its name (pitchpoling) from its being likened to that preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance, in the exercise called pitchpoling, previously described. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon, returning to a horizontal position, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew, churning the water sideways in his vengeful wake, as if whipping himself up to yet another and deadlier attack. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries, cast before Antiochus's elephants in the book of Maccabees, maddened them. Meanwhile Ahab, half smothered in the foam of the whale's insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim — though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of a whirlpool like that — helpless Ahab's head could be seen like a tossed bubble that the slightest chance shock might burst. From the broken-off stern of the boat Fedallah watched him with mild indifference; the clinging crew at the other drifting end could not help him; it was more than enough for them to look after themselves. For the White Whale's aspect as he revolved was so appalling, and the ever-tightening circles he made were so swift, like a planet's, that he seemed to be swooping horizontally upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered close by, they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, for fear that would be the signal for the instant destruction of the endangered castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. So, with straining eyes, they stayed on the outer edge of the dreadful zone, whose center had now become the old man's head.

Meanwhile, from the beginning all this had been seen from the ship's mastheads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so near that Ahab in the water hailed her! "Sail on the" — but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and overwhelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted: "Sail on the whale! Drive him off!"
The Pequod's prows were pointed; and breaking up the charmed circle, she effectually parted the white whale from his victim. As he sullenly swam off, the boats flew to the rescue.

Dragged into Stubb's boat with bloodshot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; the long tension of Ahab's bodily strength did crack, and helplessly he yielded to his body's doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb's boat, like one trodden underfoot by herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, as desolate sounds from out ravines.

But the very intensity of his physical collapse only made it the shorter. Within the span of an instant, great hearts sometimes condense into one deep pang the sum total of those shallow pains that are mercifully spread through the whole lives of feebler men. And so such hearts, though brief in each single suffering, still, if the gods decree it, pile up in their lifetime a whole age of woe, made up entirely of instantaneous intensities; for even in their centers, mere points though these are, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
"The harpoon," said Ahab, half-rising and draggingly leaning on one bent arm — "is it safe?"
"Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it," said Stubb, showing it.
"Lay it before me; any missing men?"
"One, two, three, four, five; there were five oars, sir, and here are five men."

"That's good. Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! There! There! Going to leeward still; what a leaping spout! — Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab's bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!"

It often happens that when a boat is stove, its crew, once picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is then continued with what are called double-banked oars. So it was now. But the added power of the boat did not match the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked every fin, swimming at a speed that plainly showed that if the chase were pushed on now, under these circumstances, it would prove an indefinitely prolonged one, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure such unbroken, intense straining at the oar for so long a period — a thing barely bearable even for one brief spell. The ship itself, then, as sometimes happens, offered the most promising way of overtaking the chase in the meantime. Accordingly, the boats now made for her and were soon swayed up to their cranes — the two parts of the wrecked boat having already been secured by her — and then, hoisting everything up to her side, piling her canvas high, and stretching it out sideways with stunsails like the double-jointed wings of an albatross, the Pequod bore down in Moby Dick's leeward wake. At the familiar, regular intervals, the whale's glittering spout was duly announced from the manned mastheads; and whenever he was reported as just gone down, Ahab would note the time, and then, pacing the deck binnacle-watch in hand, the moment the last second of the allotted hour ran out, his voice was heard: "Whose is the doubloon now? Do you see him?" And if the reply was "No, sir!" he at once ordered them to hoist him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab now aloft and motionless, now pacing the planks without rest.

As he was thus walking, uttering no sound except to hail the men aloft, or to bid them hoist a sail still higher, or to spread one to a still greater breadth — thus pacing to and fro beneath his slouched hat, at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped upon the quarter-deck, and lay there reversed; broken bow to shattered stern. At last he paused before it; and as in an already overclouded sky, fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across, so over the old man's face there now stole some such added gloom.

Stubb saw him pause; and perhaps intending, not vainly, to display his own undaunted spirit and thus keep up a valiant place in his captain's mind, he advanced, and eyeing the wreck exclaimed: "The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too keenly, sir; ha! ha!"

"What soulless thing is this that laughs in front of a wreck? Man, man! If I did not know you to be as brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical), I could swear you were a coward. Neither groan nor laugh should be heard in front of a wreck."
"Aye, sir," said Starbuck, drawing near, "it is a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one."

"Omen? Omen? — the dictionary! If the gods mean to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads and give an old wives' dark hint. — Begone! You two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and you two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, with neither gods nor men for his neighbors! Cold, cold — I shiver! — What now? Aloft there! Do you see him? Sing out for every spout, even if he spouts ten times a second!"
The day was nearly done; only the hem of its golden robe was rustling. Soon it was almost dark, but the lookout men still remained at their posts.
"Can't see the spout now, sir; too dark," cried a voice from the air.
"How heading when last seen?"
"As before, sir — straight to leeward."

"Good! He will travel slower now that it's night. Down royals and topgallant stunsails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he's making a passage now, and may heave to for a while. Helm there! Keep her full before the wind! — Aloft! Come down! — Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-masthead, and see that it's manned till morning." Then, advancing toward the doubloon on the mainmast: "Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it stay here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whichever of you first raises him on the day he is killed, this gold is that man's; and if on that day I raise him again myself, then ten times its sum shall be divided among all of you! Away now! — the deck is yours, sir!"
And so saying, he placed himself halfway within the scuttle, and slouching his hat, stood there till dawn, except when at intervals rousing himself to see how the night wore on.

chapters.title: Chapter 134 — The Chase—Second Day
paragraphs: At daybreak, the three mastheads were promptly manned again.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab, after allowing a little time for the light to spread.
"See nothing, sir."
"Turn up all hands and make sail! He travels faster than I thought — the topgallant sails! — aye, they should have been kept on her all night. But no matter — he's only resting for the rush."

Let it be said here that this persistent pursuit of one particular whale, kept up through day into night and through night into day, is by no means unheard of in the South Sea fishery. For such is the wonderful skill, the foresight born of experience, and the unshakable confidence acquired by some great natural geniuses among the Nantucket captains, that from simply observing a whale when last sighted they will, under certain given circumstances, predict pretty accurately both the direction in which he will keep swimming for a while out of sight, and his probable rate of progress during that time. In these cases the whale-fisherman does somewhat as a pilot does when he is about to lose sight of a coast whose general trend he knows well, and which he wants to return to shortly, but at some further point: just as this pilot stands by his compass and takes the exact bearing of the cape now in view, so as to be surer of hitting the remote, unseen headland he will eventually reach, so the fisherman stands at his compass with the whale; for after the creature has been chased and carefully marked through several hours of daylight, then, when night hides the fish, its future wake through the darkness is almost as settled in the hunter's shrewd mind as the pilot's coast is in his. So, to this hunter's wondrous skill, a wake — that proverbially fleeting thing written in water — is for all desired purposes nearly as reliable as the steadfast land. And just as the mighty iron Leviathan of the modern railway is so familiarly known in its every pace that men, watches in hand, time his rate as doctors time a baby's pulse, and say casually that the up train or the down train will reach such and such a spot at such and such an hour, so, almost, there are occasions when these Nantucketers time that other Leviathan of the deep by the observed humor of his speed, and say to themselves that so many hours from now this whale will have gone two hundred miles, and will have about reached this or that degree of latitude or longitude. But for this sharpness to succeed at all in the end, the wind and the sea must be the whaleman's allies; for what use at the moment to the becalmed or windbound sailor is the skill that assures him he is exactly ninety-three leagues and a quarter from his port? Many further subtle points touching the chase of whales can be inferred from these statements.
The ship tore on, leaving a furrow in the sea like the one a stray cannonball makes when it turns plowshare and furrows up the level field.

"By salt and hemp!" cried Stubb, "but this swift motion of the deck creeps up one's legs and tingles at the heart. This ship and I are two brave fellows! — Ha, ha! Someone pick me up and launch me spine-first on the sea — for, by live-oaks! my spine's a keel. Ha, ha! We go the gait that leaves no dust behind!"
"There she blows — she blows! — she blows! — right ahead!" was now the cry from the masthead.

"Aye, aye!" cried Stubb. "I knew it — you can't escape — blow on and split your spout, O whale! The mad fiend himself is after you! Blow your trumpet — blister your lungs! — Ahab will dam off your blood, as a miller shuts his watergate on the stream!"

And Stubb was only speaking for nearly the whole crew. The frenzies of the chase had by now worked them up into a bubbling ferment, like old wine fermenting anew. Whatever pale fears and forebodings some of them might have felt before, these were now not only kept out of sight by their growing awe of Ahab, but broken up and routed on all sides, like timid prairie hares scattering before the bounding bison. The hand of Fate had snatched all their souls; and by the stirring dangers of the day before, the torment of the past night's suspense, and the fixed, unfearing, blind, reckless way their wild ship went plunging toward its flying target — by all these things their hearts were bowled along. The wind that swelled their sails into great bellies and rushed the vessel on with arms as invisible as they were irresistible seemed the symbol of that unseen power which so enslaved them to the race.

They were one man, not thirty. For just as the one ship that held them all, though it was put together from all sorts of contrasting things — oak, and maple, and pine; iron, and pitch, and hemp — yet had all these running into one another in the single solid hull, which shot on its way both balanced and steered by the long central keel, so all the individualities of the crew — this man's courage, that man's fear, guilt and guiltiness — all these varieties were welded into oneness, and all were directed toward that fatal goal which Ahab, their one lord and keel, pointed to.

The rigging was alive. The mastheads, like the tops of tall palms, sprouted outspreading tufts of arms and legs. Clinging to a spar with one hand, some reached out the other with impatient waves; others, shading their eyes from the vivid sunlight, sat far out on the rocking yards; every spar bore its full crop of mortals, ready and ripe for their fate. Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!

"Why don't you sing out for him, if you see him?" cried Ahab, when some minutes had passed since the first cry and no more had been heard. "Sway me up, men; you have been deceived. Moby Dick does not cast one odd jet that way and then disappear."

It was just so; in their headlong eagerness the men had mistaken something else for the whale's spout, as the event itself soon proved; for hardly had Ahab reached his perch, hardly was the rope made fast to its pin on deck, when he struck the keynote for an orchestra that made the air vibrate as if with the combined discharge of rifles. The triumphant shout of thirty buckskin lungs was heard as — much nearer the ship than the place of the imaginary jet, less than a mile ahead — Moby Dick burst bodily into view! For the White Whale now revealed his nearness not by any calm and lazy spouting, not by the peaceful gush of that mystic fountain in his head, but by the far more wondrous phenomenon of breaching. Rising at his utmost speed from the farthest depths, the Sperm Whale in this way booms his entire bulk into the pure element of air, and, piling up a mountain of dazzling foam, shows where he is to a distance of seven miles and more. At such moments the torn, enraged waves he shakes off seem to be his mane; in some cases this breaching is his act of defiance.

"There she breaches! There she breaches!" was the cry, as in his immeasurable bravado the White Whale tossed himself salmon-like to Heaven. Seen so suddenly in the blue plain of the sea, and set off against the still bluer edge of the sky, the spray he raised glittered and glared unbearably for the moment, like a glacier; and it stood there, gradually fading and fading from its first sparkling intensity to the dim mistiness of a shower advancing up a valley.
"Aye, breach your last to the sun, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Your hour and your harpoon are at hand! — Down! Down, all of you, but one man at the fore. The boats! — stand by!"

Ignoring the tedious rope-ladders of the shrouds, the men slid to the deck like shooting stars by the lone backstays and halyards, while Ahab, less dartingly but still rapidly, was lowered from his perch.
"Lower away," he cried, as soon as he had reached his boat — a spare one, rigged the afternoon before. "Mr. Starbuck, the ship is yours — keep away from the boats, but keep near them. Lower, all!"

As if to strike quick terror into them, being by this time the first to attack, Moby Dick had turned and was now coming for the three crews. Ahab's boat was in the center; and cheering his men on, he told them he would take the whale head-and-head — that is, pull straight up to his forehead — which is not an uncommon thing; for within a certain distance such a course keeps the coming attack out of the whale's sideways vision. But before that close range was reached, and while all three boats were still as plain to his eye as the ship's three masts, the White Whale, churning himself into a furious speed, rushed among the boats almost in an instant, as it were, with open jaws and lashing tail, and offered appalling battle on every side; and heedless of the irons darted at him from every boat, he seemed intent only on annihilating each separate plank those boats were made of. But skillfully maneuvered, wheeling ceaselessly like trained war-horses on the field, the boats evaded him for a while, though at times only by a plank's breadth; while all the time Ahab's unearthly war cry tore every other cry but his to shreds.

But at last, in his untraceable twists and turns, the White Whale so crossed and recrossed, and in a thousand ways so tangled the slack of the three lines now fast to him, that they shortened and, of themselves, hauled the doomed boats toward the irons planted in him; though now for a moment the whale drew a little aside, as if to rally for a more tremendous charge. Seizing that chance, Ahab first paid out more line, and then began rapidly hauling and jerking it in again — hoping that way to clear it of some snarls — when look! — a sight more savage than the embattled teeth of sharks!

Caught and twisted — corkscrewed in the tangles of the line — loose harpoons and lances, with all their bristling barbs and points, came flashing and dripping up to the chocks in the bow of Ahab's boat. Only one thing could be done. Seizing the boat-knife, he reached with precise care within — through — and then out beyond — the rays of steel; dragged in the line beyond them, passed it inboard to the bowsman, and then, cutting the rope twice near the chocks, dropped the intercepted bundle of steel into the sea, and was all fast again. At that instant the White Whale made a sudden rush among the remaining tangles of the other lines; by doing so he irresistibly dragged the more entangled boats of Stubb and Flask toward his flukes, dashed them together like two husks rolling on a surf-beaten beach, and then, diving down into the sea, disappeared in a boiling maelstrom, in which, for a while, the fragrant cedar chips of the wrecks danced round and round like grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch.

While the two crews were still circling in the water, reaching out after the revolving line-tubs, oars, and other floating gear; while little Flask, slanting, bobbed up and down like an empty vial, twitching his legs upward to escape the dreaded jaws of sharks; and Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to ladle him up; and while the old man's line — now parting — allowed him to pull into the creamy pool to rescue whom he could — in that wild simultaneous rush of a thousand massed perils, Ahab's still unstruck boat seemed drawn up toward Heaven by invisible wires, as, arrow-like, shooting straight up out of the sea, the White Whale dashed his broad forehead against its bottom and sent it turning over and over into the air, until it fell again, gunwale downward, and Ahab and his men struggled out from under it like seals from a seaside cave.

The whale's first upward momentum — changing its direction as he struck the surface — carried him along it, without his willing it, to a little distance from the center of the destruction he had made; and with his back to it he now lay for a moment, slowly feeling from side to side with his flukes; and whenever a stray oar, a bit of plank, or the least chip or crumb of the boats touched his skin, his tail swiftly drew back and came sideways, smiting the sea. But soon, as if satisfied that his work for that time was done, he pushed his pleated forehead through the ocean and, trailing the intertangled lines after him, continued on his way to leeward at a traveler's steady pace.
